idea: We propose a targeted, paper-ready study of a coupled metabolite-barrier mechanism linking gut dysbiosis to neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease: dysbiosis-associated loss of protective microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives, together with accumulation of pro-inflammatory metabolites such as selected secondary bile acids or TMAO, may weaken intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity, amplify peripheral cytokine signaling, and drive microglial activation that accelerates amyloid and tau pathology. The novelty is not the general microbiome-Alzheimer’s association, but a predefined joint mediation framework that tests whether a small, mechanistically coherent panel of microbial metabolites and barrier-injury markers explains more variance in neuroinflammation than single-mediator models, while also generating clearer intervention logic. The approach is feasible as a compact mouse study or tightly phenotyped human cohort using targeted microbiome profiling, serum metabolomics, permeability assays, cytokine measurements, and standard brain readouts of microglial activation and amyloid/tau burden. Expected impact is a more actionable map of which dysbiosis signals are merely correlated versus which coupled mediator states are most likely to transmit disease-relevant inflammatory effects. The main risk is that metabolite and permeability markers may be noisy and underpowered for formal mediation, so the design should restrict hypotheses to a small literature-grounded panel. A minimal validation experiment would combine one metabolite rescue, such as indole supplementation, with one barrier-protective intervention in an Alzheimer’s mouse model and test whether joint rescue reduces microglial activation more than either manipulation alone.

idea: We propose a budget-aware learning framework for real-time AI that jointly improves deployment efficiency and training convergence by combining calibrated early exits, difficulty-aware routing, and lightweight self-distillation under an explicit energy-cost objective. A compact backbone is augmented with intermediate prediction heads, and each sample is dynamically allowed to exit early when a calibrated confidence rule indicates that deeper computation is unlikely to change the decision; hard samples continue to later layers, while easy samples consume less compute. During training, the model optimizes task loss together with an exit-calibration term, distillation from the final head to earlier heads, and a penalty based on per-exit latency or FLOPs so that convergence is encouraged toward representations that are both accurate and cheap to evaluate. The main novelty is not any single component, but the unified objective that links convergence efficiency during training with adaptive energy savings at inference in one reproducible formulation for real-time settings. The approach is feasible with standard compact architectures and commodity hardware, and could improve the accuracy-latency-energy tradeoff for edge vision or audio systems. The main risk is that confidence-based routing may be brittle under distribution shift, reducing accuracy or exit reliability. A minimal validation experiment would compare a small ResNet or MobileNet on CIFAR-10 or Speech Commands against standard training, early-exit-only, and distillation-only comparisons, measuring accuracy, expected exit depth, latency/FLOPs proxy, calibration, and wall-clock time to reach a target accuracy.

idea: We propose a physics-informed hierarchical Bayesian tomography framework for non-destructive fossil analysis under sparse-view or low-dose scanning, aimed at recovering internal anatomical structure while quantifying where the reconstruction is trustworthy. The method combines an explicit X-ray projection likelihood with fossil-specific multi-material priors that distinguish fossil tissue, surrounding matrix, and irregular mineral infill, plus a weak morphology-aware regularizer learned from a small archive of fossil or extant volumetric scans so that prior knowledge stabilizes ill-posed reconstructions without overwhelming observed evidence. The main novelty is tailoring uncertainty-aware inverse imaging to paleontological heterogeneity and decision-making, producing posterior mean volumes together with voxelwise uncertainty maps that can guide interpretations of cavities, canals, or internal landmarks. Feasibility is supported by avoiding large end-to-end training and instead using compact probabilistic inference on retrospectively undersampled CT data and digital phantoms. A minimal validation experiment would start from existing high-resolution fossil-like scans, simulate sparse-angle and noisy acquisitions, and compare reconstruction fidelity, internal feature recovery, and uncertainty calibration against filtered backprojection and total-variation iterative reconstruction. If successful, the approach could reduce reliance on destructive sampling and make fragile specimens more accessible, although its main risk is that limited and biased training priors may generalize poorly across rare taxa or unusual mineralization patterns.

idea: We propose a psychology-focused reproducibility audit framework that automatically compares public preregistrations with their corresponding published articles to quantify structured deviation profiles, including hypothesis drift, outcome switching, exclusion-rule changes, covariate changes, and statistical-test substitution. The core mechanism is a pairwise alignment pipeline that extracts planned study elements from preregistration documents and reported elements from manuscripts using a combination of section-aware rules and LLM-assisted structured parsing, then scores both the presence of deviations and whether those deviations were explicitly disclosed. The novelty is not the general observation that preregistration adherence matters, but the creation of a reusable benchmark and unified taxonomy that measures several deviation types within one compact, executable system and connects them to reproducibility-relevant proxies such as reporting transparency, sample-size adequacy, and known replication outcomes where available. The project is feasible because psychology offers a growing pool of public OSF and AsPredicted records, and the initial study can operate on a modest sample of 50 to 100 preregistration-paper pairs with gold annotation on a smaller subset. Expected impact is a practical auditing tool for meta-science and editorial screening. The main risk is that heterogeneous documents and justified amendments may blur harmful and benign deviations. A minimal validation experiment would manually annotate 20 to 30 matched pairs and compare rule-based, LLM-assisted, and hybrid methods for category-level deviation detection accuracy.

Problem: The reproducibility crisis, particularly in fields like psychology and biomedicine, highlights significant challenges in ensuring scientific research can be consistently replicated.

idea: This project proposes a sociological study of misinformation sharing as audience-facing status signaling rather than simple belief transmission. The core mechanism is that users may be especially likely to reshare misinformation when the content affirms in-group identity, when their immediate network is dense and reciprocal, and when visible prior endorsement from in-group members makes reputational rewards salient. The novelty is not the broad claim that identity matters online, but the integrated test of whether local social structure and public approval jointly amplify identity-congruent misinformation diffusion, distinguishing a status-performance account from standard exposure or homophily explanations. The design is feasible with observational repost or retweet network data from a bounded issue domain and time window: content can be labeled for misinformation status and group alignment, local cohesion can be measured with density, reciprocity, and clustering, and endorsement visibility can be proxied by prior likes, shares, or repost counts from inferred in-group accounts. Expected impact is a sharper explanation of why tightly knit communities may intensify false content circulation even without stronger belief. The main risk is measurement error and endogeneity in identity alignment and reputational incentives. A minimal validation experiment is a multilevel logistic resharing model testing whether identity-congruent misinformation is disproportionately shared, and whether that association strengthens under higher local cohesion and prior in-group endorsement, relative to matched non-misinformation identity-congruent content.

Problem: The spread of misinformation in social networks is a significant challenge.

idea: We propose a passive microfluidic stabilization strategy that combines spatially patterned anisotropic wall boundary conditions with a weakly viscoelastic carrier fluid to preserve ordered laminar co-flow across a broader range of channel shapes and operating conditions than conventional geometry-tuned designs. The core mechanism is to place alternating slip/no-slip or wettability-derived low-friction patches along channel walls so that near-wall momentum is redistributed in a way that suppresses cross-stream perturbation growth, while mild fluid elasticity damps transient distortions and helps the flow relax back toward layered streamlines without continuous feedback control. The novelty is not the individual ingredients, both of which are established in adjacent microfluidic literature, but their deliberate use as a joint passive stabilization principle evaluated as an expansion of the steady ordered-flow region rather than as a drag-reduction, focusing, or mixing technique. The approach appears feasible because both surface patterning and dilute polymer additives are experimentally accessible and can be modeled first with standard CFD using Oldroyd-B or FENE-P in the weak-elasticity regime. If successful, this could reduce dependence on highly precise channel geometry and enable more scalable high-throughput microfluidic platforms. The main risk is that any apparent stabilization may come mainly from added dissipation or reduced effective throughput rather than genuine perturbation damping. A minimal validation experiment is a comparative simulation in straight and mildly curved channels measuring interface distortion and transverse kinetic energy decay for smooth Newtonian, patterned Newtonian, smooth viscoelastic, and patterned viscoelastic cases under matched flow-rate constraints.
task_context:

idea: We propose a decision-aware probabilistic post-processing framework for coronal mass ejection forecasting that takes outputs or summary features from existing physics-based or machine learning CME models and converts them into calibrated distributions over arrival time windows, impact severity, and sector-specific disruption risk. Rather than optimizing only forecast accuracy, the method explicitly links uncertainty estimates to downstream operational decisions in power grids, satellites, aviation, and telecommunications through transparent cost matrices that penalize false alarms, missed severe events, and delayed warnings differently across sectors. The central novelty is to evaluate CME prediction as an economically consequential decision problem while keeping the predictive layer lightweight and interpretable, using simple probabilistic classifiers or quantile models plus calibration methods such as isotonic regression or Platt scaling. This makes the approach feasible with public historical CME datasets and avoids requiring a new heliophysics simulator. Expected impact is improved warning precision and more rational alert thresholds, reducing avoidable operational inefficiency when forecast uncertainty is high. The main risk is that conclusions may depend strongly on stylized economic assumptions and sparse severe-event data. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively compare calibrated and uncalibrated post-processors against climatology and standard accuracy-oriented comparisons on historical CME events, measuring both proper scoring rules and expected sector-specific decision loss.
task_context:

idea: We propose a physics-guided microplastic removal strategy based on magnetically recoverable colloidal collectors whose surface charge, hydrophobicity, and nanoscale roughness are deliberately tuned to promote heteroaggregation with dilute suspended microplastics before low-field magnetic separation. Rather than relying on conventional size-exclusion filtration or generic adsorption, the concept targets the attachment-limited regime that makes diffuse microplastic capture difficult in realistic water systems, using interfacial design to increase collision efficiency between collector particles and common polymers such as polyethylene or polystyrene across micron to tens-of-microns size ranges. A feasible first implementation would use inexpensive magnetic core particles coated into three interaction modes, for example cationic hydrophilic, amphiphilic moderately rough, and anionic control, followed by short mixing, magnetic settling, and collector recovery. The main novelty is framing magnetic removal as selective colloidal assembly under environmentally relevant salinity and natural-organic-matter conditions rather than bulk sorption alone, which could improve performance in flow-through or distributed treatment settings where filtration is impractical. Expected impact is a low-energy, regenerable capture platform for dilute microplastic pollution, though the principal risk is loss of selectivity or incomplete recollection if collectors bind natural colloids, sediments, or organic matter too strongly. A minimal validation experiment would compare polymer- and size-resolved removal, collector recovery fraction, and microscopy-confirmed collector-plastic association for tuned versus untuned magnetic particles in freshwater and saline water with added natural organic matter.

idea: We propose an adaptive anti-predator training curriculum for captive-bred animals that replaces the common one-size-fits-all approach with individualized progression through visual, olfactory, and acoustic predator cues. The core mechanism is a rule-based training pipeline that escalates cue realism or intensity only when an animal shows predator-specific vigilance, appropriate shelter-seeking or escape responses, and rapid recovery, while pausing or de-escalating when behavior suggests generalized fear, chronic stress, or maladaptive suppression of feeding and exploration. The novelty is not predator-aversion training itself, but making the curriculum state-adaptive, explicitly reproducible, and evaluated on retention and transfer to unfamiliar predator scenarios rather than immediate reactions alone. This is feasible in standard captive facilities because it relies on short repeated sessions, behavioral scoring, and optional noninvasive welfare measures such as feeding latency, body condition, or fecal glucocorticoid proxies. If successful, the approach could improve survival after reintroduction by producing more robust and discriminative anti-predator behavior while reducing unnecessary stress. The main risk is that stronger captive responses may reflect generalized arousal that does not transfer to field survival. A minimal validation experiment would randomize one focal species into adaptive-training, fixed-training, and handling-control groups, then compare comparison-adjusted predator discrimination, escape latency, retention after a delay, response to novel predator presentations, and welfare indicators.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware rolling-horizon resource allocation framework for emergency response that couples short-term incident-demand and travel-time prediction with dynamic redeployment optimization. At each decision epoch, the system forecasts zone-level demand and network travel conditions over the next 15 to 60 minutes, produces calibrated quantiles or scenario sets rather than only point estimates, and solves a small stochastic allocation problem that repositions a limited number of idle units using chance constraints or a CVaR-style objective to hedge against response failures during surges and disruptions. The central novelty is not generic prediction-plus-optimization, but explicitly testing the decision value of forecast calibration: whether better uncertainty estimates change operational choices enough to outperform point-forecast control under nonstationary conditions while keeping relocation churn manageable. The approach is feasible because it can be implemented on coarse city zones with bounded actions and solved as a compact mixed-integer or flow-style model in real time. Its expected impact is a practical recipe for integrating modern predictive models into dispatch policies without abandoning operational constraints or interpretability. The main risk is that gains may stem mostly from improved forecasts rather than uncertainty handling, or that historical replay may miss counterfactual queueing dynamics. A minimal validation experiment would compare static coverage, reactive rebalancing, rolling-horizon point forecasts, and calibrated-scenario control in a synthetic or replay-based EMS simulator under demand spikes and travel-time shocks, measuring mean and tail response times, coverage, and relocation counts.

idea: We propose a microclimate-aware adaptation allocation benchmark for urban heat that tests whether fine-scale climate inference changes where limited adaptation resources should be deployed. The core mechanism is to fuse heterogeneous public data, including weather stations, low-cost sensors, satellite land-surface temperature, canopy cover, impervious surface, topography, and built-form indicators, to estimate neighborhood- or grid-level heat exposure and convert those estimates into priority scores for interventions such as tree planting, shade infrastructure, or cooling investments under a fixed budget. The main novelty is not another high-resolution heat map alone, but a decision-focused framework that directly compares resource-allocation outputs from coarse regional climate indicators against microclimate-aware estimates, quantifying when coarse planning mis-ranks locations, how uncertainty affects rankings, and which environmental features drive decision shifts. The study is feasible because it can be scoped to one city with public remote sensing and station data, and the first version can use transparent models and proxy objectives such as extreme local heat exposure or population-weighted exposure. Expected impact is a more efficient and potentially fairer adaptation planning workflow that reveals where localized heat patterns matter most for policy. The main risk is limited ground truth for true intervention benefit and possible bias from sparse sensors. A minimal validation experiment would compare coarse and microclimate-aware priority maps on a shared grid, then assess disagreement and predictive accuracy using held-out local sensor observations.

idea: We propose a sustainability-aware closed-loop active learning framework for combinatorial high-throughput experimentation in drug discovery that prioritizes which reaction conditions or building-block combinations to test under fixed plate, material, and waste budgets. A surrogate model trained on an initial seed set would predict hit utility or reaction performance across the discrete combinatorial space, while an acquisition function would jointly reward high predicted value and uncertainty reduction and penalize estimated reagent cost, hazardous solvent use, and waste generation through explicit proxy terms. The key novelty is not a wholly new optimization primitive, but the integration of batch active learning with green-chemistry and laboratory-budget constraints in the specific setting of combinatorial HTE, together with evaluation based on hits found per experiment, per cost unit, and per waste unit rather than raw hit count alone. The approach is feasible because it can be implemented retrospectively on public reaction-screening datasets using standardized cost and waste proxies derived from reagent counts, stoichiometry, molecular weight, and solvent hazard classes, without requiring new wet-lab infrastructure. If successful, it could reduce unnecessary screening, lower consumable usage, and improve the efficiency of lead discovery. The main risk is that proxy cost and waste annotations may be noisy and could distort acquisition behavior. A minimal validation experiment is a sequential replay benchmark comparing random sampling, diversity sampling, standard uncertainty-based selection, and the proposed constrained policy across several seed and batch sizes.

idea: We propose a regime-aware, uncertainty-calibrated meta-strategy for cryptocurrency trading that treats market participation as a selective decision rather than an always-on prediction problem. The method maintains a small library of transparent base policies, such as momentum, mean-reversion, breakout, and cash, and uses strictly causal rolling features capturing trend, volatility, and liquidity to infer latent market regimes in walk-forward fashion. Conditioned on the inferred regime, a lightweight selector estimates the expected utility of each base policy together with a calibrated confidence score, using residual-based or conformal-style uncertainty estimates to determine when the apparent edge is reliable enough to trade. A position is taken only when both regime confidence and strategy advantage exceed thresholds; otherwise the system abstains and remains in cash. The main novelty is the unified framing of regime switching, uncertainty calibration, and abstention as a modular decision layer for robustness in highly nonstationary crypto markets, rather than as separate forecasting or ensemble components. The approach is feasible with standard OHLCV data and simple models, and could improve risk-adjusted performance by reducing exposure during unstable periods while preserving interpretability. Its main risk is that regime assignments and uncertainty estimates may become unreliable during abrupt heavy-tailed shocks, leading to missed opportunities or false confidence. A minimal validation experiment would compare this method in walk-forward backtests against buy-and-hold, the best single strategy, a regime-only selector, and an uncertainty-only selector under transaction costs, reporting return, Sharpe, drawdown, turnover, exposure, and confidence calibration.

idea: We propose an individualized daily load-prescription system for resistance training that replaces fixed percentage-of-1RM rules with a multimodal readiness model inspired by accounting-style state tracking. For each athlete and exercise, the system updates a compact training-capacity ledger from recent workload, prior session performance, sleep duration and quality, heart-rate variability or resting heart rate, and simple soreness or readiness self-reports, then recommends the session load most likely to achieve a target repetition and effort zone while avoiding excessive next-day fatigue risk. The novelty is not autoregulation alone, but the explicit fusion of low-burden wearable and log-derived signals into exercise-specific recommendations with uncertainty estimates, so the model can issue more conservative loads when signals are missing, noisy, or contradictory. Feasibility is high because the approach can be implemented as an offline decision-support benchmark on retrospective training logs augmented with common wearable features, using interpretable tabular models alongside stronger machine-learning comparisons. The expected impact is a more realistic prescription framework that adapts to daily physiological variation and may improve session target attainment, adherence, and safety-oriented decision quality. The main risk is overlap with existing RPE/RIR, velocity-based, and readiness-guided training methods, so contribution depends on clear benchmarking and calibration analysis. A minimal validation experiment would compare this model against fixed %1RM, last-session carry-forward, and simple readiness rules for predicting the load needed to hit a target rep-RPE zone in grouped athlete-by-time test splits.

idea: This project proposes a traceable local guideline translation engine that converts universal evidence-based recommendations into context-sensitive care options for settings where rigid guidelines break down. The core mechanism is to represent a guideline as modular condition-action statements linked to their evidentiary justifications, then pass those modules through a compact context ontology that captures resource constraints such as staffing and supply shortages, cultural factors such as household decision structure, language and interpretation needs, and local explanatory models, along with explicitly elicited patient preferences. The novelty is not a claim to invent contextual adaptation in general, but to operationalize it at the recommendation level with auditable evidence-to-adaptation links spanning material, social, and preference dimensions that are often handled separately. The approach is feasible as a lightweight protocol using structured rules, annotated vignettes, and expert review rather than large clinical deployments. Its expected impact is a more flexible form of evidence-based practice that remains transparent about what can be adapted, what is non-negotiable, and why. The main risk is oversimplifying culture into checklist variables and thereby legitimizing inappropriate deviations. A minimal validation study would compare fixed-guideline outputs, resource-only adaptation, and the full translation engine on 12-20 systematically varied vignettes, with blinded experts rating contextual fit, faithfulness to evidence, transparency, and actionability.

idea: We propose a unified uncertainty-aware chemistry model that jointly predicts molecular properties and coarse reaction-path quantities from shared molecular and reaction representations, aiming to reduce the cost of screening in drug design and materials discovery. The core mechanism is a multi-task graph or equivariant encoder that ingests molecule graphs, optional lightweight 3D conformer descriptors, and reaction pairs, then feeds task-specific heads for property regression or classification, reaction barrier estimation, and pathway likelihood or ranking. The key novelty is not a wholly new architecture, but the targeted integration of cross-task transfer with calibrated uncertainty so that the same model can support both broad candidate screening and triage of reactions for expensive simulation or experiment. This is feasible with existing public molecular property datasets and reaction-related benchmarks, and can be implemented with matched single-task comparisons under the same parameter budget. Expected impact is improved sample efficiency on scarce reaction tasks and better prioritization decisions through uncertainty-aware ranking rather than score-only selection. The main risk is negative transfer or weak calibration when property and reaction datasets are chemically mismatched or labels are noisy. A minimal validation experiment is to train joint and single-task models on one public property benchmark and one public reaction benchmark, then compare held-out accuracy, calibration, and top-k prioritization quality in both full-data and low-data regimes.

idea: We propose an attribution-focused analysis of the Hubble tension that replaces the rigid late-time expansion history assumed in standard fits with a low-dimensional, physically regularized reconstruction of H(z) or w(z), jointly inferred from Type Ia supernovae, BAO, and an early-universe anchor such as compressed CMB distance information. The core mechanism is to allow smooth, localized late-time departures from LambdaCDM while enforcing high-redshift consistency and stability priors, then measure whether the inferred H0 shift is driven by specific redshift windows or by globally distributed tension across probes. The novelty is not simply another dark-energy extension, but a common inference framework that separates where the pull on H0 originates from which phenomenological model happens to absorb it, making the result more diagnostic than solution-claiming. The study is feasible with public summary likelihoods and existing cosmology samplers because it only requires a compact 2-4 parameter basis plus systematic probe-removal and redshift-masking tests. Its expected impact is to clarify whether the tension points to localized late-time mismodeling, broader dataset inconsistency, or a need for genuinely new physics. The main risk is that conclusions may depend on basis choice or regularization strength, allowing flexibility to absorb noise rather than revealing structure. A minimal validation experiment is to compare LambdaCDM, w0waCDM, and the flexible reconstruction on the same SN+BAO+early-anchor dataset, then quantify how H0 and fit quality change when selected supernova or BAO redshift intervals are relaxed or removed.

idea: We propose a context-aware shared-autonomy framework for robotic surgery that targets narrow, repetitive subtasks such as camera positioning, peg transfer alignment, or short suturing micro-steps, rather than full procedure automation. The system fuses endoscopic video and robot kinematics to infer near-term surgical intent and subtask phase, then uses an imitation-learned policy to propose brief assistive action segments such as tremor-aware smoothing, waypoint alignment, or camera recentering. A calibrated uncertainty module gates execution: the robot assists only when confidence is high and otherwise defers to, or hands control back to, the surgeon through an explicit handoff mechanism. The main novelty is not autonomy alone, but selective micro-autonomy driven by multimodal intent prediction and confidence-aware assist/defer decisions, which directly addresses surgeon fatigue while remaining compatible with existing master-slave platforms. The approach is feasible because it can be trained offline from surgical demonstrations with commonly available video and kinematic logs, and evaluated first in simulation or bench-top shared-control settings. The main risk is miscalibrated uncertainty under operator or viewpoint shift, which could cause unsafe or distracting interventions. A minimal validation experiment would compare teleoperation-only, always-on behavioral-cloning assistance, and confidence-gated assistance on one benchmark subtask using task time, path efficiency, autonomous intervention quality, takeover latency, and false-autonomy rate.

idea: This project proposes a venue-specific environmental justice memo generator that converts tract-level pollution disparities, demographic vulnerability, and local governance context into concise advocacy memos tailored to concrete municipal decision arenas such as city council hearings, zoning boards, or permitting reviews. The core mechanism is a structured pipeline that links hyperlocal exposure and health-burden proxies to community characteristics, then constrains recommended policy asks by observed local authority, permitting history, and relevant public actors so that outputs are politically actionable rather than generic summaries. The novelty lies in moving beyond environmental justice maps and dashboard-style burden documentation toward decision-support that explicitly matches unequal exposure patterns to feasible institutional leverage points while presenting evidence and uncertainty in a form communities can directly use. The approach is feasible as a small-scale study because it can rely on publicly available pollution indicators, census-based vulnerability measures, and municipal records from a handful of cities. Its expected impact is to help marginalized communities articulate more specific, evidence-grounded claims without overstating causal certainty. The main risk is that incomplete or heterogeneous local governance data could produce misleading venue selection or embed normative assumptions about preferred strategies. A minimal validation experiment would compare generated memos across ablations of exposure-only versus full governance context against held-out advocacy briefs for venue correctness, specificity, and evidentiary grounding.

idea: We propose a real-time gait coaching system for wearable IMUs that separates gait analysis from feedback decision making by adding a confidence-gated intervention layer on top of a lightweight online detector. A compact sequence model running on phone or watch streams would estimate gait events and a small set of practical deviation markers such as cadence irregularity, asymmetry, or instability proxies at each time step, while an uncertainty module based on Monte Carlo dropout or a small ensemble would quantify prediction confidence. Feedback would be issued only when the deviation score exceeds a threshold and uncertainty remains low for a short persistence window, reducing distracting false alarms and mistimed cues that make current real-time gait systems hard to trust. The novelty is not new sensing hardware or a new gait detector alone, but an explicit policy for safe, low-latency feedback under uncertainty and cross-subject variability. The approach is feasible because it can be implemented with commodity inertial sensors and evaluated on prerecorded gait datasets in a streaming loop with strict latency constraints. Its main risk is that uncertainty may be poorly calibrated across subjects, limiting trigger reliability. A minimal validation experiment would compare always-on feedback, score-threshold feedback, and uncertainty-gated feedback on streaming IMU sequences, measuring alert precision, missed alerts, calibration error, and end-to-end inference latency.

idea: We propose an education-oriented hybrid reduced-order plate tectonics simulator that approximates expensive geodynamic modeling while keeping the main controls interpretable to non-experts. The core mechanism is a coarse 2D or graph-level engine in which plates interact through simplified, physically motivated rules for boundary motion, buoyancy contrast, slab pull, ridge push, and convergence geometry, while a lightweight learned residual model corrects systematic errors only in qualitative outcome prediction, such as divergence, convergence, transform behavior, subduction likelihood, and coarse deformation class. The novelty is not merely speedup, but the explicit design of a simulator whose user-facing parameters map to recognizable geologic concepts and whose outputs are intentionally limited to scientifically meaningful qualitative regimes suitable for classroom exploration and rapid hypothesis testing. Feasibility is high because the rule-based backbone reduces data demand and the correction model can be trained on a compact library of canonical synthetic or published tectonic scenarios rather than full global simulations. If successful, the system could broaden access to tectonics modeling for teaching, exploratory reasoning, and many-query scenario sweeps on commodity hardware. The main risk is that simplified rules and narrow calibration data may fail to preserve realistic regime transitions outside the reference set. A minimal validation experiment would compare the hybrid model against a pure rule comparison and a pure black-box surrogate on held-out canonical scenarios, measuring runtime and accuracy in predicting qualitative boundary regimes and subduction onset.
task_context:

idea: This project proposes a crop-focused evaluation of spectrally selective heat-mitigation covers that transmit most photosynthetically active radiation (400-700 nm) while rejecting a substantial fraction of near-infrared wavelengths that primarily drive canopy and soil heating, aiming to reduce agricultural greenhouse stress without the yield penalty of conventional shading. The key novelty is not inventing spectral films in general, where prior art likely exists, but testing whether crop-tailored spectral selectivity and limited peak-stress deployment can deliver a better temperature-yield tradeoff than equal-area shade nets under realistic growing conditions. Feasibility is high because the study can use commercially available NIR-rejecting films or covers and simple mechanical deployment rather than requiring new smart materials. Expected impact is a practical pathway for growers to suppress heat load, maintain photosynthetic light, improve water-use efficiency, and protect yield under warming climates. The main risk is that altered humidity, condensation, airflow, or disease pressure could confound the apparent benefit of spectral filtering, and effects may be crop specific. A minimal validation experiment would compare no cover, conventional shade, and static or midday-only spectrally selective cover in a greenhouse or tunnel over one growth cycle, measuring spectral transmission, leaf and canopy temperature, PAR, humidity or VPD, chlorophyll fluorescence or stomatal conductance, water use, and final biomass or fruit yield.

idea: We propose an inflammation-gated tolerogenic biologic for autoimmune disease in which a Treg-biased IL-2 mutein is sterically masked by a peptide linker engineered to be cleaved by proteases enriched in inflamed lesions, such as matrix metalloproteases, thereby restoring activity mainly at diseased tissue rather than throughout the body. The central hypothesis is that lesion-restricted unmasking will expand or stabilize regulatory T cells locally, reduce pathogenic effector responses, and achieve disease control with less systemic immunosuppression than conventional steroids or anti-cytokine therapies. The novelty is not simply a cytokine prodrug, but the combination of autoimmune-site protease sensing, a deliberately tolerogenic payload, and an evaluation framework centered on preserving host defense while treating inflammation. The concept is feasible because IL-2 muteins, protease-cleavable masks, and standard autoimmune mouse models already exist as modular building blocks, allowing a focused proof-of-concept study without requiring entirely new platforms. Expected impact is a safer therapeutic window for chronic autoimmune indications where infection risk limits current care. The main risk is imperfect specificity, since inflammatory proteases may also be present in non-target settings, causing unwanted activation or spillover. A minimal validation experiment would compare masked versus pre-cleaved biologic in inflamed and healthy tissue lysates, then test Treg-selective signaling and disease control versus dexamethasone in one tractable model such as collagen-induced arthritis while measuring a simple vaccine-recall immune proxy.

idea: We propose compute-elastic low-rank adapters that reduce deep learning cost by allowing each input to use only the adapter rank it appears to need. A frozen backbone is augmented with LoRA-style adapters whose highest-rank factors are trained so that lower ranks are usable as prefixes, enabling a single set of parameters to support ranks such as 2, 4, 8, and 16. Training combines standard task loss with cross-rank consistency or distillation and a mild compute regularizer, so low-rank modes remain accurate while higher ranks preserve headroom for difficult examples. At inference time, a lightweight budget-conditioned controller, or even a simple entropy or margin threshold, selects the smallest rank that is likely to meet a confidence target for each example, producing an explicit accuracy-compute tradeoff without retraining separate models. The novelty is not dynamic compute alone, but rank elasticity inside parameter-efficient adapters with per-example control under matched average compute budgets, which is more targeted and easier to deploy than token routing or architecture search. The approach is feasible because it reuses standard backbones and adapter training pipelines, and it could broaden efficient deployment on resource-constrained hardware. The main risk is that dynamic rank switching may yield limited wall-clock gains due to batching or kernel overhead, or provide little benefit on homogeneous tasks. A minimal validation is to fine-tune one frozen transformer on a benchmark with static versus adaptive ranks and compare accuracy, average active rank, FLOPs, and measured latency at equal compute budgets.
task_context:

idea: We propose an event-aware adaptive monitoring framework for workplace airborne contaminants that addresses the blind spots of fixed periodic sampling by coupling scarce high-fidelity air measurements with continuous proxy and context streams such as machine-state logs, ventilation changes, and low-cost sensor readings. The core mechanism is a two-stage statistical system: a sequential risk score detects likely spike windows and triggers intensified reference sampling under a fixed budget, while a probabilistic state-space or hidden semi-Markov reconstruction model estimates the timing, duration, magnitude, and short-term exposure-limit exceedance probability of spikes that remain only partially observed. The novelty is not generic anomaly detection alone, but the integration of budget-matched adaptive sampling with explicit inference of unobserved hazardous episodes in an occupational hygiene setting where short-duration exceedances matter more than average exposure. The approach is feasible because it can be developed first in simulation using bursty contaminant processes driven by task events and environmental covariates, with interpretable outputs aligned to existing safety metrics. If successful, it could improve early warning, reduce missed hazardous peaks, and support more defensible exposure assessment without requiring continuous gold-standard sampling. The main risk is that proxy signals may be weakly or site-specifically related to true contaminant spikes, reducing trigger value and reconstruction accuracy. A minimal validation experiment would compare periodic, random, trigger-only, and trigger-plus-reconstruction strategies at equal sample budgets on simulated burst scenarios, measuring missed-spike probability and short-term exceedance-duration error.
task_context:
Task ID: lb_problem_370
Domain: Statistics
Problem: Current reliance on periodic air sampling for monitoring workplace contaminants can miss dangerous short-term exposure spikes.

idea: We propose an attention-constrained psychophysics protocol that replaces rigid step-size testing with Bayesian stimulus selection, dynamic step sizes, explicit handling of missed or delayed responses, and uncertainty-based early stopping for participants with limited attention or mobility. The core mechanism maintains a posterior over threshold and slope, chooses each new stimulus to maximize expected information near the current uncertainty region, increases step sizes when responses suggest lapses or poor engagement, and terminates once posterior uncertainty falls below a prespecified criterion rather than after a fixed trial count. The novelty is not Bayesian adaptation alone, which is established, but its integration into a short-session protocol that treats omissions and timeouts as informative constraints instead of simple data loss, making the method more suitable for clinical, developmental, and low-mobility settings. Feasibility is high because the approach can be implemented with standard psychometric models and evaluated first in simulation before any specialized recruitment. Expected impact is a practical reduction in testing burden while preserving interpretable threshold estimates. The main risk is model misspecification: if lapse or omission processes are poorly modeled, the procedure could stop too early or bias thresholds. A minimal validation experiment would simulate observers with varying thresholds, slopes, lapse rates, and strict trial caps, comparing this protocol against fixed-step staircases and standard QUEST- or PSI-style methods on trials to criterion, threshold error, and calibration of stopping uncertainty.
task_context:
Task ID: lb_problem_371
Domain: Psychology
Problem: Traditional psychophysic methods are time-intensive due to rigid step sizes, making them impractical for populations with limited attention or mobility.

idea: This project proposes a diversity-preserving adaptive expertise-routing framework for digital collective-intelligence platforms that are prone to cognitive bottlenecks when many contributors compete for limited attention. Instead of aggregating all inputs in a flat pool or relying on a few high-reputation actors, the platform would estimate each participant’s topical expertise and marginal viewpoint diversity, route subproblems to overlapping micro-groups chosen for both relevance and complementarity, and then merge subgroup outputs through a staged synthesis protocol designed to limit overload at the final decision layer. The core novelty is not task routing alone, but the combination of dynamic expertise matching, explicit protection of minority-relevant perspectives, and bottleneck-aware recombination as a sociotechnical mechanism for large-scale collaboration. The idea is feasible because it can be implemented first in simulations or retrospective analyses of collaboration traces using lightweight proxy measures rather than a full platform deployment. Its expected impact is a more inclusive and accurate form of aggregation that reduces dominance concentration while preserving useful heterogeneity in problem solving. The main risk is that gains may depend heavily on noisy or biased estimates of expertise and diversity, and may trade off against short-run coordination efficiency. A minimal validation experiment would compare flat aggregation, random subgrouping, expertise-only routing, and the proposed method on fixed-budget collaborative tasks, measuring idea coverage, minority-expertise retention, solution quality, and attention centralization.
task_context:
Task ID: lb_problem_372
Domain: Sociology
Problem: Existing digital platforms for collective intelligence often fail to effectively aggregate diverse expertise, leading to cognitive bottlenecks in large group collaborations.

idea: We propose a geometry-aware neural operator for solving families of 2D elliptic PDEs on irregular domains by conditioning the solver on a continuous signed distance field (SDF) of the domain together with an explicit boundary-focused training objective. Instead of relying only on raster masks or boundary-fitted meshes, the model receives spatial coordinates, PDE coefficients, and local SDF values so that domain geometry is represented continuously across shapes with varying curvature, concavity, holes, and thin channels. A lightweight optional boundary attention module can further aggregate nearby boundary context for points close to complex interfaces. The central claim is not a wholly new operator paradigm, but a targeted improvement: continuous geometry encoding plus explicit boundary residual or boundary-condition loss should better preserve boundary behavior and improve cross-shape generalization under matched model capacity. The approach is feasible as a controlled small study on Poisson problems with Dirichlet conditions using procedurally generated irregular domains and standard numerical solvers for supervision. Its expected impact is a clearer recipe for geometry representation in learned PDE solvers for nontrivial domains. The main risk is that SDFs may blur sharp corners or narrow structures, making gains sensitive to sampling design rather than true inductive bias. A minimal validation experiment would compare the same backbone with no geometry input, raster-mask input, and SDF input, with and without boundary loss, measuring in-domain error, boundary-condition violation, and out-of-distribution generalization to unseen shape families.

idea: We propose a decision-aware probabilistic tectonic nowcasting framework that fuses heterogeneous monitoring streams, including recent seismic waveform summaries, GNSS deformation time series, and lower-frequency deformation or environmental proxies, to estimate the probability of elevated seismic hazard over short horizons such as the next 1 to 24 hours. Rather than claiming deterministic earthquake prediction, the system is designed to produce calibrated risk distributions that can trigger threshold-based actions such as transport slowdowns, grid protection, or localized evacuations under an explicit cost-loss model. The key novelty is linking multimodal geophysical nowcasts to economically actionable intervention rules and quantifying the marginal value of each sensing modality and data-latency reduction for loss minimization, which is more defensible than searching for universal precursors alone. The approach is feasible with public seismic catalogs, regional GNSS networks, and delayed deformation products, using interpretable comparisons before more flexible multimodal models. If successful, it could improve disaster preparedness by reducing false reassurance, missed events, and unnecessary shutdowns. The main risk is that class imbalance, noisy target definitions, and sparse non-seismic updates may yield unstable gains or unacceptable false-alarm burdens. A minimal validation experiment is a rolling historical backtest in one tectonically active region comparing catalog-only, seismic-only, and seismic-plus-GNSS forecasts on calibration, Brier or log score, alert lead time, and decision utility.

idea: We propose a minimal quantum-corrected mechanics framework for nanoscale resonators in which the usual Newton or Langevin equation is replaced by a generalized Langevin model obtained by integrating out environmental quantum modes, producing a memory kernel and colored stochastic force linked by fluctuation-dissipation constraints. The central idea is not a new open-system formalism, but an executable regime map showing when standard classical Markovian damping becomes quantitatively unreliable for observables that matter in nanodevices, such as resonance linewidth, phase diffusion, and steady-state energy variance. Novelty comes from converting established quantum Brownian ingredients into a compact, device-facing benchmark protocol with explicit crossover criteria in dimensionless parameters such as kT over hbar omega_0, damping ratio, and bath cutoff relative to resonance frequency. Feasibility is high because the study can use a harmonic or weakly nonlinear resonator with an Ohmic or Drude-Lorentz bath, and the non-Markovian dynamics can be simulated efficiently through auxiliary-variable embeddings of exponential memory kernels. The expected impact is a practical correction layer for classical mechanics in mesoscopic design workflows, clarifying when quantum fluctuations remain relevant above fully microscopic scales. The main risk is that deviations may be small outside narrow low-temperature or long-memory regimes. A minimal validation experiment is a simulation sweep comparing classical white-noise dynamics against the quantum-corrected model and identifying thresholds where predicted linewidth or phase-noise differences exceed a preset tolerance.

idea: We propose an energy-aware synonymous coding strategy that reduces the ATP and GTP cost of protein synthesis by redesigning coding sequences to minimize elongation pauses, ribosome collisions, and mistranslation-associated rescue events specifically under energy-limited conditions. Rather than optimizing codons for maximal expression in rich media, the key idea is to optimize for protein yield per unit energetic and translational burden, using codon patterns predicted to maintain smoother decoding when charged-tRNA pools and ATP availability are constrained. The novelty lies in reframing codon design as a stress-conditional energy-efficiency problem, distinct from standard codon optimization and from generic translational repression approaches. This is feasible with existing synonymous reporter libraries, fluorescent or enzymatic reporters, ATP-limitation perturbations, and readouts such as protein output, mRNA abundance, growth burden, and ribosome occupancy or pausing proxies. If successful, the approach could improve cellular efficiency for long, aggregation-prone, or highly expressed proteins and suggest a general design principle for synthetic biology and stress-resilient expression systems. The main risk is that apparent efficiency gains could instead arise from altered mRNA stability, initiation, or protein folding rather than reduced elongation waste. A minimal validation experiment is to compare optimized, deoptimized, and energy-aware synonymous variants of the same reporter in E. coli or yeast under control versus ATP-limited conditions, testing whether the energy-aware design preserves protein output with lower inferred translational burden.

idea: We propose a regime-conditioned surrogate optimization framework for complex operational processes in which simulation is expensive and environmental conditions change unpredictably. The core mechanism is to train a surrogate model that maps both decision variables and compact context descriptors of the current operating regime, such as demand intensity, resource availability, and disruption indicators, to predicted performance and calibrated uncertainty, then embed that model inside the optimization loop. Unlike static metamodeling, the method explicitly detects out-of-distribution contexts or high-risk uncertainty patterns at optimization time and triggers selective high-fidelity resimulation only for candidate decisions whose predicted value is sensitive to regime shift, allowing the optimizer to adapt without paying the full cost of repeated simulation everywhere. The novelty lies in integrating context conditioning, uncertainty calibration, and shift-triggered resampling for nonstationary process optimization rather than treating variability only as noise or handling robustness through fixed worst-case scenarios. The approach is feasible because it can be built on standard surrogate models, calibration methods, and lightweight drift detectors, and it could improve objective quality per simulation call in settings such as production scheduling, logistics, or service operations. The main risk is miscalibrated uncertainty under rare disruptions, which could either miss dangerous shifts or over-trigger simulation. A minimal validation experiment would compare equal-budget optimization performance on a synthetic operations simulator with stationary noise, gradual drift, and abrupt regime changes against direct search, a static surrogate, and a context-conditioned surrogate without the trigger.
task_context:

Problem: Variability and unpredictability challenges in complex operational environments cause inefficiency in process simulation and optimization.

idea: We propose an adaptive climate-smart marine protected area planning framework that treats reserve design as a rolling-horizon, multi-objective optimization problem over spatial planning units updated every few years. At each update, the method jointly prioritizes biodiversity representation, coverage of climate refugia identified from warming-exposure proxies, avoidance of cumulative human pressures such as fishing and pollution, and implementation realism through penalties on boundary churn, minimum patch size, and contiguity constraints. The main novelty is not a claim of a new conservation paradigm, but an integrated benchmark that evaluates these ingredients together in one marine adaptive-management setup and compares them directly with static and partial-objective alternatives under equal protected-area budgets. The approach is feasible with public regional datasets for habitats or species features, sea-surface-temperature anomalies, fishing pressure, and habitat condition, making a data-rich case study such as the California Current or Mediterranean plausible. Expected impact is a more policy-relevant picture of when dynamic MPAs can outperform static coverage targets by retaining protection as species and stressors shift under climate change. The main risk is that ecological benefits will rely on proxy outcomes and may be sensitive to objective weights or limited by sparse spatiotemporal data. A minimal validation experiment would compare four strategies—static, dynamic biodiversity-only, dynamic climate-only, and full multi-objective dynamic planning—across three to four time periods, reporting representation, refugia coverage, pressure avoidance, and boundary-turnover cost.
task_context:

idea: We propose a constraint-regularized digital twin for pharmaceutical batch manufacturing that predicts final critical quality attribute drift and batch inconsistency risk from partial multistage process trajectories, enabling earlier and more trustworthy intervention than end-of-batch release checks alone. The core mechanism is a sequence model that ingests routine sensor streams, recipe events, and sparse assay data while being trained with lightweight process priors such as approximate mass-balance relations, monotonic phase progression, and bounded state transitions, so the learned dynamics remain plausible under delayed labels and limited batch counts. The novelty is not a generic digital twin, but the use of simple, auditable constraint penalties to improve robustness, calibration, and stage-level deviation attribution in low-data, regulated manufacturing settings where black-box models are hard to justify. The approach is feasible because it relies on data already collected in many plants and only requires partial mechanistic knowledge rather than a full first-principles simulator. Its expected impact is better batch-to-batch consistency, earlier risk flagging, and clearer localization of problematic stages or controllable variables. The main risk is that available public pharmaceutical data may be scarce and the chosen constraints may be too weak or misspecified. A minimal validation experiment would compare this hybrid model against chemometric and standard sequence comparisons on held-out batches, measuring quality-risk prediction, calibration, and how early reliable warnings emerge at intermediate checkpoints.

idea: We propose a multi-view regime-aware probabilistic forecasting model for volatile financial markets that combines four daily information streams: technical price and volume features, market volatility context such as realized volatility and VIX, macro-event calendar indicators, and aggregated news sentiment when available. Each view is encoded with a lightweight temporal module, then fused through a latent regime gate that learns to weight views differently across calm, trending, and stress periods, producing a calibrated predictive distribution over next-day or next-week returns rather than a single point estimate. The central novelty is not any one modality alone, but the controlled integration of multimodal signals with latent regime adaptation and explicit calibration objectives, aimed at improving robustness under distribution shift. The design is feasible with public data and a compact universe of liquid ETFs or major indices, making it practical to train and evaluate with expanding-window backtests. Expected impact is a forecasting tool that is more reliable during unstable periods and more useful for risk-aware decision making because it quantifies uncertainty directly. The main risk is that the latent regime module may collapse into a simple volatility detector and add little beyond richer inputs. A minimal validation experiment would compare this model against historical mean, a standard point forecaster, and a probabilistic multimodal model without regime gating on 5-10 liquid ETFs, evaluating calibration, interval coverage, negative log-likelihood, and directional accuracy across calm versus stress periods.

idea: We propose a physics-aware probabilistic fusion model for sea-ice thickness retrieval that treats snow depth as an explicit latent variable rather than an unmodeled source of error. The method would combine radar-altimetry freeboard features with passive-microwave indicators of snow conditions and thermal or optical context priors, using a lightweight hierarchical Bayesian model or probabilistic neural regressor constrained by simple freeboard-consistency and monotonicity relationships. The novelty is not a new sensor, but a compact joint-inference framework that estimates thickness and uncertainty while accounting for snow-depth variability directly, which should make retrievals more robust than radar-only inversion or naive feature concatenation when regimes shift across season, region, or ice type. The design is feasible because it can be trained on collocated satellite products over a limited Arctic window, without requiring dense snow-depth labels everywhere, and can use external snow products only for weak supervision or sanity checks. Its expected impact is better-calibrated thickness estimates for operational and scientific use, especially in high-snow-variability conditions where current single-sensor methods are unstable. The main risk is that cross-sensor co-registration error or sparse snow references may obscure whether gains come from the model itself. A minimal validation experiment would compare radar-only, direct multi-sensor regression, and the proposed latent-snow model on a train-one-region-season, test-held-out-region-or-later-season setup, measuring both thickness error and uncertainty calibration.

idea: This project proposes a preservation-first archaeological prospection framework that combines multimodal non-invasive sensing with active survey planning to reduce reliance on excavation while improving subsurface feature discovery. The core mechanism is a spatial probabilistic model that fuses drone or satellite RGB imagery, multispectral or thermal data, LiDAR, and optional geophysical inputs such as magnetometry or ground-penetrating radar to produce calibrated prospect maps and uncertainty estimates for buried structures. An active-learning policy then recommends the next sensing location, transect, or modality by optimizing expected information gain under explicit survey-cost and disturbance penalties, so field teams can focus effort on the least invasive actions with the highest expected value. The novelty is not a new sensor, but the integration of multimodal fusion, uncertainty-aware abstention, and sequential decision-making under a heritage-protection objective. The approach is feasible because many landscapes already have partial remote-sensing coverage and published survey maps that can support retrospective benchmarking without new excavation. Its expected impact is a more efficient and ethically safer workflow for discovery, documentation, and protection of cultural heritage. The main risk is sparse, incomplete, and site-specific ground truth, which may limit transfer and calibration. A minimal validation experiment would simulate sequential acquisition on a small set of previously surveyed sites and compare the method against random and fixed-grid policies under matched sensing budgets.

idea: This project proposes a biodegradable hydrogel supercapacitor for short-life electronics built from a protein-polysaccharide network such as gelatin-alginate or chitosan-alginate, loaded with biochar as the conductive phase and naturally sourced redox mediators such as tannic acid or lignin-derived quinone motifs to introduce pseudocapacitive charge storage beyond simple double-layer behavior. The central novelty is not only replacing persistent components with biodegradable ones, but establishing a quantitative composition-property-degradation map that links mediator loading, crosslink density, and biocarbon fraction to capacitance retention, ionic transport, mechanical integrity, and compost-like degradation, with an additional comparison between free and network-immobilized mediators to test whether leaching can be suppressed without sacrificing end-of-life breakdown. The concept is feasible because each component is accessible from established biopolymer and biomass-processing routes, and the study can be kept compact through a 9-12 formulation matrix assembled into benign aqueous-salt cells. If successful, the work could provide a design rule for transient power sources in disposable sensors or medical patches, reducing electronic waste from non-biodegradable storage materials. The main technical risk is that redox species may leach or swelling may disrupt conductivity, so a minimal validation experiment is to fabricate matched control cells with and without mediator immobilization and compare CV, GCD, EIS, and short-horizon compost or enzymatic mass-loss behavior.

idea: We propose a transparent Planetary Health Index (PHI) for exoplanets that moves beyond liquid-water and atmospheric checklists by integrating four interpretable dimensions of planetary health: environmental stability, shielding from external stellar stress, volatile persistence, and long-term dynamical viability. Concretely, the framework would combine features that are already available or derivable for many confirmed systems, such as incident flux, equilibrium-temperature proxies, mass-radius based escape or retention indicators, stellar type or age based activity proxies, eccentricity, and tidal-locking likelihood, then normalize them into modular subscales and aggregate them with equal-weight, expert-weighted, and uncertainty-aware ranking schemes. The novelty is not a claim to invent the first composite habitability score, but to recast exoplanet assessment as a resilience-oriented, systems-level health problem with explicit uncertainty and ablation analysis, making the ranking more physically interpretable and less dependent on a single arbitrary scalar. The approach is feasible with public exoplanet catalogs and modest derived modeling, and could improve target prioritization for follow-up observations by distinguishing planets that look superficially habitable from those likely to sustain stable conditions over time. The main risk is that poorly observed factors such as magnetic shielding, atmospheric mass, and interior cycling must be represented by coarse proxies, so weighting choices may dominate conclusions. A minimal validation experiment would compute PHI for a public sample plus Solar System reference planets, compare rankings against habitable-zone and Earth-similarity comparisons, and test robustness under subscale ablations and uncertainty propagation.

idea: We propose a value-aware energy budget controller for intermittently connected IoT data pipelines that jointly decides, for each short time horizon, how much energy to spend on sensing rate, local feature extraction fidelity, compression level, buffer retention, and transmission timing. The core mechanism is a lightweight predictive policy, such as a constrained contextual bandit or receding-horizon greedy optimizer, that uses current battery state, short-horizon forecasts of connectivity and harvested energy, and a per-record utility estimate derived from event rarity, uncertainty, or downstream task importance. Unlike prior approaches that usually optimize only communication, sampling, or compression in isolation, this formulation treats the device as an end-to-end data-engineering system and allocates scarce energy across multiple pipeline stages to maximize retained analytic value subject to freshness constraints. The approach is feasible because it can be implemented with simple models and trace-driven simulation rather than heavy reinforcement learning, and it could improve energy efficiency, delay tolerance, and data usefulness for remote sensing and edge monitoring deployments. The main risk is that most gains may come from one dominant lever, such as upload batching, or depend heavily on the chosen utility model. A minimal validation experiment would compare the joint controller against static periodic upload, battery-threshold transmission, sampling-only adaptation, and communication-only adaptation on sensor traces with bursty connectivity, measuring energy consumed, data freshness, retained utility, drop rate, and policy overhead.

idea: We propose a near-real-time coastal marine plastic monitoring system that couples probabilistic satellite hotspot detection with short-horizon drift forecasting to support cleanup operations and policy response. The core mechanism is to treat public Earth observation signals, such as optical imagery, SAR, ocean color, and contextual indicators like river plumes and coastal meteorology, not as definitive plastic labels but as noisy seeds of likely floating debris. These seeded hotspots are then propagated 24-72 hours forward using lightweight transport modeling driven by publicly available surface currents, winds, and tides, producing ranked response maps that indicate where cleanup teams should expect aggregation or landfall risk. The novelty is in the operational integration: rather than offering only static detection or generic ocean drift simulation, the system explicitly links near-real-time debris proxy sensing to actionable short-term forecasting in a way that is evaluation-ready for public decision support. The approach is feasible because it relies on public satellite and reanalysis products and can be scoped to a small number of well-observed coastal regions. Its expected impact is improved prioritization of scarce cleanup resources and better evidence for local pollution governance. The main risk is low specificity, since seaweed, foam, sediment, or wood may generate false hotspot seeds. A minimal validation experiment would compare this detect-plus-drift pipeline against detection-only persistence and drift-only comparisons in 1-3 coastal sites by testing overlap with later satellite observations at 24, 48, and 72 hours.

idea: We propose a cost-aware adaptive multi-representation meta-compressor for heterogeneous modern datasets, motivated by the observation that a single codec increasingly fails on mixtures of text, logs, tables, JSON, code, and binary-like records. The system partitions input into medium-sized chunks, extracts lightweight descriptors such as byte entropy, repetitiveness, n-gram concentration, sparsity, and simple structural markers, and then routes each chunk to one codec from a modest portfolio spanning entropy/dictionary methods, transform codecs, and optionally a compact learned latent codec. The key novelty is not inventing a new compressor, but formulating fine-grained codec routing as a systems optimization problem that explicitly trades off compressed size, encode time, decode time, memory use, and routing overhead, with a selector trained or tuned to approximate this multi-objective score. The approach is feasible because it relies mostly on off-the-shelf codecs and cheap features, making implementation and comparison straightforward. If successful, it could improve compression efficiency for rapidly growing heterogeneous corpora while preserving practical throughput. The main risk is that metadata, feature extraction, and switching costs may erase gains, especially on homogeneous or small inputs. A minimal validation experiment would compare a best single codec, a static portfolio chooser, a feature-based router, and an oracle per-chunk chooser across mixed-system datasets while measuring ratio, throughput, memory, and overhead.

idea: We propose a misconception-aware stoichiometry tutor that targets the specific reasoning failures that make conventional instruction ineffective, such as equation-to-ratio mapping errors, mole-mass conversion breakdowns, limiting-reagent misidentification, and ratio reversals. The core mechanism is a compact, pre-registered taxonomy of recurrent stoichiometry errors linked to an explicit feedback policy: when a student’s step work indicates a particular misconception, the system delivers targeted prompts, contrasting examples, and lightly faded worked steps designed to repair that error class rather than merely indicate correctness. The novelty is not tutoring alone, but the tight coupling of a domain-specific misconception model with mechanism-sensitive evaluation of whether students actually change how they structure solutions across mole ratios, limiting reagents, and percent yield. The approach is feasible as a lightweight web intervention because it can operate on a small set of interpretable error categories and standard chemistry problem formats. If effective, it could improve transfer and reduce persistent error patterns more efficiently than generic hints. The main risk is that student responses may be too sparse or ambiguous for reliable classification, making adaptive feedback noisy. A minimal validation experiment would compare this tutor with an active-control version offering correctness-only hints under matched time and problem volume, using pretest-adjusted posttest accuracy, transfer items, and shifts in labeled error distributions as outcomes.

idea: We propose a model-guided bioengineering strategy to improve crop yield potential by co-optimizing Rubisco activase with Calvin Cycle RuBP-regeneration capacity, rather than modifying either module in isolation. The core mechanism is to tune activase abundance or isoform properties together with one or two regeneration-phase enzymes, prioritizing SBPase and PRK and optionally FBPase, so that Rubisco re-activation kinetics, ATP use, and sugar-phosphate regeneration remain matched during heat stress, fluctuating light, and elevated CO2. The novelty lies in treating Calvin Cycle optimization as an environment-conditioned co-design problem: predictive photosynthesis modeling would be used to rank a small combinatorial design space and identify pairs expected to relieve activation and regeneration bottlenecks simultaneously, which is more mechanistically targeted than common single-gene overexpression approaches. Feasibility is supported by existing chloroplast-targeted transgene engineering and standard gas-exchange phenotyping, while the expected impact is improved photosynthetic robustness under field-relevant variability, increasing the chance that biochemical gains translate into biomass and yield. The main risk is that combined engineering could create ATP/redox imbalance or source-sink constraints, causing condition-specific benefits or penalties. A minimal validation experiment would compare wild type, activase-only, regeneration-only, and combined lines in a tractable model plant, measuring A/Ci curves, photosynthetic induction and recovery after light transitions, chlorophyll fluorescence, and temperature responses to test whether the combined design outperforms single interventions specifically under stress-relevant conditions.

idea: We propose a constrained, patient- and task-specific CT protocol recommendation system that selects from an interpretable menu of already approved acquisition presets using readily available context such as age, body size, anatomy, and clinical indication, with the goal of minimizing estimated radiation exposure while preserving predicted diagnostic adequacy. The key novelty is to shift optimization from post hoc low-dose reconstruction to acquisition-time decision support, explicitly modeling the tradeoff between dose and task sufficiency and auditing whether recommendations improve protection for children and other high-risk groups rather than merely matching average population performance. A practical implementation would learn separate models for radiation burden and adequacy proxies from retrospective exams, then train a constrained contextual policy that recommends only clinically used settings and can expose the main factors behind each recommendation. This is feasible because it does not require autonomous scanner control or prospective deployment, only retrospective metadata, finite protocol choices, and proxy outcomes such as report confidence, repeat imaging, or downstream task labels. The main risk is counterfactual validity, since each patient was observed under only one protocol and adequacy labels may be noisy. A minimal validation experiment would focus on one anatomy-specific CT task, compare the learned policy against standard fixed or weight-banded protocols using off-policy or simulator-based evaluation, and report dose, adequacy, and subgroup fairness metrics under site-held-out testing.

idea: We propose a reasoning-oriented 3D pretraining framework for molecular representation learning that targets a core weakness of current AI systems: poor spatial reasoning over scientifically meaningful structure. Instead of relying mainly on generic masked reconstruction or denoising, an equivariant molecular encoder would be pretrained on public conformer data using auxiliary tasks that require global relational inference, including symmetry-class prediction, pairwise distance-order comparison, rigid transformation consistency, and motif completion from partial geometry. The novelty is not a new backbone alone, but a pretraining objective family explicitly designed to teach comparison, transformation, and long-range spatial structure understanding in molecules. The approach is feasible because it can be built from existing equivariant graph neural networks, standard conformer datasets, and automatically generated self-supervised labels, making it practical without costly annotation. If successful, it could improve geometry-sensitive molecular prediction and provide a more reliable foundation for downstream drug discovery tasks where 3D arrangement matters. The main risk is that the proposed reasoning tasks may be either too artificial or insufficiently aligned with downstream objectives, yielding little advantage over standard 3D self-supervision. A minimal validation experiment would compare, under matched model size and compute, supervised-only training, generic 3D self-supervised pretraining, and the proposed reasoning-oriented pretraining on a small set of conformer-dependent molecular property tasks plus held-out spatial probes for symmetry, distance ranking, and motif completion.
