Rather than replacing examiners with a black-box score, the system produces calibrated triage recommendations: fast-track likely clear cases, escalate ambiguous applications to deeper review, and surface disagreement zones where consistency checks across similar historical cases are most needed. Its expected advantage is not merely faster throughput, but more transparent, auditable reasoning and lower variance across examiners because the same evidentiary decomposition is reused across related cases. Feasibility is high because patent texts, office actions, citation networks, and examiner histories already exist in machine-readable form, allowing construction of a retrospective pipeline without changing substantive patent law. The main risk is that historical office actions may encode inconsistent or biased standards, causing the model to reproduce path-dependent errors; to control this, the method explicitly flags low-confidence alignments, separates descriptive evidence extraction from decision recommendation, and measures whether its consistency gains hold after conditioning on technology class and application complexity. A minimal convincing benchmark would test one office’s retrospective queue, comparing backlog reduction, cross-examiner variance, explanation completeness, and appeal-reversal prediction against keyword search plus first-come manual assignment, with success defined as simultaneous improvement on throughput and reason-giving quality without increased false allowances.

We propose ReflexShield-MPC, a dual-timescale adaptive control architecture that closes a novelty gap in cybernetics by targeting the regime where plants, disturbances, and sensing quality all drift during operation, making fixed-model robust control too conservative and standard online learning controllers too brittle. The unmet gap is not merely faster parameter tuning, because trivial explanations such as increasing controller gain, retraining a policy offline, or switching among a small bank of preset models fail when the source of nonstationarity is itself changing and partially hidden; these approaches either overreact to noise or lag behind real shifts. Our mechanism combines a safety-certified comparison model predictive controller with a reflexive meta-adaptation layer that updates a low-dimensional latent “control context” from streaming prediction residuals, actuator saturation patterns, and delay signatures, then uses that context to modulate horizon length, constraint tightening, estimator trust, and a small residual control term. Unlike conventional adaptive MPC that directly chases parameter estimates, the context layer treats abrupt residual structure as evidence about which adaptation mode is trustworthy, allowing the controller to slow, freeze, or redirect learning when uncertainty spikes. The expected advantage is real-time adaptation without surrendering hard safety margins, especially in networked or human-in-the-loop systems where delay and disturbance statistics evolve faster than plant parameters can be identified. Feasibility is high because the method reuses existing MPC solvers and adds only a compact online inference module. The main risk is that latent context updates may misclassify rare transients as persistent regime shifts, causing unnecessary conservatism or oscillatory adaptation; we control this with hysteresis, uncertainty-gated updates, and rollback to the certified comparison. A minimal convincing benchmark is a simulated cyber-physical control suite with time-varying delays, sensor dropouts, and plant drift, comparing constraint violation rate, cumulative tracking error, adaptation latency, and recovery after abrupt regime changes against robust MPC, gain-scheduled control, and direct adaptive MPC.

We propose LithoLoop, a concept-trajectory teaching system that turns the rock cycle into an interactive causal map linking hand specimens, field images, thin-section microscopy, and process simulations so learners can move across time scales and evidence types while constructing explanations. The novelty gap is not simply that current rock-cycle lessons are static or visually dull, because many classrooms already use videos, 3D models, or virtual labs; the unmet gap is that these tools rarely force students to reconcile why the same material can be classified differently as conditions change, or how uncertainty in texture, pressure, heat, and weathering evidence propagates through explanations. LithoLoop addresses this by combining adaptive case sequencing with contradiction-driven prompts: students classify a sample, inspect additional evidence layers, revise their causal path, and then compare their reasoning against expert-generated transformation pathways that explicitly include ambiguous branches rather than one canonical loop. This mechanism is intended to improve engagement and accessibility for both students and early-stage researchers by making the rock cycle less like a memorized diagram and more like evidence-based geological inference, while remaining feasible because it can be built from existing specimen collections, open petrographic image sets, and lightweight browser-based simulations. A main risk is that the added interactivity could increase cognitive load or reward guessing over understanding, especially for novices with weak spatial reasoning; to control this, the system should cap branch complexity, log revision behavior, and distinguish productive uncertainty from random trial-and-error. A minimal validation benchmark is a randomized comparison against a standard illustrated lesson and a conventional virtual lab, measuring delayed transfer to unfamiliar rock histories, accuracy under ambiguous cases, reasoning-quality rubrics, and engagement persistence, with success defined as better transfer and ambiguity handling without longer completion time or lower confidence calibration.

We propose RhizoLoop Pyro-Ferment Atlas, a decentralized waste-to-fertility method that converts mixed agricultural residues into crop- and soil-specific amendment blends by coupling low-temperature pyrolysis, targeted solid-state microbial fermentation, and a simple decision model trained on local soil constraints. The novelty gap is that most circular fertilizer proposals assume that any composted or biochar-treated waste will improve fertility, but this is a false positive: nutrient release kinetics, pH shifts, salinity, and micronutrient immobilization vary sharply across residue types, so “recycling more waste” alone does not solve declining fertility or synthetic fertilizer dependence. Our method explicitly rejects that trivial explanation by treating residues as programmable feedstocks rather than generic organic matter. The core mechanism is a two-stage transformation in which lignocellulosic fractions are partially pyrolyzed to create stable carbon and sorption sites, while nutrient-rich fractions are fermented with phosphate-solubilizing and potassium-mobilizing consortia, then recombined into tailored pellets whose carbon:nutrient:mineralization profile is selected to match soil texture, comparison nutrient deficits, and crop demand windows. Expected impact is a fertilizer substitute that simultaneously improves nutrient retention, recycles waste locally, and reduces yield penalties often seen when raw compost or single-source biochar is used alone. Feasibility is high because the unit operations already exist at farm or cooperative scale; the scientific move is their rule-based integration around agronomic matching. The main risk is inconsistent performance due to feedstock heterogeneity, pathogen carryover, heavy metals, or over-alkalinization, so the system includes residue screening, ash and electrical-conductivity thresholds, and a holdout rule that defaults high-risk wastes to energy use rather than soil application. A minimal validation benchmark is a three-crop pot and microplot trial comparing tailored blends against raw compost, standard biochar, and reduced-rate synthetic fertilizer, with success defined by equal or better yield at 25-40% lower synthetic input plus significant gains in soil organic carbon, available phosphorus, and seasonal nitrogen retention.

We propose RarePath Navigator, a counselor-extending framework that couples phenotype-aware case retrieval with uncertainty-gated family history reasoning to deliver pre-counseling genetic risk summaries for underserved patients and rare-disease referrals. The novelty gap is not simply that tele-genetics capacity is low or that large language models can draft education materials; those are partial workflow fixes and often fail exactly where rare conditions and fragmented records create the highest counseling burden. Instead, the unmet need is a mechanism that can transform sparse symptoms, family narratives, and low-resource clinical documentation into a structured, triage-ready hypothesis set while explicitly refusing overconfident inheritance claims when evidence is weak. RarePath Navigator would align three modules: a patient-facing multilingual intake that converts free-text family history and symptom descriptions into a pedigree-and-phenotype graph; a retrieval engine that matches this graph against curated rare-disease and hereditary cancer exemplars plus prior counselor-reviewed cases; and a calibrated inference layer that outputs candidate counseling pathways, missing-information questions, and a deferral flag when specialist escalation is required. Its expected advantage is not automated diagnosis, but reducing time-to-useful counseling by giving non-genetics clinicians and navigators a transparent first-pass workup that is more inclusive of rare presentations and lower-literacy populations. Feasibility is strengthened by relying on existing guideline sources, ontology mappings, and retrospective counseling notes rather than new wet-lab infrastructure. The main risk is false reassurance or biased retrieval for underrepresented ancestries and atypical pedigrees, so the system must optimize abstention, expose evidence provenance, and track subgroup calibration rather than only top-1 suggestion accuracy. A minimal convincing benchmark would compare RarePath Navigator against standard referral intake on retrospective multi-site cases, measuring correctness of triage urgency, completeness of key follow-up questions, counselor editing time, and safe abstention rate, followed by a small prospective pilot in community clinics assessing whether more patients reach a counselor with an actionable pre-visit summary.

We propose Sparse Regime-Causal Koopman Mixture Networks, a forecasting framework for chaotic scientific and economic systems that targets a specific novelty gap: most current models either scale brute-force sequence learners that memorize local correlations at high compute cost, or impose oversimplified dynamics assumptions that fail under abrupt regime shifts, while many apparent improvements are false positives caused by smoother datasets, shorter horizons, or leakage from dense exogenous features rather than genuine understanding of nonlinear structure. The core mechanism is to decompose trajectories into a small set of latent regimes, learn within each regime a sparse Koopman-style linear evolution in a lifted state space, and couple this with a causal interaction graph that adaptively gates which variables may influence one another across time, so the model only spends capacity on dynamically active relationships instead of recomputing dense attention over every variable pair. A lightweight uncertainty head estimates transition instability and increases regularization when the system appears near bifurcation boundaries, reducing overconfident extrapolation in highly chaotic intervals. The expected advantage is a better accuracy-compute tradeoff and improved interpretability because forecast updates are tied to explicit regime transitions and sparse cross-variable operators rather than opaque global embeddings. Feasibility is reasonable because all components can be trained end to end with standard backpropagation and sparsity penalties, and each part has precedent even though their combination for chaotic multivariate modeling is underexplored. The main risk is that the discovered regimes collapse into arbitrary partitions or the sparse graph misses weak but critical interactions. A minimal convincing benchmark would compare against a transformer and a neural ODE on Lorenz-96, a medium-scale climate reanalysis subset, and limit-order or sector-index market data, measuring long-horizon error, calibration under perturbations, graph stability, and accuracy per unit training FLOP.

We propose Causal Cross-Field Influence Graphs, a method for measuring research impact by estimating whether a paper or idea changes the downstream problem-solving behavior of multiple disciplines rather than merely accumulating citations. The novelty gap is that most alternatives to citation counts still treat impact as a static popularity signal derived from co-citation, text similarity, altmetrics, or network centrality, which creates false positives from fashionable but non-transformative work and fails to distinguish genuine interdisciplinary transfer from superficial referencing. Our core mechanism constructs a temporal graph linking papers, concepts, datasets, and methods, then uses matched counterfactual trajectories to estimate whether the appearance of a contribution causes new combinations of concepts, methods, or benchmark adoption in fields that were previously disconnected. Instead of rewarding raw attention, the model scores cross-field causal uplift: the incremental probability that a target field adopts a concept, method family, or problem framing after exposure, while controlling for prior trend growth, author prestige, venue effects, and broad topic drift. This should better surface under-cited bridge work, early methodological catalysts, and hidden knowledge brokers that standard metrics systematically miss, improving knowledge discovery and collaboration targeting. Feasibility is strong because the required inputs already exist in publication metadata, abstracts, full text where available, and time-stamped citation networks. The main risk is confounding from simultaneous external shocks, such as new funding programs or major benchmark releases, which could mimic causal transfer; we address this by negative-control concepts, placebo intervention times, and robustness checks across fields with distinct publication cultures. A minimal validation benchmark would test whether the metric predicts future cross-disciplinary method adoption, new coauthorship edges, and benchmark migration better than citation count, PageRank, and semantic centrality on a held-out multi-field corpus.

We propose Reciprocity-Trace Reframing, a behavioral intervention that increases altruistic action by making people see each helping act not as a one-off moral sacrifice but as the start of a personally traceable prosocial chain whose downstream effects may later return to the group, though not necessarily to the actor. The novelty gap is that many existing altruism interventions rely on empathy boosts, moral reminders, or reputational visibility, yet these often produce short-lived intentions, social desirability effects, or helping only when an audience is present; our approach explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that people merely need stronger prosocial values, and instead targets a neglected cognitive bottleneck: people undervalue helping because they cannot mentally simulate how small actions propagate through real social networks over time. The core mechanism is a structured reflection protocol combined with lightweight network feedback: participants are shown short, believable community scenarios, asked to map one concrete helping act to three plausible second-order consequences, and later receive anonymized summaries of how peers believe such acts would alter trust, mood, and future willingness to help within the group. This should outperform generic empathy appeals by converting altruism into a forecastable coordination process rather than a diffuse virtue signal, while remaining feasible in schools, workplaces, and online communities because it requires only brief guided exercises and simple feedback dashboards. The main risk is that participants could treat the task as abstract moral storytelling rather than updating real behavior, or that effects depend on unusually collectivist samples; to calibrate this, the minimal validation benchmark is a preregistered randomized study comparing Reciprocity-Trace Reframing against empathy-message and neutral-control conditions, with success defined by higher rates of costly anonymous helping in an incentive-compatible resource-sharing game, greater one-week follow-up volunteering or donation choice, and mediation through increased perceived downstream efficacy rather than mood alone.

We propose the Civic-Cosmic Choice Bell Architecture, a loophole-closing method that combines kilometer-scale entangled-photon stations with real-time random setting generation derived from synchronized, independent streams of socially generated urban activity and high-redshift astronomical photons, fused through a precommitted extractor that is hardware isolated from the source and detectors. The novelty gap is that prior Bell tests have often closed locality or freedom-of-choice strongly, but not both at once under a design that explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that the setting choices were still vulnerable to hidden common causes, timing leakage, or latent laboratory coupling. Our core mechanism is to place the analyzers far enough apart for strict space-like separation, while deriving each side’s basis choice from two causally distant randomness reservoirs: one from local human collective behavior measured through public transit gate timing or encrypted civic sensor bursts, and one from ancient stellar photon arrival parity. This mixed-origin randomization is intended to make false-positive claims harder because neither purely terrestrial pseudorandomness nor purely cosmic randomness alone can explain a violation if both streams must agree through a transparent fusion rule announced before data collection. The expected advantage is a more credible closure of freedom-of-choice without sacrificing locality, using existing photonic Bell infrastructure plus auditable randomness hardware. The main risk is that civic data may introduce subtle temporal structure or adversarial predictability, and cosmic channels may suffer low-rate bias, so the system must continuously estimate min-entropy, publish extractor diagnostics, and discard trials failing predeclared timing and independence thresholds. A minimal convincing benchmark is a three-site field test showing, over a fixed trial budget, simultaneous space-like separation, statistically significant Bell violation, extractor-certified entropy on both wings, and no detectable correlation between hidden source variables and setting generators under pre-registered independence tests.

We propose Topology-Conditioned Counterfactual Residual Detector, a dynamic-network anomaly detection method that targets a specific novelty gap: most current models treat structural evolution itself as suspicious, so they over-flag benign growth, community reorganization, or seasonal rewiring, while methods that adapt online often explain away true anomalies after only a few updates. The key scientific move is to separate expected structural change from truly inconsistent behavior by learning a compact causal forecast of the next graph state under normal evolution and then testing whether observed local subgraph transitions remain plausible under multiple counterfactual futures. Concretely, the method combines a temporal graph state-space model with motif-level transport matching, producing for each node and edge a distribution over expected neighborhood rewiring, degree drift, and role transition; anomalies are scored not by raw prediction error alone, but by residuals that persist after conditioning on inferred regime shifts such as densification, bursty interaction phases, or community splits. This explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that any large topological change is anomalous, because a change is only flagged when it violates the forecasted family of structurally coherent futures. Expected advantage is lower false positives during evolving but healthy network phases, while preserving sensitivity to coordinated attacks, stealthy fraud rings, or abnormal bridge formation that cannot be justified by normal dynamics. Feasibility is reasonable because the model can operate on sampled ego-graphs and low-order motifs rather than full-graph simulation. The main risk is misspecified regime inference causing real anomalies to be absorbed as normal adaptation, so uncertainty-aware thresholds and delayed consistency checks are built into the detector. A minimal convincing benchmark would compare this method against temporal GNN and reconstruction comparisons on synthetic evolving graphs with controlled drift plus one real dynamic network, measuring event-level AUROC, false-positive rate under benign distribution shift, and detection delay.

We propose EcoFiscal Twin, a hierarchical causal digital-twin method that fuses ecological state dynamics with economic planning so policymakers can optimize growth, resource use, and ecosystem resilience in one decision system rather than treating ecology as a downstream constraint. The novelty gap is that most integrated assessment tools either aggregate nature into coarse damage coefficients, which cannot guide local or sectoral action, or they join environmental and economic datasets descriptively without identifying which ecological changes actually propagate into productivity, prices, health, or public finance; our method explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that “more data integration” alone solves the problem by requiring causal pathways and counterfactual policy estimates. The core mechanism couples a dynamic input-output economic model with ecological stock-flow modules for water, land, biodiversity proxies, and carbon sequestration, linked through Bayesian structural equations that estimate lagged bidirectional effects between ecosystem conditions and economic variables under policy interventions such as taxes, restoration subsidies, extraction caps, or zoning changes. A constrained planner then searches for policies that maximize a welfare objective under ecological tipping-point and budget constraints, while uncertainty is handled through posterior predictive intervals, stress tests on hidden confounding, and robust optimization against climate and market shocks. The expected advantage is actionable policy sequencing: instead of choosing between conservation and growth, decision makers receive intervention portfolios that quantify when ecological repair increases long-run fiscal stability and sector productivity. Feasibility is high because national accounts, satellite land and water indicators, emissions inventories, and sector statistics already exist at usable resolution in many countries. The main risk is misspecified ecological feedbacks or omitted institutional confounders, so the minimal validation benchmark is a retrospective policy test in two regions comparing EcoFiscal Twin against standard cost-benefit and static IAM comparisons on out-of-sample prediction of GDP, ecosystem condition, and public revenue, with success defined by better forecast calibration and a superior ecological-economic Pareto frontier.

We propose Spectator-Calibrated Correlated Error Distillation, a hardware-aware mitigation method that targets a neglected gap in current quantum reliability work: most schemes either assume near-independent noise, absorb drift into coarse calibration updates, or rely on heavy logical error correction overhead, so they miss short-range, time-varying correlated faults that dominate many NISQ failures; the key novelty is to reject the false-positive explanation that reliability is limited only by higher single-qubit fidelity or larger shot counts, because those improvements do not expose hidden spectator-induced phase kicks, bursty crosstalk, and readout-conditioned error propagation. Our mechanism inserts lightweight spectator probe circuits interleaved with the computation, using idle or sacrificial qubits to sense local crosstalk and drift in real time, then feeds those probe outcomes into a sparse graphical noise estimator that infers edge-specific correlated error rates over a short moving window; the inferred structure is used to adapt Pauli-twirling choices, schedule local recompilation of vulnerable gate blocks, and apply correlation-conditioned readout reweighting during post-processing. The expected advantage is better effective logical fidelity without full fault tolerance, especially for medium-depth circuits where static calibration tables are already stale but full syndrome extraction is infeasible; feasibility is strong because the probes reuse native gates and only require classical side processing plus limited circuit rewrites. The main risk is that probe insertion itself perturbs the device or that estimated correlations overfit transient fluctuations, yielding negative net benefit; we control this by constraining estimator sparsity, using held-out calibration windows, and falling back to standard mitigation when confidence drops. A minimal convincing benchmark is a comparison on randomized mirror circuits and small chemistry or Ising instances under induced drift and crosstalk, measuring improvement in heavy-output probability, cycle fidelity, and final observable error versus zero-noise extrapolation and static readout mitigation, with success defined as consistent gains under equal shot budgets and under at least two distinct noise regimes.

We propose MorphoPulse-CRISPR, a two-input developmental gene-control platform that couples optically gated transcriptional activation with morphogen-responsive RNA logic to achieve true spatiotemporal regulation in vivo. The novelty gap is that existing methods usually deliver either spatial precision without dynamic timing, as in localized promoters or tissue-specific recombinases, or temporal precision without fine positional encoding, as in inducible systems, while apparent exceptions often rely on static tissue boundaries, slow diffusion-limited drugs, or irreversible lineage marking that cannot write transient expression programs during morphogenesis. Our method addresses this gap by placing a target effector gene under a split control architecture: a light-activated CRISPRa module provides millisecond-to-hour temporal gating, while a synthetic untranslated-region switch senses a local developmental cue, such as Wnt, BMP, or Notch activity, to permit translation only where the morphogen state matches a programmable threshold. A degradation tag and self-limiting guide RNA circuit sharpen pulse duration and reduce carryover, allowing repeated on-off cycles rather than one-time activation. The expected advantage is transient, position-specific gene expression that can track moving developmental boundaries, enabling causal tests of timing versus location in tissue patterning with less ectopic expression than current inducible or tissue-specific systems. Feasibility is supported by the modularity of existing CRISPRa, optogenetic dimerizers, RNA sensors, and degron engineering, but the main risk is crosstalk between endogenous signaling noise and the synthetic RNA gate, which could blur spatial selectivity or attenuate output; this is controlled by threshold tuning, orthogonal sensor designs, and dual fluorescent reporters that separate transcriptional activation from translational permission. A minimal convincing benchmark is in zebrafish or gastruloid embryos, where a fluorescent reporter is induced only when both blue-light pulses and a chosen morphogen domain coincide, with success defined by at least threefold higher reporter signal in the targeted spatiotemporal window, boundary leakage below 10%, and reversible shutoff within two hours after stimulation ends.

We propose Context-Latent Safety Tube Control, a control adaptation method that addresses a novelty gap in rapidly changing environments: most existing adaptive controllers either assume slow drift that can be handled by gain scheduling or online identification, or they treat abrupt shifts as generic disturbances, which is a false-positive explanation because the real failure often comes from hidden changes in contact, delay, actuator health, or constraint geometry that alter which model family is valid at all. The core mechanism combines a bank of lightweight local dynamics experts with a latent context switcher that infers, from short recent trajectory fragments, which environment regime is active and how uncertain that assignment is; the controller then solves a receding-horizon objective inside a safety tube whose width expands or contracts according to regime uncertainty, while a meta-update rule only commits parameter adaptation when prediction residuals are persistent and structurally consistent rather than transient noise. This differs from trivial robustification because it does not merely increase margins everywhere, and it differs from standard hybrid control because regime selection is uncertainty-aware and tied to conservative action shaping during ambiguous transitions. The expected advantage is faster recovery after abrupt environmental shifts with less instability and less overconservatism during steady periods, making it feasible for robotics, process control, and autonomous platforms where conditions can change faster than full model relearning. The main risk is mode fragmentation, where the latent switcher overfits spurious contexts and induces unnecessary switching; we control this with dwell-time regularization, residual consistency tests, and a fallback safe expert. A minimal convincing benchmark is a simulated control suite with sudden changes in friction, delay, payload, and actuator saturation, comparing against robust MPC, online system identification MPC, and gain-scheduled control on adaptation latency, cumulative constraint violation, regret after shift, and stability recovery rate.

We propose Reactive-State Twin Assimilation, a multiscale method that quantifies dynamic fluid-rock interactions by coupling time-lapse geophysical sensing, sparse produced-fluid chemistry, and physics-constrained pore-network simulation into a continuously updated digital twin of reactive permeability evolution. The novelty gap is that current recovery models usually treat permeability damage, dissolution, fines migration, and wettability alteration as separable static corrections, which can fit historical production yet fail when reaction fronts reorganize flow paths; our premise explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that more dense monitoring or a larger black-box surrogate alone solves this, because the missing quantity is the hidden state linking mineral alteration to transport connectivity under changing injection chemistry. The core mechanism is a latent reactive-state field that is inferred from streaming pressure, resistivity or seismic attributes, and ion concentrations, while hard constraints enforce mass balance, mineral stoichiometry, and admissible pore-throat topology changes, allowing the model to distinguish true channel opening from sensor drift or pressure-driven redistribution without reaction. Expected impact is better optimization of injection composition and rate, earlier detection of unsustainable breakthrough pathways, and more defensible forecasts of recovery versus geochemical risk in geothermal, carbon storage, or enhanced oil recovery settings. Feasibility is strong because each data source already exists operationally, and the method only requires moderate-resolution core-informed priors rather than exhaustive imaging of the whole reservoir. The main risk is identifiability: multiple reaction mechanisms can produce similar production responses. We therefore calibrate uncertainty with ensemble state estimation and mechanism dropout tests. A minimal convincing benchmark is a meter-scale reactive core-flood or sand-pack network with controlled salinity and pH switching, where success means at least a 30% reduction in forecast error for permeability evolution and breakthrough timing versus static-history-matched reactive transport comparisons.

We propose Adaptive Collateral-Sensitivity Graph Therapy, a platform that designs antibiotic sequences by exploiting evolutionarily stable tradeoffs rather than searching for yet another single drug, addressing a novelty gap in resistance control because most current approaches either optimize immediate bacterial kill, rely on static susceptibility panels, or assume any drug cycling is beneficial, even though many cycling schemes fail once pathogens adapt through cross-resistance or strain-specific trajectories. The core mechanism is to build, for a target pathogen, a probabilistic graph in which nodes are resistance states inferred from longitudinal phenotypes and low-cost genotype markers, and edges encode measured transitions in collateral sensitivity under short antibiotic exposures; a constrained planner then selects two- or three-step treatment schedules that maximize expected bacterial clearance while steering evolution toward states that re-sensitize the organism to older antibiotics and explicitly rejects trivial explanations such as simple class rotation, higher dosing, or rediscovery of known synergistic pairs that do not alter the resistance landscape. The expected advantage is that therapy becomes adaptive to bacterial evolvability itself, potentially extending the useful life of existing antibiotics without requiring de novo compounds, and feasibility is supported by the fact that collateral sensitivity can be measured in standard microbiology workflows and sequence optimization can run on modest clinical data. The main risk is that collateral sensitivity may be unstable across strains, hosts, or biofilm contexts, producing false optimism, so the method calibrates uncertainty by penalizing edges with high inter-isolate variance, requiring robustness across replicate evolution lines, and defaulting to standard of care when confidence is low. A minimal convincing benchmark is an in vitro prospective test on clinical Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates comparing planner-chosen sequences against best single-drug therapy and naive cycling, with success defined as delayed resistance emergence, lower final MICs, and non-inferior short-term bacterial reduction across serial passage experiments.

We propose Provenance-Contrastive Diamond Authentication, a multimodal verification method that distinguishes natural from synthetic diamonds by learning provenance-linked microstructure signatures rather than relying on single spectral cues that are already partially exploitable or vulnerable to treatment-induced false positives. The novelty gap is that most existing approaches treat the problem as direct binary classification from Raman, infrared, fluorescence, or inclusion images alone, which can mistake heat-treated natural stones, lab-grown stones with engineered defects, or low-quality measurements for decisive evidence; our method explicitly rejects these trivial explanations by modeling whether observed signals are jointly consistent with a geologically formed growth history. The core mechanism combines three inputs available in practical grading workflows: hyperspectral luminescence maps, high-magnification inclusion imagery, and polarization-dependent strain patterns. A physics-guided contrastive encoder aligns these modalities into a latent “formation trajectory” space, while a graph-based consistency module checks whether local features co-occur in patterns plausible for natural mantle growth versus HPHT or CVD synthesis. Instead of forcing a hard label on every sample, the system outputs an authenticity score plus a reject option when evidence is sparse, contradictory, or consistent with post-growth treatment, improving trust and valuation decisions by reducing overconfident misclassification. The expected advantage is higher robustness to adversarially engineered synthetic stones and better calibration under real-world measurement noise, while remaining feasible because all sensing modes already exist in advanced gem labs. The main risk is domain shift across labs, instruments, and rare natural stones with atypical defect chemistry. A minimal convincing benchmark would use a multi-lab dataset of certified natural, HPHT, and CVD diamonds, plus treated and ambiguous edge cases, evaluating AUROC, false-authentication rate at fixed high recall, and selective abstention quality, with success defined as materially fewer high-confidence false positives than unimodal comparisons.

We propose EthicsLedger, a counterfactual risk graph for auditing research proposals that targets a novelty gap in current ethical review: most automation efforts either checklist obvious keywords or summarize proposals, which creates false positives on harmless technical language and misses cross-section risks that only emerge when aims, data sources, incentives, and deployment plans interact. The core mechanism converts a proposal into a structured ledger of claims, resources, stakeholder exposures, and governance commitments, then builds a typed graph linking each methodological choice to possible ethical hazards such as hidden human-subject involvement, downstream misuse, inequitable exclusion, undeclared data provenance issues, and incentive misalignment. Instead of scoring risk from surface frequency, the system performs counterfactual consistency tests: it asks whether a flagged concern still holds if a cited safeguard is truly implemented, whether the same concern disappears when a risky dependency is removed, and whether the proposal contains evidence required to justify a low-risk classification. This explicitly rejects trivial explanations like merely mentioning sensitive populations or using generic compliance language. The expected advantage is a narrower but more defensible audit output: fewer noisy alerts, clearer rationale chains, and actionable requests for missing evidence, making review faster without replacing human oversight. Feasibility is strong because proposals already contain the needed semi-structured signals, and the graph can be derived from standard sections rather than requiring new reporting burdens. The main risk is ontology brittleness, where uncommon disciplines or novel methods produce incomplete hazard graphs; to control this, the system marks low-coverage regions and routes them to conservative human review instead of forcing confident predictions. A minimal convincing benchmark is a blinded set of historical and synthetic proposals with expert-annotated concern chains, measuring concern recall, false-alert rate, rationale completeness, and calibration under section ablations, with success defined by higher recall at equal or lower false alerts than checklist and summarization comparisons.

We propose Stratigraphic Counterfactual Radar Parsing, a physics-guided probabilistic interpretation method that addresses a key novelty gap in archaeological Ground Penetrating Radar: most current pipelines either enhance reflections or classify anomalies, but they do not explicitly distinguish culturally meaningful subsurface structures from the many soil layering, root, moisture, and plow-disturbance signatures that create convincing false positives, so apparent progress often comes from better visualization rather than better archaeological discrimination. The core mechanism is to represent each radargram and its neighboring transects as a set of competing latent explanations generated by a lightweight forward radar model: candidate buried features such as walls, pits, ditches, floors, and graves are encoded as geometrically simple priors, while common natural and modern confounds are encoded as alternative counterfactual priors, and Bayesian inference selects interpretations that remain stable across slices, frequencies, and survey directions instead of rewarding any single strong reflector. This makes the scientific move more than routine segmentation, because the system must actively reject trivial explanations and can output calibrated posterior maps showing where the evidence supports an archaeological feature versus where ambiguity remains unresolved. The expected advantage is more trustworthy non-destructive site mapping, especially in noisy or heterogeneous soils where experts now over-interpret isolated hyperbolas or amplitude contrasts. Feasibility is reasonable because the priors can be deliberately simple, using existing survey metadata and small expert-labeled examples rather than massive training corpora. The main risk is model misspecification, where real archaeological forms are more irregular than the priors or local soil physics violates assumptions; to control this, the method should preserve an abstention option and report explanation instability as uncertainty rather than forcing a label. A minimal convincing benchmark would use a small multi-site dataset with known excavation outcomes or tightly constrained legacy maps, comparing false-positive rate, calibration, and feature-boundary overlap against expert reading, amplitude-slice heuristics, and standard learning-based segmentation.

We propose Buoyant Reactive Olivine Microcapsules, a coastal carbon sequestration method that addresses a specific gap in current carbon capture: most scalable options either require energy-intensive plant infrastructure or disperse alkalinity or biomass interventions broadly enough to risk ecological disruption, while many apparent alternatives are false positives because they merely shift carbon between reservoirs, dissolve too fast to be controllable, or depend on unrealistic mining-to-ocean transport economics. The core mechanism is to encapsulate finely ground Mg-rich olivine inside porous, biodegradable hollow microspheres whose shell composition and pore architecture are tuned to keep particles suspended in the upper mixed layer for weeks, where wave-driven motion accelerates controlled weathering and bicarbonate formation, then gradually lose buoyancy and sink once reactivity declines, limiting chronic surface exposure. Each capsule also contains a small iron-binding additive that suppresses trace metal release spikes by co-precipitation, explicitly targeting one of the main ecological objections to enhanced weathering rather than assuming dilution solves it. The expected advantage is high air-sea CO2 uptake efficiency per unit mineral because reaction kinetics are enhanced in turbulent, high-gas-exchange waters without constructing industrial contactors, yet the intervention remains spatially targetable and retrievable during pilot phases using magnetic or fluorescent tracer fractions. Feasibility is supported by existing spray-drying and biopolymer encapsulation processes, but the main risk is that shell degradation, local pH transients, or unforeseen plankton responses could offset sequestration benefits. A minimal convincing benchmark is a mesocosm study comparing encapsulated olivine, free olivine powder, and no-addition controls under identical wave-mixed seawater, with success defined by significantly higher net dissolved inorganic carbon retention per gram, bounded trace metal release, less than 10 percent deviation in plankton productivity from control, and modeled sequestration durability beyond 100 years.

We propose Time-Delay Event Tomography, a streaming lensing method that treats each strongly lensed field as a dynamic causal system rather than a static magnification map, targeting the novelty gap that current gravitational-lensing pipelines recover only time-averaged mass structure and therefore miss short-lived anomalies from microlens caustic crossings, compact-subhalo perturbations, and transient source variability that appear only in relative image timing and morphology. The core mechanism is a hierarchical state-space model coupled to a physics-constrained neural operator: one layer jointly predicts latent source light-curve evolution across multiply imaged sightlines, while a second layer infers temporally localized perturbations to the lens potential by enforcing consistency between image-specific arrival-time residuals, chromatic flux changes, and evolving centroid distortions. False-positive rejection is built in by explicitly modeling intrinsic source transients, atmospheric/systematic cadence artifacts, and detector drift as separate nuisance processes, so the method only flags an event when a perturbation explains cross-image timing structure better than source-only or instrument-only alternatives. The expected advantage is temporal super-resolution of lensing, enabling discovery of transient substructure signatures that static reconstructions average away, with feasible deployment on Rubin, Roman, and high-cadence follow-up streams because the inference can run online on small image cutouts rather than full survey mosaics. The main risk is degeneracy between microlensing by stars and genuine mesoscopic dark-structure perturbations, especially under sparse cadence; we control this by requiring multi-band coherence tests and posterior predictive checks on image-pair delay residuals. A minimal convincing benchmark is a simulated-and-retrospective study on known lensed quasars and supernovae with injected transient potential perturbations, measuring event-detection AUROC, delay-recovery error, and false-alarm rate against static lens models and source-variability-only comparisons, with success defined by materially better transient detection at matched specificity.

We propose Tensorized Phase-Lift Indexing, a data-engineering method that replaces repeated angle-based trigonometric evaluation with a learned but physically constrained lookup-and-refine pipeline for robotic navigation and microscopy streams. The novelty gap is not simply that sine and cosine are computationally expensive, because hardware acceleration and approximation tables already address raw throughput; the unresolved issue is that angle-centric pipelines still propagate discretization error, branch instability near wraparound boundaries, and repeated coordinate re-projection costs when systems must fuse heterogeneous sensor traces under tight latency. Our method rejects the trivial explanation that more calibration alone solves this problem by treating calibration constants as dynamic data products rather than fixed corrections. The core mechanism stores local motion and orientation evidence in a tensorized phase-lift representation that encodes directional state as bounded complex embeddings and local Jacobian summaries, then retrieves candidate transforms through sublinear nearest-neighbor indexing before a lightweight constrained optimizer performs one refinement step without invoking full trigonometric chains. Because the representation is closed under composition and uncertainty tagging, the system can join microscope stage drift updates, inertial increments, and image-registration cues in a common dataflow, reducing repeated transcendental calls while preserving geometric consistency. Expected impact is lower end-to-end latency and improved precision under high-frequency updates, especially in edge cases where conventional angle normalization amplifies jitter. Feasibility is strong because the index can be trained from synthetic trajectories and calibrated with existing logs, while runtime uses standard vector operations and small tables. The main risk is representation bias under out-of-distribution motion or optical distortion, so each retrieved transform carries a confidence residual that triggers fallback to conventional trigonometric estimation when consistency checks fail. Minimal validation is a benchmark on one robotic localization stream and one microscopy drift-correction stream, measuring transform error, latency, fallback rate, and stability near angle wraparound, with success defined as statistically consistent error reduction or equal error at materially lower runtime.

We propose PolicyPulse-SciCast, a real-time scientometrics forecasting framework that fuses streaming signals from preprints, grants, policy documents, conference programs, code repositories, and citation updates to predict which research areas are likely to become strategically important for science policy within the next 6 to 24 months. The novelty gap is not simply that existing scientometrics are slow or descriptive; many already ingest large publication datasets and produce trend maps, but they mostly treat science as a backward-looking citation graph and therefore miss early coordination signals that appear before citations accumulate. Our method explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that adding more data alone solves this problem: the key move is a dynamic multi-layer temporal graph in which papers, investigators, institutions, funding calls, and policy priorities are linked through time-stamped events, while a hazard-style forecasting module estimates whether a topic will cross policy-relevant thresholds such as rapid funding concentration, regulatory attention, or mission-oriented program creation. To reduce false positives from hype cycles, media shocks, or database coverage artifacts, the model separates durable scientific momentum from transient attention by contrasting source-specific lead-lag patterns, estimating uncertainty intervals, and penalizing signals that fail to propagate across independent layers. The expected advantage is actionable early warning for policy agencies, allowing portfolio adjustment before conventional indicators mature, yet the design remains feasible because all inputs are already digitally observable and incrementally updateable. The main risk is that policy salience is partly endogenous to political events rather than scientific development, so forecasts may confuse exogenous agenda shocks with genuine field emergence. A minimal convincing benchmark is a rolling prospective backtest over recent years: using only data available up to each month, predict which topics later receive major funding surges or formal policy attention, and compare lead time, calibration, and false-alarm rate against citation-only trend detection and static topic-model comparisons.

We propose PhaseSwitch-MPC, a dual-timescale control method for biomanufacturing that treats growth-production balance as a reversible state-transition problem rather than a fixed tradeoff. The novelty gap is that most existing strategies either statically optimize media and induction schedules, or enforce hard two-stage growth/production separation, implicitly assuming the burden of product synthesis is predictable and uniform; this is a likely false positive because the main loss often comes from transient, history-dependent metabolic overload, population heterogeneity, and delayed stress responses that make fixed schedules suboptimal even when average kinetics look favorable. Our core mechanism combines a low-order digital twin with online state estimation from inexpensive signals such as oxygen uptake, base addition, substrate concentration, and product proxy measurements, then uses model predictive control to compute short pulse interventions in feed rate, inducer level, and stress-relief cofactor supplementation that keep cells near a controllable production-ready manifold instead of pushing them fully into growth or production extremes. The expected advantage is higher integrated space-time yield with less wasted substrate and fewer nonproductive stress episodes, while remaining feasible because it relies on sensors and actuators already common in fed-batch platforms and a compact model that can be identified from standard runs. The main risk is model mismatch from unobserved intracellular states, clone-to-clone variability, or slow adaptation causing the controller to chase noisy proxies; we address this by embedding confidence bounds, conservative fallback policies, and a penalty on rapid phase switching. A minimal convincing benchmark is a replicated fed-batch comparison against constant-feed and standard two-stage induction comparisons in one burden-sensitive host-product pair, with success defined by at least 15% improvement in final product per carbon input and 10% improvement in viable production time without increased batch failure or byproduct accumulation.

We propose Adaptive Anatomical Twin Tutor, a mixed-reality anatomy learning system that converts low-cost smartphone video of plastic models, textbook plates, or limited cadaver access into a continuously explorable 3D “anatomical twin” linked to misconception-aware tutoring. The novelty gap is not merely that anatomy lacks 3D visualization, since many atlas and VR tools already render organs interactively; the unmet gap is that existing systems usually present fixed expert-built models and assume seeing more geometry automatically improves learning, while they do not infer what structure a learner is confusing, which spatial transformation caused the confusion, or how scarce local teaching materials can be turned into interactive instruction. Our mechanism combines neural pose reconstruction from ordinary classroom captures with a concept graph of anatomical relations and a Bayesian student model that detects likely confusions such as left-right reversal, layer-order mistakes, or vessel-nerve misbinding. The tutor then generates targeted spatial interventions: transparent peeling of overlying tissue, contrastive morphing between neighboring structures, and short retrieval prompts that force the learner to predict orientation before revealing the answer. This is expected to outperform static 2D images and generic VR because feedback is tied to inferred error states rather than passive exploration, while feasibility remains high because the 3D twin is anchored to lightweight scans of already available teaching objects instead of requiring expensive full-fidelity specimen digitization. The main risk is hallucinated geometry or overconfident misconception diagnosis that could teach wrong relations; we control this by restricting reconstruction to confidence-calibrated regions, displaying uncertainty overlays, and falling back to canonical atlas geometry when evidence is weak. A minimal convincing benchmark is a 4-week study in two anatomy modules comparing this system against standard atlas study and ordinary 3D viewer use, with success defined by higher transfer on unseen cross-sectional identification, lower misconception recurrence one week later, and acceptable instructor-rated anatomical fidelity.

We propose NutriRoute Commons, a hyperlocal food-access planning method that couples nutrition-weighted demand mapping with cooperative mobile micro-markets and adaptive pickup hubs for urban food deserts. The novelty gap is that many existing responses assume low access is solved by simply adding a grocery outlet, subsidizing transport, or expanding generic food delivery, yet these are false positives because they often ignore unstable demand, perishability, mistrust of vendors, digital exclusion, and the fact that calorie access does not equal reliable access to culturally acceptable, nutritious food. Our method addresses this unmet gap by estimating block-level nutrition deficits from publicly available demographic, transit, land-use, clinic, and retail data, then using a constrained routing algorithm to place small refrigerated pickup lockers and schedule mobile produce vans through trusted community anchors such as schools, libraries, and clinics. The core mechanism is a joint optimization that maximizes expected nutrient availability per dollar while penalizing stockout risk, walking burden, and mismatch between supply and local food preferences, with a simple paper-voucher fallback so participation does not depend on smartphones or bank cards. Expected impact is higher effective access to fresh foods at lower infrastructure cost than building full stores, while remaining feasible because it reuses existing vans, municipal parcels, and standard cold-chain equipment. The main risk is demand uncertainty causing waste or underuse, especially if modeled need does not translate into actual household uptake; we handle this by conservative uncertainty bounds, phased deployment, and preference calibration from short intercept surveys and redemption data. A minimal convincing benchmark is a six-month pilot across matched neighborhoods comparing NutriRoute Commons against a static farmers-market schedule, with success measured by reduced average walk-time to nutritious food, higher fruit and vegetable purchase redemption, lower stockout-adjusted spoilage, and improved household Healthy Eating Index proxies from repeated surveys.

We propose TrialTrace-Causal, a falsification-detection framework for medical research that targets a specific novelty gap: most current integrity screens rely on generic statistical anomalies, plagiarism signals, or image forensics, which miss semantically consistent fabrication and also flag honest but unusual studies as suspicious. The key idea is to test whether a paper’s reported patient-level or arm-level results are causally reconstructable from its stated protocol, measurement process, enrollment flow, and known clinical constraints. TrialTrace-Causal builds a structured provenance graph from manuscripts, registries, protocols, tables, and supplementary material, then fits a constrained generative model that samples many plausible latent datasets under inclusion criteria, endpoint definitions, adverse-event rates, missingness mechanisms, and site-level heterogeneity. Instead of asking whether numbers merely look rare, the method asks whether the joint pattern of outcomes, subgroup effects, dropout, and timing is compatible with the claimed trial mechanics. To reject trivial false positives, the detector explicitly conditions on small sample size, adaptive designs, strong treatment effects, and specialty-specific biomarkers that can naturally create strange-looking distributions. Its expected advantage is a sharper distinction between legitimate outliers and internally inconsistent evidence, enabling editors, auditors, and sponsors to prioritize cases where reported findings appear impossible to generate without undisclosed manipulation. Feasibility is supported by the increasing availability of trial registries, CONSORT-style reporting, and supplementary appendices that provide enough structure for partial reconstruction. The main risk is under-specification: badly reported but honest studies may appear irreconcilable, while sophisticated falsifiers may imitate plausible generative signatures. A minimal convincing benchmark would combine clean published trials, prospectively blinded synthetic falsification injections, and a small expert-adjudicated set of historical concern cases, with success defined by materially lower false-positive rate than anomaly-only comparisons at matched recall and by calibrated uncertainty scores that defer ambiguous cases rather than over-accuse.

We propose Counterfactual Trace Graphs, a transparency method that explains an AI conclusion by reconstructing the smallest causally sufficient chain of intermediate evidence states and then stress-testing that chain against targeted counterfactual perturbations. The novelty gap is that most current explainability tools either highlight correlated features, produce post hoc rationales that sound plausible without being causally tied to the prediction, or summarize internal attention patterns that do not reliably distinguish genuine reasoning from shortcut behavior; simply making models more verbose or exposing weights does not solve the reliability and bias problem because those signals can still validate spurious pathways. Our mechanism builds a sparse graph linking latent representations, retrieved evidence fragments, and decisive input regions, then searches for a minimal set of nodes whose removal or substitution flips the conclusion while preserving overall input fluency and task semantics. Explanations are returned only when the same graph remains stable under semantically matched paraphrases, demographic attribute swaps, and evidence masking, which creates an explicit rejection step for false-positive explanations that merely co-occur with the output. The expected advantage is a more actionable notion of transparency: users can inspect not only what influenced the decision, but whether the claimed influence is causally necessary and robust to bias-relevant perturbations. Feasibility is reasonable because the method can be layered onto existing multimodal or tabular-text models using logged activations and lightweight graph induction rather than full retraining. The main risk is that the induced graph may oversimplify distributed reasoning or miss redundant pathways, making explanations appear cleaner than the model truly is. A minimal convincing benchmark is to test whether accepted traces predict output flips under held-out counterfactual edits better than attention maps and feature attributions, while also reducing demographic disparity in explanation stability across matched examples.

We propose Hierarchical Transport-Calibrated Atmospheric Deconvolution (HTCAD), a statistical method for planetary atmosphere assessment that closes a key novelty gap: current retrieval pipelines largely treat sparse spectra, in situ probe samples, and atmospheric transport as separable estimation problems, so apparent biosignature or habitability signals can be inflated by unresolved mixing, sampling bias, or instrument-specific artifacts rather than true composition. The central mechanism is a multiscale Bayesian inverse model that couples three layers: a latent compositional field over altitude, latitude, and local time; a transport-consistent stochastic process encoding diffusion, circulation, and photochemical transformation; and a sensor model for heterogeneous observations such as transit spectra, occultation data, and localized probe measurements. Instead of reporting only posterior gas abundances, HTCAD infers composition jointly with a source-attribution score that quantifies whether a claimed atmospheric feature is robust to transport aliasing and cross-instrument mismatch, explicitly rejecting trivial explanations where a single anomalous spectral line, calibration drift, or unrepresentative plume sample would otherwise dominate. The expected advantage is not merely lower error, but better scientific decision quality: habitability assessments become conditional on whether inferred compounds are globally persistent, dynamically plausible, and reproducible across sensing modes. Feasibility is strong because the model can be trained on existing radiative-transfer simulators and run with variational inference or sequential Monte Carlo over moderate-dimensional latent states. The main risk is model misspecification, especially if the transport prior is too rigid for poorly understood atmospheres, which could suppress real anomalies; to control this, the framework includes posterior predictive checks and sensitivity analysis over transport kernels. A minimal convincing benchmark is a synthetic-to-real retrieval study where known atmospheric fields with localized confounds are generated, partially observed through mixed sensors, and evaluated on composition recovery, false biosignature rejection, calibrated uncertainty, and correct ranking of habitability candidates relative to standard independent retrieval comparisons.

We propose Adaptive Cognitive State Matching (ACSM), a personalized learning method that infers a learner’s moment-to-moment cognitive style from short behavioral traces and then assigns micro-interventions matched to that state rather than to broad trait categories. The novelty gap is that most personalization systems either optimize for past performance only or rely on coarse self-report labels such as “visual” versus “verbal,” which often produce false-positive personalization because they mistake preference, motivation, or prior knowledge for a stable mechanism of learning difficulty. ACSM explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that weaker learners merely need more practice or that one content format should dominate for everyone; instead it models hidden bottlenecks such as working-memory overload, slow relational integration, attentional variability, or overconfident retrieval using response time distributions, confidence judgments, brief secondary-task probes, and error transitions during study. Its core mechanism is a lightweight Bayesian state estimator that updates these latent bottlenecks online and chooses among tightly defined interventions such as segmentation, retrieval spacing, contrastive examples, dual-code support, or reduced extraneous load, with a guardrail that prevents switching unless evidence exceeds a reliability threshold. The expected advantage is more mechanistically valid personalization that can improve transfer and retention, not just immediate quiz scores, while remaining feasible because it uses data already collectible in digital learning platforms within a single session. The main risk is misclassifying temporary fatigue or anxiety as enduring cognitive style, producing unstable recommendations; ACSM addresses this by modeling uncertainty explicitly, decaying old evidence, and defaulting to neutral instruction when posterior confidence is low. A minimal validation benchmark is a randomized crossover study in one learning domain comparing ACSM against uniform instruction and performance-only adaptation, with success defined by better delayed retention, better near-transfer, calibrated confidence, and lower variance of benefit across learners.

We propose Civic Evidence Inoculation Networks (CEIN), a community-level intervention that links misinformation correction to locally trusted social structures rather than to generic fact-checking or one-shot science lessons. The novelty gap is that most current responses assume people mainly lack correct information, media exposure, or general critical-thinking skills, but those explanations are often false positives: many individuals can repeat scientific facts yet still reject evidence when it arrives through distrusted institutions, partisan frames, or socially costly public positions. CEIN instead models low science literacy and misinformation resilience as a coordination problem between credibility, identity safety, and evidence interpretation. The core mechanism is a three-part pipeline: first, map neighborhood trust networks to identify cross-cutting messengers such as teachers, nurses, religious volunteers, union leaders, and peer moderators; second, train them with compact evidence translation templates that force claim decomposition into source quality, uncertainty range, and actionable implication; third, deploy synchronized “micro-dialogue cascades” in schools, clinics, community groups, and messaging channels so the same evidence is encountered through multiple trusted ties before false narratives consolidate. The expected advantage is not merely better recall of facts, but stronger transfer from scientific evidence to public decisions because acceptance is scaffolded by social redundancy and uncertainty-aware explanation. Feasibility is high because the method uses existing institutions, short modular training, and lightweight network mapping instead of expensive media campaigns. The main risk is that trust mapping could overfit local elites or amplify hidden polarization, so the design should include diversity constraints and monitor whether message acceptance clusters by faction rather than diffusing across them. A minimal validation benchmark is a prospective field pilot across matched communities, measuring pre-registered changes in misinformation susceptibility, uncertainty calibration, source discrimination, and willingness to revise policy-relevant beliefs after exposure to contested science topics.

We propose Latency-Certified Reconfiguration via Shadow Commodity Potentials, a network reconfiguration method that addresses a specific novelty gap: most large-scale reconfiguration algorithms either optimize topology changes while treating routing as a secondary repair step, or they accelerate routing with heuristics that assume static congestion patterns, so their latency gains often disappear during the transient period when flows, queues, and rule updates interact; this is not simply a matter of insufficient hardware parallelism or larger link capacities, because the persistent failure is a mathematical mismatch between discrete reconfiguration actions and continuous traffic redistribution. Our mechanism introduces a shadow multicommodity flow layer that maintains low-dimensional dual potentials for destination clusters and uses them to score each candidate switch, link, or rule update by predicted downstream latency change under transient congestion, then selects a sequence of reconfiguration moves through a constrained lookahead search with a monotone safety certificate that forbids any step whose worst-case queue growth exceeds a calibrated bound. The expected advantage is that routing and reconfiguration are co-optimized online rather than patched together, reducing packet detours, oscillatory rerouting, and tail-latency spikes while remaining feasible because the dual state is compressed and can be updated incrementally from local traffic counters instead of solving a full multicommodity program each time. The main risk is model misspecification: if destination clustering or queue bounds are too coarse, the controller may become overconservative or mis-rank actions under bursty traffic. A minimal convincing benchmark is a simulator on fat-tree and random regular topologies with nonstationary demand matrices, comparing against shortest-path rerouting, two-phase update schedules, and min-cost reconfiguration heuristics, with success defined by lower 99th-percentile flow completion time and lower transient packet loss at matched reconfiguration budget, while never violating the certified queue-growth threshold.

We propose Disruption-Calibrated Multi-Node Digital Twin Control (DCMDTC), a supply-chain operations method that closes a specific gap left by current visibility dashboards, static optimization tools, and single-firm forecasting systems: they detect disruption signals but do not convert them into coordinated, real-time decisions across suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, and retailers under partially missing and strategically delayed information. The novelty is not merely adding more sensors, faster data, or another reinforcement-learning scheduler, because those are false positives that fail when upstream reports are noisy, substitution options are heterogeneous, and local actors optimize selfishly. Instead, DCMDTC combines a graph-based digital twin of the end-to-end supply network with event-triggered Bayesian belief updates for disruption severity, node-level reliability scoring, and a constrained recourse optimizer that jointly chooses expediting, rerouting, safety-stock repositioning, temporary supplier substitution, and demand-priority rationing. Its core mechanism is a rolling coordination layer that passes probabilistic disruption states and shadow prices across nodes, allowing each participant to act on a shared uncertainty-aware state rather than stale deterministic forecasts. Expected impact is lower stockout propagation and lower overreaction costs than traditional ERP-driven replanning, while remaining feasible because it can be layered onto existing transaction, shipment, and inventory feeds without requiring full data centralization. The main risk is model misspecification or incentive misalignment causing cascading bad recommendations when one node manipulates or delays data; we address this by down-weighting unreliable nodes, stress-testing policies under adversarial missingness, and imposing robust action bounds. A minimal convincing benchmark would simulate a multi-echelon network with supplier outages, port delays, and demand shocks, comparing service level, total cost, recovery time, and bullwhip amplification against static safety-stock rules, myopic rerouting, and deterministic MPC, with success defined as consistent gains under both observed and partially hidden disruptions.

We propose Stroboscopic Physics-Informed Diffractive State Tracking, a real-time X-ray diffraction framework that reconstructs transient phase evolution in electromechanical and electrochemical materials by fusing compressed reciprocal-space measurements with a mechanistic state-space model of lattice distortion, domain switching, and reaction-front propagation. The novelty gap is not simply that existing XRD is too slow, because faster detectors, pump-probe timing, and sparse scanning already exist; the unresolved problem is that these tools still assume either repeatable cyclic dynamics or quasi-static refinement, so they fail when transformations are partially irreversible, spatially heterogeneous, and coupled to voltage, stress, or ion transport. Our method addresses this by deliberately measuring only a small set of adaptively chosen diffraction arcs at each time step, then inferring the hidden microstructural trajectory with a physics-constrained sequential estimator whose latent variables encode phase fractions, strain tensors, texture evolution, and interface velocity, while a control policy reallocates future sampling toward reflections predicted to be most informative under current uncertainty. This mechanism should convert limited photon budget and detector bandwidth into dynamic observability rather than denser but redundant frames, enabling millisecond-scale tracking of non-equilibrium transformations without requiring full-pattern acquisition at every instant. Feasibility is supported by the fact that diffraction kinematics, electrochemical current, and actuator load already provide strong priors that can regularize the inverse problem. The main risk is model bias: if an unmodeled intermediate phase or beam-induced effect appears, the tracker could hallucinate smooth transitions. We therefore include innovation-based anomaly flags and a residual branch that triggers temporary broader-angle scans when predictive confidence and measured peaks disagree. A minimal validation benchmark is to compare our method against full-frame synchrotron XRD on a ferroelectric switching sample or battery cathode undergoing a programmed transient, and require recovery of phase-transition onset time, transient phase fraction, and hysteresis-path differences within predefined error bounds while using at least fivefold fewer measured diffraction points per unit time.

We propose Mineral-Gated Proto-Replication Cycling, a prebiotic systems method in which short, chemically diverse oligomers emerge inside wet-dry microcompartments on redox-active mineral surfaces and are selectively retained only when they jointly accelerate their own fragment capture and re-ligation, addressing the novelty gap left by RNA-world and protein-first models that assume a fully formed informational polymer or catalytic polypeptide already exists. The key move is to replace the search for a single first replicator with a physically coupled network of subcritical fragments, amphiphiles, and mineral-bound cofactors that becomes heritable at the level of cycle dynamics: drying concentrates feedstock, metal sulfide or borate surfaces orient phosphoester, thioester, or mixed anhydride formation, and rehydration releases only those fragment ensembles that regenerate a similar composition after partial breakdown. This explicitly rejects false-positive explanations based on mere passive concentration, crystal templating without compositional inheritance, or transient autocatalysis that cannot survive dilution and environmental resetting. The expected advantage is that replication begins as selection on a mesoscale chemical regime rather than on a rare perfect macromolecule, making the first evolvable system more plausible under heterogeneous early-Earth chemistry while still allowing a later transition to RNA-dominant encoding. Feasibility is strengthened because each component process, compartment cycling, surface catalysis, and oligomer ligation, is individually prebiotically credible, though the main risk is that observed persistence may reflect generic enrichment or mineral adsorption instead of true regenerative inheritance. A minimal validation benchmark is a serial-transfer microfluidic wet-dry experiment seeded with simple activated monomers, fatty acids, and candidate minerals, where success requires at least five disturbance cycles showing reproducible recovery of a specific fragment-composition signature and above-background re-ligation kinetics in descendant compartments after dilution, surface exchange, and partial compositional scrambling controls.

We propose CrackPath-Conditioned Microalloy Design, a fatigue-life optimization method that couples in situ crack-path sensing with graph-based microstructure control to create alloys whose local grain-boundary chemistry and precipitate topology actively deflect, blunt, and slow fatigue cracks under variable loading. The novelty gap is that most current fatigue programs either search composition space for higher average strength, apply generic surface treatments, or fit life-prediction models from coupon data, implicitly assuming that better static properties or larger datasets will translate into longer service life; this is a false positive because many high-strength alloys still fail early once crack initiation localizes along a few vulnerable microstructural corridors, and purely predictive models do not change those corridors. Our method instead learns a crack-vulnerability graph from multimodal microscopy, acoustic emission, and cyclic loading traces, then uses a constrained inverse-design loop to place nanoscale precipitate formers and boundary segregants only where they are predicted to maximize crack tortuosity while preserving manufacturability, weldability, and tensile performance. The expected advantage is not just longer mean fatigue life but reduced life variance across nominally identical parts, which matters directly for aerospace and automotive reliability certification. Feasibility is reasonable because the pipeline relies on existing EBSD/SEM characterization, standard thermodynamic simulations, and alloying additions already used in industrial systems, but recombines them around crack-path control rather than bulk property maximization. The main risk is that the learned vulnerability graph may overfit lab loading spectra or produce interventions that help one stress ratio while harming another, so the design loop includes domain-shift penalties and rejects candidate microstructures that improve life only through trivial hardness increases.
