The novelty gap is that most current approaches treat real-world uncertainty either as noise around a deterministic model, which misses ambiguity in model structure itself, or as fully distribution-free robustness, which often becomes too loose to support useful decisions; our method targets the overlooked middle ground where uncertainty concerns which equations, couplings, or logical dependencies should be trusted in the first place. To reject trivial explanations, we do not merely add stochastic terms, wider confidence intervals, or worst-case bounds to an existing model, because those moves preserve a possibly misspecified structure and therefore cannot distinguish aleatoric variability from structural ambiguity. The core mechanism is to represent candidate model components as weighted constraint modules, infer a sparse posterior over compatible module subsets from partial observations, and compute prediction or optimization outputs as intervals and ranked actions that remain stable across the surviving structures. This should improve decision quality in settings such as planning, control, and resource allocation by exposing when a recommendation is robust to structural doubt and when it is not, while remaining feasible because the sparse module posterior can be approximated with variational updates and branch-and-bound pruning. The main risk is combinatorial blowup or overconservative intervals if too many structures survive; we control this by penalizing redundant modules, calibrating interval width against held-out violations, and forcing abstention when stability is low. A minimal convincing benchmark is a suite of synthetic and semi-synthetic inverse problems with hidden regime switches and missing mechanisms, where success is measured by tighter calibrated intervals, fewer catastrophic decision errors under shift, and better recovery of the true active constraint family than deterministic, Bayesian parametric, and robust-optimization comparisons.

We propose Habitat-Coupled Adaptive Quota Insurance, a fisheries management method that fills a novelty gap left between conventional catch quotas, marine protected areas, and static ecosystem models by explicitly treating habitat degradation and harvest pressure as a jointly managed economic risk rather than two separately regulated problems. The key claim is not the trivial one that stricter limits reduce overfishing, nor the already explored idea of adding more biological covariates to stock assessment, but that regulators can improve both conservation and fishery income stability by linking annual catch rights to a dynamic habitat-recovery index and a contingent insurance transfer. Concretely, each fishery receives a quota schedule generated by a bioeconomic state-space model in which expected future stock growth depends on observed habitat quality, local gear damage intensity, and fleet behavior; when operators adopt verified low-damage practices or temporarily avoid stressed nursery zones, they earn habitat credits that relax future quota cuts and lower their insurance premium, while severe habitat shocks automatically trigger compensating payments tied to precommitted effort reductions. This mechanism should outperform blunt closures because it prices the externality of habitat damage directly, creates a private incentive to preserve recruitment capacity, and reduces political resistance by smoothing short-run income losses. Feasibility is high because the required inputs already exist in fragmented form through satellite vessel tracking, benthic habitat maps, landing records, and periodic ecological surveys. The main risk is measurement error or strategic displacement of effort into unmonitored areas, which could create false gains; to control this, the design uses conservative uncertainty bands, random audits, and no-credit zones where habitat attribution is weak. A minimal benchmark is a retrospective counterfactual on 2 to 3 fisheries with habitat monitoring, comparing stock trajectory, revenue variance, and habitat condition against standard quota and closure policies, with success defined by simultaneous improvement on at least two of the three outcomes without higher collapse risk.

We propose Quantum-Controlled Synthetic Slits, a double-slit architecture in which the slits are not fixed apertures but coherently programmable transmission channels created by an ancilla-controlled matter-wave potential, allowing the same interferometer to move continuously between path-resolved and interference-preserving regimes without rebuilding the apparatus. The novelty gap is that standard double-slit experiments treat slit geometry and which-path measurement as separate, invasive elements, so apparent wave-particle complementarity may partly reflect hardware rigidity rather than the most general measurement design; by contrast, our method tests whether path information can be encoded in a tunable quantum control register before irreversible amplification, explicitly rejecting trivial explanations based on ordinary delayed-choice switching, weak-measurement averaging, or classical slit modulation that merely repackage known tradeoffs. The core mechanism is to couple each effective slit to a distinct ancilla phase state through a fast electro-optic or atom-optic potential, then perform post-interaction readout in selectable ancilla bases, so the experimenter can choose whether the ancilla reveals path distinguishability, erases it, or partially interpolates between them while the underlying propagation remains unchanged. This should expose a finer operational map of complementarity, reveal whether apparent paradoxes are artifacts of fixed measurement boundaries, and provide a platform for testing generalized visibility-distinguishability relations under one calibrated device. Feasibility is supported by existing dynamic beam shaping, quantum erasure, and phase-stable ancilla control technologies, though the main risk is that decoherence or control cross-talk will mimic partial complementarity and falsely suggest new physics. The minimal validation benchmark is a table-top photonic implementation showing, in one apparatus and under matched flux and alignment, continuous, reversible tuning between high-visibility fringes and high which-path predictability, with quantitatively modeled intermediate points and statistically significant exclusion of a classical time-multiplexed modulation model.

We propose PulsePTM-Seq, a time-resolved perturb-and-capture platform that maps causal PTM state transitions in living cells by combining synchronized enzymatic pulse labeling, rapid microfluidic fixation, PTM-selective nanopore peptide reading, and a state-space inference model that reconstructs modification order rather than static abundance alone. The novelty gap is that most PTM tools still provide endpoint inventories or bulk enrichment snapshots, which cannot distinguish whether a modification initiates, propagates, or merely correlates with a signaling event; this is not simply a sensitivity problem, because even deeper proteomics often amplifies false temporal associations caused by asynchronous cells, peptide enrichment bias, or crosstalk between nearby modifications. Our method addresses that gap by delivering a short orthogonal chemical pulse to mark newly accessible substrates immediately before and after a controlled perturbation, then using microfluidic subsecond sampling to preserve transient PTM states and a graph-constrained decoder to infer conditional transition paths across phosphorylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination on the same protein regions. The expected advantage is a shift from descriptive PTM catalogs to dynamic, direction-aware maps of regulatory logic, enabling identification of transient driver modifications that standard workflows would average away. Feasibility is supported by existing components in pulse labeling, microfluidics, nanopore peptide sensing, and Bayesian dynamical modeling, with the key contribution being their integration around dynamic PTM causality. The main risk is sparse or noisy single-molecule PTM reads, especially for low-stoichiometry marks, so the platform explicitly calibrates uncertainty with spike-in phosphopeptide ladders, decoy PTM sites, and posterior confidence thresholds that reject trivial co-occurrence explanations. A minimal convincing benchmark is stimulation of a well-characterized stress pathway in synchronized cells, with success defined by recovering the known early-late ordering for at least two canonical PTMs and correctly predicting one perturbation-sensitive transition validated by targeted mutagenesis or enzyme inhibition.

We propose Resource-Aware Event-Triggered Replanning Graphs (RATER-G), a supply chain optimization method that fills a specific gap between static robust planning and expensive full-horizon re-optimization: existing approaches often treat dynamic replanning as either a faster solver engineering problem or a generic forecasting problem, but that is a false positive because the core failure under unforeseen disruptions is structural, namely that scarce trucks, buffer stock, labor time, and compute budget must be reallocated selectively across a changing dependency network rather than globally recomputed at every event. The mechanism is a hierarchical graph model of suppliers, plants, warehouses, lanes, and demand nodes with two coupled decision layers: an offline layer learns disruption-sensitive slack policies and substitute flow motifs from historical perturbation traces, while an online event-triggered layer performs localized repair by expanding only the subgraph whose feasibility margin collapses after a shock, then solving a constrained recourse problem with explicit budgets on inventory moves, mode switches, overtime, and optimization time. A lightweight uncertainty gate ranks whether an observed event is likely to propagate, so trivial disturbances are absorbed without replanning and severe but contained events trigger bounded regional intervention before they cascade. The expected advantage is materially lower response latency and fewer service failures than full-network rolling optimization under the same limited resources, while remaining feasible because the learned motifs warm-start the recourse solver and keep decisions interpretable for operators. The main risk is myopic localization missing long-range interactions, especially when multiple small disruptions synchronize; this can be controlled by a shadow escalation rule that expands the repair frontier when residual infeasibility or forecast divergence crosses calibrated thresholds. Minimal validation would use a discrete-event benchmark with stochastic supplier outages, transport delays, and demand spikes, comparing service level, total cost, recovery time, and compute time against rolling-horizon MILP and robust comparison policies under fixed emergency budgets.

We propose Climate-Analog Counterfactual Fisheries Inference, a method that learns stock-specific catchability and recruitment dynamics by pairing sparse fishery observations with climate analogs drawn from other regions and years, then testing whether those analogs improve short-horizon management decisions beyond standard interpolation or purely mechanistic stock assessment. The novelty gap is that current responses to data-limited fisheries under climate change usually assume either more monitoring will eventually solve the problem or that transferring ecological knowledge across systems is too noisy to be useful; both are false positives, because many fisheries will remain chronically under-sampled while climate-driven shifts create repeated, partially comparable environmental regimes that can be exploited if transfer is uncertainty-aware and biologically constrained. The core mechanism is a hierarchical state-space model with two coupled layers: a latent population layer for biomass, recruitment, and fishing mortality, and an analog-retrieval layer that selects donor episodes with similar temperature, stratification, productivity, and exploitation context, then borrows only the portions of donor dynamics that pass causal plausibility filters such as life-history similarity and non-overlapping management shocks. Instead of predicting a single stock trajectory, the model outputs counterfactual decision distributions for quotas, closures, or effort caps, which should improve robustness when local time series are short. Its expected impact is more credible adaptive management for small or emerging fisheries facing regime shifts, using already available oceanographic reanalysis, eDNA or survey fragments, and logbook data. The main risk is negative transfer from superficially similar but ecologically mismatched analogs, so the method explicitly downweights analogs under covariate shift and flags low-identifiability cases. A minimal validation benchmark is retrospective management simulation on several historically data-rich stocks artificially thinned to data-poor settings, measuring whether the method better recovers biomass trends and reduces overfishing probability relative to data-limited assessment comparisons and climate-naive transfer models.

We propose Microbiome-Triggered Vitamin Microcapsules, an oral supplement platform that pairs low-dose vitamins with enteric microcapsules engineered to open only when exposed to a user’s characteristic colonic enzyme profile, addressing a novelty gap that is not solved by simply increasing dose, using liposomal delivery, or making generalized time-release tablets, because poor vitamin benefit in real use often arises from person-specific degradation, food-timing variability, and inconsistent intestinal liberation rather than absolute vitamin scarcity alone. The core mechanism is a two-stage capsule: an outer shell protects the payload through stomach acid and proximal small intestine, while an inner polysaccharide-peptide matrix is computationally tuned to be cleaved by a narrow combination of bacterial glycosidases and pH conditions associated with each user’s stool-metagenomic signature, releasing vitamins together with matched absorption cofactors such as emulsifiers for fat-soluble vitamins or transporter-sparing mineral ratios for water-soluble ones. This creates a feasible precision-supplementation approach that could improve effective uptake without requiring unrealistic diet overhaul, because the manufacturing components are extensions of existing microencapsulation and microbiome assay workflows rather than new drug entities. A key false-positive explanation we explicitly reject is that any observed improvement would come merely from higher adherence caused by novelty packaging; to counter this, the regimen keeps dose frequency and capsule appearance identical across arms. The main risk is inter-day microbiome fluctuation causing mistimed release or incomplete liberation, so the design includes conservative trigger windows and a fallback fraction that dissolves conventionally. A minimal convincing benchmark is a randomized crossover pilot in adults with low-normal vitamin D or B12 status comparing standard capsules versus personalized trigger-microcapsules over four weeks each, with success defined by higher isotopically traced fractional absorption, lower between-subject variability, and at least 20% greater improvement in serum biomarker response at matched nominal dose.

We propose Orbital Infrastructure Finance Securitization with Adaptive Milestone Clearing, a financing architecture that lowers the capital and logistics barrier to space station deployment by turning construction and servicing obligations into performance-contingent, tradable mission tranches. The novelty gap is that most proposals treat high cost as a pure engineering-scale problem, implying that cheaper launch, public subsidy, or a single mega-prime contractor will eventually solve deployment; this is a false positive because the binding constraint is the inability to coordinate heterogeneous investors, insurers, launch providers, module manufacturers, and in-orbit service operators under deep technical uncertainty and long settlement horizons. Our method creates a contract graph in which each station subsystem, launch window, docking operation, and resupply commitment is represented as a milestone-verified cash flow claim, while an adaptive clearing algorithm reprices tranche exposure using telemetry-linked progress proofs, cross-contractor dependency risk, and delay contagion estimates. This mechanism should reduce upfront capital concentration, allow phased participation by smaller firms, and align logistical commitments with verifiable readiness rather than fixed calendar promises, making deployment more financeable without assuming unrealistic reductions in hardware cost. Feasibility is supported by the fact that structured project finance, catastrophe-linked securities, and milestone procurement already exist separately, but have not been integrated into a dynamic orbital infrastructure instrument. The main risk is that telemetry or milestone verification could be gamed, or that contract complexity amplifies systemic fragility instead of dampening it; we address this by requiring independent verification nodes, conservative dependency buffers, and automatic tranche freezes when correlated delays exceed calibrated thresholds. A minimal validation benchmark is a simulated multi-module station deployment with historical aerospace delay distributions, comparing our mechanism against fixed-price consortium financing on total required committed capital, contractor participation breadth, schedule slippage, and default cascade frequency.

We propose CarbonLedger-Cal, a locality-aware radiocarbon calibration method that treats carbon-14 variation as an auditable regional accounting system rather than a single global correction curve. The novelty gap is that current practice mainly explains misdating by measurement noise, generic calibration uncertainty, or simple regional offsets, yet these are often false-positive explanations because they ignore locally mixed carbon sources such as marine reservoir input, freshwater hard-water effects, volcanic carbon, and old-wood reuse that can shift apparent ages in structurally different ways. CarbonLedger-Cal builds a hierarchical Bayesian “source-and-sink ledger” for each site or microregion, combining local tree rings, annually laminated sediments, known-age botanical remains, and paired terrestrial-aquatic samples to estimate time-varying contributions from distinct carbon reservoirs under mass-balance and temporal smoothness constraints. Instead of fitting a free local curve that may overfit sparse anchors, the method reconciles multiple proxy streams, flags imbalance events as anomaly periods, and shrinks poorly observed local estimates toward broader regional dynamics, producing calibrated dates with explicit provenance-weighted uncertainty. The expected advantage is better chronological resolution in settings where global curves systematically blur local excursions, while remaining feasible because the required data types already exist for many archaeological and paleoenvironmental contexts and can be integrated incrementally. The main risk is false localization: sparse anchors or unmodeled contamination could make a site-specific correction look real, so the model must include contamination sensitivity terms, leave-one-anchor-out stability checks, and posterior predictive tests that reject local curves unsupported by independent evidence. A minimal convincing benchmark is a multi-site evaluation on historically dated or dendrochronologically anchored samples, comparing calendar-age coverage, interval width, and cross-material consistency against IntCal-only and simple regional-offset comparisons, with success defined as better age coverage and narrower intervals without inflated miscalibration on held-out anchors.

We propose ContextWeave, a community-steered endangered-language preservation method that records and models language as bundles of speech, activity, social role, place, and ritual significance rather than as isolated words or grammar rules. The novelty gap is not simply that existing archives are small or poorly digitized; many already store stories, transcripts, and dictionaries, but they rarely encode when a form is appropriate, who can say it, what co-occurring gesture or object gives it meaning, or how speech choices change across ceremony, childcare, conflict resolution, trade, and ecological practice. This rejects the trivial explanation that more audio or better translation alone would solve preservation, because decontextualized records cannot support culturally valid reuse or transmission. The core mechanism is a situational annotation and retrieval framework that links each utterance to a structured context graph built from speaker-validated metadata: participant relations, material setting, activity sequence, taboo status, emotional stance, and culturally salient nonverbal cues. A lightweight model then learns context-conditioned usage patterns, not to replace speakers, but to surface contrastive examples such as how the same lexical item shifts meaning across kinship or ritual settings, enabling richer teaching materials and safer revitalization support. The expected advantage is preservation of pragmatic competence and cultural grounding, which are often what disappear first when speaker communities shrink. Feasibility comes from combining portable multimodal recording, low-resource annotation, and active-learning suggestions that minimize expert burden. The main risk is false contextual inference, especially where sacred, gendered, or restricted speech is involved; we address this by permission tiers, uncertainty flags, and mandatory community adjudication for sensitive labels. A minimal validation benchmark would compare ContextWeave against a transcript-only archive on two languages, measuring whether community teachers more accurately select context-appropriate utterances for scenario cards and whether learners transfer usage to novel social situations with fewer pragmatically inappropriate responses.

We propose Pulsed HAT-Gated Relay Catalysis, a dual-catalyst electro-photochemical platform for site-selective C–H activation that addresses a genuine gap left by current transition-metal insertion and undirected radical methods: they often succeed only because the substrate already contains a strong directing group, an activated benzylic position, or harsh oxidants that mask poor intrinsic selectivity, so apparent generality is frequently a false positive rather than a solution to inert aliphatic C–H bonds. The core mechanism is to pair a weakly coordinating, recyclable Lewis-acid anchor that transiently organizes the substrate near a photocatalytically generated hydrogen-atom-transfer mediator, while millisecond pulsed electrochemical bias continuously regenerates only the productive mediator oxidation state and suppresses over-oxidation. This creates a relay in which reversible preassociation determines where HAT occurs, but downstream radical capture by a nickel or copper partner rapidly converts the chosen C–H site into C–C or C–N products before scrambling can occur. The expected advantage is that selectivity is encoded by transient microenvironment control rather than permanent directing groups or extreme bond strength differences, enabling late-stage functionalization under milder conditions and with broader substrate compatibility. Feasibility is supported by the fact that each component, reversible Lewis-acid binding, photocatalytic HAT, and electro-regeneration, already exists separately, but has not been integrated as a kinetic gating strategy specifically for inert C–H bonds. The main risk is that substrate preorganization may be too weak to outcompete background HAT, causing diffuse reactivity or catalyst poisoning. A minimal convincing benchmark is a head-to-head test on three substrates containing multiple similar secondary and tertiary aliphatic C–H sites, comparing regioisomer ratio, yield, over-oxidation level, and catalyst turnover against a standard photocatalytic HAT protocol, with success defined as at least 10:1 site selectivity at one otherwise unbiased position, over 50% isolated yield, and substantially reduced byproduct formation under ambient conditions.

We propose ChronoMergerDM, a causally regularized temporal graph inference method that reconstructs galactic evolutionary timelines by fusing stellar-population spectra, resolved kinematics, gas-phase metallicity structure, weak-lensing maps, and environment context into a latent event sequence model explicitly designed to detect merger episodes and dark-matter-driven perturbations. The novelty gap is that current timescale estimators mainly smooth galaxies onto coarse evolutionary tracks or infer ages from isolated observables, which makes transient dynamical events appear as noise and confuses dark matter interactions with ordinary secular evolution, starburst feedback, or projection artifacts; our method rejects these false positives by requiring cross-modal causal consistency, so a putative event must jointly explain spectral age discontinuities, kinematic asymmetries, spatial metallicity offsets, and halo-response signatures rather than any single anomaly. The core mechanism is a Bayesian neural controlled differential equation on a galaxy state graph, where each latent jump corresponds to an interpretable event token such as minor merger, major merger, tidal stripping, or dark subhalo passage, while counterfactual branches test whether simpler explanations can reproduce the same observables with lower event complexity. This should improve precision in evolutionary timescale estimates because event timing is anchored to physically constrained state transitions instead of static template matching, and it remains feasible because all inputs are already available in modern survey combinations and high-resolution simulations. The main risk is model misidentification under sparse or biased observations, especially if feedback-induced disturbances mimic interaction signatures; we control this with simulation-to-observation forward modeling, uncertainty-calibrated posteriors, and explicit abstention when evidence for an event class is not separable. A minimal convincing benchmark is to train on hydrodynamic mock surveys with injected merger and dark-subhalo events, then test whether the method recovers event type and timing more accurately than spectral-only and kinematics-only comparisons, achieving lower calibration error and at least a 20 percent gain in event-time localization within predefined tolerance windows.

We propose Experience-Linked Change Tracing, a data engineering method that creates a real-time feedback loop between code commits and end-user experience by fusing runtime telemetry, UI interaction traces, and code-diff semantics into a continuously updated causal impact graph. The novelty gap is that current observability and APM pipelines mostly stop at service metrics or alerting, while product analytics stop at aggregated behavior, so teams still cannot attribute a specific code change to a measurable degradation in latency, task completion friction, or workflow abandonment with enough precision to act during development; this is not already solved by dashboards, canary releases, or error monitoring because those tools detect anomalies without resolving whether the root cause is the code change itself, a traffic mix shift, or a benign infrastructure fluctuation. The core mechanism is a stream processor that converts each deployment into a structured intervention event, aligns it with fine-grained user-session segments and backend traces, then performs online counterfactual matching against recent comparable sessions and services to estimate a commit-conditioned experience delta, producing developer-facing feedback such as “this refactor increased checkout hesitation after autocomplete by 8% under mobile network variance.” Its expected advantage is earlier, more actionable detection of user harm than offline experimentation, while remaining feasible because it reuses existing logs, traces, and CI metadata rather than requiring new instrumentation everywhere. The main risk is false attribution from hidden confounders such as seasonality, concurrent feature flags, or heterogeneous user cohorts, so the system explicitly withholds high-confidence claims unless stability checks agree across multiple matched comparisons and intervention windows. A minimal validation benchmark would replay several weeks of deployment, telemetry, and user-journey data from a medium-scale web product, compare ranked harmful-change alerts against post hoc incident analyses, and measure top-k precision, median detection delay, and the reduction in engineer triage time versus standard observability workflows.

We propose Equity-Calibrated Palliative Access Compacts, a governance method that links cross-system policy design to local cultural adaptation through a structured package of trigger rules, implementation contracts, and equity audits for end-of-life care. The novelty gap is that most existing reforms assume disparities mainly reflect low funding, general workforce shortages, or diffuse cultural reluctance, then recommend broad expansion of hospice capacity or awareness campaigns; this is a false-positive explanation because unequal access often persists even where services formally exist, owing to misalignment between national entitlements, provider incentives, referral timing, and culturally acceptable decision pathways. Our method treats disparity as a coordination failure across policy, clinic, and family levels. The core mechanism is a compact that requires each jurisdiction to map the patient pathway from diagnosis to final-stage care, identify where disadvantaged groups drop out, and then bind providers and payers to a small set of adaptive rules: automatic palliative consultation triggers for high-risk conditions, protected reimbursement for goals-of-care conversations, community mediator involvement where family-centered decision norms dominate, and quarterly equity audits that compare referral timing, symptom control, place of death, and caregiver burden across social groups. This should outperform generic end-of-life reforms by making implementation fidelity and cultural fit jointly measurable rather than assumed. Feasibility is strong because the compact uses routinely collectable administrative and survey indicators and can be layered onto existing health systems without full institutional redesign. The main risk is that standardized triggers could become box-ticking tools or unintentionally override minority preferences; the design therefore embeds opt-out documentation, community review panels, and disparity monitoring by subgroup. A minimal validation benchmark is a two-region pilot comparing matched hospitals before and after adoption, with success defined by earlier palliative referral, reduced group gaps in pain management and family satisfaction, and no decline in preference-concordant care.

We propose Adaptive Digital Twin Dosimetry, a personalized real-time radiation monitoring method that closes a genuine novelty gap between passive cumulative dosimeters and generic alarm-based wearables by estimating patient-specific biological dose as treatment or exposure unfolds rather than merely reporting ambient radiation after the fact. The key claim is not that more sensors alone solve the problem, because false-positive explanations such as adding a faster badge reader, using population-average correction factors, or displaying raw dose rate on a mobile app still fail to account for anatomy, motion, tissue sensitivity, prior dose history, and changing treatment context. Our mechanism combines a lightweight wearable sensor stream, treatment-device or environmental beam metadata, and a continuously updated patient digital twin that fuses body location, movement, recent cumulative exposure, and individualized radiosensitivity priors into a Bayesian state estimator. The estimator outputs a calibrated personalized effective-dose trajectory with uncertainty bounds and drives closed-loop feedback such as immediate repositioning prompts, adaptive shielding suggestions, or clinician alerts when projected risk exceeds a patient-specific threshold. The expected advantage is earlier and more meaningful intervention: instead of discovering overdosing retrospectively, the system identifies harmful trajectories while they are still preventable, while remaining feasible because the twin can be initialized from standard clinical records and updated with low-cost inertial and dosimetric sensors. The main risk is model misspecification causing overconfident recommendations under unusual anatomy or sensor drift, so the design explicitly carries uncertainty, detects out-of-distribution patterns, and falls back to conservative alarms when confidence degrades. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective phantom-plus-pilot study comparing our personalized online estimates against ground-truth reconstructed dose maps and standard dosimeter readings, with success defined by lower real-time dose estimation error, earlier hazard detection, and fewer missed high-risk exposure events without excessive false alarms.

We propose Museum-in-a-Boxless, a telepresence science museum method that turns ordinary phones and low-cost household objects into synchronized micro-exhibits guided by adaptive curator agents. The novelty gap is that current access solutions for museum education mostly assume the barrier is content distribution, so they offer videos, virtual tours, or static simulations; however, those already-solved formats rarely reproduce the participatory, artifact-linked reasoning that makes museum visits effective, and they fail most for learners constrained by mobility, geography, or repeated access costs. Our method instead treats the missing ingredient as embodied inquiry without physical co-location: each exhibit is redesigned as a “domestic twin” composed of common materials, phone sensors, and computer-vision checks that verify whether a learner’s local setup can instantiate the intended scientific phenomenon. An adaptive agent then sequences observation prompts, predicts likely misconceptions from sensor traces and verbal responses, and dynamically switches between explanation, challenge, and repair moves, while a lightweight telepresence layer optionally connects remote learners to a live museum educator or peer cohort around the same exhibit state. The expected advantage is museum-grade interactivity at near-zero travel cost, with accessibility gains for homebound, rural, and low-income learners, while remaining feasible because it relies on commodity devices and a small library of carefully engineered exhibit twins rather than full VR or robotics. The main risk is that domestic replicas may produce noisy or scientifically weak experiences, especially when households lack required materials or lighting; this is handled by confidence-gated sensing, alternate object substitutions, and fallback “observation-only” modes that explicitly preserve conceptual integrity instead of pretending equivalence. A minimal validation benchmark would compare this system against standard virtual museum videos in a three-exhibit pilot, measuring concept gain, misconception correction, engagement persistence, and successful exhibit completion across geographically constrained learners, with success defined as higher post-test gains and completion without increased facilitator time.

We propose TerrainTwin-Guidance, a rover-drone cooperative mapping and prescription system that builds centimeter-scale field terrain twins for precision agriculture by fusing low-altitude multispectral drone imagery, wheel-slip-aware ground rover inertial sensing, and sparse soil-moisture probes into a physics-regularized elevation and trafficability graph. The novelty gap is not merely that farms need better maps, because satellite DEMs, RTK guidance, and standard UAV photogrammetry already exist; the unmet gap is a field-operational method that resolves microtopography, wetness-driven sink zones, and passability changes at the scale where irrigation runoff, fertilizer pooling, and machine path errors actually occur, while explicitly rejecting the trivial explanation that denser imagery alone solves guidance, since photogrammetry often fails over crop canopy, reflective water patches, and repeated textures. The core mechanism is a cross-view graph neural estimator constrained by shallow-water flow and vehicle terramechanics priors: drone images infer surface shape candidates, rover dynamics identify hidden slope and compaction cues beneath partial canopy, and the model outputs both a high-resolution terrain map and uncertainty-aware action layers for variable-rate input placement and low-slip machinery routing. Expected impact is reduced over-application of water and fertilizer on convex ridges and avoidance of rut-forming wet depressions, improving input efficiency without requiring expensive full-field LiDAR. Feasibility is supported by currently available UAVs, compact rovers, and low-cost RTK modules. The main risk is domain shift across soil textures, crop stages, and residue cover, which could create overconfident but wrong traversability estimates; to control this, the method predicts calibrated uncertainty and falls back to conservative guidance when confidence is low. A minimal convincing benchmark is a multi-plot field trial comparing against RTK plus UAV photogrammetry and terrain-only routing, with success defined by lower elevation error, better wet-zone detection, fewer guidance deviations, and reduced input waste per hectare.

We propose VectorTag-LAMP, a field-deployable diagnostic that couples host-response microRNA fingerprinting with pathogen-family barcoded isothermal amplification on a disposable paper microfluidic chip to identify active vectorborne infection at the point of care. The novelty gap is that most rapid tests either detect a single known pathogen with brittle specificity or infer infection from nonspecific fever markers, so they fail when patients present early, have low pathogen load, or are exposed in regions where dengue, malaria, chikungunya, Zika, rickettsial disease, and arboviruses overlap; this is not solved by simply miniaturizing PCR or adding another antigen strip because cross-reactive antibodies and transient viremia still drive false positives and missed mixed infections. Our method addresses this by jointly reading two orthogonal signals: a compact panel of host microRNAs associated with acute endothelial injury and interferon programs seen in vectorborne infection, and a multiplex reverse-transcription LAMP panel targeting conserved but discriminative genomic anchors from several pathogen families, with a small on-phone model performing constrained fusion so a positive call requires mechanistic agreement between host-state and pathogen-family evidence. Expected impact is faster on-site triage, earlier outbreak mapping, and actionable referral without central lab dependence, while feasibility is supported by mature LAMP chemistry, paperfluidics, low-cost smartphone imaging, and existing microRNA extraction shortcuts compatible with capillary blood. The main risk is confounding from non-vectorborne febrile illnesses or prior exposure, especially where inflammation profiles overlap, so the fusion model explicitly includes an abstain class, contamination controls, and calibration against malaria-negative bacterial and viral febrile controls rather than only healthy donors. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective multisite study on finger-prick samples from 250 acute febrile patients, testing whether VectorTag-LAMP achieves at least 0.88 macro-AUROC, under 30 minutes turnaround, and fewer false positives than single-signal rapid assays against centralized PCR and clinician-adjudicated diagnosis.

We propose Causal Trace Cards, a transparency method for AI models that learns compact, testable causal summaries of internal reasoning instead of relying on post hoc free-text explanations or attention heatmaps, which often look plausible without reflecting the real decision process. The novelty gap is that many current transparency approaches either expose raw internals that humans cannot interpret, or generate verbal rationales that may be faithful only by coincidence; our method explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that better wording alone creates understanding by requiring every explanation unit to correspond to a measurable intervention on the model’s computation. Concretely, the method segments a model’s forward pass into latent reasoning steps, then fits a sparse graph of concept-level variables, evidence transfers, and confidence updates whose edges are retained only if targeted activation patching or feature ablation produces the predicted downstream change. Each prediction is returned with a Trace Card: a short causal chain, a confidence interval over its faithfulness, and a counterfactual statement describing what evidence would have changed the output. The expected advantage is transparency that is simultaneously human-readable, mechanistically anchored, and comparable across examples, making it more useful for debugging, auditing, and scientific analysis than descriptive rationales. Feasibility is supported by existing tools for representation probing, sparse autoencoding, and activation intervention, but the main risk is that the extracted concepts may be unstable or fragmented across inputs, yielding explanations that are locally faithful yet globally inconsistent. To control this, we impose cross-instance stability regularization and report uncertainty when the same concept cannot be recovered reliably. A minimal validation benchmark would compare Trace Cards against standard rationales on a dataset with known evidence structure, measuring intervention faithfulness, counterfactual accuracy, and human task performance in error localization, with success defined by substantially higher causal faithfulness without large loss in predictive accuracy.

We propose Bayesian Sentinel Streams, a fixed-sensor statistical monitoring method that detects water contamination events by fusing high-frequency proxy signals such as conductivity, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature, and flow into an online causal residual model with false-alarm rejection. The novelty gap is that most existing monitoring pipelines either depend on sparse manual grab samples and lab assays, which are too delayed for fast response, or on simple threshold alarms from in situ sensors, which are already known to be brittle because storms, diurnal cycles, maintenance drift, and seasonal hydrology can mimic contamination. Our method explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that more sensors or lower thresholds alone solve the problem: the unmet need is a statistically calibrated detector that distinguishes anomalous pollutant signatures from normal but abrupt environmental variation. The core mechanism is a hierarchical state-space model that learns site-specific comparison dynamics and cross-sensor dependence, then computes real-time posterior predictive residuals; a contamination alarm is triggered only when multivariate residual trajectories match a learned contamination shape prior while remaining inconsistent with weather-driven and flow-driven nuisance patterns. To improve feasibility, the model is designed for fixed installations and weak supervision from historical lab-confirmed incidents, simulated injection profiles, and routine non-event periods, allowing deployment without dense labels. The expected advantage is earlier warning with fewer false positives, enabling targeted confirmatory sampling and faster mitigation rather than blanket manual testing. The main risk is covariate shift, especially rare contamination chemistries or sensor fouling that produce unfamiliar signatures, so the system includes uncertainty inflation, abstention regions, and drift flags that route cases to manual review. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective or replay study across several monitoring sites comparing detection delay, false alarms per month, and event recall against threshold rules and standard control charts, with success defined by materially earlier detection at matched false-positive rates.

We propose Autobiographical Loci Distillation, a memory-palace construction method that replaces generic imagined buildings with a compact set of personally verified, emotionally moderate, and spatially distinctive locations drawn from a participant’s own routine life. The novelty gap is that prior mnemonic systems largely assume any vivid palace is sufficient, so poor performance is often dismissed as low effort, weak imagery, or lack of training; however, this is a false-positive explanation because generic palaces may fail even for motivated users when the scene lacks self-referential structure, retrieval cues tied to lived navigation, and stable contextual priors. Our core mechanism is to elicit a large pool of autobiographical places, score each candidate on familiarity, route stability, emotional valence, semantic richness, and interference with other memories, then algorithmically select loci that maximize distinctiveness while avoiding highly emotional or repetitive settings. Each target item is bound not just to a location but to a personal micro-event schema, such as where one usually hesitates, reaches, or turns, so encoding exploits sensorimotor prediction and self-memory integration rather than imagery alone. The expected advantage is higher recall durability and lower training burden because the user reuses already consolidated spatial models instead of learning arbitrary architecture. Feasibility is high because the method needs only structured self-report, simple ranking, and brief guided encoding. The main risk is that autobiographical cues could trigger distraction, mood-congruent intrusions, or excessive overlap between similar places; the method therefore excludes high-arousal memories and penalizes confusable routes. A minimal validation benchmark is a randomized within-subject study comparing generic palaces, freely chosen personal palaces, and Autobiographical Loci Distillation on immediate recall, one-week delayed recall, intrusion rate, and setup time, with success defined as significantly better delayed recall and equal or lower intrusion without increased preparation burden.

We propose Latent Social Micro-Interaction Reconstruction, a multimodal observational framework that infers fine-grained social acts in animal groups by jointly modeling short-lived body orientation shifts, approach-retreat asymmetries, gaze proxies, spacing fluctuations, and context-dependent vocal or movement microbursts that standard ethology pipelines usually compress into coarse contact or proximity events. The novelty gap is not merely that current data collection is sparse, because adding more cameras or higher frame rates alone does not recover nuanced affiliative, coercive, or deceptive exchanges when annotation schemes remain behaviorally blunt; likewise, existing pose-tracking systems mainly improve individual localization and therefore can falsely appear sufficient while still missing relational intent. Our method treats social interaction as a latent sequence of micro-states between dyads and triads, learned with a graph neural state-space model that fuses asynchronous video, audio, and wearable or positional streams, then constrains inferred states using ethological priors such as reciprocity timing, dominance consistency, and impossible-transition rejection. This mechanism is expected to reveal interaction motifs that are invisible to proximity thresholds, improve cross-observer consistency, and generate interpretable social episode summaries without requiring exhaustive manual coding. Feasibility is strong because the system can operate on modest multimodal recordings and a small seed set of expert-labeled interaction clips, then expand through uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling. The main risk is that latent states may absorb environmental coincidence, sensor occlusion, or species-specific movement stereotypes rather than true social meaning; we address this by confidence calibration, counterfactual ablations removing non-social context cues, and held-out testing across enclosures or subgroups. A minimal convincing benchmark would compare this method against proximity-only and pose-only comparisons on a curated dataset of manually coded subtle interactions, with success defined by higher event-level F1, better cross-context generalization, and earlier detection of socially meaningful episodes before overt contact occurs.

We propose Conflict-Profile Guided Branch-and-Cut with Certified Neighborhood Compression, a method for large-scale integer programs that targets a novelty gap between generic machine-learned branching heuristics and classical decomposition: existing accelerations often either overfit solver traces, merely reweight known cuts, or assume separable block structure, so they fail when constraint interactions are dense, heterogeneous, and globally coupled; our idea explicitly rejects the false-positive explanation that large instances are hard only because current cut pools are too small or node selection is suboptimal. The core mechanism is to construct an online conflict profile graph whose nodes are variables and constraints and whose edges summarize observed integrality conflicts, dual degeneracy, and repeated LP basis instability during the early search. This graph is used to identify a small set of certified interaction neighborhoods, and for each neighborhood the solver solves a compressed local integer subproblem to generate composite branching objects and bundled cuts that preserve globally valid implications while avoiding full problem decomposition. These neighborhood objects are injected only when they reduce a proof-based surrogate of downstream tree entropy, so the intervention is selective rather than always-on. The expected advantage is a sharper reduction in search tree size on instances where useful structure is hidden in overlapping local couplings that standard cuts or branching scores treat independently, while remaining feasible because conflict profiles can be updated from information already produced by modern branch-and-cut solvers. The main risk is that the learned neighborhoods become noisy and produce expensive local subproblems with little global payoff; to control this, we cap neighborhood diameter, require validity certificates for bundled cuts, and disable the module when early entropy reduction fails to exceed a fixed threshold. A minimal convincing benchmark is to compare against a strong commercial-style comparison on large MIPLIB-style set covering, scheduling, and facility-location families, measuring time-to-first-feasible, final optimality gap under a fixed time budget, and search-tree nodes, with success defined as consistent node reductions and wall-clock gains on at least two structurally distinct families.

We propose Adaptive Spectrum Leasing Wave Farms, a hybrid techno-economic control method that couples tunable wave energy converters with a market-layer optimizer that leases incoming wave-frequency bands across heterogeneous devices in real time. The novelty gap is that most prior work treats the narrow-band efficiency problem as either a pure mechanical tuning issue or a device-design limitation, implicitly assuming each converter must individually broaden its capture width; that is likely a false positive because broad-band hardware often becomes too costly, lossy, or maintenance-intensive, while resource smoothing by geographic diversification alone does not solve local spectral mismatch at the farm level. Our method instead views the wave spectrum as an allocable economic resource: a farm is built from several lower-cost converters with partially overlapping resonance ranges, each equipped with modest stiffness, damping, or PTO retuning, and a controller assigns devices to the most profitable spectral slices given forecasted sea states, degradation costs, and grid-price signals. The mechanism combines short-horizon spectral forecasting, convex dispatch over converter operating envelopes, and a degradation-aware switching penalty so gains do not come from unrealistic retuning frequency. Expected impact is higher annual energy yield and lower levelized cost without requiring every unit to become broadband, making deployment more feasible in mixed sea states and secondary markets. The main risk is that forecast error, hydrodynamic coupling, and actuator wear could erase theoretical gains, especially if real spectra shift faster than practical retuning can follow. A minimal validation benchmark would compare this farm-level spectrum-leasing controller against fixed-tuned converters and independently retuned converters in a wave-tank or high-fidelity digital twin using measured irregular spectra, with success defined by statistically significant improvement in annualized capture efficiency per capital dollar, bounded switching frequency, and no increase in modeled maintenance cost beyond a preset threshold.

We propose ThermoTopochem, a cascade thermal storage architecture that couples a metastability-tuned phase-change matrix with reversible gas-solid chemisorption microcapsules and model-predictive charge routing to store renewable heat across daily and multi-day timescales. The novelty gap is not simply that thermal storage lacks higher capacity materials, because many candidate phase-change and thermochemical media already exist; the unmet problem is that systems optimized for energy density usually sacrifice cycling speed, thermal conductivity, or dispatch flexibility, while fast sensible-heat tanks remain too bulky for long-duration renewable balancing. ThermoTopochem rejects the trivial explanation that better insulation alone solves this, since standing losses are only one bottleneck and do not address the mismatch between short, volatile charging windows and variable discharge temperatures. The core mechanism is a hierarchical bed in which a conductive graphite-foam scaffold hosts phase-change domains for rapid heat capture, while embedded microcapsules containing a reversible ammonia-free salt-hydrate sorbent absorb excess heat into a chemically stored state when the melt fraction saturates; a controller routes heat between the two subsystems to minimize exergy destruction and maintain outlet temperature quality. Expected advantage is simultaneously higher usable energy density, faster round-trip thermal response, and flatter discharge temperature than either subsystem alone, using materials and fabrication routes compatible with current encapsulation and packed-bed manufacturing. The main risk is interfacial degradation: repeated volume change, vapor transport limits, or side reactions could decouple the fast and long-duration modes and cause apparent gains that vanish over cycling. A minimal validation benchmark is a 1-5 kWhth lab module cycled under realistic solar-curtailed charging pulses and industrial-process-heat discharge demands, with success defined by at least 30% higher usable exergy density than a matched latent-heat comparison, 500 stable cycles with less than 10% capacity fade, and discharge temperature control within plus or minus 5 C.

We propose MycoPatch, a modular desertification-reversal method that pairs locally sourced biodegradable microcatchment mats with drought-tuned microbial and cryptobiotic soil consortia chosen by a causal site-matching algorithm. The novelty gap is that many restoration programs already use seeding, mulch, biochar, or irrigation support, but they often treat degraded drylands as a generic water-limitation problem; this creates false positives because short-term greening can come from rare rain pulses or fertilizer effects without rebuilding infiltration, aggregate stability, or native recruitment. MycoPatch explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that “more planting density” or “more amendments” alone solves desertification, and instead targets the coupled failure of surface crusting, seed loss, and soil-biota collapse that keeps landscapes locked in a degraded state. Its core mechanism is a low-cost hexagonal mat that traps runoff, reduces wind erosion, and slowly releases a tailored inoculum of arbuscular mycorrhizae, cyanobacteria, and drought-resilient rhizobacteria, while a lightweight selection model matches inoculum composition to soil texture, salinity, rainfall variability, and remnant vegetation so that intervention is adaptive rather than one-size-fits-all. The expected advantage is scalable restoration with fewer water inputs, higher seedling establishment, and more durable recovery of soil function than planting-only approaches, using manufacturable materials and organisms already present in regional drylands. The main risk is ecological mismatch or unintended microbial competition that suppresses native succession, especially under highly saline or heavily grazed conditions; to calibrate this, the method includes exclusion rules for incompatible sites, native-only inoculum sourcing, and early failure indicators based on infiltration and crust integrity rather than greenness alone. A minimal convincing benchmark is a one-season replicated field trial across three degradation classes comparing MycoPatch against seed-only and mulch-only controls, with success defined by statistically meaningful gains in infiltration rate, soil aggregate stability, native seedling survival, and reduced bare-ground expansion after rainfall events.

We propose ThermoSplit-MPC, a fuel-cell balance-of-plant control method that treats waste heat not as a passive byproduct to be removed, but as a dynamically allocable resource that can be redirected in real time across membrane hydration, inlet reactant conditioning, and a compact bottoming thermoelectric stage. The novelty gap is that most efficiency work either improves stack materials or adds fixed heat-recovery hardware, implicitly assuming heat losses are spatially and temporally uniform; this is a false-positive simplification because transient load changes, local dehydration, and cathode flooding make the same joule of heat beneficial in one subsystem and harmful in another. ThermoSplit-MPC closes this gap by combining a reduced-order digital twin of stack electrochemistry and thermal transport with model-predictive control over microvalves, bypass channels, and phase-change microbuffers that store and release heat on short horizons. Instead of merely cooling hot zones, the controller estimates the marginal efficiency gain of sending recovered heat toward membrane temperature stabilization, fuel humidification, or low-grade power scavenging, then selects the allocation that maximizes net electrical efficiency minus parasitic pumping and control costs. The expected advantage is a measurable improvement in part-load and transient efficiency, where conventional fixed heat exchangers underperform, while remaining feasible because it relies on sensors and actuators already near commercial balance-of-plant complexity. The main risk is model mismatch: poorly estimated local water-heat coupling could shift the system toward flooding or membrane dry-out, so the controller includes conservative safety envelopes, online parameter adaptation, and fallback rules that revert to standard thermal management when confidence drops. A minimal convincing benchmark is a hardware-in-the-loop PEM fuel-cell testbed with scripted drive-cycle load profiles, comparing comparison thermal control against ThermoSplit-MPC on net system efficiency, parasitic power, cell voltage uniformity, membrane hydration stability, and usable recovered heat, with success defined as at least 3% relative efficiency gain without increased degradation proxies.

We propose Tidal-Seismic Magnetogravity Inversion (TSMI), a cross-moon inference framework that reconstructs subsurface ocean geometry, ice shell thickness, and active interior energy pathways in outer solar system moons by jointly assimilating time-variable magnetic induction, gravity harmonics, libration, plume chemistry, and sparse passive seismic signals into a physics-constrained Bayesian digital twin. The novelty gap is that current studies usually infer habitability proxies from one modality at a time, which leaves a false-positive regime where conductive salty oceans, warm but stagnant ice shells, or plume-fed local pockets can each mimic signs of a globally habitable ocean world; TSMI explicitly rejects these trivial explanations by requiring consistency between tidal dissipation patterns, phase-lagged induction response, flexural shell mechanics, and chemically plausible transport from rock-water interaction zones to the surface. The core mechanism is a hierarchical inversion that couples orbital forcing, viscoelastic shell deformation, electroconductive ocean response, and fracture-mediated venting, while allowing moon-specific priors so Europa, Enceladus, Titan, and Ganymede can inform one another without forcing identical interiors. The expected advantage is that geologic activity and habitability become testable structural hypotheses rather than isolated signatures, improving mission targeting for landers, flybys, and seismic payload placement with feasible use of datasets already planned or partially available. The main risk is structural non-identifiability, especially if multiple deep models fit the same sparse measurements, plus confounds from magnetospheric variability and transient plume behavior; we control this by posterior predictive checks against withheld observables, synthetic perturbation tests, and explicit model comparison between global-ocean, regional-brine, and dry-warm-shell alternatives. A minimal validation benchmark is a blind synthetic-to-real study showing that TSMI recovers known interior parameters within uncertainty on simulated missions and then predicts one withheld observable, such as induction phase or plume composition trend, better than single-modality comparisons by a statistically credible margin.

We propose AcidLock Mosaic Microparticles, an oral drug delivery platform that combines an acid-tight transient shell with inflammation-triggered site unlocking to protect fragile therapeutics in the stomach and release them only at diseased intestinal or colonic tissue. The novelty gap is that many existing systems solve only one half of the problem: enteric coatings survive gastric acid but release broadly based on pH transition alone, while ligand-targeted carriers often lose payload or targeting function before reaching the target site; this is not a trivial formulation-tuning issue because premature leakage, mucus trapping, and off-target release remain common even when standard polymers and ligands are optimized. Our mechanism is a two-layer particle in which a dense hydrogen-bonded tannic acid-chitosan outer shell is further mineralized with a thin calcium-phosphate mosaic to resist low pH, while the inner depot contains drug-loaded nanoparticles tethered by reactive-oxygen-species-cleavable linkers and decorated with a mucus-penetrating zwitterionic brush plus a secondary disease-site adhesion peptide exposed only after shell dissolution in the distal gut. This creates a sequential logic gate: survive acid, pass mucus with minimal sticking, then activate local retention and payload release only where inflammatory oxidative chemistry is elevated. The expected advantage is higher effective local concentration with reduced systemic exposure and reduced dose loss in transit, using materials and fabrication steps that are already individually feasible. The main risk is biological heterogeneity, especially if oxidative triggers vary across patients or if the shell dissolves too late, causing under-release. A minimal convincing benchmark is a three-stage test comparing this system against standard enteric microparticles and always-on targeted particles: less than 10% cargo release after 2 hours in simulated gastric fluid, greater than 70% triggered release in inflamed-intestine-mimicking media within 6 hours, at least 2-fold higher retention on inflamed versus healthy intestinal organoids, and superior local drug efficacy in a murine colitis model without increased systemic drug levels.

We propose CanopyAdvance, a pre-carbon financing method that converts early agroforestry biophysical signals into tradable, risk-tiered transition claims so farmers can receive cash within one season rather than waiting years for conventional credit issuance. The novelty gap is not merely that farmers lack credit access or insurers already solve the problem; those are false positives because generic loans ignore plot-level carbon uncertainty, and standard carbon forward contracts still depend on slow, expensive verification designed for mature sequestration. Our method instead defines a new asset class tied to near-term indicators that are observable long before full carbon accrual, such as survival-adjusted sapling density, species mix, soil moisture trajectory, and geolocated management events. A Bayesian monitoring engine fuses satellite time series, low-cost phone photos, local weather, and sparse field audits to estimate the probability distribution of future verified carbon delivery for each plot cohort, then issues only a conservative tranche of transition claims priced with uncertainty haircuts and automatic reserve buffers. Buyers fund these claims because they obtain discounted priority access to future certified credits plus auditable environmental optionality, while farmers gain immediate liquidity for labor and maintenance, improving adoption and reducing early abandonment. The main risk is that early proxies may be gamed or may correlate weakly with long-run sequestration under drought, species failure, or land-use reversal, so the system uses random audit escalation, fraud-sensitive image consistency checks, weather-normalized priors, and dynamic caps that shrink issuance when posterior uncertainty widens. A minimal validation benchmark would pilot the method on 150 to 300 farms across two agroecological zones, testing whether first-year financing speed, farmer retention, and prediction calibration of three-year verified carbon outcomes outperform a conventional ex post credit pathway, with success defined by materially earlier payouts, lower default-adjusted over-issuance, and acceptable monitoring cost per hectare.

We propose LedgerTwin-PFC, an accounting-aware digital-twin method that treats data-center power-converter losses not as a purely hardware efficiency problem but as a continuously auditable cost-allocation and control problem, addressing a novelty gap left by prior work that optimizes converter topology or cooling in isolation while assuming stable load composition, uniform power quality, or easily observable loss sources. That assumption is a likely false positive: much of the avoidable waste arises from transient, tenant-specific, and rack-specific workload patterns that conventional facility accounting collapses into coarse aggregate energy reports, making it impossible to identify which converter stages, operating modes, and business activities jointly drive losses. Our method builds a hierarchical loss ledger that fuses high-frequency telemetry from UPS, rectifiers, DC-DC stages, and rack PDUs with workload and financial attribution data, then fits a physics-informed state-space model that separates comparison conversion loss, harmonic-induced excess loss, and ramping-related switching loss under changing utilization. A constrained control layer uses these decomposed estimates to recommend phase balancing, converter mode scheduling, and workload placement shifts that minimize marginal loss per accounting unit of service rather than only total power. The expected advantage is that operators gain both lower energy waste and a defensible audit trail linking efficiency actions to cost centers, enabling interventions that are financially actionable instead of technically generic. Feasibility is high because the method uses instrumentation already present in many enterprise facilities plus lightweight additional metering at selected feeders. The main risk is confounding from unobserved thermal effects or delayed load interactions that could misattribute losses; we control this with counterfactual residual checks, uncertainty bands, and holdout periods during topology-stable operations. A minimal validation benchmark would compare LedgerTwin-PFC against aggregate-PUE monitoring and static efficiency curves on one instrumented hall, with success defined by significantly better loss-source attribution accuracy and at least a measurable reduction in converter losses during controlled rebalancing trials.

We propose Reciprocity-Aware Ethnobotanical Knowledge Graph Discovery, a method that addresses the novelty gap that current plant knowledge cataloguing is either a shallow digitization of scattered ethnographies or a purely biochemical search pipeline, neither of which can reliably preserve cultural meaning, reject already-solved documentation claims, or identify medicinal hypotheses grounded in indigenous use-context. The core mechanism links three layers: multilingual extraction of plant-use narratives from community-approved archives and oral-history transcripts, a knowledge graph that encodes plant part, preparation, ailment category, ecology, seasonality, and ritual or social context, and a reciprocity-aware inference module that separates transferable therapeutic signals from culturally specific practices that should not be decontextualized. This rejects false positives such as assuming that any frequently mentioned plant is medicinally promising, or that generic text similarity across cultures implies the same pharmacological action; instead, candidate discoveries must show convergent use patterns across partially independent traditions while remaining ecologically and symptomatically coherent. Expected impact is a more defensible map of undercatalogued medicinal leads that simultaneously supports conservation prioritization and community-controlled heritage protection, because the system can flag culturally sensitive knowledge for restricted handling rather than maximizing extraction. Feasibility is high because the first version can operate on existing digitized ethnobotanical texts plus a small number of consented oral-history collections, using expert-in-the-loop ontology alignment instead of requiring massive labeled data. The main risk is overfitting to colonial-era documentation biases or mistranslating indigenous disease concepts; we control this through uncertainty tags, source provenance weighting, and abstention when semantic alignment is weak. A minimal validation benchmark would compare this method against frequency-based and standard retrieval comparisons on a curated cross-cultural dataset, measuring whether blinded ethnobotanists judge the top ranked plant-use hypotheses as more novel, context-faithful, and pharmacologically plausible, while also verifying correct sensitivity labeling for restricted knowledge.

We propose Solar-Swelling Imprinted Heterojunction Beads, a visible-light photocatalyst architecture in which red-light-absorbing carbon nitride nanosheets and copper single-atom oxidative sites are immobilized inside a hydrophilic, lightly crosslinked molecularly imprinted polymer shell that preferentially sorbs oxidized polyethylene and polystyrene oligomers while swelling at the particle-water interface. The novelty gap is not simply that UV-dependent catalysts need bandgap tuning, because many visible-light materials already generate reactive oxygen species yet still fail on real microplastics due to poor contact, buoyancy mismatch, and rapid quenching in natural water; likewise, merely grinding plastics smaller or adding surfactants is a false solution because it increases dispersal without mineralization. Our mechanism instead couples three functions in one recoverable bead: interfacial enrichment of weathered microplastics by imprint-guided adsorption, localized swelling that traps oxygen and polymer fragments near catalytic hotspots, and a Z-scheme-like charge separation between carbon nitride and an iron oxyhydroxide subdomain that biases formation of singlet oxygen and surface-bound holes under sunlight rather than nonselective hydroxyl radicals. The expected advantage is practical solar activity in turbid surface waters, reduced need for UV lamps, and higher apparent degradation because photon use is spent where polymer chains actually reside rather than in bulk water. Feasibility is supported by existing syntheses of imprinted hydrogels, visible-light carbon nitride, and single-atom copper motifs, combined here in a contact-engineering framework rather than a purely bandgap-engineering one. The main risk is that adsorption may favor only pre-weathered plastics and that dissolved organic matter could outcompete the polymer shell. A minimal validation benchmark is a 6-hour simulated-sunlight test in river water comparing these beads against plain carbon nitride, with equal absorbed photon flux, on weathered polyethylene microplastics, requiring at least 3-fold higher carbonyl-index loss, measurable CO2 evolution, and less than 10 percent activity decay after three recovery cycles.

We propose DustField-Consistent Multiband Inversion, a physics-guided inference method that jointly reconstructs distant compact sources and intervening dust structure from sparse multiwavelength observations of star-forming regions and exoplanetary environments. The novelty gap is that current pipelines usually treat dust as either a nuisance blur to be removed by generic deconvolution or a foreground to be fit independently, which creates false positives by hallucinating sharp sources from wavelength-dependent extinction, scattering halos, or point-spread-function mismatch; in contrast, our method explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that better denoising alone solves the problem by requiring every recovered object to remain consistent with a shared three-dimensional dust field and radiative transfer constraints across infrared, submillimeter, and visible bands. The core mechanism is a coupled latent model with two interacting components: a morphology-preserving source prior that favors astrophysically plausible disks, jets, and compact companions, and a dust transport module that predicts extinction, reddening, and anisotropic scattering under line-of-sight geometry, with uncertainty propagated through a Bayesian ensemble or diffusion-posterior sampler. This should improve object separability in heavily obscured regions, reduce spurious detections of clumps or exoplanetary companions, and recover more reliable source photometry because the reconstruction is forced to explain both the scene and the dust with one consistent generative account. Feasibility is high because the model can be trained on existing magnetohydrodynamic plus radiative-transfer simulations and adapted to telescope-specific point-spread functions without new hardware. The main risk is model misspecification: real dust grain distributions and unresolved background emission may violate the assumed transport family, causing overconfident reconstructions. A minimal validation benchmark is to create synthetic telescope observations from held-out simulated star-formation scenes with controlled dust opacity and compare against standard deconvolution and independent foreground-fitting comparisons using source recovery F1, astrometric error, photometric bias, dust-map calibration, and false-companion rate under increasing obscuration.

We propose DesignTrace Fusion, a retrieval-augmented generative design orchestration method that learns from historical CAD edit logs, simulation outputs, and part-constraint graphs to cut manual design and simulation cycles by predicting which local geometry changes are most likely to satisfy downstream performance targets before full re-simulation. The novelty gap is not simply “using AI for CAD,” which is already crowded, nor generic surrogate modeling of final performance, which often fails because it ignores the sequential structure of design reasoning; instead, the unmet gap is a data-engineering problem: existing pipelines rarely convert fragmented design histories into a queryable, causally organized substrate that links design intent, constraint propagation, and simulation deltas across iterations. DesignTrace Fusion addresses this by building a versioned design-state lakehouse where each edit is encoded as a typed graph delta, aligned with parameter changes, solver traces, and outcome shifts, then training a planner that retrieves analogous past trajectories and proposes ranked next-step edits with uncertainty estimates and constraint-violation forecasts. This should outperform black-box geometry generation because it narrows search to historically productive edit motifs, reduces wasted simulations, and remains feasible within industrial workflows since it can sit beside existing CAD and PLM systems without replacing them. A likely false-positive explanation is that any gains come merely from replaying frequent edits or from easier part families; we reject that by requiring evaluation on held-out product line variants and by comparing against frequency-based recommenders, pure surrogate optimization, and LLM-only CAD assistants. The main risk is distribution shift when novel topologies lack close precedents, so the system must abstain or escalate to full simulation when retrieval confidence is low. A minimal convincing benchmark is a multi-family dataset of design sessions where success is measured by fewer iterations to reach target constraints, reduced unnecessary simulations, and preserved compliance on unseen designs.

We propose LexOrbit, a treaty-linked adaptive governance method that converts broad space-law principles into a modular rulebook for resource utilization, orbital environmental protection, and traffic coordination through conditional legal protocols triggered by observable mission characteristics. The novelty gap is not simply that current frameworks are old or incomplete, because many reform proposals already call for new treaties, best-practice codes, or technical registries; the unmet gap is the absence of a mechanism that can generate issue-specific obligations without waiting for full treaty renegotiation and without assuming that soft-law guidance alone will solve strategic ambiguity. LexOrbit rejects the trivial explanation that better compliance comes merely from more monitoring: instead, it links monitoring outputs to pre-agreed escalation clauses, creating a governance stack in which licensing authorities, insurers, and multinational launch providers recognize a shared set of default obligations for extraction volumes, debris externalities, and conjunction response duties.
