The novelty gap is that most placebo research treats culture as background variation or demographic noise, then generalizes mechanisms derived from Western clinical encounters; CAPMM instead rejects the false-positive explanation that cross-cultural differences are merely differences in suggestibility, language comprehension, or comparison trust, by explicitly modeling those factors alongside ritual meaning. The core mechanism is to decompose placebo response into three measurable channels: symbolic congruence between treatment ritual and local healing cosmology, relational legitimacy of the healer or institution, and communal witnessing or endorsement that may amplify embodied expectation through social accountability. The method pairs ethnographic elicitation to derive locally valid ritual elements with a harmonized experimental protocol that manipulates these channels independently while holding inert treatment substance constant, allowing comparison of which configurations trigger analgesic, stress, or symptom-report changes across populations. Its expected impact is a mechanistic account of why placebo responses vary across cultural settings and a feasible template for designing ethically sensitive interventions and trials that do not misclassify culturally patterned effects as noise. The main risk is overfitting culture into simplistic categories or confounding ritual meaning with demand effects; CAPMM addresses this by preregistering competing explanations, including expectancy, acquiescence bias, and provider charisma, and by using both self-report and physiological outcomes. A minimal convincing benchmark is a three-site pilot comparing culturally congruent versus incongruent inert healing rituals, with success defined as reproducible site-specific placebo gains that are statistically mediated by symbolic congruence rather than generic expectation alone.

We propose PhotoSwitch Mineral-Seeded Flocculation, a wastewater-compatible microplastic removal method that targets a neglected gap between broad adsorbents that also capture benign organic matter and membrane systems that foul rapidly, by using visible-light-switchable amphiphilic ligands grafted onto biodegradable iron-silicate colloids to bind oxidized and hydrophobic polymer surfaces only during a short activation window and then collapse into dense flocs for easy magnetic-sedimentation recovery. The novelty is not merely adding another sorbent, because the central claim explicitly rejects common false positives: apparent removal caused by sieving large particles, nonspecific trapping of natural suspended solids, or simple coagulation that works equally on sand, cellulose, and plastics. Instead, the mechanism couples polymer-selective interfacial recognition with reversible aggregation, so capture and separation are decoupled: activated ligands increase affinity for polyethylene, polypropylene, and polystyrene fragments in the 1 to 100 micrometer range, while a timed conformational switch reduces colloid stability and drives recoverable floc formation. This should outperform passive coagulants by improving selectivity, lowering sludge volume, and preserving operation in saline or organic-rich waters without requiring high-pressure infrastructure, making deployment plausible in treatment plants or decentralized polishing units. The main risk is that dissolved organic matter, biofilms, or weathering heterogeneity could dominate surface interactions and erase selectivity, so feasibility depends on calibrating ligand density, light dose, and ionic conditions against realistic confounds rather than pristine lab plastics alone. A minimal convincing benchmark is a blinded side-by-side test in synthetic wastewater and real secondary effluent seeded with mixed-size weathered microplastics plus cellulose and mineral particulates, measuring polymer-specific removal by pyrolysis-GC/MS or Raman mapping, floc recoverability, sludge mass, and performance retention across three regeneration cycles, with success defined as at least 70 percent microplastic removal and at least 2 times selectivity over nonplastic particulates relative to ferric coagulation controls.

We propose Counterfactual Biosignature Retrieval with Stellar-Activity Nulling, a hierarchical inference framework for exoplanet transmission and emission spectra that targets a key novelty gap in current biosignature detection: most pipelines optimize molecular detectability but do not explicitly test whether an apparent O2, O3, CH4, or disequilibrium signal is better explained by stellar heterogeneity, cloud-aerosol degeneracy, photochemical abiotic production, or instrumental systematics, which makes many positive claims fragile or effectively non-falsifiable. The core mechanism is to replace single-atmosphere retrieval with a library of coupled counterfactual worlds in which the same observed spectrum is jointly fit under biotic, abiotic, contaminated-star, and cloud-dominated hypotheses, while enforcing physical consistency through shared priors on planetary bulk properties, host-star UV activity history, vertical mixing, and redox budgets. A contrastive evidence module then ranks not only what molecules are present, but whether any inferred disequilibrium remains uniquely hard to reproduce under false-positive pathways; this explicitly rejects trivial wins where one biomarker is detected without ruling out known non-biological routes. The expected advantage is a shift from “can we see a molecule” to “can we eliminate the strongest confounders,” which should produce fewer spectacular but misleading detections and more defensible target prioritization for JWST-class and future direct-imaging missions. Feasibility is high because the method can be built on existing retrieval codes, stellar contamination models, and photochemical grids rather than requiring new hardware. The main risk is model misspecification: if the abiotic library is incomplete, the system could overstate confidence, so the design must stress-test out-of-distribution atmospheres and adversarial stellar states. A minimal convincing benchmark is a blinded synthetic challenge with realistic noise and time-variable stellar contamination, where success means improved calibration, lower false-positive biosignature rates, and correct identification of truly biotic versus abiotic spectra across matched signal-to-noise regimes.

We propose OceanGenomeAtlas-CR, a climate-aware probabilistic data-engineering framework that maps phytoplankton genomes to oceanic regions by fusing fragmented metagenomes, isolate genomes, and satellite-linked ocean context into a region-resolved genomic atlas with calibrated provenance. The novelty gap is not merely that marine genomic data are scattered, because repositories and metagenomic portals already exist; the unsolved problem is that they rarely produce a unified, region-level genome-to-ocean mapping that distinguishes true biogeographic signal from sampling density, taxonomic redundancy, and transient bloom artifacts, so simple database integration or coordinate tagging would be a false solution. Our mechanism is a cross-resolution record-linkage pipeline that first builds genome entities from assembled MAGs, reference genomes, and marker-gene neighborhoods, then aligns them to ocean regions through a hierarchical Bayesian assignment layer combining sequence signatures, co-occurring environmental variables, seasonal circulation zones, and uncertainty-aware geospatial metadata. A contrastive deconfounding module explicitly penalizes mappings explainable only by cruise frequency, lab-specific assembly bias, or repeated sequencing of cosmopolitan taxa, while a temporal stability prior separates persistent regional associations from short-lived dispersal events. The expected advantage is a database that is useful not just for lookup but for downstream prediction of how marine ecosystem genomic composition may reorganize under warming, stratification, or nutrient shifts, while remaining feasible because it reuses existing ocean omics and Earth observation streams rather than requiring new global sampling. The main risk is biased regional assignment in undersampled waters or for horizontally transferred genes, which we control through abstention thresholds, lineage-level uncertainty propagation, and explicit unknown-region outputs. Minimal validation is a benchmark on held-out ocean expeditions where the system must recover masked source regions and improve region prediction over metadata-only and sequence-only comparisons, with success defined by higher top-1 accuracy, better calibration, and stronger temporal robustness across seasons.

We propose PolicyPulse-GDE, a governance-aware dynamic evidence engine that continuously fuses remote sensing, administrative text, local media, mobility traces, and disaster reports into policy-ready spatiotemporal indicators for environmental regulation, urban growth, and emergency response. The novelty gap is not merely that existing global datasets become outdated; many already offer frequent updates, but they remain sector-siloed, weakly aligned to political decision cycles, and vulnerable to false positives from one-off shocks, sensor drift, or reporting bias, so they cannot reliably tell policymakers whether observed change reflects real governance-relevant transformation rather than transient noise. Our method addresses this by building a hierarchical graph over places, infrastructures, ecological assets, agencies, and hazard events, then using change-point detection plus cross-source causal consistency checks to update latent state estimates only when multiple signals cohere under known institutional and geographic constraints. A key mechanism is a confidence-calibrated “decision layer” that converts raw environmental and urban change into interpretable alerts such as zoning pressure, infrastructure stress, enforcement weakening, or disaster exposure escalation, while explicitly flagging when evidence is too sparse or politically distorted to support action. The expected advantage is a global data product that is fresher than static comparisons yet more policy-credible than simple nowcasting dashboards, making it useful for comparing regions with uneven state capacity. Feasibility is strong because the inputs already exist in fragmented form and the main contribution is the integration logic and uncertainty discipline rather than a wholly new sensor system. The main risk is systematic bias where media silence or weak administrative capacity mimics stability; we mitigate this through missingness modeling, source reliability weights, and counterfactual stress tests. A minimal validation benchmark would test whether the system improves 3- to 12-month prediction of independently observed land-use change, pollution enforcement events, and disaster impact hotspots across a small cross-national panel, with success defined by better calibrated alerts and earlier detection than standard single-source update pipelines.

We propose NeuroLatent-Fuse, a cross-timescale state-space framework that converts slow fMRI into near-real-time feedback by fusing subsecond peripheral and behavioral streams with physics-constrained latent hemodynamic inference. The novelty gap is not simply that fMRI is slow, because faster decoding from the same blood-oxygen signal alone is largely a solved illusion: most apparent gains come from leakage, retrospective smoothing, or predicting task blocks rather than moment-to-moment brain state. Instead, the unmet opportunity is to use fMRI as a spatially precise anchor while learning a subject-specific latent neural state that is continuously updated by concurrent high-rate signals such as respiration, pulse, eye dynamics, button force, speech envelope, or low-density EEG, with a generative module enforcing biologically plausible hemodynamic delay and region-specific coupling. The mechanism combines an online Bayesian filter, a neural operator that approximates forward neurovascular dynamics, and confidence-gated feedback that only emits control signals when posterior uncertainty is low enough to avoid misleading users. Expected impact is practical neurofeedback and adaptive experiment control with temporal responsiveness closer to real behavior, while preserving the spatial specificity that motivates fMRI in the first place. Feasibility is high because all inputs are already co-collectable in scanners and the model can be trained from synchronized recordings without changing hardware. The main risk is that auxiliary streams may reflect arousal or motion confounds rather than neural content, producing deceptively responsive but biologically empty feedback; we address this by explicit nuisance channels, adversarial confound removal, calibration against held-out task transitions, and abstention under uncertainty spikes. A minimal validation benchmark is a prospective closed-loop study comparing standard fMRI neurofeedback against NeuroLatent-Fuse on time-to-detect induced state changes, correlation with later full-window fMRI estimates, and behavioral adaptation latency, with success defined as earlier reliable detection without loss of spatial specificity.

We propose EcoTrace Studio, a school-scale environmental inquiry method in which students build evidence-backed “local impact chains” by combining low-cost field measurements, neighborhood observations, and public municipal data into causal maps of how everyday systems such as stormwater, heat islands, waste streams, or air quality affect their own community. The novelty gap is not simply that environmental science lacks projects or digital tools, because many schools already run isolated recycling campaigns, generic citizen-science apps, or cookbook labs; the unmet gap is that students rarely connect personally collected evidence to authentic local decisions, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and concrete intervention proposals, so activities feel real in topic but not in scientific consequence. EcoTrace Studio addresses this by structuring each unit around a three-stage mechanism: students first collect multisource local evidence using phone cameras, simple sensors, and location-tagged observation templates; they then use a guided modeling interface that forces each claim to be linked to evidence quality, alternative explanations, and missing data; finally, they generate a community-facing recommendation with explicit confidence bounds and a “next measurement” plan. This should improve scientific literacy because students practice data interpretation, causal reasoning, and policy tradeoffs on phenomena they can directly observe, while remaining feasible for high schools through inexpensive materials and open civic datasets. The main risk is false confidence from noisy local data or the mistaken belief that relevance alone drives learning, so the design includes contradiction prompts, calibration rubrics, and required comparison against at least one plausible rival explanation. A minimal validation benchmark is a semester pilot comparing EcoTrace Studio with a standard lab-based environmental science unit, measuring gains in transfer-oriented scientific literacy, quality of evidence-to-claim reasoning in blind-scored student artifacts, retention after six weeks, and the proportion of intervention proposals judged actionable by external local stakeholders.

We propose MicroBind-GeoFlux, a geomorphology framework that treats microplastics not as passive contaminants or generic tracers, but as active modifiers of soil aggregate stability, pore-network connectivity, and near-surface sediment entrainment thresholds across hillslopes and channels. The novelty gap is that current erosion and sediment transport studies largely explain anomalous runoff, crusting, and fine-particle mobility through texture, organic matter, salinity, or moisture history alone, which creates false positives because several observed instabilities may instead arise from polymer-specific fiber and fragment interactions with clay bridges, microbial exudates, and capillary forces. Our core mechanism couples fractionated microplastic traits, including shape, polymer class, and weathering state, into a process model that predicts how they alter aggregate breakup, infiltration heterogeneity, splash detachment, and selective transport of silt-clay fractions under repeated wetting and rainfall pulses. Rather than merely correlating plastic concentration with erosion, the method uses controlled additions and trait-resolved parameters to separate true geomorphic effects from trivial co-occurrence with fertilizer residues, tillage disturbance, or urban dust inputs. The expected advantage is a mechanistic correction to erosion-risk mapping and sediment budgeting in agricultural landscapes where microplastic loading is increasing but hidden inside standard soil property measurements. Feasibility is high because the framework can be implemented with rainfall simulators, aggregate stability assays, X-ray or dye-based flow-path imaging, and standard sediment yield measurements. The main risk is confounding from concurrent changes in organic matter, salinity, and bioturbation, so the design calibrates uncertainty by comparing inert mineral particle amendments, sterilized versus live soil microcosms, and aged versus pristine polymers. A minimal convincing benchmark is a factorial test on two contrasting agricultural soils showing that trait-resolved microplastic variables improve prediction of infiltration decline and event sediment yield by at least 20% over comparison models using texture, moisture, and organic carbon alone.

We propose GutBarrier-Glia Circuit Editing, a staged precision intervention that targets the specific microbial-to-brain signaling axis most likely to amplify Alzheimer’s neuroinflammation rather than treating gut dysbiosis as a generic correlate. The novelty gap is that current microbiome approaches in Alzheimer’s disease largely test broad probiotics, fecal transfer, or associative taxa signatures, which cannot distinguish causal gut-derived immune drivers from trivial consequences of aging, diet, constipation, or advanced neurodegeneration; our idea explicitly rejects the false-positive explanation that any microbiome normalization is beneficial, and instead focuses on a narrow, mechanistically anchored circuit in which dysbiotic bile acid and tryptophan catabolite profiles impair intestinal barrier function, expand peripheral Th17-like inflammatory tone, and prime microglia toward a tau- and amyloid-permissive state. The concrete intervention is a modular two-part regimen: a bacteriophage or CRISPR-based microbial editing cocktail to deplete pathobionts predicted to overproduce barrier-disrupting metabolites, paired with an orally delivered engineered commensal that restores indole-derived aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling and mucosal tight-junction support. This should outperform untargeted microbiome therapies by reducing peripheral inflammatory noise while preserving colonization resistance and allowing patient stratification by metabolite-defined dysbiosis subtype, making the approach feasible with existing metagenomic and metabolomic tools. The main risk is that observed brain benefit may still reflect systemic anti-inflammatory effects rather than a gut-brain causal route, or that microbial editing may be unstable across hosts. A minimal convincing benchmark is a two-stage validation in APP/PS1 or tauopathy mice colonized with humanized dysbiotic microbiota: demonstrate selective correction of the targeted metabolite module, restoration of gut permeability markers, and reduced circulating IL-17/GM-CSF, then require concordant reduction in microglial activation states, soluble phospho-tau or amyloid burden, and memory impairment versus broad probiotic and sham controls, with success defined by pathway-level mediation rather than microbiome diversity shifts alone.

We propose Event-Triggered Low-Rank Progressive Distillation, a real-time learning method that targets a neglected gap in energy-efficient AI: most existing approaches reduce inference cost with pruning, quantization, or smaller models, but they do not directly address the repeated optimization waste that causes slow convergence during continual or streaming adaptation, and simple claims that better hardware, lower precision, or generic early stopping solve this problem are false positives because they often shift cost elsewhere or degrade responsiveness under distribution drift. The core mechanism is a dual-timescale training scheme in which a compact student model updates every step using sparse event-triggered gradients only when incoming data changes exceed an uncertainty threshold, while a low-rank memory of recent gradient subspaces approximates second-order curvature and periodically absorbs knowledge from a larger teacher through selective distillation on only the most informative windows. This intervention is intended to cut redundant gradient computation, shorten the path to stable performance after abrupt context changes, and preserve accuracy without requiring constant full-model retraining. Feasibility is high because the components are implementable with standard tensor operations and streaming buffers, and the novelty lies in coupling event-triggered optimization with low-rank curvature reuse and selective teacher refresh rather than treating compression and convergence as separate problems. The main risk is threshold miscalibration: if event triggers are too conservative, the system may miss subtle drift, while aggressive triggering can erase the energy benefit; this can be controlled with uncertainty-bounded trigger schedules and a fallback refresh budget. A minimal convincing benchmark is a streaming tabular and time-series classification setup with abrupt and gradual drift, comparing energy per adaptation episode, wall-clock recovery time to 95% of pre-drift accuracy, and final accuracy against online SGD, quantized online training, and lightweight continual-learning comparisons.

We propose FossilLatentCT, a statistical reconstruction method that combines ultra-low-dose multi-angle X-ray snapshots, surface photogrammetry, and a morphology-constrained Bayesian latent variable model to recover internal fossil structure without destructive sampling. The novelty gap is not simply that imaging exists already, because conventional micro-CT often fails on dense matrices, fragile specimens, or field-scale collections due to radiation limits, cost, and poor contrast, while surface-only scans miss hidden chambers, vascular traces, and repair patterns; likewise, claiming that generic super-resolution or standard tomography is sufficient would be a false positive, since these methods usually assume either many views or directly observable contrast boundaries. Our core mechanism instead treats internal anatomy as a structured probability distribution learned from a reference library of related specimens, mineral matrices, and taphonomic deformation patterns, then updates that prior using sparse radiographs and external geometry through hierarchical Bayesian inference with explicit uncertainty maps over each recovered internal region. The expected advantage is that paleontologists could screen rare specimens non-destructively, prioritize only the most informative samples for costly scanning or drilling, and quantify confidence rather than forcing binary interpretations from weak images. Feasibility is supported by the fact that museums already collect surface meshes and limited radiographs, so the method mainly changes statistical integration rather than requiring exotic hardware. The main risk is hallucinated anatomy driven by biased reference priors or taxonomic mismatch, especially for highly novel fossils; we address this by out-of-distribution detection, posterior predictive checks, and a reject option that flags regions where the data do not support reconstruction. A minimal validation benchmark would use extant-shell and sacrificial fossil analog specimens with known high-resolution CT interiors, compare recovered internal segmentation, void topology, and uncertainty calibration from only 6 to 12 low-dose projections, and define success as materially better structure recovery than sparse-view tomography and surface-only inference at equal radiation budget.

We propose Replication Sensitivity Mapping, a study-design and analysis method that targets a novelty gap at the center of the reproducibility crisis: many failed replications are treated as evidence that an original claim was false, while many successful replications are treated as proof that the underlying effect is robust, even though both outcomes can be driven by hidden design fragility rather than theory-level truth or error. The method explicitly rejects trivial explanations such as “just increase sample size,” “preregister everything,” or “use stricter p-value thresholds,” because those moves improve discipline without identifying which concrete procedural assumptions make a psychological finding transportable across labs, populations, and measurement implementations. The core mechanism is to formalize each study as a set of manipulable sensitivity dimensions, including recruitment channel, incentive structure, stimulus wording, timing, exclusion rules, measurement transformation, and analyst degrees of freedom, then generate a constrained multiverse of protocol variants that preserves the same theoretical construct while perturbing implementation details. A hierarchical model estimates not only the average effect but a reproducibility surface: which combinations of seemingly minor choices preserve, attenuate, or reverse the result. The expected advantage is a sharper distinction between genuinely generalizable phenomena and effects that only survive within narrow procedural corridors, yielding more informative claims for psychology and biomedicine than binary replicate-or-fail judgments. Feasibility is high because the method can be layered onto existing multi-lab workflows with shared templates and standard analysis software. The main risk is that sensitivity dimensions may be chosen post hoc or may miss the truly causal fragilities; to calibrate this, dimensions are specified prospectively, bounded by theory, and subjected to adversarial review from an independent lab before data collection. A minimal validation benchmark is a prospective multi-lab test on several canonical effects, where success means the reproducibility surface predicts between-lab effect variation better than standard pooled meta-analysis or single-protocol replication.

We propose Exposure-Path Inoculation, a network-aware misinformation control method that targets not the most visible false posts or the most influential users in isolation, but the specific social pathways through which dubious claims repeatedly gain credibility as they travel across loosely connected communities. The novelty gap is that most existing approaches implicitly assume misinformation spreads because bad content is intrinsically persuasive or because a few hubs dominate diffusion, which risks false-positive explanations because many viral falsehoods actually succeed only after being reinterpreted by trusted local peers, while many hubs amplify both true and false information. Our method models each claim as a sequence of community-to-community translations and identifies bridge accounts whose reposting behavior systematically converts low-credibility content into high-trust narrative variants. The intervention is a lightweight, platform-feasible ranking layer that selectively inserts friction at these bridge transitions by attaching context prompts, slowing reshare velocity, or boosting prebunking messages only when a claim’s diffusion pattern matches a high-risk exposure path, rather than globally suppressing content or bluntly flagging users. This should improve precision, reduce unnecessary moderation, and better preserve legitimate discussion because the mechanism acts on risky transmission structures instead of crude popularity signals. The main risk is confounding bridge behavior with ordinary cross-community brokerage, especially around contested but legitimate news, so the model explicitly calibrates decisions using source diversity, disagreement intensity, and historical correction uptake to avoid treating all boundary-crossing communication as harmful. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective simulation-plus-field evaluation on time-stamped repost networks comparing our path-triggered friction against content-only flagging and hub-targeting comparisons, with success defined by larger reductions in downstream false-belief proxy exposure and cascade depth at equal or lower intervention volume and lower collateral impact on verified information diffusion.

We propose Vorticity-Canceling Electroosmotic Wall Coding, a microfluidic method that sustains laminar-like coflow by programming boundary conditions rather than depending on highly optimized channel geometry or globally low Reynolds number. The novelty gap is that most existing approaches either passively preserve laminarity by making the channel itself do all the work, which limits layout freedom and scale-up, or actively suppress mixing with pumps, valves, or acoustic forcing that add energy cost and control complexity; a likely false-positive explanation is that simply reducing average velocity, shrinking dimensions, or polishing walls already solves the problem, but those moves only recover the conventional regime and do not generalize to flexible geometries or higher-throughput operation. Our mechanism is to tile the channel walls with low-voltage electroosmotic electrode segments coated by a thin charge-selective layer and drive them with a spatially phase-coded waveform that generates weak, alternating near-wall slip velocities chosen to cancel the onset of transverse shear gradients before they amplify into cross-stream recirculation. Instead of forcing the bulk, the system shapes only the boundary layer, so the energy scales with wall area rather than total fluid volume and can be embedded into bends, junctions, or wide manifolds where standard laminar design rules break down. The main risk is that electrode heterogeneity, Joule heating, bubble nucleation, or zeta-potential drift could create exactly the disturbances the method is meant to suppress, so feasibility depends on low-conductivity buffers, Faradaic-shielded coatings, and feedback from two-point impedance or optical streak measurements to retune the phase code. A minimal convincing benchmark is a Y-junction or serpentine chip operated at matched throughput against passive geometry-only and uniform electroosmotic controls, with success defined by at least a 50% reduction in interface broadening and secondary-flow indicators over 100 channel widths while using less than 20% of the control power of bulk active methods.

We propose EconCME-Gate, a cost-sensitive coronal mass ejection forecasting method that couples physics-aware multimodal sequence modeling with an explicit economic decision layer and selective false-alarm rejection. The novelty gap is that most CME predictors optimize geophysical event accuracy alone, then treat downstream operations as an external scheduling problem, which leaves a major source of inefficiency untouched: economically costly false positives that trigger unnecessary satellite safing, grid precautions, or mission replanning even when arrival probability is poorly identified. This is not solved by simply adding more solar images, larger transformers, or post hoc threshold tuning, because those approaches still collapse heterogeneous uncertainty into a single score and cannot distinguish ambiguous eruptions from truly actionable threats. Our core mechanism is a dual-head architecture that ingests coronagraph images, magnetograms, flare metadata, and solar wind context, then jointly predicts CME arrival severity and a calibrated reject option that abstains when the event lies in a known ambiguity region; a second layer maps the predictive distribution into action recommendations by minimizing expected operational loss under user-specific cost matrices. The expected advantage is higher net economic utility, not merely higher hit rate, because the model is trained to suppress expensive false alarms while preserving recall for rare severe events. Feasibility is strong because all inputs already exist in standard heliophysics archives and the decision layer only requires approximate operational cost ranges rather than perfect accounting. The main risk is domain shift across solar cycles and instruments, plus biased cost assumptions that could over-penalize precaution. We control this with conformal calibration, temporal holdouts, and stress tests over cost scenarios. A minimal benchmark would compare against standard probability-only comparisons on a historical rolling-window dataset, with success defined by lower expected decision cost, improved calibration under shift, and fewer unnecessary intervention alerts at matched severe-event recall.

We propose Electroadhesive Swarm Flocculation, a flow-through remediation method that captures microplastics by driving biodegradable, magnetically recoverable colloidal capsules to seek and bind dispersed polymer particles under weak oscillatory electric fields. The novelty gap is that most current approaches assume microplastics must be removed by size exclusion, dense coagulation, or centralized membrane infrastructure, which becomes energy intensive, fouling prone, and impractical for dilute, heterogeneous particles in rivers, stormwater, and treatment outfalls; this is not already solved by standard flocculants, because they are optimized for mineral turbidity and often fail when microplastics vary widely in surface oxidation, shape, and buoyancy. Our method instead uses soft capsules with amphiphilic coronae and patchy charge domains that form reversible polymer-selective bridges, while embedded iron oxide nanograins allow low-gradient magnetic harvesting after capture. Alternating fields are used not to electrolyze water or shred plastics, but to induce dielectrophoretic micro-mixing and repeated capsule-particle encounters, increasing collision efficiency at low concentrations without physical sieving. The expected advantage is scalable polishing of diffuse flows with lower pressure drop, lower fouling, and tunable selectivity across polyethylene, polypropylene, and polystyrene fragments and fibers. Feasibility is supported by known ingredients from colloid science, dielectrophoresis, and magnetic separations, but the main risk is nonspecific aggregation with natural organic matter or clay, which could reduce selectivity or generate secondary residues; we therefore design the capsules to degrade after magnetic recovery and tune surface chemistry against humic adsorption. A minimal convincing benchmark is a recirculating channel test using environmentally realistic mixed microplastics at parts-per-million to parts-per-billion levels in clean and natural waters, with success defined by at least 80% particle count reduction across major size bins, less than 10% dissolved carbon increase, and stable capsule recovery over five reuse cycles.

We propose Predator Contingency Curriculum, a reintroduction training method that targets a specific novelty gap: most anti-predator programs expose captive-bred animals to predator cues or live predators, but they rarely teach when to freeze, flee, mob, or seek cover under shifting ecological contexts, and they often mistake short-term arousal for true predator competence. To reject that false-positive, our method does not treat elevated vigilance, cortisol, or one-off avoidance as sufficient; instead it trains and measures context-appropriate action selection across predator type, distance, habitat structure, and social setting. The core mechanism combines multisensory predator simulations with adaptive contingency learning: animals experience repeated trials in semi-natural enclosures where predator cues are paired with different escape affordances, refuge layouts, and group compositions, and the sequence is adjusted so individuals must infer which defensive response is optimal rather than memorize a single routine. A lightweight reinforcement schedule strengthens flexible response mapping while periodic cue-transfer trials test whether learning generalizes to novel exemplars, preventing a trivial habituation effect. The expected advantage is a more portable anti-predator repertoire that should reduce post-release mortality without requiring full exposure to lethal risk, making the approach feasible for endangered species and facilities with limited access to live-predator setups. The main risk is that trained behavior could become overgeneralized, producing unnecessary hiding or reduced foraging, or that captive enclosures fail to capture field complexity; this is controlled by embedding non-threat discriminations, recovery-period measurements, and novel-context probes. A minimal convincing benchmark is a randomized pre-release study comparing standard cue exposure versus this curriculum in one target species, with blinded scoring of correct response selection, retention after four weeks, transfer to unseen predator scenarios, and early post-release survival or predator-encounter escape success as the key success criteria.

We propose Predictive Robust Dispatch MPC, a rolling-horizon emergency resource allocation method that closes a specific gap between static operations research dispatch and purely predictive systems that forecast demand but do not translate uncertainty into actionable, reliable allocation decisions. The novelty is not simply adding machine learning to ambulance or fire deployment, because that is already a common and often superficial framing; instead, the unmet need is a decision layer that explicitly rejects false positives from volatile short-term predictions, distinguishes actionable demand shifts from noise, and optimizes only on forecast structure that remains stable under perturbation. The core mechanism combines a spatiotemporal incident predictor with conformal uncertainty sets, a causal drift detector for regime changes such as weather or crowd events, and a distributionally robust model-predictive control allocator that repositions units, reserves slack capacity, and triggers staged redeployment only when predicted gains survive worst-case uncertainty tests. This creates a concrete intervention: each dispatch cycle solves for allocations that maximize expected coverage and response-time reduction while penalizing fragility, prediction sensitivity, and inter-station depletion, producing decisions that are adaptive but intentionally conservative when the signal is weak. The expected advantage is better real-time performance than static integer programs and better safety than myopic prediction-driven dispatch, especially in rapidly changing demand landscapes. Feasibility is high because all components can run on standard dispatch logs, GIS travel-time estimates, and existing fleet constraints without requiring new sensors. The main risk is over-conservatism, where robust guards suppress useful repositioning, or hidden confounding, where forecast shifts reflect reporting artifacts rather than true incidents. A minimal convincing benchmark is a replay simulation on historical emergency data with injected regime shifts, comparing against static allocation, forecast-only dispatch, and robust optimization without calibrated prediction, measuring 90th-percentile response time, missed high-priority coverage, relocation churn, and degradation under forecast error.

We propose MicroAdapt Twin, a hyperlocal climate-adaptation planning method that learns actionable microclimate response zones from fused street-scale sensing, satellite thermal imagery, land-surface descriptors, and utility-demand traces, then allocates adaptation resources through counterfactual optimization rather than coarse regional averages. The novelty gap is not simply that existing strategies use low-resolution climate maps; many already downscale weather, but they still treat microclimate variation as descriptive background noise or assume that finer maps automatically improve decisions. We explicitly reject that false-positive explanation by targeting the missing decision layer: a model that identifies where microclimates systematically change intervention effectiveness, such as tree planting, reflective surfaces, cooling centers, irrigation timing, or flood-retention assets. The core mechanism combines a physics-guided spatiotemporal graph neural model with causal representation learning to infer latent microclimate regimes and estimate localized treatment-response curves under different adaptation portfolios, while a resource-constrained optimizer selects interventions that maximize avoided heat stress, water waste, or runoff damage per dollar. Expected advantage comes from reallocating limited budgets toward blocks whose canopy, building geometry, soil moisture, and human exposure interact nonlinearly, yielding larger resilience gains than uniform citywide rules. Feasibility is strong because most inputs already exist through municipal sensors, open Earth observation products, cadastral maps, and infrastructure records. The main risk is confounding from unobserved socioeconomic and behavioral factors that may masquerade as microclimate effects, so the system uses uncertainty-aware policy bounds, placebo interventions, and transfer-stability checks across neighborhoods to suppress overconfident recommendations. A minimal validation benchmark is a retrospective holdout study in two cities and one prospective district pilot, where success means at least 15% lower prediction error for localized hazard exposure and at least 10% higher simulated benefit-per-budget than conventional grid-based adaptation planning.

We propose Waste-Aware Counterfactual Reaction Search, a closed-loop combinatorial chemistry platform that replaces brute-force high-throughput experimentation with a generative planner that selects only reactions whose expected information gain and synthetic value justify their material, time, and waste cost. The novelty gap is that most current optimization schemes merely rank promising conditions for yield or potency, assuming that more miniaturized screening solves inefficiency; this is a false positive because even smaller assays still consume broad reagent grids, propagate biased historical reaction preferences, and rarely quantify whether an experiment is worth running relative to the waste it creates. Our method couples a reaction encoder trained on prior combinatorial campaigns with a Bayesian surrogate that predicts not only product success but also uncertainty, by-product burden, purification difficulty, and E-factor proxies, then uses counterfactual acquisition to choose experiments that either maximize the probability of discovering a new productive scaffold region or aggressively eliminate redundant regions already explainable by known structure-reactivity patterns. A hard feasibility constraint restricts proposals to purchasable reagents, instrument-compatible conditions, and a bounded solvent and catalyst budget, making the system deployable in existing medicinal chemistry workflows. The expected advantage is fewer assays per useful hit, lower solvent and reagent consumption, and faster exploration of chemically diverse space rather than repeated local optimization around familiar motifs. The main risk is model misspecification under sparse early data, causing overconfident pruning of rare but valuable chemotypes; we control this with uncertainty penalties, diversity floors, replicate-triggered recalibration, and periodic random sentinel experiments. Minimal validation is a prospective benchmark on 3 to 5 historical or live combinatorial campaigns, comparing against grid search and standard active learning on hit rate, unique scaffold discovery, experiments per validated hit, and waste per hit, with success defined as matching or improving hit quality while reducing total experiments and estimated waste by at least 30%.

We propose Liquidity-State Counterfactual Policy Learning, a crypto trading method that fills a novelty gap between price-only reinforcement strategies and simplistic sentiment-driven signals by explicitly modeling when apparent alpha is merely a byproduct of transient exchange-specific liquidity distortions, funding shocks, or survivorship in backtests rather than a true exploitable pattern. The core mechanism builds a latent market-state model from limit-order-book imbalance, cross-exchange basis, perpetual funding rates, realized volatility, stablecoin flow proxies, and liquidation intensity, then trains a constrained policy that chooses among momentum, mean-reversion, and stay-flat actions only when a counterfactual filter predicts that the expected edge survives transaction costs and regime shifts under alternative liquidity states. This rejects trivial explanations such as “more features improve prediction” or “high volatility always creates opportunity,” because the policy is rewarded only for strategies whose advantage remains after perturbing spreads, slippage, and exchange lead-lag structure. The expected impact is a more stable and interpretable decision process for dynamic crypto markets, especially during abrupt transitions when standard black-box agents overtrade or chase noisy breakouts. Feasibility is high because all required inputs exist in standard exchange data and the method can be implemented with offline training plus lightweight online inference. The main risk is latent-state misspecification: if the inferred regimes collapse distinct stress events into one state, the policy may become overconfident and concentrate risk exactly when liquidity evaporates. A minimal convincing benchmark is a walk-forward test on major crypto pairs across bull, bear, and shock periods, comparing against buy-and-hold, volatility-scaled momentum, and unconstrained RL, with success defined by statistically better net Sharpe, lower turnover-adjusted drawdown, and smaller performance decay when transaction costs and slippage are stress-amplified.

We propose LedgerLoad, a readiness-conditioned resistance prescription method that replaces fixed percentage-of-1RM planning with a daily latent capacity estimate derived from short pre-session signals and an accounting-style exposure ledger. The novelty gap is that current adaptive training ideas often stop at simple velocity loss rules, subjective readiness questionnaires, or occasional autoregulated set adjustments, which do not formally separate transient physiological capacity from accumulated training liability across days; this makes them vulnerable to false positives where apparent adaptation is actually sleep, dehydration, caffeine, or random performance noise. LedgerLoad addresses this by maintaining an individual state-space model that updates a hidden daily strength-readiness variable using bar-speed from two standardized warm-up lifts, heart-rate recovery, grip-strength deviation, and prior-session strain, while a companion ledger records unresolved fatigue “obligations” from volume, eccentric load, and proximity to failure. The intervention is to choose the day’s working load and target repetitions by maximizing expected productive tension subject to a fatigue solvency constraint, so the athlete receives slightly higher loads on unexpectedly good days and protective downshifts on biologically poor days without needing a new max test. Expected impact is better strength gain per unit fatigue, fewer nonfunctional overreaching episodes, and more stable progression for lifters whose capacity fluctuates substantially. Feasibility is high because all inputs can be collected with common gym sensors or simple field measures. The main risk is overfitting noisy readiness markers and mistaking acute arousal for durable capacity, so the model should impose shrinkage toward athlete-specific comparisons and reject adjustments unless multiple signals agree. A minimal convincing benchmark is a 6- to 8-week prospective study against fixed-percentage programming and standard RPE autoregulation, with success defined by improved prediction of same-day top-set performance, lower session-to-session performance variance, and superior strength gain relative to accumulated fatigue exposure.

We propose Context-Layered Guideline Translation (CLGT), a method that converts evidence-based practice recommendations into locally negotiable care pathways by combining ethnographic constraint mapping, resource-aware decision rules, and patient-preference weighting. The novelty gap is not simply that clinicians ignore guidelines or that implementation is underfunded, because those explanations are already well known and do not explain why the same guideline succeeds in one clinic yet fails in another with similar staffing and disease burden. The unresolved problem is that most guidelines encode evidence as if contexts were interchangeable, while real decisions are shaped by household obligations, local moral norms, supply instability, language, trust, and acceptable tradeoffs between biomedical efficacy and social feasibility. CLGT addresses this by first eliciting a structured “context profile” from rapid ethnographic interviews with clinicians, patients, and caregivers, then translating each guideline step into a tiered menu of actions labeled by evidence strength, cultural sensitivity, material requirements, and preference dependence. A simple rule engine then recommends the highest-fidelity feasible pathway rather than forcing binary adherence versus nonadherence. This should improve uptake because it preserves the core causal ingredients of the intervention while making adaptation explicit, auditable, and comparable across sites, instead of leaving it as hidden improvisation. Feasibility is strong because the data burden is modest and the translation layer can be piloted on one clinical workflow before wider deployment. The main risk is that local adaptation could drift into unjustified dilution or encode local power asymmetries as “culture,” so the method includes red-flag constraints that prohibit dropping high-benefit elements without documented reasons and requires patient-side preference capture rather than clinician-only interpretation. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective comparison across 6 to 8 resource-variable clinics implementing one guideline, with success measured by improved pathway uptake, preserved core clinical process fidelity, patient-reported acceptability, and fewer undocumented deviations.

We propose Counterfactual Active Reaction Graph Distillation (CARGD), a molecular-property and reaction-pathway prediction framework that targets a real novelty gap: most current chemistry ML systems either fit benchmark labels without modeling why a pathway is chosen, or they rely on expensive quantum calculations that remain too slow for broad design loops, while many apparent gains come from scaffold leakage, memorized reaction templates, or trivial correlations between composition and labels rather than transferable mechanistic understanding. CARGD addresses this by coupling a 3D equivariant molecular encoder with a reaction-state graph generator that predicts not only end properties but a compact sequence of latent intermediate states, then trains those states using counterfactual consistency constraints: if electronically irrelevant substituents are perturbed, the model should preserve the same causal reaction core, whereas perturbations at the reactive center must induce calibrated pathway changes. A lightweight teacher-student distillation stage uses sparse high-fidelity quantum evaluations only on uncertainty-triggered samples, allowing the student to learn barrier-sensitive structure without paying full simulation cost across the dataset. The expected advantage is faster screening with better extrapolation to novel chemotypes and reaction families because the model is forced to represent mechanistic invariants instead of shortcut features. Feasibility is reasonable because all components build on available conformer generation, equivariant graph networks, and active learning infrastructure. The main risk is that latent intermediates may become chemically unfaithful yet still improve benchmark error, so uncertainty estimates and counterfactual invariance tests must explicitly reject such false positives. A minimal convincing benchmark would compare CARGD against strong property-only and reaction-template comparisons on scaffold-split molecular property prediction and held-out reaction family pathway ranking, with success defined as lower error, improved top-k transition-state pathway recall, and better calibration under distribution shift using no more than a modest quantum labeling budget.

We propose Causal Time-Delay Cosmography with Environment-Conditioned Early Energy, a joint inference framework that treats the Hubble tension as a possible breakdown of the assumption that all distance ladders and all early-universe probes can be compressed into one homogeneous background expansion history with negligible line-of-sight structure coupling. The novelty gap is that most proposals either add smooth early dark energy, invoke generic late-time systematics, or modify gravity globally, but they rarely test whether percent-level shifts in inferred H0 can arise from a specific, redshift-dependent interaction between transient pre-recombination energy injection and the environment-sensitive lensing/time-delay observables used at intermediate redshift; this explicitly rejects trivial explanations such as simple Cepheid recalibration, unrestricted extra relativistic species, or an arbitrary free w(z) fit that absorbs tension without physical discriminability. The core mechanism introduces a short-lived scalar sector that changes the sound horizon before recombination while simultaneously generating a calibrated correction operator for strong-lens time-delay distances based on resolved matter-environment descriptors from imaging and weak-lensing maps, forcing the model to explain both early and late inferences with one causal parameterization rather than independent nuisance shifts. Its expected advantage is that it can reduce the tension by splitting what is currently treated as a single discrepancy into a physically linked pair of effects, while remaining feasible because both components can be embedded in existing Boltzmann codes and hierarchical lens analyses. The main risk is degeneracy: the lens-environment operator could mimic flexible systematics and falsely rescue a weak early-energy signal, so the model must enforce sparsity, sign constraints, and leave-one-survey-out stability. A minimal validation benchmark is a blinded fit to Planck plus BAO plus Pantheon-like supernovae and a small set of gold-standard lensed quasars, with success defined by materially lowering joint residual tension, improving out-of-sample predictive likelihood for held-out lenses, and recovering null corrections on realistic mock universes where standard LambdaCDM is true.

We propose SurgGraph-Assist, a data-centric autonomy layer that converts direct teleoperation into continuously queryable procedural state graphs for shared-control robotic surgery. The novelty gap is not simply that surgical robots lack better motion planning or stronger vision models, because those explanations are already heavily explored and still leave surgeons cognitively overloaded by having to manually maintain context, intent, and safety constraints across long procedures. The unmet need is a reliable data-engineering substrate that fuses heterogeneous signals into a structured, low-latency representation of surgical progress, instrument roles, tissue state, and allowable next actions, so automation can be introduced as bounded assistance rather than brittle full autonomy. SurgGraph-Assist would ingest synchronized endoscopic video, instrument kinematics, foot-pedal events, force surrogates, and operating-room metadata, then build a temporal procedure graph whose nodes represent validated micro-states and whose edges encode clinically permitted transitions with uncertainty scores. A constrained policy layer can then offer context-conditioned subtask execution such as camera repositioning, suture following, retraction stabilization, or repetitive clip placement only when the graph shows high confidence and hard safety predicates are satisfied; otherwise control reverts immediately to the surgeon. The expected advantage is reduced fatigue and higher consistency without requiring end-to-end autonomous surgery, making deployment more feasible in existing systems. The main risk is graph misclassification under bleeding, occlusion, or rare anatomy, which could create confidently wrong assistance; we therefore use abstention thresholds, out-of-distribution alarms, and patient-specific online recalibration from the first minutes of the case. A minimal convincing benchmark is a retrospective-plus-simulator evaluation on multi-modal partial-procedure datasets, measuring micro-state accuracy, unsafe action suggestion rate, intervention latency, and reduction in manual camera or repetitive manipulation commands versus pure teleoperation, with success defined by materially fewer surgeon-issued low-level actions at no increase in safety violations.

We propose Equity-Weighted Causal Exposure Ledger, a policy-advocacy method that converts local pollution and health data into neighborhood-specific, legally interpretable evidence on whether marginalized communities bear excess exposure and how much of that burden is plausibly preventable under concrete regulatory actions. The novelty gap is that existing environmental justice dashboards mostly map disparities or correlations, which is useful for awareness but weak for advocacy because officials can dismiss them as demographic sorting, lifestyle differences, or already-known hotspot patterns; our method explicitly rejects those false-positive explanations by estimating disparity only after decomposing background risk, land-use history, mobility, and healthcare access, and by flagging cases where apparent inequity disappears once these are accounted for. The core mechanism is a causal evidence pipeline that fuses satellite and low-cost sensor pollution estimates, administrative health records, zoning and permitting histories, complaint logs, and school or workplace mobility traces into a matched neighborhood panel, then computes a community exposure debt score: the cumulative excess pollution-linked health burden attributable to modifiable policy choices such as truck routing, industrial permitting, or buffer-zone design. Instead of only ranking harm, the system generates counterfactual policy briefs showing which intervention would most reduce disparity per dollar and how uncertain that estimate is, making it more actionable for community groups with limited technical capacity. The main risk is overclaiming causality when unobserved confounding or measurement error remains, so the method reports abstention zones, sensitivity bounds, and negative-control tests rather than forcing a verdict everywhere. A minimal validation benchmark is a three-city retrospective study in which the method must outperform standard disparity maps in predicting where independently documented policy changes later reduced pollution-linked emergency visits, while maintaining calibrated uncertainty and producing stable neighborhood rankings under sensor and model perturbations.

We propose PhaseShift-Gait, a real-time gait feedback method that couples self-supervised phase estimation with uncertainty-gated micro-interventions to close a specific novelty gap: most current gait analysis systems either deliver accurate but offline post hoc summaries, or provide simplistic real-time cues based on thresholded step timing, force asymmetry, or wearable heuristics that treat feedback as a generic alerting problem rather than a dynamically personalized control problem. The key claim is not that sensors or streaming inference are missing, but that existing approaches often produce false-positive corrections because they ignore moment-to-moment phase confidence, terrain-induced variability, and person-specific compensation patterns, so users receive cues that are late, noisy, or behaviorally disruptive. PhaseShift-Gait addresses this by learning each user’s latent gait phase and deviation manifold from short calibration walks using inertial and optional pressure signals, then running a lightweight online state-space model that predicts the next stable correction window 150 to 300 milliseconds ahead; feedback is only issued when predicted deviation is both clinically meaningful and confidence-calibrated, and the modality is adapted between haptic pulse, auditory metronome fragment, or no cue to minimize overload. This mechanism should improve actionability because it targets the correct phase of the gait cycle rather than merely flagging abnormality after it occurs, while remaining feasible on commodity wearables due to compact streaming inference and sparse cueing. The main risk is overfitting to short calibration sessions or misclassifying benign variability as pathology under speed changes, fatigue, or uneven surfaces, so the system explicitly tracks uncertainty and suppresses interventions during unstable estimates. A minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective treadmill and overground study comparing PhaseShift-Gait against offline-only analysis and fixed-threshold live cueing, with success defined by lower cue latency, fewer unnecessary cues, and larger immediate improvement in gait symmetry or variability metrics within one session.

We propose TectoSketch, a concept-constrained surrogate simulator for plate tectonics education that converts a few teacher- or student-specified boundary conditions into fast, interpretable continental-drift scenarios without requiring full geodynamic expertise or expensive numerical solvers. The novelty gap is not merely that existing simulators are slow, because lightweight visual demos already exist, nor that plate tectonics is hard to teach, because many animations simplify it; the unmet gap is a middle layer between toy animations and research-grade finite-element models: a scientifically anchored system that is fast enough for classroom hypothesis testing while still exposing causal assumptions such as spreading rate, subduction angle, lithospheric age, and mantle upwelling. TectoSketch addresses this by combining a sparse rule-based tectonic graph, where plates, boundaries, and mantle cells are explicit nodes, with a distilled neural surrogate trained on a library of offline high-fidelity simulations and textbook reconstructions, so users manipulate physically meaningful controls while the surrogate predicts deformation trajectories, basin formation likelihood, mountain-building regions, and qualitative stress maps in seconds. This is not a trivial interface wrapper, because the key intervention is a constraint layer that rejects geologically inconsistent state transitions, flags when multiple mechanisms can explain the same map pattern, and offers uncertainty bands rather than a single authoritative animation. The expected advantage is broader accessibility for teaching and rapid hypothesis screening, especially for comparing “what if” scenarios in lab or lecture settings. The main risk is oversmoothing rare tectonic behaviors or giving false confidence in visually plausible outputs; feasibility comes from limiting scope to mesoscale educational scenarios and exposing uncertainty explicitly. A minimal validation benchmark would compare TectoSketch against both a standard educational animation tool and a small set of expert-run numerical models on runtime, parameter usability, qualitative reconstruction accuracy, and learners’ ability to correctly predict consequences of altered boundary conditions after short guided use.

We propose Spectral-Shift Radiative Cooling Mulch, a crop-row intervention that cools the canopy microclimate without the yield penalty of conventional shading by decoupling heat mitigation from photosynthetically useful light removal. The novelty gap is that most agricultural greenhouse-effect countermeasures treat excess heat as a problem to block from above, which trivially lowers leaf temperature but also suppresses photosynthetically active radiation and often reproduces an already-known tradeoff rather than solving it; our method explicitly rejects that false-positive path by leaving direct overhead sunlight largely available to leaves while instead manipulating the radiation balance from below and between rows. The core mechanism is a biodegradable mulch film patterned with angular-selective mineral microparticles and near-infrared reflective bands that redirect non-photosynthetic infrared away from the canopy-root zone system, increase longwave thermal emission to the sky, and mildly enhance diffuse visible light back into lower leaves, thereby reducing midday canopy temperature and vapor pressure stress while preserving or even improving whole-canopy light use efficiency. Because the intervention sits on soil rather than over plants, it is operationally compatible with existing row-crop management and can be tuned by particle loading, band geometry, and crop architecture. The main risk is that reflected radiation could warm lower leaves or soils under some sun angles, or alter humidity and disease pressure in ways that offset cooling benefits; therefore the smallest convincing benchmark is a replicated field-plot comparison against black mulch and shade-net controls, measuring canopy temperature, leaf gas exchange, incident PAR, soil moisture, disease incidence, and final marketable yield, with success defined as at least 1.5 to 2.0 degrees Celsius midday canopy cooling relative to control while maintaining no more than 2 percent PAR loss and achieving equal or higher yield.

We propose AutoAntigen-Logic CAR-Treg, a precision tolerance-induction platform that uses patient-specific autoantigen discovery plus combinatorial sensing regulatory T cells to silence autoimmune inflammation only inside disease-relevant tissues rather than suppressing immunity system-wide. The novelty gap is that most current “targeted” autoimmune therapies still block shared cytokines or deplete broad lymphocyte classes, so they reduce symptoms by dampening normal host defense; conversely, simply expanding polyclonal Tregs or giving soluble antigen is a likely false-positive solution because those effects are diffuse, unstable, and often insufficient in inflamed tissues where pathogenic effector programs dominate. Our method engineers autologous Tregs with a two-layer circuit: one receptor recognizes a disease-linked autoantigen peptide-MHC or tissue-enriched antigen, while a second synNotch input senses an inflamed target-tissue cue and triggers local release of IL-10/CTLA4-biased suppressive modules only when both signals co-occur, thereby restricting activity to the pathological niche. The expected advantage is selective restoration of immune tolerance with lower infection risk, less malignancy liability, and longer remission than chronic systemic immunosuppression. Feasibility is supported by existing autologous cell-manufacturing workflows, clinical experience with CAR-Treg concepts, and growing single-cell/peptidomic methods for identifying dominant autoimmune targets. The main risk is antigen heterogeneity or epitope spreading, which could let disease escape or misdirect the cells; to control this, the initial design uses a small multiplexed antigen panel and excludes ubiquitously expressed targets to reduce off-tissue tolerance. A minimal convincing benchmark is an ex vivo human assay followed by one mouse model: demonstrate that engineered Tregs suppress autoreactive T-cell cytokine production and tissue damage markers only in cultures containing both target antigen and inflammatory tissue cue, while preserving unrelated antiviral recall responses, then show reduced disease score without excess infection susceptibility versus steroid or anti-cytokine controls.

We propose Gradient Forecasted Sparse Routing (GFSR), a training method that cuts deep learning compute by learning when full backpropagation is unnecessary and replacing it with calibrated local gradient forecasts on low-value updates. The novelty gap is that most efficiency work treats high computational cost as a hardware scaling issue, a compression problem after training, or a fixed sparse architecture problem, yet these explanations are partly false positives because a large fraction of cost is wasted during training on repeatedly recomputing similar gradients for examples, layers, and steps whose update directions are predictable. Rather than pruning the network statically or lowering precision uniformly, GFSR adds a lightweight controller that monitors per-layer gradient volatility, loss curvature proxies, and sample novelty, then routes each training event to either exact backpropagation or a cheap forecast path that reuses a short-horizon gradient state model with periodic correction. The mechanism is a two-timescale loop: a fast forecast module predicts layerwise updates from recent optimizer trajectories, while a slower verifier enforces trust-region bounds and triggers exact recomputation whenever prediction uncertainty, distribution shift, or rare-example signatures exceed a calibrated threshold. The expected advantage is lower end-to-end training FLOPs without requiring custom hardware, while preserving convergence because expensive exact gradients are concentrated on informative or unstable regions of training. Feasibility is strong because the controller can be inserted into standard transformer or CNN training stacks and relies only on signals already produced during optimization. The main risk is silent bias accumulation, where forecasted updates overfit common patterns and under-serve minority modes; we control this by uncertainty-gated fallbacks, mandatory exact refresh intervals, and stratified monitoring of subgroup error and optimization drift. A minimal convincing benchmark is to train a medium transformer and a ResNet on standard text and image tasks, comparing equal-accuracy compute, wall-clock time, and final accuracy against full training, mixed precision, and static sparse comparisons, with success defined as at least 30% lower training FLOPs at no more than 0.5% accuracy loss.

We propose SpikeGuard-Stat, a Bayesian extreme-event reconstruction framework that turns sparse periodic air samples into continuous estimates of short-lived contaminant peaks by fusing low-cost surrogate signals, task logs, and physics-informed prior structure on emission bursts. The novelty gap is that most workplace exposure programs still treat missed spikes as a hardware sampling-frequency problem, leading either to expensive continuous monitors or to simple interpolation of periodic samples, yet neither addresses the statistical question of how to infer unobserved excursions from partial evidence while rejecting false explanations such as ordinary temporal smoothing, threshold alarms on noisy proxies, or generic anomaly detection that cannot produce calibrated peak concentration estimates. Our core mechanism is a hierarchical state-space model with a burst process linked to discrete work activities, ventilation state changes, and continuously available surrogates such as particle counts, sound, vibration, or process telemetry, with informative priors enforcing chemically plausible rise and decay dynamics; posterior inference then outputs both peak probabilities and uncertainty-bounded short-term exposure summaries aligned with occupational limits. The expected advantage is earlier identification of dangerous transient exposures without universal deployment of high-end continuous contaminant sensors, making the method feasible for retrofitting existing monitoring programs in high-risk settings. The main risk is confounding, because surrogates may correlate with production intensity but not the contaminant itself, causing false spike reconstruction; we control this by embedding negative-control periods, shrinkage on weak proxy links, and explicit posterior checks for proxy-only explanations. A minimal validation benchmark would pair periodic reference sampling with temporary continuous direct-reading instruments in several work zones over a few weeks, then compare reconstructed versus observed spike timing, peak magnitude, exceedance detection, and uncertainty calibration, with success defined by materially better short-term exceedance recall than periodic sampling alone at matched false-alarm rates.

We propose Attention-Bounded Bayesian Staircase with Micro-Burst Sampling, a psychophysical threshold estimation method designed for participants who cannot tolerate long, rigid testing sessions. The novelty gap is not merely that classic staircases are slow, because adaptive psychophysics already exists; the unresolved problem is that most adaptive procedures still assume sustained engagement, fixed trial pacing, and stable response quality across many reversals, which fails in children, frail older adults, neurological patients, or bed-bound participants. Our method addresses this by replacing long continuous staircases with short, uncertainty-targeted trial bursts separated by optional rest windows, while a hierarchical Bayesian state model jointly infers sensory threshold, lapse rate, fatigue trend, and momentary disengagement from both responses and response times. This explicitly rejects the trivial explanation that smaller step sizes or fewer trials alone solve the problem, because those changes usually trade precision for speed without modeling why data quality deteriorates. The core mechanism is a risk-aware controller that chooses the next stimulus intensity only when the expected information gain exceeds an attention-cost budget; otherwise it terminates early with calibrated posterior uncertainty or switches to a more diagnostic contrast level. Expected impact is a clinically feasible threshold test that preserves inferential quality under sparse, noisy, interrupted data and therefore broadens access to psychophysics outside ideal laboratory conditions. The main risk is model misspecification, especially if fatigue and sensory sensitivity become confounded, so the minimal convincing benchmark is a prospective comparison against a standard QUEST or transformed up-down staircase in adults tested under experimentally imposed interruption and time limits, with success defined by equal or better threshold error against a high-trial reference, at least 35% fewer trials, and tighter uncertainty calibration under dropout.

We propose Expertise Routing with Dissent-Aware Synthesis, a platform protocol that treats large-group collaboration not as a simple averaging problem but as a dynamic allocation problem in which different subproblems require different constellations of expertise. The novelty gap is that most collective-intelligence systems assume cognitive bottlenecks arise mainly from insufficient participation, poor incentives, or lack of recommendation quality; however, these are false-positive explanations when the real failure is that platforms collapse heterogeneous knowledge into a single undifferentiated discussion stream, allowing fluent generalists and early dominant frames to crowd out specialized but crucial contributions. Our mechanism first decomposes a shared task into evolving micro-claims, uncertainty flags, and evidence requests, then learns a bipartite routing graph between contributors and micro-claims using a joint signal of demonstrated domain competence, cross-domain translation ability, and disagreement productivity. Instead of ranking people globally, the system forms rotating synthesis cells that must include at least one high-fit specialist, one bridge contributor from an adjacent field, and one calibrated dissenter whose role is to surface incompatible assumptions before convergence. A lightweight aggregation layer then merges local syntheses only when claim-level confidence and diversity thresholds are met, reducing premature consensus while preserving scalability. The expected advantage is better use of dispersed expertise, more accurate integration of minority knowledge, and fewer coordination failures in large collaborations without requiring unrealistic full attention from all participants. The main risk is over-fragmentation, where decomposition and routing create siloed micro-deliberations or reward performative disagreement; we address this through merger triggers, redundancy checks, and penalties for dissent that does not improve downstream prediction or explanation quality. A minimal validation benchmark would compare this protocol against threaded discussion and upvote-based expert ranking on complex collaborative forecasting or policy-design tasks, measuring final solution accuracy, minority-signal retention, integration quality, participation load, and time to stable consensus.

We propose Boundary-Consistent Neural Atlas Elements, a PDE solver that decomposes an irregular domain into a learned atlas of overlapping curvilinear patches whose local coordinates are jointly optimized with the solution field and stitched together by physics-constrained interface conditions. The novelty gap is that most current approaches either embed the domain in a regular grid and pay a large penalty near jagged boundaries, or rely on expensive meshing and hand-designed basis functions; simply using more expressive neural operators or signed-distance penalties is a false positive because those methods still blur boundary layers, leak errors across narrow channels, or depend on geometry discretizations that become unstable under small shape irregularities. Our mechanism is to learn patch maps from the irregular geometry to near-rectangular reference cells, solve the PDE locally with shared spectral blocks in each cell, and enforce boundary conditions through a dual residual that separately penalizes physical boundary mismatch and cross-patch flux inconsistency, while an uncertainty gate downweights patches whose coordinate distortion exceeds a calibrated threshold. This should improve accuracy on complex geometries because local spectral structure is retained without requiring a globally regular parameterization, yet feasibility remains high since the method only needs boundary samples, PDE residual evaluations, and lightweight overlap constraints rather than a high-quality conforming mesh. The main risk is that patch learning may collapse or produce poorly conditioned overlaps in domains with re-entrant corners or extremely thin features; we control this by distortion regularization, topology-aware patch seeding, and rejecting degenerate atlases before full training.
