idea: We propose a regime-aware adaptive simulation-optimization framework for complex operational systems such as manufacturing lines or warehouse networks operating under shifting demand, failures, and congestion. The core mechanism combines a discrete-event simulator with online latent-regime inference over streaming operational signals, a bank of mode-specific surrogate models, and an uncertainty-triggered budget allocator that selectively runs expensive simulations when the current regime is ambiguous or the decision impact is high. Unlike static surrogate-based simulation optimization or generic robust optimization, the method explicitly coordinates regime detection, surrogate switching, and adaptive resampling so that optimization remains stable when the environment is nonstationary and rare transitions dominate downstream cost. The approach is feasible because it only requires event logs already available in many operational settings and can be implemented with standard change-point detection, probabilistic surrogates, and receding-horizon search. Expected impact is improved sample efficiency and more reliable scheduling or control under variability without requiring a uniformly large simulation budget. The main risk is that noisy or delayed observations may cause incorrect regime assignments and oscillatory decisions, reducing any benefit from adaptation. A minimal validation experiment would compare this method against static simulation optimization and distributionally robust optimization under equal compute budgets on a calibrated discrete-event benchmark with injected demand surges and machine-failure shifts, measuring cost, throughput, adaptation lag, and robustness across random seeds.

idea: We propose a climate-adaptive marine protected area planning framework that redesigns MPA zoning on a fixed multi-year review cycle rather than treating protection as static. The system fuses public spatiotemporal layers for habitat extent, sea-surface temperature anomalies, chlorophyll, fishing effort, pollution proxies, and existing protected-area boundaries with forecasts of species redistribution and larval connectivity. A robust multi-objective optimizer then selects no-take, limited-take, and restoration zones to maximize expected biodiversity persistence, climate-refugia coverage, and connectivity while minimizing conflict with fisheries, enforcement burden, and zoning turnover, so recommendations remain ecologically responsive but administratively realistic. The key novelty is integrating climate refugia, dynamic human pressure, and governance frictions in one adaptive decision loop instead of optimizing reserve placement once under static assumptions. The approach is feasible for a single coastal region because the required inputs are increasingly available from remote sensing, habitat maps, AIS-derived fishing data, and existing conservation inventories. Its expected impact is a more credible path to expanding insufficient MPA coverage while improving adaptive management under warming, habitat loss, and overexploitation. The main risk is that forecast error or sparse biodiversity observations could overstate benefits, especially if species shifts are poorly estimated. A minimal validation would use hindcasting: optimize zoning from earlier years, then test whether the selected network better covers later observed or modeled habitats, refugia, and connectivity than static area-target and biodiversity-only comparisons under the same spatial budget.

idea: We propose an interpretable multimodal batch digital twin for pharmaceutical manufacturing that improves batch-to-batch consistency by predicting critical quality attribute (CQA) risk early enough to support corrective action within validated operating limits. The system would fuse routinely available Process Analytical Technology (PAT) sensor trajectories, recipe and event logs from manufacturing execution systems, raw-material descriptors, and equipment-context variables to estimate a latent batch state over time, then use that state to forecast final CQA deviation or out-of-specification risk from partial batch trajectories. Novelty comes from combining trajectory-aware soft sensing with compliance-aware attribution: instead of issuing opaque control commands, the model would rank likely contributing critical process parameters (CPPs) and generate constrained what-if analyses that recommend only adjustments consistent with Quality by Design design-space boundaries and standard operating procedures. This makes the approach more feasible for regulated deployment than black-box adaptive control while still offering actionable early warning and root-cause support in unit operations such as granulation or blending. Expected impact is fewer failed batches, faster investigations, and more consistent product quality without changing existing release frameworks. The main risk is that historical failure cases may be sparse and multimodal plant data may be asynchronous or incomplete, which could weaken generalization and attribution credibility. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively compare partial-batch CQA-risk prediction and deviation lead time against SPC and PLS comparisons on historical batches from one high-impact unit operation.

idea: We propose a regime-aware multi-view probabilistic forecasting framework for volatile financial markets that predicts full return distributions rather than only point estimates by fusing three complementary signals: a temporal encoder over historical prices and volumes, a dynamic cross-asset graph module that tracks evolving dependence and contagion structure, and a timestamp-aligned text and macro encoder that captures exogenous news and policy shocks. A latent market-state mechanism modulates the fusion weights and predictive uncertainty so that the model can adapt differently during crisis, recovery, and calm regimes, addressing the core failure of stationary forecasters under structural breaks and heavy tails. The novelty is not any single modality, but the joint combination of dynamic relational structure, exogenous event signals, and regime-dependent calibration in one modular architecture that remains feasible with public equity, macroeconomic, and news datasets and can be trained with standard rolling windows. Expected impact is more reliable risk intervals, better calibrated tail forecasts, and more robust support for downstream portfolio or hedging decisions under market instability. The main risk is overfitting noisy multimodal signals or introducing leakage through imperfect time alignment. A minimal validation experiment would compare this model against price-only probabilistic transformers and multimodal variants without latent regimes in a strict rolling backtest across calm and crisis periods, measuring CRPS or NLL together with interval coverage and calibration.

idea: We propose a physics-guided multisensor inversion framework for sea-ice thickness retrieval that explicitly models snow depth as a latent state rather than treating it as a fixed climatology correction. The method fuses radar freeboard, laser freeboard, and optional contextual features from SAR or passive microwave observations within a probabilistic model constrained by hydrostatic equilibrium and sensor-specific observation operators, so the system can jointly infer ice thickness, snow depth, and calibrated uncertainty. Its novelty is to exploit the complementary sensitivities of radar and laser altimetry to disentangle snow loading from ice freeboard while allowing weak priors from reanalysis or snow climatology to act only as soft regularizers where observations are sparse. This is feasible with partial supervision because sparse airborne snow and thickness measurements can be combined with self-consistency losses on collocated satellite observations, and regime-aware components can account for first-year versus multiyear ice differences. The expected impact is lower bias and better uncertainty quantification across regions and seasons where snow variability currently dominates retrieval error. The main risk is identifiability: co-registration errors, footprint mismatch, and imperfect assumptions about radar penetration or snow density may cause the model to rely too heavily on priors. A minimal validation experiment would compare the proposed system against radar-only, laser-only, and fixed-snow-climatology comparisons on a shared collocation dataset, with ablations on each sensor source and evaluation of both thickness error and uncertainty calibration.

idea: We propose a preservation-aware archaeological prospection framework that reduces unnecessary excavation by fusing non-invasive geophysical survey data, such as ground-penetrating radar, magnetometry, and electrical resistivity, with LiDAR-derived terrain models and aerial or satellite imagery to generate calibrated probability maps of buried cultural features. The core mechanism is a multimodal spatial model with modality-specific encoders, site-adaptive normalization for soil and instrument variation, and modality dropout so predictions remain usable when some sensors are unavailable; a lightweight uncertainty module then converts scores into excavation-triage recommendations, while attribution maps highlight which anomaly signatures, geometric regularities, and landscape cues supported each prediction. The novelty is not just higher detection accuracy, but decision support tailored to heritage preservation: the system is designed to rank micro-areas for minimal-disturbance verification, explicitly exposing confidence and explanatory evidence rather than replacing archaeologist judgment. The approach is feasible because the required sensing modalities and GIS workflows already exist in archaeological remote sensing practice, and weak supervision can be derived from known site plans, expert annotations, and limited trench records. The main risk is verification bias and cross-site confounding, where sparse labels or modern disturbance may mislead the model. A minimal validation experiment would use leave-one-site-out testing on several surveyed sites to measure calibration and how much excavation area is needed to recover a fixed fraction of known features versus single-modality comparisons.

idea: We propose a compostable supercapacitor for short-lifetime electronics that co-designs energy-storage performance and end-of-life degradation at the full-stack level rather than replacing only one plastic component. The device uses a cellulose-chitosan paper substrate for mechanical support, biomass-derived hierarchical porous carbon electrodes for double-layer charge storage, and an alginate or gelatin hydrogel containing a benign aqueous salt to provide ionic transport without persistent organic solvents. A thin humidity-tuned barrier layer is introduced as the key mechanism: during use it suppresses ambient water uptake, swelling, and leakage current, but under compost conditions it rapidly loses integrity, allowing the substrate to soften and the electrolyte network to disconnect so conductivity and capacitance collapse in a controlled way. The novelty is a materials-and-lifetime design rule that explicitly couples electrochemical stability during service with triggered loss of function after disposal, backed by a component-level biodegradability audit covering substrate, binder, electrolyte, and interfaces. This approach is feasible because all layers can be processed at low temperature from abundant bio-derived feedstocks and are better matched to aqueous supercapacitor chemistry than to high-energy battery architectures. Its expected impact is safer disposable power sources for smart packaging, environmental sensors, and medical patches with reduced persistent e-waste, though the main risk is that moisture resistance and compostability may be inversely coupled, causing premature self-discharge or weak degradation. A minimal validation experiment would compare devices with and without the barrier layer for capacitance retention and self-discharge under humid storage, then track mass loss and impedance growth during standardized compost exposure.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware Exoplanet Planetary Health Framework that replaces static habitability heuristics with a hierarchical Bayesian assessment of planetary health across interacting subsystems. Rather than asking only whether a planet lies in the habitable zone or may host liquid water, the framework maps sparse observables and inferred stellar-history variables into interpretable subsystem scores for climate stability, atmospheric retention, water persistence, geodynamic recycling, and radiation shielding, while explicitly propagating measurement noise, missing data, and prior uncertainty. The key novelty is to treat exoplanet habitability as a multidimensional health profile with uncertainty bars and failure-mode diagnostics, so astronomers can distinguish planets that appear similar under conventional Earth-similarity or equilibrium-temperature metrics but differ in resilience to volatile loss, stellar activity, or long-term climate collapse. Feasibility is supported by existing catalogs from Kepler, TESS, and follow-up spectroscopy, combined with established forward models for atmospheric escape, stellar evolution, and interior cooling. The expected impact is a more transparent target-prioritization tool for scarce telescope time and a principled way to identify which new measurements would most reduce uncertainty. The main risk is that poorly constrained latent variables, such as magnetic shielding or tectonic cycling, may make rankings sensitive to modeling assumptions. A minimal validation experiment would compare ranking shifts and uncertainty calibration against habitable-zone and Earth-similarity comparisons on terrestrial exoplanet catalogs, plus synthetic planets with known unstable versus stable regimes.

idea: We propose a query-aware energy-adaptive data pipeline for intermittently connected IoT devices that treats sensing, buffering, compression, and synchronization as a unified data-management problem rather than a pure duty-cycling problem. Each device maintains a lightweight utility score for buffered records using three signals that are feasible on embedded hardware: freshness decay, anomaly likelihood from simple local detectors, and relevance to downstream aggregates or alerting queries. Given current battery level, buffer occupancy, and a short-horizon prediction of connectivity opportunities, the device solves a small online scheduling decision: whether to sample at full or reduced rate, aggregate or compress selected records, defer low-value items, or transmit only the highest-utility subset during the next contact window. The novelty is in explicitly aligning synchronization semantics with query value under power and link uncertainty, aiming to minimize radio activations and bytes sent while maintaining bounded Age of Information, aggregate error, or event recall targets. This could improve the operational lifetime and reliability of remote monitoring deployments without requiring heavy models or new hardware. The main risk is that utility estimation or connectivity prediction may be too brittle across workloads, causing uneven quality degradation. A minimal validation would use trace-driven simulation with real outage and battery or harvesting traces, comparing against periodic upload, connectivity-aware threshold upload, and compression-only comparisons on energy, AoI, query error, anomaly recall, and buffer overflow rate.

idea: We propose a decision-aware, near-real-time system for monitoring floating marine plastic hotspots in coastal waters by fusing weak remote-sensing evidence with physical transport priors and sparse human observations. The model ingests satellite optical and SAR imagery, river discharge, tides, winds, surface currents, and delayed cleanup or citizen reports on a coastal spatiotemporal graph, and outputs hotspot probability maps, calibrated uncertainty, and ranked cleanup targets for the next 6-72 hours. The key novelty is to treat plastic monitoring as probabilistic hotspot inference under partial observability rather than as direct universal plastic recognition, allowing the system to combine ambiguous visual cues with ocean-drift dynamics and recent incident signals. Feasibility is supported by the growing availability of Earth observation streams, operational ocean products, and municipal cleanup logs, while the expected impact is improved lead time for cleanup deployment and more interpretable risk maps for regulators deciding where to allocate surveillance and mitigation resources. The main risk is confounding from foam, algae, wood, or oil, together with biased supervision concentrated near accessible shorelines, which could produce overconfident false alarms; accordingly, the model should support abstention in low-confidence regions. A minimal validation experiment would compare this multimodal physics-informed approach against remote-sensing-only, drift-only, and generic spatiotemporal forecasting comparisons on leave-one-region-out hotspot detection and short-horizon top-K cleanup targeting.

idea: We propose a workload-aware hierarchical compression system for edge-to-cloud telemetry, logs, and multimodal sensor streams that addresses the declining effectiveness of static compressors on high-volume, nonstationary data. The core mechanism combines lightweight modality-specific learned encoders with classical entropy coding, while an online controller selects chunk size, compression mode, and fidelity level for each incoming segment to maximize downstream utility under storage, bandwidth, and decode-latency budgets. Unlike prior compression methods that optimize only rate-distortion on fixed distributions, the novelty is a closed-loop systems design that explicitly adapts to distribution shift, changing query patterns, and task sensitivity, so critical segments for anomaly detection or forecasting can retain more semantic detail while routine segments are compressed more aggressively. The approach is feasible because it reuses existing neural codecs and mature entropy coders, adding a budgeted decision layer rather than requiring an entirely new compression stack, and can be deployed incrementally in observability or industrial monitoring pipelines. Its expected impact is lower end-to-end infrastructure cost without sacrificing operational usefulness of compressed data. The main risk is that adaptation overhead or task-specific tuning could offset practical gains, especially under strict latency constraints. A minimal validation experiment would stream a shifting telemetry dataset through the system and compare it against strong classical and learned comparisons on compression ratio, decode latency, controller overhead, and preserved anomaly-detection accuracy.

idea: We propose a representation-aware adaptive stoichiometry tutor that targets a persistent weakness of chemistry instruction: students often learn stoichiometric procedures as disconnected arithmetic and fail to coordinate balanced equations, mole ratios, unit analysis, and particulate meaning. The core mechanism is a short diagnostic sequence that classifies common misconception profiles, such as treating coefficients as masses, ignoring conservation constraints, or misreading limiting-reactant relationships, and then routes learners to matched scaffold pathways. Each pathway combines contrastive worked examples, step-level feedback, and prompts that explicitly translate among symbolic equations, quantitative calculations, and particulate diagrams, with scaffolds faded as students demonstrate stable accuracy. The novelty lies in making misconception-to-scaffold mapping explicit and chemistry-specific rather than offering generic practice or hinting, while remaining feasible through a rule-based web platform with a compact item bank and low teacher overhead. The expected impact is improved conceptual transfer across mole conversion, limiting reactant, and percent-yield tasks, especially for learners with weak proportional reasoning. The main risk is that brief diagnostics may misclassify students, reducing the value of personalization and making gains indistinguishable from extra practice time. A minimal validation study would compare this adaptive tutor with non-adaptive digital worked-example practice under matched time-on-task in an introductory chemistry unit, using pre/post and delayed assessments of procedural accuracy, explanation quality, representation translation, and reduction of specific misconception patterns.

idea: We propose a crop bioengineering strategy that improves Calvin-Benson cycle efficiency by dynamically increasing RuBP-regeneration capacity only when chloroplast energy supply is high, rather than relying on constitutive overexpression. The core construct would stack chloroplast-targeted SBPase and phosphoribulokinase, with optional inclusion of FBPase, under light- or redox-responsive regulatory control so enzyme abundance or activity rises during high irradiance and relaxes as light declines. The novelty is the shift from static Calvin-cycle enhancement to adaptive control designed for fluctuating field light, where many previous photosynthetic engineering gains are lost through metabolic imbalance, unnecessary protein cost, or poor transition performance. This design is feasible because the target enzymes are well characterized, their manipulation has prior precedent, and the proposed module remains compact enough for multigene transformation in staple crops such as rice or wheat. The expected impact is higher daytime carbon assimilation and better translation of photosynthetic gains into biomass and grain yield without chronic resource penalties. The main risk is that added Calvin-cycle capacity may still be masked by sink limitation or by weak and mistimed regulatory responses. A minimal validation experiment would compare dynamic SBPase-PRK lines against wild type and matched constitutive-expression controls under steady versus fluctuating light, measuring enzyme activity, gas exchange, chlorophyll fluorescence, and leaf carbohydrate accumulation to test whether adaptive RuBP-regeneration control specifically improves photosynthetic performance.

idea: We propose a task-aware prior-informed ultra-low-dose CT framework for children and other patients who undergo repeated follow-up imaging, aiming to reduce radiation exposure without sacrificing the clinical question that motivated the scan. The core mechanism is to reconstruct the current sparse-view or low-mAs CT from raw measurements while conditioning on the patient’s most recent prior CT through a change-sensitive fusion module that is explicitly designed to preserve interval differences rather than simply copy anatomy forward. Unlike conventional low-dose CT methods that optimize generic image similarity, the model is jointly trained with a downstream follow-up task such as lung nodule change detection or organ segmentation stability, and it outputs both a reconstructed image and an uncertainty map that highlights regions where aggressive dose reduction may be unreliable. The novelty is the combination of prior-scan conditioning, task-level supervision, and safeguards against pathology suppression in a clinically narrow repeated-scan setting that is realistic for retrospective study. Feasibility is high because many surveillance cohorts already contain serial standard-dose CTs that can be used to emulate lower-dose acquisition and train the system without changing scanner hardware. A minimal validation experiment would compare filtered back projection, iterative reconstruction, generic deep low-dose reconstruction, and the proposed method on a repeated-imaging cohort, measuring task accuracy and uncertainty calibration across dose levels and cases with newly appearing lesions. The main risk is that prior information could obscure new pathology if interval change is large.

idea: We propose GeoSymbolic Reasoner, a scientific discovery model designed to address the persistent weakness of current AI systems in spatial reasoning and abstract pattern recognition for drug and materials design. The core mechanism combines an SE(3)/E(n)-equivariant geometric encoder over molecular conformers, protein pockets, or crystal lattices with an explicit constraint reasoning layer that scores and propagates scientific relations such as symmetry consistency, chirality preservation, steric distance and angle feasibility, pocket-ligand complementarity, and lattice periodicity. The novelty is not another geometric backbone, but a neuro-symbolic interface that turns learned 3D representations into reusable relational abstractions and makes predictions conditional on physically meaningful structural rules. This is feasible because all components can be built on existing 3D datasets and strong equivariant architectures, while constraint modules can be trained with weak supervision or synthetic perturbations rather than requiring dense expert annotation. If successful, the approach could improve candidate prioritization, reduce scientifically implausible predictions, and transfer better across chemistry and materials domains. The main risk is that gains may come mainly from stronger inductive bias rather than genuine reasoning, or that hard constraints may destabilize training. A minimal validation experiment is to compare the full model against matched geometric comparisons on counterfactual chirality, symmetry, and pocket-fit diagnostics where only one spatial relation is changed and success requires scientifically coherent prediction shifts.

idea: We propose a heterogeneous exobiology exploration system in which a conventional rover is paired with one or more fast scouts, such as micro-aerial or hopping probes, to overcome the coverage bottleneck of rover-only missions while preserving the high-fidelity confirmation needed for biosignature search. The key mechanism is an uncertainty-aware scout-to-rover handoff policy: scouts rapidly screen large regions for weak biosignature proxies, update a probabilistic spatial field over candidate scientific value, and nominate follow-up targets only when the expected value of rover validation exceeds the mobility, energy, and delay cost of reaching them. Unlike generic multi-robot coverage methods, the formulation is centered on rare-target exobiology, explicitly modeling asymmetric sensor fidelity, false-negative control for subtle signals, traversability constraints, and communication latency. The approach is feasible because it relies on lightweight Bayesian belief updates and receding-horizon planning rather than full map-wide optimization, allowing onboard adaptation under mission resource limits. If successful, it could increase validated discoveries per sol and reduce wasted rover traverses in sparse, uncertain terrains. The main risk is that prescreening may filter out scientifically important but ambiguous sites if biosignature priors or proxy models are poorly calibrated. A minimal validation experiment would compare rover-only search, naive scout-rover teaming, and the proposed uncertainty-aware coordination in simulated planetary terrains with sparse clustered targets, measuring time-to-first-validated target, missed high-value sites, and discovery yield under fixed energy budgets.

idea: We propose an all-optical closed-loop platform for inducing and measuring synapse-specific plasticity in vivo with millisecond temporal control and spine-level spatial precision during behavior. The system would combine two-photon imaging of identified dendritic spines expressing calcium or glutamate sensors with holographic optogenetic stimulation targeted to presynaptic ensembles and postsynaptic dendritic compartments, while a low-latency controller detects predefined pre-post activity patterns and triggers stimulation to impose STDP-like timing rules. This mechanism is novel because it unifies three capabilities that are usually separated across ex vivo and bulk in vivo methods: precise timing of induction, subcellular targeting of individual synapses, and longitudinal tracking of how local changes propagate to population coding and memory performance. Feasibility is supported by existing components in two-photon spine imaging, holographic stimulation, and real-time neural event detection, but their integration is the central engineering advance. The expected impact is a causal framework for testing how single-synapse LTP or LTD contributes to learning, memory updating, and circuit dysfunction in neurological disease models. The main risk is that motion, optical scatter, or dendritic nonlinearities could reduce true single-spine specificity and confound synaptic changes with altered excitability. A minimal validation experiment would target a small set of hippocampal or cortical spines in behaving mice, vary pre-post stimulation intervals, and compare stimulated spines, neighboring unstimulated spines, and sham controls for predicted sign-specific functional or structural plasticity over hours to days.

idea: We propose a community-augmented coastal groundwater salinity surveillance framework that expands sparse official monitoring by combining agency well records with participatory measurements from household and private wells using low-cost electrical conductivity and total dissolved solids kits, plus a smaller calibration subset of lab-analyzed chloride samples. These heterogeneous observations are fused in a hierarchical spatiotemporal model with coastal drivers such as shoreline distance, elevation, tidal and sea-level anomalies, land use, and groundwater withdrawal proxies to produce neighborhood-scale salinization risk maps with explicit uncertainty and early-warning alerts for local utilities and communities. The core novelty is the tight integration of community participation with uncertainty-aware statistical data fusion, allowing broader and more equitable monitoring coverage without requiring a full mechanistic groundwater model or dense sensor infrastructure. The approach is feasible because low-cost field proxies can support frequent distributed sampling, while limited laboratory confirmation can anchor interpretation and reduce confusion between seawater intrusion and other contamination sources. Expected impact is improved detection of localized freshwater threats in underserved coastal areas, enabling more timely testing, mitigation, and adaptation planning. The main risk is that citizen-collected data may be noisy and spatially biased toward better-resourced neighborhoods, which could distort estimates if not modeled carefully. A minimal validation experiment would compare agency-only monitoring against the community-augmented system on held-out official and lab-confirmed samples, evaluating gains in spatial coverage, hotspot recall, and uncertainty calibration under realistic participation bias.

idea: We propose a misconception-driven, multi-representation learning environment for introductory set theory that targets the central bottleneck in student understanding: translating between formal notation and mental models. The system presents each concept, such as membership, subset, equality, the empty set, singleton sets, power sets, and finite cardinality, through tightly synchronized views: symbolic expressions, Euler/Venn-style diagrams where appropriate, concrete finite examples, and short natural-language explanations. Rather than only showing multiple views, it actively prompts students to move among them by judging statements, constructing examples or counterexamples, and giving brief self-explanations, while a rule-based misconception model detects common confusions such as element versus subset or empty set versus singleton containing the empty set and triggers targeted feedback. The novelty is not generic adaptivity but concept-specific representational alignment designed to build proof readiness by making definitions operational across views. The approach is feasible because it can be scoped to foundational topics, finite examples, and instructor-authored feedback templates with formal constraints, avoiding dependence on unconstrained generation. Expected impact is improved conceptual understanding and stronger transfer to short definition-based reasoning tasks. The main risk is that students may learn to interpret diagrams without improving formal reasoning, especially for concepts like power sets. A minimal validation experiment would compare this system against static worked examples and static visual aids in a pre/post study using misconception-sensitive concept inventory items plus short explanation and counterexample tasks.

idea: We propose a low-carbon electro-bioleaching platform that recovers critical minerals from mine tailings and low-grade ores, turning existing waste stocks into a secondary resource while reducing the energy, water, and land impacts of new extraction. The core mechanism couples acid-tolerant microbial consortia that selectively mobilize target metals such as copper, nickel, or lithium from heterogeneous mineral matrices with a downstream electrochemical separation unit that captures the dissolved metals, regenerates leaching chemistry, and minimizes fresh reagent demand under renewable electricity operation. The novelty is the tight integration of biological mobilization, electrochemical selectivity, and circular reagent management within a single waste-to-resource process optimized for variable feedstocks rather than virgin ore. Feasibility is supported by the maturity of both bioleaching and electrowinning components, but the key research contribution is their co-design around tailings heterogeneity, residual toxicity reduction, and system-level sustainability metrics. If successful, the approach could expand critical-mineral supply, lower lifecycle emissions, and reduce legacy mining liabilities. The main risk is that slow bioleaching kinetics and site-specific mineralogy may limit throughput or selectivity enough to erode economic advantage. A minimal validation experiment would compare the integrated process on two compositionally distinct tailings samples against conventional hydrometallurgical recovery, measuring metal yield, impurity rejection, energy per kilogram recovered, reagent loss, water use, and residual solid toxicity under matched system boundaries.

idea: We propose a noise-aware active-space embedding framework for quantum simulation of large molecular systems that treats qubit count and hardware noise as a single coupled resource-allocation problem rather than independent bottlenecks. A classical pre-screening stage estimates orbital entanglement and energy sensitivity to select a compact, strongly correlated active region, while the weakly correlated environment is handled by a lower-cost embedding model. The active region is then solved on quantum hardware with a shallow, symmetry-preserving variational ansatz, and error-mitigation effort is allocated adaptively across Hamiltonian terms and measurements according to each component’s propagated contribution to total-energy uncertainty. The key novelty is this joint policy: scarce qubits, circuit depth, shots, and mitigation overhead are concentrated only where both chemical correlation and noise sensitivity are highest, instead of using uniform truncation or uniform mitigation. This design is feasible on near-term devices because it reduces circuit size before mitigation is applied and uses standard ingredients such as active-space chemistry, variational solvers, and symmetry checks within a coordinated loop. If successful, it could improve accuracy per qubit and per shot for molecules that are too large for direct encodings. The main risk is that imperfect active-space selection or embedding error may dominate before mitigation helps. A minimal validation would benchmark small-to-medium molecular families under fixed qubit and shot budgets against unmitigated active-space VQE, uniform-mitigation variants, and embedding-only classical comparisons, while decomposing truncation and residual noise errors.

idea: We propose a mechanism-aware precision nutrition framework that replaces population-average dietary advice with person-specific meal recommendation based on gut microbiome function, host phenotype, and metabolic state. The core model represents each candidate meal by its nutrient composition and food context, and each individual by comparison clinical covariates, metabolomic markers, and microbial functional pathways rather than raw taxonomy alone. A multimodal graph or latent-factor architecture then predicts a distribution of likely responses, such as postprandial glycemia, lipid excursions, inflammatory signals, or gastrointestinal tolerance, while exposing pathway-level contributors that explain why the same nutrient profile may help one person and harm another. Recommendations are produced by constrained optimization over candidate meals, balancing predicted benefit with nutritional adequacy, uncertainty, and simple adherence constraints so the system does not overfit noisy biomarkers or propose impractical diets. The novelty is the combination of functional microbiome features, interpretable response mechanisms, and uncertainty-aware recommendation rather than black-box prediction alone. The approach is feasible with existing precision nutrition cohorts that include meal logs, microbiome sequencing, and metabolic readouts. Its expected impact is more reliable and biologically grounded dietary guidance, though the main risk is confounding and poor cross-cohort generalization from noisy diet and microbiome measurements. A minimal validation experiment would compare temporal-holdout meal-response prediction and recommendation quality against standard guidelines, nutrient-only rules, and host-only models.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware, component-level defect triage system for civil infrastructure inspection that fuses UAV RGB imagery, infrared thermography, and sparse structural-response signals within a lightweight asset graph representing beams, joints, decks, linings, and their physical adjacency. Each component node aggregates cross-modal evidence and inspection history, while a graph-based fusion model predicts defect presence, severity, and a follow-up priority score, with calibrated uncertainty and abstention when evidence is weak or modalities are missing. The novelty is not another standalone crack detector, but a conservative decision-support pipeline that jointly reasons over visible and partially hidden deterioration, uses graph context to propagate risk across connected components, and produces auditable explanations linking each recommendation to concrete observations. The approach is feasible because most agencies already collect some combination of visual inspection imagery, thermal scans, and maintenance records, and sparse vibration or strain data can be incorporated when available without making the system dependent on dense instrumentation. Expected impact is reduced inspection time and cost through better prioritization of high-risk regions while preserving human oversight. The main risk is unreliable alignment and supervision across modalities and time, especially for hidden defects such as delamination or corrosion. A minimal validation experiment would compare this system against single-modality vision and late-fusion comparisons on a bridge or tunnel dataset, measuring component-level localization, severity ranking, uncertainty calibration, and top-k defect recovery under a fixed inspection budget.

idea: We propose a process-aware multimodal spatiotemporal framework for monitoring permafrost methane that converts sparse, localized field observations into region-scale probabilistic hotspot maps across the thaw season. The model would fuse Sentinel-1 SAR for inundation and surface structure, optical and thermal imagery for vegetation and land-surface temperature, topography and hydrologic indices for flow accumulation and wetness, and meteorological or reanalysis variables for thaw dynamics, then align these predictors with chamber and eddy-covariance measurements through a hierarchical supervision scheme that accounts for point-to-pixel scale mismatch. Rather than predicting absolute methane flux everywhere, the system would estimate hotspot probability or ordinal emission classes with calibrated uncertainty, which is more defensible under sparse supervision and more useful for targeting follow-up sampling. The main novelty is the combination of cross-scale label aggregation, temporal thaw-state modeling, and uncertainty-aware multi-sensor fusion tailored to permafrost landscapes where emissions are highly episodic and heterogeneous. The approach is feasible because all major predictor streams are already available at broad Arctic coverage, while sparse field measurements can supervise relative-risk learning. Its expected impact is a practical monitoring layer for identifying emerging methane hotspots and prioritizing observations, though the main risk is geographic sampling bias that could cause the model to learn site-selection artifacts. A minimal validation would hold out entire sites and years, then test hotspot retrieval and uncertainty calibration against independent methane campaigns.

idea: We propose a morphology-aware closed-loop crystallization framework for pharmaceutical purification that combines a reduced-order mechanistic crystal-growth model with in situ process analytical technology to stabilize crystal habit despite batch disturbances. Real-time ATR-FTIR or Raman estimates of supersaturation are fused with FBRM and inline imaging signals to infer both particle population evolution and habit descriptors such as aspect ratio and facet prevalence, and a model-predictive controller then adjusts cooling rate, antisolvent feed, and agitation to keep the process inside a morphology-stable operating window. The novelty is to target morphology consistency directly, rather than only polymorph or particle size, while embedding mechanistic priors so the controller can adapt to impurity shifts and mixing variability with less retraining than purely data-driven recipes. This is feasible because the sensing stack and control handles already exist in many crystallization setups, and the model can be calibrated from standard seeded-batch experiments. If successful, the approach could reduce batch-to-batch variation in dissolution, filterability, drying, and downstream handling without relying on heavy additive screening that may complicate regulatory acceptance. The main risk is that habit descriptors may be only indirectly observable and may transfer poorly across APIs with different facet-growth mechanisms. A minimal validation would compare open-loop versus closed-loop seeded antisolvent crystallization for two morphology-sensitive APIs under intentional impurity or mixing disturbances, measuring image-based habit variance while confirming unchanged polymorph and acceptable purity.

idea: We propose Contract-FMEA, a standardized failure-mode identification and assessment framework for smart contracts that adapts Failure Mode and Effects Analysis to DeFi systems. Instead of introducing another detector for isolated bugs, the framework organizes risks into a hierarchical schema spanning implementation flaws, access-control mistakes, reentrancy and logic errors, oracle and governance dependencies, upgradeability hazards, and cross-contract composability failures, then links each failure mode to explicit observable evidence from code structure, privilege assignments, external-call patterns, asset exposure, and protocol dependencies. An interaction-aware graph over contracts, privileged actors, assets, proxies, and price feeds is used to estimate not only local exploitability but also potential blast radius, while a reproducible scoring rubric operationalizes likelihood, impact, and detectability so that contract and protocol risks can be compared in a uniform way. The novelty is the combination of software-engineering-style failure analysis with DeFi-specific dependency modeling and standardized scoring, which is feasible because it can be built on existing static analysis outputs, audit artifacts, and public incident reports rather than requiring new formal methods from scratch. The expected impact is more consistent auditing, triage, and governance of smart-contract risk, although the main risk is subjective or noisy labeling of root causes and severity. A minimal validation experiment would map a public corpus of audited contracts and known exploit cases into the schema and test coverage and ranking agreement against expert audit judgments.

idea: We propose a proactive confidentiality-preserving access mediation layer for electronic health records that sits on top of existing role-based access control and evaluates each record request at the moment of access rather than after harm has occurred. The system would compute an interpretable risk score from workflow-grounded signals such as active encounter linkage, patient-provider relationship strength, department and role consistency, prior access patterns, shift timing, recent team activity, and explicit emergency indicators. Instead of a binary allow/deny decision, the score would trigger graded responses including normal access, required justification, limited minimum-necessary record views, or break-glass escalation with enhanced logging, thereby reducing unnecessary exposure while preserving care continuity. The novelty is the combination of pre-access risk assessment with minimum-necessary exposure and override-aware intervention policies, moving beyond reactive audit review and generic anomaly detection toward clinically contextualized prevention. Feasibility is high because the required inputs already exist in most EHR audit trails, scheduling systems, and encounter metadata, and deployment can begin as a policy layer without replacing the underlying EHR. Expected impact is earlier interception of curiosity-driven or inappropriate insider access with more manageable compliance workflows. The main risk is false positives that could burden legitimate cross-coverage or atypical care. A minimal validation would replay de-identified historical audit logs to estimate how often risky accesses would be flagged or stepped up, especially in emergency and rare legitimate scenarios.

idea: We propose a chronology-aware hierarchical Bayesian framework for reconstructing past human migration corridors while explicitly separating demic movement from non-demic cultural exchange. The model represents sites and populations as a spatiotemporal graph whose latent edges are typed as migration, exchange, or both, and fuses multiple evidence streams that carry different signatures of these processes: ancient DNA affinity informs shared ancestry, strontium or oxygen isotopes indicate individual mobility, radiocarbon dates constrain temporal directionality, artifact-style similarity and raw material provenance capture cultural transmission, and geographic cost surfaces encode plausible movement routes across landscapes. Novelty comes from assigning each modality a distinct probabilistic contribution to migration versus exchange edges, allowing uncertainty to propagate into posterior maps of likely routes, exchange hubs, and ambiguous regions rather than collapsing all similarity into a single explanation. The approach is feasible because it uses data types already common in archaeological case studies and remains interpretable enough for domain experts to inspect priors and edge decompositions. Its main impact would be a more defensible reconstruction of migration and interaction histories across poorly documented regions. The main risk is weak identifiability when evidence is sparse or temporally misaligned. A minimal validation experiment would test recovery of known latent migration and exchange patterns in synthetic landscapes under controlled missingness and dating error.

idea: We propose an operando electrochemistry platform that combines synchronized atomic-resolution surface imaging with chemically specific spectroscopy in a shared microfluidic cell, then reconstructs joint structural and chemical trajectories with a physics-constrained fusion model. The core mechanism is to acquire intermittent high-resolution snapshots of surface reconstruction by EC-STM or liquid-cell STEM at predefined potentials while continuously recording co-registered spectroscopic signals such as XAS, Raman, or SEIRAS under the same waveform, electrolyte, and current response. A state-space inference layer links these streams through electrochemical constraints, crystallographic priors, mass balance, and temporal continuity to estimate lattice-scale motifs, oxidation states, and adsorbate populations without requiring any single modality to directly measure all quantities. The novelty is not just correlative hardware, but explicit modeling of the mismatch in spatial resolution, probing depth, and sampling rate that has limited prior operando studies. Feasibility is supported by existing components from operando microscopy, spectroscopy, and microfluidic electrochemical cells, though the main risk is that beam, tip, or registration artifacts could dominate the inferred chemistry. A minimal validation experiment would target a well-studied potential-dependent surface transition, such as Pt oxide formation and reduction, and test whether the fused reconstruction recovers known structural and oxidation-state changes more faithfully than either modality alone.

Problem: Current methods for studying electrochemical surfaces under operating conditions do not provide simultaneous atomic-scale structural and chemical information.

idea: We propose a physics-informed amortized Bayesian inference framework for supermassive black hole spin estimation that replaces source-by-source expensive forward fitting with an offline-trained posterior estimator operating on joint X-ray reflection spectra and reverberation-lag features. The core mechanism is to generate large synthetic populations from established relativistic reflection and reverberation simulators while varying spin together with nuisance factors such as inclination, ionization, disk density, absorption, and coronal height, then train a neural simulation-based inference model to return calibrated spin posteriors rather than point predictions. The novelty is not a purely data-driven spin regressor, but a fast posterior-approximation layer that explicitly marginalizes astrophysical degeneracies and uses timing information to break ambiguities that spectroscopy alone often leaves unresolved. Feasibility is supported by existing simulator libraries and archival AGN datasets that already contain high-quality spectra and, for a smaller subset, timing measurements. Expected impact is to make uncertainty-aware spin inference scalable to larger AGN samples and to improve follow-up prioritization for observatories such as XRISM, Athena, and IXPE. The main risk is simulator-to-reality mismatch, which could produce overconfident posteriors if absorption complexity or disk/corona physics are misspecified. A minimal validation experiment would compare spectra-only and joint spectral-timing versions against conventional MCMC reflection fitting on archival AGN and held-out synthetic data, measuring posterior agreement, coverage, and runtime.
task_context:

Problem: Current methods for estimating supermassive black hole spin are inefficient or limited.

idea: We propose a compact sparse-array micro-sonar for small autonomous underwater vehicles that co-designs miniaturized acoustic hardware and low-power perception rather than scaling down a conventional imaging sonar. The system uses a physically small package of few piezoelectric or MEMS-assisted transducers arranged as a sparse aperture, transmits coded low-duty-cycle pulses instead of high-energy broad insonification, and reconstructs short-range range-angle occupancy maps through a lightweight model-based decoder with optional learned priors constrained to embedded compute budgets. The core novelty is treating payload volume, battery draw, and onboard latency as first-class design variables together with sensing quality: sparse geometry reduces array size, coded transmission preserves recoverable information at lower acoustic energy, and reconstruction compensates for lost aperture without requiring server-class processing. This is feasible for obstacle avoidance and local mapping because many AUV missions only need reliable perception over limited ranges in cluttered spaces rather than full long-range survey sonar performance. If successful, the approach could expand sonar adoption in low-cost AUVs for inspection, cave exploration, and environmental monitoring. The main risk is that reduced source level and aperture may interact badly with reverberation, motion, and multipath, causing reconstruction failures that erase system-level efficiency gains. A minimal validation experiment is a matched-range tank test against a compact conventional sonar on obstacle detection and local occupancy mapping, reporting accuracy together with sensor mass, package volume, peak and average power, and onboard latency.

idea: This project proposes an urban lake microplastic vulnerability framework that explains how specific urban source structures, rather than urbanization intensity alone, drive ecological exposure across lake compartments. The core mechanism links stormwater outfalls, wastewater influence, shoreline recreation, and atmospheric deposition to hydrologic transport and retention processes that concentrate different particle types in surface water, littoral zones, and sediments, where plankton, benthic invertebrates, fish, and microbial communities are exposed. The novelty is a policy-facing source-to-compartment-to-receptor model that integrates limnological sampling with GIS indicators of drainage connectivity, impervious cover, shoreline use, and lake morphology to identify actionable pathways and hotspots. The design is feasible because it relies on standard microplastic QA/QC protocols, routine limnological covariates, drainage maps, and comparative sampling across a small set of urban lakes with contrasting hydrologic connectivity and retention characteristics. Expected impact is a decision tool that helps municipalities rank interventions such as stormwater retrofits, wastewater upgrades, or shoreline management according to the pathways most likely to reduce ecological burden. The main risk is confounding from co-pollutants and methodological inconsistency in microplastic measurement, which could weaken causal interpretation. A minimal validation experiment would compare whether source connectivity and retention metrics predict cross-compartment microplastic burdens better than coarse urban land-use measures in a matched multi-lake observational study.
task_context:

idea: We propose a hybrid mechanistic graph state-space model for understanding and predicting partially observed complex systems in which many interacting components generate nonlinear feedback, rare cascades, and regime shifts. The model learns latent node states, a sparse time-varying interaction graph, and probabilistic transition dynamics from noisy multivariate observations, while soft mechanistic constraints enforce stability, conservation, or monotone flow patterns when appropriate. A regime-aware inference module identifies latent operating modes and early-warning precursors of critical transitions, and an action-conditioned rollout head estimates how candidate local interventions alter downstream system-wide risk, enabling mitigation ranking with calibrated uncertainty rather than point forecasts alone. The novelty is the integration of structure learning, mechanistic regularization, rare-event anticipation, and decision-oriented counterfactual simulation in one framework that does not require fully known governing equations. The approach is feasible because each component can be implemented with existing graph neural state-space and variational inference machinery, and trained on both simulators and observational benchmarks. Expected impact is improved forecasting and more trustworthy intervention prioritization for networked ecological, infrastructural, or socioeconomic systems. The main risk is misspecified mechanistic priors or learned graphs acting as predictive surrogates instead of true interactions. A minimal validation experiment would test the model on a controlled cascade simulator with partial observability and noisy interventions, comparing forecast calibration, transition-detection lead time, and intervention-ranking regret against sequence, graph, and heuristic comparisons.

Problem: Understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems is crucial but difficult, limiting mitigation efforts.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware adaptive sequencing framework for mastery-based education that replaces static, one-size-fits-all lesson progressions with individualized next-activity and feedback decisions derived from an interpretable learner state. The system maintains concept-level mastery estimates over prerequisite skills together with calibrated uncertainty, allowing it to distinguish between true non-mastery and lack of evidence; it then selects the next exercise difficulty, pacing, and feedback intensity by balancing expected learning gain, risk of premature advancement, and excess remediation under simple instructor-set constraints. The novelty is not personalization alone, but using decision-aware uncertainty as a first-class signal for pedagogical action selection rather than merely for prediction, while preserving inspectability through human-readable concept states and overrideable policy thresholds. The approach is feasible with existing tutoring or online course interaction logs because it can be trained from sequential student-response data and evaluated through offline replay or a validated simulator without requiring new classroom deployment. Its expected impact is improved learning efficiency, better cold-start support, and more equitable progression for heterogeneous learners whose prior knowledge and response reliability differ substantially. A main risk is that uncertainty may correlate with underrepresented or sparse-data students, unintentionally slowing their advancement, so fairness-aware constraints and subgroup analysis are necessary. A minimal validation experiment would compare this policy against static curricula, rule-based mastery progression, and standard knowledge-tracing-driven greedy sequencing on an existing tutoring dataset using time-to-mastery, excess practice, advancement calibration, and subgroup disparity metrics.

idea: We propose a function-linked soil ecotoxicology study testing whether environmentally realistic, weathered microplastic fibers and fragments disrupt subterranean invertebrates and the ecosystem processes they drive in agricultural soils. The core mechanism is that particle shape and aging state alter ingestion, cuticle and burrow contact, and soil pore structure, thereby changing earthworm and collembolan behavior, oxidative-stress responses, and feeding activity, with downstream effects on litter decomposition, aggregate stability, and mineral nitrogen release. The novelty lies in moving beyond common acute single-species toxicity assays with pristine beads toward a two-taxon microcosm design that explicitly connects organism-level responses to soil-function outcomes under field-plausible exposure conditions. The study is feasible because it can be run in one standardized loam soil with a modest concentration gradient and two particle classes, while using established endpoints such as avoidance or burrowing, reproduction, litter mass loss, wet-aggregate stability, and ammonium or nitrate flux. Its expected impact is to clarify whether microplastics threaten soil health mainly through direct invertebrate stress, habitat modification, or both, informing risk assessment for agricultural systems. The main risk is confounding from polymer additives or bulk soil physical changes rather than particle shape itself, so the minimal validation experiment should compare weathered fibers versus fragments and particle-free leachate controls in short-term earthworm and collembolan microcosms before scaling to longer function assays.

idea: We propose a physics-informed unrolled reconstruction framework for low-dose CT that targets the core clinical tradeoff between radiation reduction and poor soft-tissue conspicuity. The model embeds a Poisson-based measurement likelihood and scanner-aware data-consistency steps inside an iterative neural reconstruction pipeline, then adds a soft-tissue structure module that emphasizes low-contrast organ boundaries and subtle lesion interfaces through anatomy-preserving gradient, local contrast, and cross-scale feature constraints. A lightweight uncertainty head is trained jointly to identify regions where enhancement may be unreliable, addressing the main safety risk that learned restoration can hallucinate or shift diagnostically important soft-tissue detail while improving image appearance. The key novelty is to couple explicit CT acquisition physics with soft-tissue-specific preservation objectives rather than optimizing only global fidelity metrics, making the approach feasible for retrospective datasets with routine or simulated paired low-dose scans and without requiring contrast agents or dual-energy hardware. Expected impact is a more deployable path to dose reduction that preserves clinically relevant visibility in non-contrast and low-contrast settings such as abdominal or thoracic soft tissues. A minimal validation experiment would compare the method against model-based iterative reconstruction, a generic deep denoiser, and a standard unrolled comparison on paired low-dose CT, reporting not only PSNR and SSIM but also local contrast-to-noise ratio, boundary accuracy for one soft-tissue segmentation task, and calibration of uncertainty in enhanced regions.

idea: We propose a mechanism-aware multimodal framework for drug discovery that predicts target engagement, off-target liabilities, and cell-context phenotypic effects by jointly modeling three complementary views of a compound: its molecular graph, the sequence or structure representation of candidate proteins, and perturbation-response signatures from treated cells. The core mechanism is a shared representation space in which compound, protein, and cellular states are aligned, followed by propagation over pathway and protein-protein interaction networks so that predictions must remain consistent with plausible biological cascades rather than isolated pairwise associations. The novelty lies in combining cross-scale fusion with explicit mechanistic regularization: instead of treating pathway knowledge as a side feature, the model uses network constraints to discourage biologically implausible predictions and to transfer information when labels are sparse or modalities are missing. The approach is feasible with public resources such as DrugBank-derived interaction sets, MoleculeNet or TDC tasks, protein language embeddings, and LINCS-style perturbation data. If successful, it could improve robustness for polypharmacology, toxicity, and translational response prediction beyond traditional cheminformatics pipelines. The main risk is that heterogeneous assays and incomplete biological networks may introduce noisy alignment and bias toward well-studied mechanisms. A minimal validation experiment is to compare this model against molecular-only and unconstrained multimodal comparisons on a scaffold-split drug-target and phenotypic-response benchmark, with ablations removing protein, cell, and network components.

idea: We propose a bias-aware dynamic biogeography model that reconstructs species ranges and community turnover from uneven biodiversity records by separating ecological change from the observation process. The framework combines occurrence records, collection metadata, environmental rasters, and optional trait, phylogenetic, and fossil or historical inputs in a hierarchical spatiotemporal joint species distribution model. Latent occupancy or abundance states evolve across space and time through colonization, extirpation, and environmental response components, while a linked detection submodel accounts for collector effort, accessibility, taxonomic popularity, and temporal shifts in sampling practice. Partial pooling across related taxa using phylogenetically and trait-structured priors allows rare species and poorly sampled clades to borrow strength without collapsing to a single static niche estimate. The main novelty is to make temporal nonstationarity, taxonomic imbalance, and observation bias first-class objects in one interpretable uncertainty-calibrated framework that can degrade gracefully when some auxiliary data sources are missing. The approach is feasible because it relies on data types already common in museum repositories and remote sensing products, though identifiability between true absence and low detectability remains the main risk when effort metadata are sparse. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively mask recent records and well-sampled regions in a benchmark clade, then test whether the model better recovers held-out distributions and turnover patterns than static or bias-corrected species distribution comparisons.

idea: This project tests whether stress-inducible microRNAs function as an active developmental buffering layer that preserves embryonic patterning under environmental perturbation, addressing a gap in evo-devo research that has focused more on conserved gene regulatory network architecture than on mechanisms of robustness. The central hypothesis is that a defined microRNA family, selected for known links to stress responsiveness and developmental targeting in a tractable model such as Drosophila, dampens environmentally induced expression noise in patterning or differentiation circuits, thereby limiting embryo-to-embryo variation in developmental timing, fate specification, and morphology during temperature or nutritional stress. The novelty lies in reframing microRNAs not simply as developmental regulators but as conditional robustness modules whose primary signature is stress-dependent variance control rather than a large shift in mean phenotype. Feasibility is high because the system allows precise environmental manipulation, established genetic perturbation of microRNA function, and quantitative readouts of robustness including penetrance variance, fluctuating asymmetry, developmental timing dispersion, and single-embryo trajectory divergence. A minimal validation experiment would compare wild-type and microRNA-perturbed embryos under control and mild heat or diet stress, testing for a specific environment-by-buffer interaction in which perturbation has limited effects in benign conditions but disproportionately amplifies developmental variance under stress. The main risk is pleiotropy, since loss of the microRNA may cause primary developmental defects or generalized sickness rather than revealing a dedicated buffering role.

idea: We propose a sociology-oriented multimodal sentiment analysis framework for social media that treats sentiment as a meaning-making process distributed across text, images, emojis, and lightweight social-context signals such as engagement patterns and topic context, rather than as a property recoverable from words alone. The core mechanism is a conflict-aware fusion architecture with separate encoders for each modality and a gating module that explicitly estimates whether modalities agree, intensify one another, or contradict one another, allowing the model to identify cases such as ironic captions paired with positive imagery, protest symbolism that reverses literal wording, or emojis that amplify or soften stance. To support substantive interpretation, the model also outputs dominant-modality and uncertainty estimates, making it possible to distinguish strong sentiment judgments from culturally ambiguous posts. The novelty lies less in adding more modalities than in modeling cross-modal override and disagreement as socially meaningful signals. The approach is feasible because it can build on existing multimodal social-media datasets and require only targeted additional annotation for contradiction and ambiguity. Its expected impact is more valid sociological inference about affect, identity expression, and contentious discourse online. The main risk is that the system may learn platform-specific cues or reflect annotation disagreement rather than genuine multimodal understanding. A minimal validation experiment would compare this model against text-only and standard fusion comparisons on matched posts, with a focused test set of disagreement cases and an ablation under missing-modality conditions.

idea: We propose an observability-aware inverse framework for reconstructing a restricted history of cosmological spacetime geometry from present-day light-cone observations, addressing the fact that past metric configurations are not directly observable and are often only partially identifiable. The method represents homogeneous or weakly perturbed universes with a low-dimensional latent trajectory for temporally resolved geometric quantities such as the expansion history, effective curvature evolution, and coarse metric class, and couples this representation to a differentiable forward simulator that predicts multimodal observables including supernova distance-redshift curves, large-scale structure statistics, and CMB-derived summaries. Posterior inference is performed under explicit physical constraints, using Einstein-equation residuals, causal consistency, and energy-condition checks to rule out geometrically implausible histories while separating observation noise from irreducible structural non-identifiability. The novelty is to shift cosmological inference from static parameter fitting toward uncertainty-calibrated recovery of recoverable spacetime histories, together with a map of which geometric features can be reconstructed under given observational channels and priors. The approach is feasible because it operates within restricted metric families and uses existing cosmological simulators as differentiable components. Its main impact would be a principled language for reconstructing and auditing the universe’s geometric past, though the central risk is that posterior ambiguity may remain large even after strong physical regularization. A minimal validation would use synthetic universes with known metric histories to test recovery error, posterior calibration, and physical-consistency residuals under single- versus multi-modal observations.

idea: We propose a decision-focused disaster-risk economics framework that converts extreme-weather forecasts into targeted mitigation actions to reduce mortality and economic damage. The system fuses numerical weather predictions, satellite imagery, infrastructure and land-use maps, historical outage and claims data, and neighborhood-level socioeconomic vulnerability indicators in a spatiotemporal model that predicts not only hazard severity but also localized human and asset losses with calibrated uncertainty. These forecasts feed a constrained optimizer that recommends ex ante actions such as shelter placement, backup power deployment, medical-team staging, grid hardening, and evacuation assistance, with the explicit objective of minimizing expected social loss under budget, time, logistics, and fairness constraints. The novelty is the tight integration of multimodal impact prediction with an economically interpretable welfare objective, rather than treating forecasting and response allocation as separate problems. The approach is feasible because the required data sources increasingly exist for floods, hurricanes, heatwaves, and wildfires, and the optimization layer can be built from operational constraints already used by emergency agencies. Expected impact is better prioritization of scarce resources, especially for high-vulnerability communities. The main risk is bias from data harmonization challenges and from training on losses shaped by past interventions. A minimal validation would run retrospective simulations on several major disasters, comparing predicted impacts and recommended allocations against weather-only, damage-only, and rule-based comparisons in terms of avoided expected losses and equity-sensitive targeting.

idea: We propose a paper centered on a minimal hidden-sector dark matter model in which a stable fermionic dark matter particle is accompanied by a slightly heavier coannihilation partner and coupled to the Standard Model through a weak Higgs or vector portal. The central idea is that a compressed dark-sector spectrum can preserve the correct thermal relic abundance through coannihilation while naturally suppressing present-day direct-detection rates, thereby opening viable parameter regions that are inaccessible to conventional single-species WIMP portal scenarios. The novelty lies not in adding many new states, but in defining a tightly constrained benchmark family with only a few physical parameters and systematically identifying where relic-density consistency, perturbativity, mediator-width bounds, and current collider and underground limits can all be satisfied simultaneously. The approach is feasible because the main ingredients can be analyzed with standard Boltzmann freeze-out calculations, simplified-model collider simulations, and overlays of public exclusion data. If successful, the work would provide a sharper set of experimentally relevant targets for dark matter searches and clarify how nonminimal thermal relic structures can remain testable despite null results. The main risk is that existing cosmological and collider constraints may leave only narrow viable regions. A minimal validation experiment is to scan the compressed mass-splitting and portal-coupling plane and compare predicted direct-detection cross sections and mono-X or soft-lepton plus missing-energy signatures against a matched single-species WIMP benchmark.

idea: We propose a field-scale pest early-warning system for integrated pest management that fuses three low-cost, already-deployable signals: automated insect counts from pheromone or sticky-trap images, local weather streams converted into phenology-aware features such as degree-day accumulation and humidity/rainfall transitions, and sparse historical scouting notes. A multimodal spatiotemporal model would estimate current latent pest pressure and forecast outbreak risk 3-14 days ahead for each plot, while explicitly modeling uncertainty so farmers can distinguish between confident spray triggers and cases that require additional scouting. The novelty is not only combining vision and agronomic forecasting, but doing so in a decision-facing way that is robust to missing modalities, trap failures, and irregular scouting, which are common in real farms. This is feasible because the sensing stack is inexpensive, the biological priors are well grounded, and supervision can come from existing trap counts and infestation records rather than dense manual annotation. If successful, the system could reduce delayed interventions, crop damage, and unnecessary insecticide use by shifting spraying from routine schedules to risk-targeted actions. The main risk is limited transfer across crops, regions, and seasons because weather-pest relationships and trap image quality vary substantially. A minimal validation experiment would compare multimodal forecasts against manual scouting schedules and weather-only or recent-count comparisons on cross-season outbreak prediction lead time, false alarms, and estimated spray reduction.

idea: We propose a mechanics-informed composite laminate architecture that strengthens only the interfaces most likely to trigger delamination, rather than uniformly modifying the entire part. The core mechanism is a spatially graded interlaminar reinforcement map that combines thin toughened interleaves with sparse through-thickness bridges such as z-pins or tufted fibers at free edges, ply drops, holes, and impact-prone zones identified by finite-element interlaminar stress analysis. In these local hotspots, crack deflection in the interleaf and crack bridging or pullout from the through-thickness reinforcement are intended to work together to raise mode I and mode II fracture resistance, while leaving low-risk regions unchanged to preserve in-plane stiffness, compressive strength, weight, and manufacturing simplicity. The novelty is not a new reinforcement material alone, but a physics-guided placement and grading rule that explicitly targets the classic tradeoff between delamination toughness and property penalties caused by uniform z-reinforcement or full-area interleaving. The concept is feasible because it can be integrated into established CFRP layup and curing workflows with only localized additions. Expected impact is improved damage tolerance for load-bearing aerospace, wind, and automotive laminates with lower mass and less fiber disruption than blanket toughening strategies. The main risk is transition-zone stress concentration or process variability at reinforcement boundaries. A minimal validation experiment would compare a selective laminate against conventional and uniformly reinforced controls using DCB and ENF fracture tests plus X-ray CT of crack paths and reinforcement-induced defects.
