idea: We propose a hybrid exoplanet detection framework that targets small and wide-orbit planets by combining ultra-precise astrometric micro-wobble tracking with weak gravitational microlensing precursor alerts in a single Bayesian inference pipeline. The core mechanism is to monitor nearby bright stars with long-comparison optical interferometry or next-generation space astrometry, extracting sub-microarcsecond stellar motion signatures that are usually too weak or ambiguous when modeled alone, then use predicted foreground-background alignments from deep survey catalogs to identify time windows where the same systems may also produce low-amplitude lensing perturbations from distant background stars. The novelty is not a new instrument but a coordinated inference strategy that fuses two sparse, complementary signals: astrometry constrains planetary mass and orbital geometry, while lensing boosts sensitivity to distant or non-transiting companions that radial velocity and transit surveys systematically miss. Feasibility is supported by existing survey streams, Gaia-like catalog precision, and Rubin-class alerting infrastructure, with the main technical risk being false positives from stellar activity, unresolved binaries, and imperfect background-source forecasts. A minimal validation experiment would inject synthetic Earth-to-Neptune-mass companions into archival astrometric time series for nearby stars, pair them with simulated catalog-derived alignment events, and test whether the joint model recovers more true wide-orbit planets at fixed false-alarm rate than astrometry-only or transit/radial-velocity-style selection.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware latent operator framework for jointly predicting system dynamics and control signals in complex autonomous systems by combining a sparse graph state encoder, a neural Koopman-style latent transition model, and a distributionally robust control head. The encoder maps heterogeneous sensor and actuator histories into a compact graph-structured latent state that preserves subsystem interactions while reducing computational burden; the latent transition model evolves this state with linear operators conditioned on regime tokens, enabling fast rollout and interpretable stability constraints; and the control head optimizes actions against an uncertainty set estimated from residual dynamics, sensor dropout patterns, and domain shifts, rather than a single point forecast. The novelty is the tight coupling of structured latent linearization with online uncertainty calibration, so the predictor and controller share a common low-dimensional model yet remain robust to disturbances and model mismatch. Feasibility is high because each component can be trained from logged trajectories with standard differentiable objectives and lightweight convex robustness penalties. Expected impact is lower inference cost and more reliable closed-loop behavior in safety-critical autonomous platforms. The main risk is that aggressive compression may discard rare but crucial nonlinear events. A minimal validation experiment would compare one-step prediction error, rollout stability, and control degradation under synthetic perturbations on a simulated multi-subsystem autonomous platform against a non-structured sequence model.

idea: We propose a Rapid Evidence and Deliberation Engine for science policy that replaces one-shot expert consensus with a continuously updated, transparent forecasting-and-argument system. The core mechanism combines three layers: structured evidence retrieval from publications, grants, patents, regulatory filings, and public comments; a panel of diverse domain experts and stakeholder representatives who submit short probabilistic forecasts and written rationales on policy options; and an aggregation model that weights inputs not only by credentials, but by calibration history, conflict-of-interest disclosures, and viewpoint diversity. Novelty lies in treating science policy as an auditable prediction-and-revision problem rather than a static consensus exercise, while preserving expert judgment instead of fully automating it. Feasibility is high because the required data streams already exist and the workflow can be piloted inside a single policy domain such as AI safety, biomedical funding, or climate innovation. Expected impact is faster, more explainable, and less bias-prone policy advice, especially when evidence is evolving quickly. The main risk is that formal aggregation could still encode hidden institutional biases or incentivize strategic forecasting. A minimal validation experiment would compare this system with a conventional expert panel on a set of historical science-policy decisions, measuring speed, forecast calibration, rationale diversity, and the stability of recommendations under new evidence updates.

idea: We propose a standardized comparative framework for primate vocal complexity that represents each call sequence as a multiscale communication graph combining acoustic units, transition structure, and interaction context. The core mechanism is a pipeline that first segments continuous recordings into probabilistic vocal units using self-supervised acoustic embeddings, then builds individual- and group-level sequence models that quantify complexity through a small, interpretable panel of metrics: repertoire diversity, transition entropy, context specificity, temporal recurrence, and compressibility under hierarchical grammars. Novelty lies in unifying these currently fragmented dimensions into a species-agnostic standard with explicit controls for recording effort, observer bias, and ecological context, so that complexity scores are comparable across datasets rather than tailored to one field site or annotation convention. Feasibility is high because the approach can be implemented on existing archived recordings with moderate manual labeling used only for calibration and biological interpretation, not full hand coding. The expected impact is a reproducible benchmark for primatology that enables stronger cross-species tests of social and cognitive hypotheses. The main risk is that unsupervised units may not align cleanly with biologically meaningful calls, potentially making complexity estimates unstable. A minimal validation experiment would apply the framework to two well-studied primate datasets with different social systems, measure metric reliability across annotators and recording subsamples, and test whether the standardized scores remain consistent while still distinguishing known communicative regimes.

idea: We propose a calculus learning environment built around Conceptual Tension Loops, in which students repeatedly predict, simulate, explain, and generalize core ideas such as limit, derivative, accumulation, and optimization before formal procedures are introduced. Each lesson begins with an everyday or scientific phenomenon, for example motion near a turning point or water filling an irregular container, and asks learners to commit to qualitative forecasts. The system then provides linked visual, symbolic, and verbal representations, highlights where intuition fails, and guides students to repair misconceptions through short counterexample-driven dialogues and micro-construction tasks that require creating meanings for formulas rather than only applying them. The novelty is the explicit orchestration of productive cognitive conflict across multiple representations, combined with automatic generation of near-transfer and far-transfer tasks from the same underlying concept graph, so engagement and deep understanding are targeted together rather than treated as separate goals. The approach is feasible with current web-based interactive notebooks and lightweight student modeling. Expected impact is stronger conceptual retention, greater willingness to engage, and better transfer from graphical and physical reasoning to formal calculus. The main risk is excess cognitive load for weaker students, which can be mitigated with adaptive pacing. A minimal validation experiment would compare one unit of this environment against a conventional worked-example lesson on limits, measuring concept inventory gains, explanation quality, and delayed transfer.

idea: We propose a biodegradable dual-function aquaculture pellet that couples feeding control with localized drug delivery by embedding nutrient cores and medication-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid)/alginate microcapsules inside a water-stable starch-chitosan matrix whose degradation rate is tuned to fish or shrimp feeding behavior and pond chemistry. The mechanism is to keep the pellet structurally intact during the expected feeding window, then trigger staged softening afterward so uneaten pellets gradually sink and release microbial enzyme stimulants that accelerate biodegradation and reduce sludge accumulation, while ingested microcapsules provide pH- and enzyme-responsive release in the gut rather than immediate dissolution into the water. Novelty lies in integrating anti-overfeeding feedback, waste-reducing biodegradability, and controlled oral medication in one manufacturable feed format instead of treating feed, waste, and therapeutics as separate subsystems. Feasibility is high because all components are drawn from established aquafeed binders and approved biodegradable polymers, and fabrication can use extrusion plus low-temperature microencapsulation. Expected impact is lower feed loss, reduced dissolved antibiotic or antiparasitic waste, and improved water quality without major farm hardware changes. The main risk is that release timing may vary across species and salinity, causing underdosing or premature pellet breakup. A minimal validation experiment would compare this pellet against a standard medicated feed in replicated tank trials, measuring uneaten feed mass, waterborne drug concentration, sludge formation, and in vitro/in vivo release profiles over 24-72 hours.

idea: We propose a privacy-preserving dataset expansion framework for medical imaging that couples anatomy-aware generative synthesis with lightweight expert supervision to overcome the scarcity of diverse, annotated data. The core mechanism is a two-stage pipeline: first, a foundation image generator is adapted using hospital-specific unlabeled scans plus public multi-center datasets to produce pathology- and device-conditioned synthetic images while preserving realistic scanner artifacts, demographic variation, and anatomical structure through segmentation-guided constraints; second, a disagreement-driven annotation loop uses a small committee of task models and uncertainty maps to select only the most informative synthetic and real samples for rapid radiologist correction, yielding high-value labels at low expert cost. The novelty lies in treating diversity and annotation as a joint optimization problem rather than separately augmenting images or separately reducing labeling burden, which is especially relevant when rare conditions and site-specific acquisition differences drive poor generalization. The approach is feasible because it relies on existing generative, segmentation, and active-learning components that can be integrated without changing clinical workflows. Expected impact is improved robustness across hospitals with fewer manually labeled scans. The main risk is synthetic distribution drift that could reinforce artifacts or bias. A minimal validation experiment would train a classifier or segmenter on a small real dataset with and without the proposed synthetic-plus-curated expansion, then compare external-site performance and calibration on a held-out multi-institution test set.

idea: We propose an energy-adaptive pattern-recognition architecture that couples a sparse event-driven front end with a low-precision in-memory learning core to reduce the power cost of machine learning workloads without giving up practical accuracy. The key mechanism is to convert dense sensor or feature streams into asynchronous token events using learned temporal change detectors, then route only salient events to crossbar-style analog memory blocks that perform approximate multiply-accumulate operations directly where weights are stored; a lightweight digital supervisor monitors confidence and selectively triggers higher-precision refinement only for uncertain cases. This is novel in the way it jointly optimizes data representation, compute placement, and precision scheduling as one closed-loop policy, instead of treating hardware efficiency and model inference as separate layers. The design is feasible because each component builds on existing ingredients such as quantized networks, event-based encoding, and non-von-Neumann memory arrays, but combines them into a system explicitly targeted at power-hungry recognition pipelines. Expected impact is a substantial drop in energy per inference for always-on classification, anomaly detection, and edge learning settings where conventional processors waste power on redundant operations. The main risk is that analog noise, event sparsity errors, or difficult inputs could degrade robustness and calibration. A minimal validation experiment would compare this architecture against a conventional quantized neural network on a streaming image or sensor-classification task, measuring accuracy, confidence-trigger rate, and estimated energy per correct prediction under matched model capacity.

idea: We propose an adaptive sampling framework for research studies that explicitly models representation bias during data collection rather than treating it as a post hoc adjustment problem. The core mechanism combines a small set of known population marginals, uncertainty-aware stratification, and sequential recruitment: after each recruitment batch, the system estimates which subgroups are simultaneously underrepresented and high influence for the study outcome, then reallocates sampling effort toward those cells while applying a fairness-constrained weighting rule that prevents extreme variance inflation. The novelty is the joint optimization of representation and estimator stability, so the design does not merely chase demographic balance but targets the subpopulations most likely to distort inference if missed. Feasibility is high because the method only requires routinely available metadata and can be implemented as a layer on top of existing survey, clinical, or observational recruitment pipelines. Expected impact is more reliable conclusions under realistic recruitment constraints, especially when rare or hard-to-reach groups shape effect heterogeneity. The main risk is misspecification of the auxiliary population marginals or outcome model, which could redirect effort inefficiently. A minimal validation experiment would simulate a population with skewed recruitment probabilities and heterogeneous treatment effects, then compare bias, variance, and subgroup coverage between fixed stratified sampling and the proposed adaptive design.

idea: We propose a longitudinal developmental genomics framework that links polygenic liability and regulatory markers to behavioral and emotional milestones from infancy to early childhood by modeling development as a sequence of time-sensitive transitions rather than isolated outcomes. The core mechanism combines saliva-based genotyping, repeated caregiver reports, short mobile behavioral tasks, and brief home-video coding to estimate when children acquire or deviate from expected milestones in emotion regulation, social reciprocity, fear response, language-linked self-control, and adaptive behavior, then tests whether specific genetic profiles predict altered timing, coupling, or heterogeneity of these trajectories through biologically informed latent transition models. The novelty is the integration of common-variant polygenic scores with milestone timing across multiple developmental domains, which addresses the current gap between gene discovery studies and psychologically meaningful early-life phenotypes. Feasibility is high because the measurements are low burden, scalable, and compatible with existing birth cohorts or pediatric recruitment. Expected impact includes earlier mechanistic stratification of developmental risk and more precise hypotheses about when prevention should occur. The main risk is weak and noisy genotype-to-phenotype signal, especially given environmental confounding and rapid developmental change. A minimal validation experiment would follow a modest pilot cohort over 18 months with quarterly assessments to test whether preregistered genetic markers improve prediction of out-of-window emotional or behavioral milestone transitions beyond demographic and family-context variables alone.

idea: We propose an urban crime early-warning framework that treats crime risk as a short-horizon social stress contagion process rather than a simple hotspot forecast. The system would fuse routinely available neighborhood signals such as emergency-call volume, public transit crowding, nightlife density, recent eviction filings, school absenteeism, weather anomalies, and anonymized mobility flows into a dynamic multilayer city graph, then use a spatiotemporal causal model to estimate when combinations of social strain, transient congregation, and weakened informal guardianship make specific blocks unusually vulnerable to violence or property crime. The novelty is the explicit modeling of interaction between structural disadvantage and fast-changing urban rhythms, allowing the model to distinguish chronic high-risk areas from moments when ordinary areas temporarily become fragile. Feasibility is strong because most inputs already exist in municipal, transit, and open administrative systems, and privacy exposure can be limited through aggregation at block-group and hourly levels. The expected impact is more targeted prevention, such as focused outreach, transit staffing, lighting adjustments, or violence interruption deployment, instead of broad over-policing. The main risk is that biased historical records could reproduce unequal surveillance patterns, so fairness constraints and counterfactual audits must be built in. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively predict next-day block-level incidents in one dense city and compare calibration, lead time, and geographic disparity against standard hotspot and pure mobility-based models.

idea: We propose a neuro-symbolic triage system for dense brain-scan diagnostics that converts a full 3D MRI or CT volume into a compact set of lesion-centric “evidence tokens” before final classification, reducing review burden without discarding clinically meaningful context. A lightweight multiscale encoder first identifies candidate regions with uncertainty-aware saliency maps, then a graph module links these regions across slices and anatomical neighborhoods to preserve long-range structure such as edema spread, midline shift, or distributed microbleeds. Instead of predicting directly from every voxel, a diagnostic reasoner operates on the token graph and produces both a triage score and a concise machine-readable rationale highlighting which regional patterns drove urgency. The novelty is the explicit compression of dense scans into structured diagnostic evidence rather than generic latent embeddings, which should improve speed, interpretability, and robustness when scans vary in resolution or acquisition protocol. Feasibility is high because all components can be built from existing segmentation backbones, graph networks, and weak supervision from radiology reports. Expected impact is faster screening for time-critical abnormalities while keeping enough traceability for clinician trust. The main risk is that aggressive tokenization may suppress subtle diffuse pathology. A minimal validation experiment would compare this approach against a standard full-volume classifier on one urgent detection task, measuring sensitivity, inference time, and whether highlighted evidence regions overlap expert-marked abnormalities.

idea: This project proposes a closed-loop water optimization market for hydraulic fracturing that couples field-level wastewater treatment decisions with regional water allocation and induced-environmental-cost pricing. The core mechanism is a techno-economic platform that jointly schedules three levers for each unconventional well pad: substitution of freshwater with treated produced water, modular onsite treatment intensity, and timed transfer of excess wastewater to nearby pads or disposal sites, all under local water scarcity, transport cost, salinity chemistry, and disposal-capacity constraints. The novelty is not wastewater recycling alone, but embedding recycling quality requirements and infrastructure bottlenecks into a dynamic contract-and-pricing framework that lets operators compare treatment, reuse, storage, and disposal on a common marginal-value basis while internalizing environmental externalities such as groundwater stress and truck traffic. The approach is feasible because operators already collect operational, water-quality, and logistics data, and compact treatment units and digital dispatch systems are commercially available. Expected impact is lower freshwater withdrawals, reduced disposal volumes, and better economic resilience in drought-prone basins. The main risk is that water chemistry variability may make reuse unreliable or raise completion-performance concerns, which could limit adoption despite favorable modeled economics. A minimal validation experiment would calibrate the model on one shale basin using public well, water-use, and disposal records, then compare simulated costs and water demand under current practice versus coordinated closed-loop scheduling for a small cluster of pads.

idea: We propose a Nuclear-Resolved Periodic Table (NRPT) that augments each chemical element with a compact, queryable layer of nuclear-state descriptors so that ground states and long-lived isomers are represented as distinct yet chemically linked entries. The core mechanism is to index every nuclide by proton number, neutron number, spin-parity, metastable lifetime, electromagnetic moment, decay channels, and a derived nuclear-structure fingerprint learned from shell-model and evaluated nuclear-data tables, then project these descriptors into a two-level table where conventional chemistry remains the top layer and a switchable nuclear layer reveals state-specific identity. The novelty is not a new chart of nuclides alone, but a principled representation that explicitly treats isomeric states as first-class members of the element system when their nuclear properties are observably different, enabling prediction and search over state-selective spectroscopy, materials activation, and isotope engineering tasks that the standard periodic table hides. The approach is feasible because the required data already exist in curated nuclear databases and can be integrated with modest machine-learning or rule-based embedding methods. Its impact would be a more faithful organizing framework for physics, radiochemistry, and nuclear technology education and design. The main risk is that the representation may become visually or conceptually too complex for broad adoption. A minimal validation experiment is to build the NRPT for a small set of medically and technologically relevant isomeric pairs, such as Tc-99m/Tc-99 or Hf-178m2/Hf-178, and test whether experts retrieve state-specific nuclear properties and application-relevant distinctions more accurately than with the conventional periodic table.

idea: We propose a disease-specific target discovery framework that treats complex disease as a context-dependent network control problem rather than a single-gene ranking task. The core mechanism combines patient multi-omics profiles, perturbational transcriptomics from compound and CRISPR screens, and cell-type-resolved protein interaction graphs to learn causal disease-state transition models, then prioritizes proteins whose modulation is predicted to push pathological cell states back toward healthy attractors while preserving essential functions in non-diseased tissues. Novelty comes from explicitly integrating targetability, state reversibility, and tissue-selective safety into one generative scoring loop, which should surface non-obvious regulatory chokepoints such as scaffold proteins, context-specific transcriptional cofactors, or synthetic-lethal partner nodes that are usually missed by static association methods. Feasibility is supported by growing public resources such as single-cell atlases, DepMap-style perturbation data, and structure-aware ligandability predictors, enabling a practical first version without requiring bespoke wet-lab datasets. Expected impact is a sharper funnel from disease biology to experimentally actionable targets for polygenic disorders where current pipelines fail. The main risk is that inferred causal edges may reflect correlation or cell-line artifacts rather than true disease mechanisms. As a minimal validation experiment, the top-ranked target and one matched lower-ranked control could be tested by CRISPR interference in a patient-relevant organoid or primary-cell model, measuring whether disease-associated transcriptional and phenotypic markers shift toward a healthy state.

Problem: Drug discovery is limited by the difficulty in predicting and validating novel drug targets for complex diseases.

idea: We propose a delamination-resistant composite architecture that combines a thin interleaf network of magnetically alignable aramid microfibers with latent self-healing tougheners confined to ply interfaces, so that the laminate resists crack initiation, bridges growing interlaminar cracks, and partially restores cohesion after overload without sacrificing in-plane stiffness. The novelty is not simply adding a tougher resin, but spatially programming the interface as a multifunctional mesoscale layer: during manufacturing, a low-volume-fraction interleaf containing short aramid fibers, reversible thermoplastic domains, and microencapsulated healing agent is placed between plies, then a magnetic field aligns the fibers normal and oblique to the interface to create crack-bridging paths that are difficult for a delamination front to bypass. This should be feasible with existing prepreg and vacuum-assisted curing workflows because the interleaf is thin, compositionally modular, and does not require redesign of the bulk laminate. Expected impact is a substantial increase in damage tolerance for aerospace, wind, and mobility structures where barely visible impact damage currently limits adoption. The main risk is that the interleaf could raise resin-rich regions or reduce fatigue life if alignment and cure viscosity are poorly controlled. A minimal validation experiment would fabricate double-cantilever-beam coupons with and without the programmed interleaf, then compare mode-I fracture toughness, post-impact residual stiffness, and microscopic evidence of fiber bridging and local healing.

idea: We propose a precision agronomy platform that couples low-cost canopy thermal imaging, hyperspectral leaf sensing, soil nitrate/moisture probes, and short-horizon weather forecasts with a crop-soil symbiosis digital twin to trigger adaptive co-management of drought resilience and biological nitrogen fixation under climate stress. The core mechanism is a closed-loop controller that infers when plants are entering a pre-stress state in which stomatal closure, root exudation, and rhizosphere oxygen balance begin to suppress both water-use efficiency and diazotroph activity, then prescribes variable-rate micro-irrigation, targeted molybdenum/iron and carbon amendments, and timed inoculation or stimulation of associative nitrogen-fixing microbes only in zones predicted to benefit. The novelty is not another static recommendation map, but a dynamic intervention policy that explicitly models the tradeoff between conserving water and sustaining microbial nitrogen fixation during heat and drought episodes. Feasibility is high because all sensing components are field-deployable and the controller can be trained from existing crop, weather, and management data before limited on-farm calibration. Expected impact is reduced fertilizer dependence and more stable yields under increasing climate volatility. The main risk is model misspecification across soil types and cultivars, which could lead to poorly timed interventions. A minimal validation experiment would compare controller-guided versus conventional uniform management in replicated drought-stressed plots while measuring canopy temperature, nodulation or rhizosphere diazotroph markers, soil nitrate dynamics, and yield.

idea: We propose a precision anti-resistance therapy that couples a bacteriophage-derived delivery particle with a CRISPR base-editing payload designed to selectively disable the most clinically common antibiotic-resistance determinants in pathogenic bacteria, such as beta-lactamase or carbapenemase genes, while sparing commensal microbes. The concrete mechanism is to package guide RNAs and a compact deaminase editor into non-replicative phage capsids that preferentially infect target superbugs, rewriting key catalytic residues or promoter motifs so resistant strains become resensitized to existing antibiotics rather than being killed directly. The novelty is the combination of sequence-specific resistance erasure, microbiome preservation, and reuse of already approved antibiotic classes, which may reduce evolutionary pressure compared with broad-spectrum escalation. Feasibility is supported by existing phage-host engineering, bacterial CRISPR delivery concepts, and rapid genomic profiling in hospital isolates to match payloads to local resistance patterns. Expected impact is a modular platform that restores the utility of failing antibiotics against multidrug-resistant infections without requiring entirely new small-molecule discovery. The main risk is incomplete delivery or rapid emergence of escape mutants through target sequence variation or phage receptor loss. A minimal validation experiment would expose a carbapenem-resistant clinical isolate panel to the engineered particles, then measure restoration of antibiotic susceptibility and off-target effects on representative gut commensals in coculture.

idea: We propose a predictive safety-engineering platform for finance that treats operational, cyber, model, and market hazards as interacting precursors in a continuously updated causal-temporal risk graph rather than as isolated threshold breaches. The system would fuse streaming telemetry from transaction flows, model confidence signals, access logs, incident tickets, and external market or news shocks into a graph neural state estimator coupled with survival and change-point models that forecast the probability, timing, and likely propagation path of hazards such as fraud cascades, liquidity stress, model drift, or control failure. An adaptive decision layer would then recommend risk responses, including throttling, stepped authentication, model fallback, hedging, or human escalation, by optimizing a constrained objective that balances safety reduction, service continuity, and intervention cost under uncertainty. The novelty is the combination of cross-layer precursor modeling and closed-loop action selection for real-time financial safety management, while feasibility is supported by the fact that most required signals already exist in enterprise monitoring stacks and can be integrated incrementally. Expected impact is earlier detection of emerging hazards and more proportionate responses than static rule systems. The main risk is spurious correlations or feedback loops that could trigger unnecessary interventions. A minimal validation experiment would replay historical incident streams in a simulator and compare lead time, false alarms, and loss containment against threshold-based monitoring with fixed response playbooks.

idea: We propose an early-warning system for scientific misconduct that models integrity risk as a longitudinal pattern rather than a single detection event. The core mechanism combines three weak but complementary signals available before formal publication problems emerge: writing-process anomalies from version histories and authorship metadata, citation-and-text reuse irregularities that fall short of obvious plagiarism, and statistical inconsistency markers in tables, figures, and reported distributions that may indicate fabrication. These signals are fused in a temporal graph linking manuscripts, coauthors, datasets, and prior submissions, and the model outputs calibrated risk trajectories with human-interpretable evidence rather than accusations. The novelty is to target precursory behaviors across the research lifecycle, especially subtle coordination between textual, numerical, and collaboration anomalies that isolated plagiarism or image forensics tools miss. Feasibility is reasonable because universities, journals, and preprint platforms already store many of the required artifacts, and the approach can start with privacy-preserving local deployment using hashed text fingerprints and derived statistical features. Expected impact is earlier triage for editors and research-integrity offices, reducing harm before problematic work propagates. The main risk is false positives against unconventional but legitimate research practices, so the system should be framed as decision support with strict audit trails and conservative thresholds. A minimal validation experiment would assemble a retrospective dataset of corrected, retracted, and matched non-problematic papers, then test whether the fused temporal model flags elevated risk earlier than standard plagiarism-only screening.

idea: We propose a community-governed Heritage Process Graph that helps endangered intangible cultural practices survive globalization by encoding not only artifacts such as songs, recipes, rituals, and stories, but also the social sequence, local meanings, permissions, and environmental cues that make them authentic in use. The core mechanism combines multimodal documentation from elders and practitioners with a graph model linking performance steps, linguistic variants, kinship roles, seasonal timing, taboo boundaries, and acceptable adaptation rules, then uses this structure to generate context-aware teaching materials for schools, diaspora groups, and local apprentices while preserving community control over what may or may not be shared. The novelty is treating cultural transmission as a living process with governance constraints rather than as a static archive, which could reduce the common failure mode where digitization accelerates flattening and commercialization. Feasibility is supported by existing speech, video, and knowledge-graph tools, plus participatory annotation workflows already familiar to museums and NGOs. Expected impact is improved intergenerational transfer and more respectful digital circulation. The main risk is codifying fluid traditions too rigidly or exposing sensitive knowledge. A minimal validation experiment would pilot one ritual or craft tradition in partnership with a single community and compare learner retention and practitioner-perceived fidelity between graph-guided materials and conventional archive-style materials.

idea: We propose a catalyst-aware reaction-mechanism discovery framework that couples operando time-resolved spectroscopy with neural-guided microkinetic state-space search to expose hidden pathways and short-lived intermediates that conventional mechanism studies often miss. The concrete mechanism is to encode catalyst surface motifs, reactant states, and spectroscopic signatures into a dynamic reaction graph, then use uncertainty-driven exploration to nominate transient adsorbates and branching elementary steps that best explain observed nonstationary spectra while remaining consistent with quantum-chemical energetics. The novelty lies in treating mechanism identification as an active latent-state inference problem rather than a fixed pathway-fitting exercise, allowing rare off-cycle states, catalyst reconstruction events, and competing routes to be discovered jointly. Feasibility is strong because the required inputs—DFT priors, operando IR/XAS or MS traces, and standard microkinetic solvers—already exist in many catalysis labs, and the model can begin with a small curated reaction network before expanding. Expected impact is faster catalyst design through more faithful identification of selectivity-determining intermediates and deactivation channels. The main risk is non-identifiability, where multiple hidden-state explanations fit the same measurements. A minimal validation experiment is to apply the framework to a well-studied benchmark catalytic reaction with pulse-perturbation operando measurements and test whether the inferred transient intermediates predict independently measured isotope-labeling responses.

idea: We propose a hierarchical autonomous exploration architecture for planetary science in which one primary rover deploys dozens of centimeter-scale sensor scouts that act as short-range, disposable extensions of its perception and sampling reach. The core mechanism combines orbital maps, onboard terrain reconstruction, and a shared probabilistic “science value” model that assigns each scout or the mothership to micro-missions such as fissure inspection, volatile sniffing, regolith imaging, or relay placement, while a delay-tolerant planner continuously reallocates roles as local evidence arrives. The novelty is not merely using multiple robots, but coupling task-specialized micro-scouts with a science-aware coordination layer that explicitly trades scientific uncertainty reduction against energy, communication, and recovery cost, allowing exploration to spread across hazardous or spatially fragmented sites that a single rover would avoid. The concept is feasible because it builds on existing rover autonomy, low-power MEMS sensors, short-hop mobility, and mesh networking, with the mothership handling high-compute planning and sample triage. If successful, this could expand explored area per mission and increase discovery of rare localized phenomena such as hydrated veins or biologically relevant mineral contexts. The main risk is brittle coordination under dust, terrain occlusion, and scout failure. A minimal validation experiment would use a Mars-analog testbed and simulated orbital priors to compare single-rover versus mothership-plus-scout coverage and science-target discovery under identical time and energy budgets.

idea: We propose a data-engineering layer for range-extended quantum key exchange that treats scarce end-to-end quantum links as a schedulable resource and uses distributed reliability coding to safely compose short QKD segments into longer secure delivery paths. The core mechanism is a control plane that continuously models link loss, key-generation rate, buffer occupancy, and trust-domain boundaries across metropolitan fiber segments, then allocates traffic through multi-path secret sharing: application session keys are split into threshold shares, each share is wrapped by locally generated QKD material on a different short-range segment chain, and shares are reassembled only when enough independent paths arrive. The novelty is not a new physical repeater, but a systems architecture that converts the range limitation into a data-placement, routing, and reconstruction problem, allowing existing short-haul QKD hardware to support wider-area communication with graceful degradation under link outages. Feasibility is high because it relies on software orchestration, telemetry pipelines, and current trusted-node deployments rather than fault-tolerant quantum repeaters. Expected impact is faster practical adoption of quantum-secured networking across campuses, cities, and data-center corridors. The main risk is that trusted intermediate nodes and routing metadata may create exploitable operational side channels or concentrate trust. A minimal validation experiment would simulate or emulate a small network of 5-10 QKD-connected nodes, compare delivery success and key-consumption efficiency against single-path forwarding under varying distance and loss, and verify that threshold reconstruction preserves service when individual segments fail.

idea: We propose a policy-facing deliberation system that detects polarization and misinformation in political discourse by modeling not only whether a claim is false or divisive, but why it spreads across identity-based communities. The core mechanism combines claim verification, stance-conditioned framing analysis, and a cross-group diffusion graph built from public speeches, legislative debate, news, and social media excerpts, then uses these signals to generate targeted interventions such as uncertainty labels, counter-framings, and policy briefs written to preserve factual correction without triggering defensive partisan backlash. The novelty is to treat misinformation and polarization as a coupled communication problem rather than separate moderation or fact-checking tasks, allowing the system to identify claims that are technically debunked yet still politically adhesive because they align with group narratives. The approach is feasible with existing language models, public fact-check corpora, congressional records, and platform data, plus human annotation for framing and identity cues. Expected impact is earlier detection of discourse patterns likely to distort public policy formation and more effective interventions for agencies, journalists, and civic organizations. The main risk is that intervention recommendations may misclassify legitimate ideological disagreement as harmful polarization. A minimal validation experiment would compare whether generated counter-framings reduce perceived credibility and partisan entrenchment more than standard fact-check labels in a controlled survey using contested policy claims.

idea: We propose a closed-loop prosthetic interface that combines event-driven tactile sensing in the artificial hand with adaptive, low-bandwidth electrotactile feedback on the residual limb to restore usable sensation without overwhelming the user. Instead of streaming raw pressure values, the controller converts contact, slip onset, grip-force margin, and joint-load changes into a small vocabulary of spatiotemporal stimulation patterns, while a lightweight online personalization module updates mapping thresholds from the wearer’s recent corrections, task context, and skin response. The novelty is the combination of sensory compression and user-specific co-adaptation: feedback is delivered only when uncertainty or manipulation risk rises, which could improve control and adaptability while reducing habituation and cognitive load compared with continuous feedback schemes. Feasibility is strong because all components rely on existing prosthetic sensors, wearable stimulators, and embedded learning methods with modest compute demands. The expected impact is more stable grasping, faster embodiment, and better handling of fragile or irregular objects in daily use. The main risk is that individualized stimulation codes may still vary too much across users or drift with fatigue and sweating. A minimal validation experiment would compare this adaptive event-driven feedback against no-feedback and continuous-feedback conditions in a small object-manipulation study measuring slip rate, grip-force overshoot, task completion time, and subjective workload.

idea: We propose a multimodal learning-analytics framework that augments response-based mastery tracing with temporally aligned behavioral evidence from ordinary classroom platforms, including writing latency, revision trajectories, mouse and scroll patterns, video-attendance events, optional webcam-derived gaze dispersion, and speech-turn metadata during discussion. The core mechanism is a student-specific state-space model that treats conceptual understanding, confidence, cognitive load, and disengagement as separate latent factors and updates them through cross-modal consistency rules, so that, for example, rapid guessing with low revision depth is distinguished from fluent competence, while long pauses paired with targeted rereading is interpreted as productive struggle rather than failure. The novelty is not simply fusing more signals, but explicitly modeling when modalities should agree or conflict and using missing-modality robustness so schools can deploy only the signals they already collect. Feasibility is high because the system can be built on existing LMS logs and commodity conferencing data, with privacy preserved through on-device feature extraction and coarse aggregates rather than raw audio or video storage. Expected impact is earlier detection of confusion and disengagement, enabling more timely, personalized support than answer-only dashboards. The main risk is that multimodal proxies may encode context or accessibility differences rather than learning states. A minimal validation experiment would compare next-assessment prediction and early-risk flagging between response-only models and the proposed multimodal model on one course, while auditing subgroup calibration and ablations over each signal family.

idea: We propose a distributed biomass densification network in which low-cost mobile preprocessing units are dispatched among farms to convert loose agricultural residues into standardized, sensor-tagged dense pellets or briquettes before long-distance transport. The core mechanism combines field-edge size reduction, moisture-aware drying using waste heat or solar-assisted airflow, and adaptive compaction controlled by a routing algorithm that assigns each unit to residue clusters based on harvest timing, road access, moisture state, and nearby demand from biogas, pyrolysis, or feed manufacturers. The novelty is not densification alone, but the coupling of mobile physical preprocessing with a digital logistics layer that treats residue quality and transportability as co-optimized variables, allowing farmers to aggregate value locally while avoiding the inefficiency of hauling bulky raw biomass to a central plant. Feasibility is supported by existing chipping, drying, and briquetting technologies, with innovation focused on modular integration and scheduling. Expected impact is lower transport cost, reduced residue burning, and improved participation of smallholders in biomass value chains. The main risk is operational complexity under heterogeneous residue moisture and seasonal peaks. A minimal validation experiment would compare transport cost, bulk density, and delivered usable energy per ton for one residue type across raw hauling versus mobile preprocessing plus hauling in a small multi-farm pilot.

idea: We propose a dynamic cancer diagnostic framework that models each patient tumor as an evolving mixture of cellular and microenvironmental states rather than a single static label. The core mechanism is a heterogeneity-aware digital pathology and liquid-biopsy fusion model: spatial transcriptomic or multiplex imaging features from an initial tumor sample are embedded into a state graph, circulating tumor DNA and blood protein markers are then used to update the graph over time, and a Bayesian progression layer estimates which subclones are expanding, which niches are therapy resistant, and when the diagnostic confidence for a conventional subtype should be revised. The novelty is not merely multimodal integration, but explicit temporal state tracking that turns diagnosis into a continuously updated inference problem aligned with tumor evolution. Feasibility is reasonable because all inputs can be built from clinically emerging assays and the model can begin with sparse longitudinal data by propagating uncertainty rather than requiring dense sampling. Expected impact is earlier detection of aggressive shifts that static pathology misses, enabling better stratification and monitoring. The main risk is that noisy, irregular longitudinal measurements may induce unstable state updates across patients. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively test whether two-timepoint blood updates improve prediction of hidden resistant subpopulations relative to a single-timepoint tissue-only diagnostic model in one heterogeneous cancer cohort.

idea: We propose an interpretable robust learning framework for noisy high-dimensional data that couples sparse concept discovery with uncertainty-aware sample reweighting. The model first maps raw features into a small set of latent concepts through a structured encoder constrained by group sparsity and prototype anchoring, so each prediction depends on a compact, human-inspectable subset of variables rather than a diffuse embedding. On top of these concepts, a graph-based denoising module estimates local consistency across samples and features, separating stable task-relevant structure from idiosyncratic noise. A Bayesian gating head then predicts both class output and epistemic uncertainty, using uncertainty to downweight suspicious samples and unstable concept activations during training. The novelty is the explicit integration of concept bottlenecks, graph denoising, and uncertainty-driven optimization in one end-to-end system targeted at the joint problem of robustness, interpretability, and high-dimensional noise, rather than treating these goals separately. The approach is feasible because all components can be implemented with standard deep learning and variational inference tools, with sparsity and prototype constraints keeping the representation tractable. Expected impact is a model that remains reliable under corrupted or redundant features while exposing which concepts drive decisions. The main risk is that overly strong concept sparsity may reduce predictive flexibility. A minimal validation experiment would compare performance, calibration, and concept stability on a noisy high-dimensional benchmark under controlled feature corruption and label noise.

idea: We propose an economics-facing causal inference framework that treats confounding as a partially testable model failure problem rather than a nuisance absorbed by stronger identification assumptions. The core mechanism combines three pieces: structured proxy adjustment from high-dimensional administrative or survey covariates, environment-wise invariance tests across naturally heterogeneous subpopulations or time periods, and simulation-based falsification that checks whether estimated treatment effects can reproduce observable policy-relevant moments under plausible hidden-confounder regimes. The novelty is to turn empirical verification into a first-class component of causal estimation: instead of reporting a single effect estimate from standard selection-on-observables or instrumental-variable pipelines, the method outputs an effect interval restricted to models that both fit the data and survive cross-environment stability and falsification checks. Feasibility is high because each component can be built from existing econometric tools such as double machine learning, sensitivity analysis, and overidentification-style diagnostics, but their integration yields a more decision-relevant procedure for policy settings where confounding is likely and ground truth is unavailable. Expected impact is a more credible workflow for estimating program, tax, or labor-market effects when conventional methods may be fragile. The main risk is that invariance tests may reject too often when environments differ for reasons unrelated to confounding, producing overly conservative intervals. A minimal validation experiment would simulate economic panel data with controlled latent confounding and policy selection, then compare coverage, interval width, and false-certainty rates against standard estimators.

idea: We propose an adaptive mixed-reality anxiety assessment platform that embeds participants in ecologically grounded social, spatial, and interoceptive stress scenarios while preserving laboratory control. The system combines immersive virtual environments such as crowded public transit, workplace evaluation, and nighttime street navigation with real-time physiological sensing from heart rate, respiration, gaze, and movement, then uses a closed-loop controller to adjust crowd density, social scrutiny, uncertainty, and escape availability to keep challenge levels individualized but safe. The novelty is not VR exposure alone, but a standardized mechanism for reproducing realistic anxiety dynamics through context-sensitive escalation rules that link environmental cues to each participant’s moment-to-moment arousal profile, enabling more valid study of triggers, avoidance, and recovery than static laboratory tasks. Feasibility is high because the required headsets, wearable sensors, and rule-based adaptation software are already accessible in research settings. Expected impact includes better phenotyping of anxiety disorders and stronger translational testing of interventions in environments closer to daily life. The main risk is that simulator discomfort or demand characteristics could confound anxiety responses. A minimal validation experiment would compare adaptive mixed-reality scenarios against standard laboratory stress tasks on subjective anxiety, physiological synchrony, and behavioral avoidance within the same participants.

idea: We propose a nursing-home intervention that creates stable resident dyads or triads for brief recurring social encounters by combining three lightweight inputs: life-history themes, broad cognitive-communication level, and same-day mood or energy noted by staff. Instead of running generic activities, the system would recommend compatible small groups and generate low-preparation reminiscence prompts built around shared work histories, hometowns, music, caregiving roles, or other overlapping memories, allowing sessions to happen during existing routines such as meals, lounge time, or short walks. The novelty is not reminiscence therapy alone, but the integration of adaptive social matching, continuity of repeated ties, and prompt structuring calibrated to capacity and readiness, which aims to reduce isolation while providing mild cognitive stimulation without new hardware or intensive training. Feasibility comes from using short resident profiles, optional family-contributed artifacts, and staff-facing guides that can be updated incrementally. Expected impact is greater frequency of meaningful repeated interaction, stronger conversational reciprocity, and more durable peer connection inside the facility. The main risk is that matching based on biography or cognition could feel paternalistic or produce poor-fit pairings, so assent, easy reassignment, and dignity-preserving criteria are essential. A minimal validation experiment would pilot the workflow on one unit, comparing matched micro-groups with usual generic group activities on repeated-contact frequency, observed engagement, and participation continuity over several weeks.

idea: We propose a retrieval-augmented nonlinear differential equation solver for repeated families of ODE and PDE instances in which past solves are stored as structured solver experience rather than only as final states. For a new problem, the method computes a cheap structural signature from the equation form, parameter regime, boundary or initial conditions, and coarse stiffness indicators, then retrieves nearby prior instances to propose a warm start, a continuation schedule, mesh or adaptivity settings, and a local preconditioner template. These retrieved hints are not trusted as final answers; instead, they are injected into a conventional Newton, Krylov, or implicit residual-minimization backend that performs the certified correction, accepts or rejects retrieved guidance using residual-based safeguards, and falls back to default behavior when transfer is poor. The novelty is the equation-family-aware solver memory and reuse interface, which targets the dominant cost of nonlinear iteration without replacing established numerical guarantees. Feasibility is high because the learned or heuristic retrieval layer sits outside trusted solvers and can be added incrementally to existing workflows. If successful, the approach could substantially reduce runtime for parameter sweeps, inverse problems, and repeated simulation campaigns. The main risk is that structural signatures may fail near bifurcations or stiffness regime shifts, leading to harmful retrievals. A minimal validation experiment would compare against strong classical solvers on a benchmark family of related nonlinear equations under matched tolerances, measuring runtime, nonlinear iterations, and recovery behavior when retrieved hints are rejected.

idea: This project proposes a modular hybrid tidal-energy breakwater for coastal regions that need both flood protection and low-carbon power, in which standard breakwater segments are redesigned to embed low-head tidal turbines or oscillating tidal gates that generate electricity during regular tidal exchange while also dissipating wave energy and reducing storm-surge penetration. The research novelty is not simply attaching turbines to coastal infrastructure, but developing a coupled hydro-economic-ecological co-design framework that determines when a dual-purpose structure can outperform separate investments in seawalls or breakwaters plus stand-alone tidal generation by jointly optimizing segment geometry, turbine placement, and operating rules under constraints on fish passage, sediment transport, maintenance access, and extreme-storm survivability. Feasibility is strengthened by the modular architecture, which supports phased piloting, localized repair, and alignment with existing coastal defense budgets rather than requiring a single large estuarine megaproject. Expected impact is lower lifecycle social cost through combined avoided flood damage and predictable tidal power revenue, especially for exposed coastlines with moderate tidal range and high asset risk. The main risk is that corrosion, ecological disruption, or conservative storm-hardening requirements could erase the economic advantage. A minimal validation experiment would compare a few site archetypes in a numerical wave-tide model coupled to simple cost and habitat metrics, benchmarking the hybrid design against separate-defense and separate-energy comparisons.

idea: We propose a thermodynamically constrained, multi-fidelity model for complex-mixture behavior under extreme conditions that learns corrections at the free-energy level rather than directly regressing individual properties. Starting from an interpretable backbone such as a classical equation of state or excess-Gibbs-energy model, the method adds a differentiable correction term conditioned on pressure, temperature, composition, and molecular descriptors of the components, then derives densities, fugacity coefficients, phase equilibria, and response functions by differentiation so cross-property consistency is preserved by construction. Its novelty is the combination of free-energy-level learning, explicit enforcement of Gibbs-Duhem consistency, stability/convexity, and correct ideal-solution or low-density limits, together with multi-fidelity training that uses scarce high-pressure experiments as the primary signal and molecular-simulation data as a regularizer in under-sampled regions, while also producing calibrated uncertainty estimates and out-of-domain warnings. The approach is feasible because it retains the structure of established thermodynamic models while only learning a constrained residual, making it more data-efficient and interpretable than black-box surrogates. If successful, it could improve prediction of non-ideal mixtures in regimes relevant to energy, separations, and planetary or process conditions. The main risk is that simulation bias or imperfect constraint enforcement could distort predictions near phase boundaries. A minimal validation experiment is to train on a mixed experimental-plus-simulation dataset and compare against tuned classical backbones and unconstrained ML models on held-out high-pressure phase-equilibrium and density data for unseen mixture families.

idea: We propose a modular AND-gated cancer therapeutic in which a nanoparticle or antibody-guided nanocarrier first binds a tumor-enriched surface marker and then unmasks its payload only in the presence of a second tumor-microenvironment cue, such as matrix metalloprotease activity or acidic pH, so cytotoxic action requires both spatial recognition and local biochemical activation. The carrier would encapsulate a highly potent drug or gene-silencing cargo in a masked prodrug form, with the outer targeting layer concentrating the construct at malignant tissue and the inner trigger-responsive linker preventing release in circulation or marker-positive normal cells that lack the abnormal microenvironment. The novelty is not any single component, but the explicit combination of orthogonal surface-binding and microenvironment-triggered unmasking to improve therapeutic index beyond conventional chemotherapy, single-antigen targeting, or enzyme-activated prodrugs alone. Feasibility is supported by existing chemistries for protease-cleavable or pH-labile linkers and by clinically familiar targeting scaffolds, making the platform adaptable across tumor types by swapping marker and trigger modules. Expected impact is a substantial reduction in off-tumor toxicity to marrow, gut, and other healthy proliferative tissues while preserving strong local anticancer activity. The main risk is heterogeneous tumors or inflamed normal tissues causing escape or false activation. A minimal validation experiment would compare payload release and cell killing across matched cancer and healthy primary cells while independently toggling marker expression and the second trigger to confirm strict dual-input behavior.

idea: We propose a proactive urban pedestrian-flow management system built around a safety-constrained pedestrian digital twin that predicts short-horizon crowd redistribution at the city-block or corridor scale and then coordinates a limited set of realistic interventions before congestion forms. The system fuses privacy-preserving multimodal sensing, transit and event schedules, weather, and temporary disruption data to estimate evolving pedestrian demand, and uses this forecast to optimize pedestrian signal timing, dynamic wayfinding messages, and reversible curb or buffer-space allocation under explicit accessibility, emergency-egress, and neighborhood-fairness constraints. The novelty is not generic adaptive traffic control transferred to walkers, but a pedestrian-specific joint prediction-control-actuation stack that treats vulnerable-user safety and interpretable operator overrides as first-class design requirements while targeting nonstationary conditions such as concerts, station closures, and construction detours. Feasibility is supported by using existing municipal assets such as fixed counters, signal controllers, and digital signage rather than requiring street reconstruction, although the main risk is that forecast errors or confusing rerouting could shift congestion or burden users with limited mobility if constraints are poorly specified. A minimal validation experiment would compare this approach against static timing and reactive threshold-based control in a simulated pedestrian network with event-driven demand shifts, measuring queue density, congestion duration, travel-time reliability, near-conflict proxies, and accessibility compliance.
task_context:

Problem: Urban pedestrian flow is often inefficient, leading to congestion and safety issues, and current infrastructure design is reactive rather than proactively adaptive to evolving patterns.

idea: We propose a climate-informed hierarchical Bayesian framework to produce high-resolution, depth-stratified maps of subsurface water-ice likelihood on Mars by fusing orbital datasets with different spatial supports and sensing depths rather than forcing them into a single uniform label space. The latent state is defined as ice probability across shallow depth intervals, while sensor-specific observation models link that state to SHARAD/MARSIS detections and non-detections, neutron-derived hydrogen abundance, thermal inertia, albedo, slope, geomorphic context, and fresh-crater ice exposures; soft priors from obliquity-driven ice-stability simulations regularize inference without dictating it. The main novelty is not generic multi-sensor fusion, but explicit treatment of depth sensitivity, resolution mismatch, and cross-sensor disagreement, yielding calibrated posterior uncertainty and interpretable disagreement maps that can distinguish likely buried ice from regions where current theory or measurements are incomplete. This is feasible with existing orbital archives and modern spatial inference or variational approximation tools, and could improve both resource prospecting and reconstruction of latitude-dependent climate history. The main risk is biased supervision and false precision when coarse or selective sensors dominate the posterior. A minimal validation experiment would hold out known fresh-impact ice exposure sites and radar-consistent regions to test whether predicted high-probability zones recover these independent indicators with sensible uncertainty calibration.

idea: We propose a niche space-manufacturing route for pharmaceutical compounds whose clinical performance depends on exceptionally tight solid-state control: crystallizing high-value, low-mass, polymorph-critical active pharmaceutical ingredients or API co-crystals in microgravity to generate defect-minimized seed crystals or small premium lots, then completing downstream finishing and formulation on Earth. The core mechanism is that reduced buoyancy-driven convection, sedimentation, and density-stratified mixing in microgravity may produce more uniform supersaturation fields during nucleation and growth, lowering impurity occlusion, dislocation density, crystal-habit variability, and unwanted polymorphic heterogeneity that remain difficult to suppress in terrestrial batches. The novelty is not microgravity crystallization alone, but its use as a targeted manufacturing strategy for drugs that fail Earth-based consistency or purity thresholds despite advanced process control, with economics justified by very high value per gram and low annual mass demand rather than bulk production. Feasibility is strengthened by focusing on compact crystallization payloads, sterile sealed vessels, and products whose regulatory value is linked to reproducible solid form. Expected impact is a new specialty route for rescue manufacturing of otherwise hard-to-make compounds. The main risk is that observed gains may be reproducible on Earth using improved flow or thermal control, undermining the need for space processing. A minimal validation experiment is a matched Earth-versus-microgravity crystallization campaign using identical solvent, vessel geometry, and supersaturation trajectory, followed by defect, impurity, polymorph, and dissolution analysis after return.

idea: We propose a delay-aware multi-view pharmacovigilance system for earlier detection of rare and delayed adverse drug reactions by treating each candidate drug-event pair as a temporally evolving evidence accumulation problem rather than a static association score. The method builds a time-aligned drug-event graph that fuses three complementary views: spontaneous safety reports for broad signal coverage, longitudinal EHR or claims trajectories for patient-level temporal patterns, and biomedical text or label evidence for mechanistic and semantic support. A source-specific hazard model estimates how evidence from each view changes the probability that a true ADR signal is emerging after drug exposure, while calibrated uncertainty scores determine when weak but concerning signals should be escalated for expert review. The main novelty is the explicit modeling of asynchronous cross-source evidence buildup for delayed ADRs, combined with source-level evidence tracing that keeps alerts auditable for regulators and clinicians. The approach is feasible because each data source already exists in many surveillance environments and can be harmonized through standard drug and outcome vocabularies, although the main risk is instability and confounding for very sparse events or poorly aligned data streams. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively test whether known delayed ADRs are prioritized earlier than with disproportionality analysis, static graph scoring, or single-source temporal comparisons, while also measuring false-alert burden.

idea: This paper proposes a constraint-aware meta-analytic framework for accounting research that augments conventional effect aggregation with an auditable coding layer for two dimensions usually left implicit: methodological limitations affecting internal validity and population constraints affecting external validity. Each study is annotated using a minimal, publicly extractable metadata schema covering design strength, measurement choices, sample type, institutional setting, and time period, and the synthesis then reports not only a pooled estimate but also limitation-adjusted evidence tiers, sensitivity ranges under alternative coding and weighting rules, and explicit statements about where conclusions should and should not generalize. The novelty is not a claim to fully correct bias, but to integrate quality assessment, heterogeneity analysis, and population-scope representation into one transparent workflow tailored to accounting literatures, where findings often span different regulatory regimes, firm sizes, and reporting contexts. Feasibility is strong because the method can be demonstrated using published accounting meta-analyses and study-level information already reported in papers. Its expected impact is to shift meta-analysis from a single decontextualized summary toward decision-relevant evidence maps with clear uncertainty and scope conditions. The main risk is subjective or sparse metadata coding, which could weaken reproducibility. A minimal validation experiment would reanalyze one published accounting meta-analysis and compare whether substantive conclusions change once bounded evidence tiers and generalizability restrictions are reported.

idea: We propose a culturally contextualized ancestry-interpretation layer for direct-to-consumer genetic testing that sits on top of existing inference pipelines and restructures how results are explained rather than how ancestry is computed. The core mechanism is a plural-ancestry report architecture that presents genetic similarity estimates alongside clearly non-substitutable dimensions of heritage such as family history, language, place attachment, and community affiliation, while explicitly stating that genetic clusters do not determine cultural membership, indigeneity, or political belonging. A companion identity-sensitive routing protocol would trigger tailored annotation modules for contexts where misinterpretation is especially harmful, such as Indigenous, Afro-diasporic, caste or tribal, and adoption-related cases, adding historically grounded migration, colonial disruption, and reference-population caveats. The novelty is to operationalize anthropological and STS critiques into a deployable reporting and auditing framework rather than another general ethics warning. Feasibility is high because the intervention can be implemented as templates, decision trees, and annotation layers without changing laboratory methods. Expected impact is reduced essentialist interpretation and improved user understanding of what genetic ancestry can and cannot say. The main risk is that fixed categories or generic cultural modules could themselves oversimplify communities. A minimal validation experiment would compare user interpretation of standard versus plural-ancestry reports in vignette form, measuring uncertainty comprehension, conflation of genetics with identity, and perceived cultural sensitivity.

idea: This project proposes a fully bio-based dynamic polyester network for durable coatings or molded parts, built from lignin- or carbohydrate-derived diacids and diols and incorporating a small fraction of exchangeable ester motifs that enable transesterification under managed conditions. The central mechanism is a switchable polymer fate: the network remains dimensionally stable during normal use, can be reshaped or repaired through mild catalytic bond exchange during manufacturing or remanufacturing, and can be driven toward faster hydrolytic or enzymatic depolymerization in a dedicated end-of-life stream. The novelty is not a claim of wholly new chemistry, but the deliberate integration of three sustainability levers in one platform: renewable feedstocks, low-toxicity organocatalytic or benign catalytic synthesis, and dual end-of-life options that combine closed-loop reprocessing with designed degradability. Feasibility is supported by the separate precedents for bio-based polyester monomers, dynamic ester exchange, and controlled polyester breakdown, although their compatibility and property balance remain open. Expected impact is a realistic route beyond petroleum-based, nondegradable thermoset-like materials. The main risk is that dynamic exchange sufficient for reprocessing may compromise creep resistance or moisture durability. A minimal validation experiment would synthesize one candidate network from a defined renewable monomer set, then compare thermo-mechanical stability, remolding ability, and accelerated depolymerization under buffered hydrolytic or enzyme-assisted conditions.

idea: We propose an interpretable geometry-growth consistency framework to probe the origin of cosmic acceleration by jointly analyzing Type Ia supernova, BAO, weak-lensing, galaxy-clustering, and optional cosmic-chronometer data with a shared late-time expansion history reconstructed through a flexible but stability-constrained nonparametric model for H(z) or w(z). The key mechanism is to fit all distance-sensitive probes under common expansion dynamics while introducing redshift-resolved residual consistency parameters only in the growth sector, so any statistically coherent mismatch between geometry and structure formation is compressed into a small set of physically readable diagnostics. This is novel relative to standard multi-probe likelihood analyses because the primary output is not merely tighter dark-energy parameters, but a robust observable-level test of whether apparent acceleration is better explained by evolving dark energy or modified-gravity-like growth departures, while explicitly accounting for cross-survey calibration and selection systematics in a hierarchical way. The approach is feasible with existing public cosmology likelihoods and can be benchmarked directly against Lambda CDM, CPL, and common spline or Gaussian-process reconstructions. Its main impact would be a clearer separation between genuine new physics and survey-driven inconsistencies. The main risk is residual degeneracy with neutrino mass, curvature, intrinsic alignments, or photometric-redshift errors. A minimal validation experiment is to test recovery on simulations of Lambda CDM, evolving-w, and modified-gravity-like growth scenarios, including leave-one-probe-out robustness checks.

idea: We propose a policy- and workload-aware crypto-agility planner for data platforms that assigns hybrid classical and post-quantum protection profiles to datasets and flows across ingestion, stream processing, storage, replication, and archival. The system combines a metadata layer with an optimization-based control plane that uses data sensitivity, retention horizon, trust boundaries, latency budgets, and migration cost models to decide where to deploy post-quantum key encapsulation and signatures immediately, where hybrid operation is sufficient, and how to schedule rotation without bulk re-encryption or schema disruption. The novelty is to treat post-quantum migration as a cross-stage data-engineering planning problem rather than a static cryptographic configuration problem, explicitly prioritizing long-lived assets exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later risk while accounting for ciphertext size, signature overhead, and metadata propagation costs. The approach is feasible because it relies on existing NIST-standardized or standardized-bound post-quantum primitives and integrates through catalog, policy, and key-management interfaces already present in modern data lakes and event pipelines. Its expected impact is lower-friction quantum-resilient migration for heterogeneous data systems, with more targeted protection than one-size-fits-all upgrades. The main risk is that the contribution could appear as systems integration unless the planner’s objective and constraints are formalized sharply. A minimal validation experiment would compare static encryption policies against planner-generated hybrid plans on a prototype data lake plus streaming pipeline under archival, sharing, and staged-migration scenarios, measuring latency, operational disruption, and long-term protection coverage.

idea: This project develops a comparative documentation framework for the Anthropocene transition that treats periodization as an empirical and policy-relevant modeling choice rather than a settled boundary question. The core mechanism is to assemble a transparent taxonomy of marker families, including Earth-system indicators such as emissions, land-use change, biodiversity pressure, and material throughput, alongside political-institutional markers such as treaty adoption, regulatory shifts, parliamentary attention, and state capacity responses, and then compare how alternative pairings generate different narratives of transition timing, responsibility, and policy urgency across global, regional, and national scales. The novelty lies in moving beyond descriptive Great Acceleration dashboards or conceptual Anthropocene debates to quantify how marker selection changes governance diagnosis itself. Feasibility is strong because the framework can rely on existing longitudinal environmental, trade, and policy text datasets and can be implemented as a reproducible comparison pipeline with divergence maps and narrative sensitivity profiles. Its expected impact is to help policymakers and scholars identify which Anthropocene narratives are most decision-relevant for accountability and intervention design without forcing a single canonical transition date. The main risk is scale mismatch and normative disagreement across heterogeneous indicators, so the framework must make assumptions explicit. A minimal validation experiment would pilot two or three competing periodizations for one region or sector and test whether they produce meaningfully different policy-priority rankings.
