idea: This project proposes a newsroom-integrated source-transparency and uncertainty-labeling protocol for science journalism that standardizes how articles disclose evidence strength, degree of expert consensus, study limitations, and unresolved questions at the point of publication. The core mechanism is sociological as well as communicative: by making the epistemic basis of reporting visible, the intervention aims to repair trust through procedural legitimacy rather than through stronger certainty claims, while also reducing the informational conditions in which sensationalism and misinformation thrive. The novelty lies not in adding generic labels, but in combining uncertainty communication, editorial workflow rules, and audience-facing trust cues into a single deployable framework that links newsroom decision practices to public interpretations of scientific authority. The design is feasible because it can be implemented as a lightweight template and style guide within existing science desks, then audited through mixed methods. Expected impact includes better calibrated trust, improved comprehension of what is known versus unsettled, and greater resistance to misleading simplifications. The main risk is that some audiences may read explicit uncertainty as incompetence or institutional weakness, especially for politicized topics. A minimal validation experiment would randomly assign readers to labeled versus standard versions of the same science story and compare multidimensional trust, comprehension, perceived accuracy, uncertainty understanding, and willingness to share.

idea: We propose a closed-loop geometry-aware additive manufacturing framework that reduces part-to-part shape inconsistency by converting standard in-situ monitoring streams into actionable geometric control during fabrication. The system fuses layerwise camera images, thermal maps, and sparse height or profilometry measurements to estimate latent geometric error modes such as shrinkage, bead-width drift, warping, and support-induced deformation, then uses a physics-informed predictor to forecast whether these deviations will accumulate into downstream geometric errors. Rather than continuously perturbing the process, the controller applies uncertainty-gated, locally bounded corrections only where predicted drift exceeds a threshold, for example by adjusting toolpath offsets, extrusion or energy input, or scan strategy on subsequent layers. The novelty is the integration of multi-view geometric state estimation, future-error prediction, and selective intervention, shifting additive manufacturing from passive defect observation or offline pre-compensation toward early prevention of cumulative geometry loss. Feasibility is supported by using sensing modalities already available or addable with modest instrumentation on many platforms, while constrained actuation limits reduce the risk of introducing new defects. If successful, the approach could lower post-processing burden and improve dimensional consistency across complex parts. The main risk is that imperfect state estimation or overcorrection may trade geometric gains for surface roughness or residual stress. A minimal validation experiment would compare this controller against open-loop printing on a small set of geometrically challenging parts, measuring layerwise deviation growth and final geometric error.

idea: We propose an operational tsunami-warning architecture that continuously updates probabilistic alerts by fusing the earliest available seismic inversion, high-rate GNSS displacement, sparse offshore pressure or buoy streams, and coastal sea-level observations into a sequential estimate of earthquake source and expected wave evolution. The core mechanism is a latency-aware Bayesian assimilation pipeline coupled to a physics-informed surrogate model trained to emulate full tsunami propagation fast enough to run real-time ensembles, so warning centers can issue not only a binary alert but calibrated exceedance probabilities for coastal wave height and inundation severity. The novelty is not a new sensor type, but the end-to-end integration of uncertainty-aware source inference, rapid ensemble propagation, and economically informed alert selection that explicitly balances earlier warning against false-alarm costs and evacuation burden. This is feasible because it can be layered onto existing seismic, GNSS, tide-gauge, and buoy networks, with the surrogate serving as a speed layer rather than replacing established hazard physics. Expected impact is improved lead time and more reliable coastal targeting, especially in events where initial seismic estimates are ambiguous. The main risk is degraded performance in regions with sparse offshore telemetry or poorly calibrated loss assumptions. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively replay historical tsunami events with realistic data-arrival delays and compare lead time, forecast calibration, and alert decisions against current operational workflows.

idea: We propose a coherence-map-driven runtime orchestration layer for scaled quantum processors that treats coherence as a time-varying systems resource rather than a fixed calibration constant. The core mechanism is a rolling hardware map built from lightweight observables already available in many platforms, such as recent calibration drift, Ramsey/echo-derived coherence proxies, spectator-shift estimates, and short-window gate error summaries; this map is exposed to a compiler-controller interface that periodically reassigns logical qubits to more stable regions, retimes gates to avoid high-risk windows, and inserts selective dynamical decoupling only on idling qubits whose predicted exposure is costly. The novelty is the closed-loop coordination across sensing, placement, scheduling, and protection, which goes beyond standalone adaptive calibration or noise-aware compilation by turning coherence nonstationarity into direct runtime decisions at short update horizons. The approach is feasible because it relies on modest signals and sparse updates rather than full tomography or continuous recompilation, and it could increase usable circuit depth and effective two-qubit gate utilization on larger devices where spatial and temporal stability are heterogeneous. The main risk is that sensing and update overhead may outweigh gains if noise changes faster than the map can track. A minimal validation experiment would compare this runtime layer against static calibration and fixed mapping on a simulator with slow-drift and bursty noise, measuring executable circuit depth and aggregate infidelity.

idea: We propose a root-localized synthetic rhizosphere module for hydroponics that recreates key soil-microbe functions without turning the entire recirculating reservoir into an uncontrolled biofilm system. Seedlings would first be precolonized with a minimal 3-5 strain consortium chosen for complementary functions such as phosphate or potassium mobilization, siderophore-mediated iron acquisition, and antagonism against common root pathogens, then transferred into hydroponic units containing an inert porous carrier or root-adjacent sleeve that provides a protected attachment niche near the roots. To improve persistence under low-organic, high-flow conditions, the system would use periodic ultra-low-dose exudate-mimic carbon pulses targeted to the root zone rather than the bulk nutrient tank, aiming to support beneficial microbes locally while limiting opportunist growth, line fouling, and chemistry drift. The novelty is not any single inoculant or carrier component, but their integration into a spatially confined, sanitation-compatible microbiome platform tailored to hydroponic constraints. This design is feasible with standard hydroponic hardware and commercially accessible microbial strains and materials, and could improve nutrient uptake efficiency and disease resistance in soilless cultivation. The main risk is that the carrier or carbon support may also favor unwanted microbes. A minimal validation experiment would compare uninoculated, inoculation-only, and module-treated plants under mild phosphorus or iron limitation while measuring root colonization persistence, bulk-solution spillover, plant nutrient status, growth, and response to a controlled root-pathogen challenge.

idea: We propose a programmable threshold-gradient smart composite that converts a single uniform external stimulus into ordered, region-specific behavior by encoding different local activation thresholds across the material. Instead of all domains responding simultaneously, the composite is fabricated with spatially varying crosslink density, filler loading, or microstructural alignment so that heating, light, humidity, or an electric field drives sequential switching of shape, stiffness, porosity, or color as the global input rises. Weak coupling between neighboring regions can be tuned to sharpen transitions or propagate wave-like state changes, enabling functions such as self-sequencing actuators, adaptive vents, or distributed mechanical logic without embedded electronics or spatially patterned stimulus sources. The novelty is not merely a graded amplitude response, but intrinsically programmed multi-step state transitions under one common trigger, which addresses the limited functional complexity of conventional uniformly responsive smart materials. Feasibility is supported by plausible fabrication routes including voxelwise printing, selective curing, gradient filler deposition, and post-fabrication training. A key risk is that fabrication tolerances and hysteresis may blur threshold separation and collapse the behavior back toward smooth or inconsistent actuation. A minimal validation experiment would fabricate a strip with three programmed threshold zones and test whether uniform heating produces reproducible, ordered local transformations compared with a uniform control and a conventional graded material.
task_context:

idea: We propose a probabilistic two-stage early-warning and impact-triage framework for climate-driven methane hydrate destabilization on continental margins. In the first stage, the system assimilates bottom-water warming trends, hydrate stability model outputs, seafloor deformation, bathymetric change, and acoustic plume observations to estimate near-term likelihood of hydrate weakening or seep activation at site scale. In the second stage, it screens the likely fate of released methane using simple sediment and water-column pathway indicators, such as sulfate-methane transition depth, local oxidation potential, plume height, and water-depth constraints, to distinguish releases likely to be oxidized or trapped from those with greater chance of reaching the upper ocean and contributing to atmospheric forcing. The novelty is not a new sensor or a fully resolved transport model, but the explicit coupling of physical destabilization signals with methane-fate relevance, enabling uncertainty-aware prioritization of monitoring and hazard assessment beyond static stability maps or temperature-only alerts. The approach is feasible because it leverages heterogeneous but already available oceanographic, geophysical, and geochemical observations and focuses on risk ranking rather than deterministic flux prediction. Its expected impact is a more defensible identification of climate-relevant methane-release hotspots. The main risk is sparse, site-specific data and difficult attribution relative to non-hydrate seepage. A minimal validation experiment is a hindcast at several well-studied margins, testing whether the framework would rank known seep or plume activation sites above matched control locations before or during observed activity.

idea: We propose a cartridge-based diagnostic that rapidly identifies antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains by combining strain-selective capture with ultra-early phenotypic susceptibility measurement directly from clinical samples. The system would use a microfluidic chip functionalized with pathogen- or strain-biased binders to enrich target cells from urine or positive blood culture aliquots, partition them into nanoliter chambers, expose them to a short pulse of clinically relevant antibiotics, and record early stress-response signatures through low-cost optical and electrochemical sensors that detect changes in membrane integrity, metabolic activity, and microcolony initiation before conventional growth is visible. A constrained classifier would integrate these signals with a small panel of resistance markers only when needed to improve strain attribution in mixed infections, reducing the failure mode of genotype-only assays that miss context-dependent resistance expression. The main novelty is the integration of selective enrichment, single-cell-scale rapid phenotyping, and lightweight inference for resistant-subpopulation resolution within a same-shift workflow. Feasibility is supported by existing microfluidic capture, short-incubation AST, and compact sensing components, although capture specificity and phenotype robustness across specimen matrices remain the principal risk. A minimal validation experiment would compare turnaround time and resistance-call agreement against standard culture and susceptibility testing using contrived mixed susceptible/resistant strain samples and a small prospective set of urine or positive blood culture specimens.

idea: We propose a probabilistic volcanic early-warning framework that integrates seismicity, ground deformation, gas emissions, thermal anomalies, and satellite observations through a missing-data-aware temporal model to estimate calibrated short-horizon probabilities of unrest escalation and eruption. The core mechanism is a multimodal sequence model with modality-specific encoders, uncertainty-aware fusion, and explicit handling of irregular sampling, delayed feeds, and sensor outages, so that forecasts remain stable when monitoring is incomplete. To address the severe data scarcity faced by many volcanoes, the framework also includes cross-volcano transfer learning with lightweight few-shot adaptation and expert-informed priors, allowing partially monitored sites to benefit from patterns learned at better instrumented volcanoes. The main novelty is not generic sensor fusion, but the combination of calibrated probabilistic forecasting, robustness to real operational data gaps, and transferability across volcanoes in one decision-ready system. This is feasible because it can be trained on retrospective multi-volcano monitoring archives without requiring full physics-based hazard simulation. Its expected impact is more reliable alert thresholds and better communication of uncertainty to observatories and civil protection agencies. The principal risk is that cross-volcano transfer may fail under strong geological differences. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively compare within-volcano and leave-one-volcano-out forecasting under simulated sensor outages, measuring lead-time-conditioned event detection and probability calibration.

idea: We propose a chronotype-aware personalized sleep recovery index that estimates whether a given night was truly restorative by combining sleep duration with circadian fit and within-person physiology. Instead of scoring eight hours uniformly, the system first learns each user’s longitudinal comparison from common wearable and app data: habitual sleep timing, timing regularity, resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, and a lightweight chronotype estimate derived from a short questionnaire or midsleep patterns. Each night is then scored by how well it matches the individual’s expected sleep need and biological timing, while penalizing social jetlag, irregular bed and wake times, and adverse deviations from personal HRV or resting-heart-rate norms. The main novelty is shifting sleep assessment from population-average duration thresholds to an individualized recovery model centered on comparison deviation and circadian alignment, while remaining feasible with existing consumer wearables and brief daily alertness check-ins. This could improve fatigue monitoring for cognitively demanding professions such as accounting, where decision quality may depend more on misalignment and incomplete recovery than on hours slept alone. The main risk is noisy chronotype and wearable physiology estimates, especially under stress, illness, or caffeine use. A minimal validation experiment would test whether this index predicts next-day self-reported alertness better than duration-only and duration-plus-stage comparisons in a longitudinal within-person dataset.
task_context:

idea: We propose a compact multi-site mixed-methods study to identify which placebo-effect mechanisms generalize across cultures and which depend on locally specific healing meanings. The core design decomposes placebo-related responses into four candidate pathways: conscious expectancy, conditioning history, ritual symbolism, and relational trust in the healer or clinician. Participants from a small set of culturally distinct populations, including at least one non-Western setting, would complete a harmonized low-risk behavioral or symptom-vignette paradigm in which treatment framing and ritual cues are experimentally varied, alongside locally adapted interviews eliciting idioms of efficacy, trust, and healing. The novelty is not merely comparing placebo magnitude across sites, but building a mechanism-level map that tests whether the same observable response arises from different cultural pathways. Feasibility is strengthened by using brief paradigms, cognitive interviewing, translation and back-translation, and a narrow symptom domain rather than a costly clinical trial. A minimal validation experiment would randomize culturally grounded versus culturally neutral treatment framings within each site and test whether changes in reported relief are differentially mediated by expectancy versus ritual-meaning and trust measures. The expected impact is a more anthropologically grounded theory of placebo processes that can inform later causal and clinical studies, while the main risk is measurement non-equivalence, where constructs such as trust or expectation may not map cleanly across populations.

idea: We propose a point-source wastewater treatment module based on magnetically recoverable porous sorbents whose surfaces combine hydrophobic, aromatic, and hydrogen-bonding motifs to capture diverse microplastics, especially from textile and municipal effluents where particle loads are high enough for controlled interception. The core mechanism is selective adsorption of suspended polymer particles onto reusable magnetic composites, followed by rapid magnetic separation and mild closed-loop regeneration using salt, pH, or low-solvent triggers that release an intact concentrated microplastic fraction for downstream recycling or high-confidence destruction rather than fragmentation in situ. The novelty is the integration of tunable polymer-affinity chemistry with magnetic recovery and explicit mass-balance handling designed to avoid the common failure mode of shifting pollution into nanoplastic or dissolved byproduct pools. Feasibility is strengthened by compatibility with existing polishing or side-stream units and by avoiding energy-intensive oxidation steps, making retrofit deployment more realistic. If successful, the system could reduce persistent plastic discharge while creating a manageable concentrate stream for regulated disposal. The main technical risk is fouling and loss of selectivity in real wastewater containing surfactants, natural organic matter, and biofilms. A minimal validation experiment would compare repeated-cycle capture and regeneration for mixed PE, PP, PET, PS, and nylon particles in synthetic versus real textile wastewater, while tracking polymer-resolved removal, magnetic recovery, and full particle mass balance.

idea: We propose a multi-epoch hierarchical retrieval framework for biosignature assessment that jointly models planetary atmospheric spectra, stellar surface heterogeneity, and time-variable contamination across repeated transmission and emission observations of the same exoplanet system. Instead of treating each visit independently, the method shares latent parameters for spot and facula populations, activity-driven spectral distortions, and persistent atmospheric structure while allowing visit-specific variability, cloud or haze changes, and wavelength-dependent noise. The key novelty is not only contamination-aware retrieval, which already exists in limited forms, but a false-positive-control layer that converts posterior gas inferences into calibrated biosignature plausibility scores and estimated follow-up value, explicitly distinguishing biotic-like gas combinations from abiotic or stellar-confounded explanations. This is feasible with JWST-class repeated spectroscopy because it works with currently plausible cadence and wavelength coverage, and computational cost can be managed through structured priors and surrogate forward models. Its expected impact is to reduce overconfident biosignature claims and make telescope time allocation more decision-relevant by identifying when additional visits materially reduce ambiguity. The main risk is identifiability: stellar variability, clouds, and trace gases can imprint similar spectral signatures at low signal-to-noise. A minimal validation experiment would compare this framework against standard single-epoch retrievals on synthetic repeated spectra with injected spots, faculae, clouds, and abiotic O2/CH4-like cases, measuring calibration of false-positive-aware plausibility scores.

idea: We propose a probabilistic phytoplankton genome-to-ocean-region atlas that harmonizes isolate genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes across public repositories and maps each record to standardized marine province systems as a distribution over region, depth layer, and season rather than a single label. The core mechanism is a provenance-aware integration pipeline that joins genome records with sampling coordinates, collection time, depth, taxonomic context, and matched environmental covariates such as temperature, nutrients, chlorophyll, and circulation regime, then infers confidence-scored regional assignments under multiple accepted ocean biogeography schemas. Novelty comes from treating missing or conflicting metadata as an uncertainty modeling problem instead of a curation failure, enabling the database to support climate-response modeling while preserving traceable evidence and compatibility with downstream ecosystem forecasts. The project is feasible because the required ingredients already exist in fragmented form across genome catalogs, cruise metadata, and public ocean environmental layers, and the main engineering contribution is schema harmonization plus calibrated assignment logic. Expected impact is a reusable resource for linking phytoplankton functional potential to changing ocean regions under climate stress. The main risk is inconsistent region definitions and sparse metadata that could yield poorly calibrated assignments. A minimal validation experiment would test whether confidence-weighted atlas assignments agree with held-out known sampling regions and remain stable across alternative province schemas.

idea: We propose a globally updateable geospatial policy-trigger framework that fuses public Earth-observation time series with climate, land-use, population, transport accessibility, infrastructure, administrative, and lightweight governance proxies to generate subnational indicators for three linked decision tasks: environmental hotspot targeting, urban growth risk screening, and pre/post-disaster resource prioritization. The core mechanism is a spatiotemporal data-fusion pipeline that converts heterogeneous layers into interpretable composite signals and rule-based triggers, such as places where rapid land conversion, rising exposure, and weak service accessibility jointly indicate regulatory intervention or resilience investment needs. The main novelty is not a new sensor or standalone map, but a unified, cross-sector framework that updates regularly, ties outputs to concrete policy actions, and remains comparable across countries using globally available inputs with optional local calibration. Feasibility is high because the required data streams already exist in public global repositories, and the framework can be implemented at common administrative or gridded resolutions. Expected impact is a more current and policy-relevant evidence base for environmental management, urban planning, and disaster preparedness in data-sparse settings. The main risk is that cross-country indicator thresholds may be too generic or sensitive to uneven data quality. A minimal validation experiment would compare the framework against single-domain or static map comparisons on a small set of case-study regions by testing whether it yields more stable and interpretable hotspot rankings before and after major environmental or hazard shocks.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware multimodal neurofeedback system that compensates for fMRI’s slow blood-oxygen-level-dependent response by coupling it with a fast auxiliary modality such as EEG or fNIRS in a subject-specific state-space model. The model treats target-circuit activity as a latent dynamical process: fast signals drive millisecond-scale provisional estimates, while delayed fMRI observations provide spatially precise correction terms that recalibrate the latent state and prevent drift. The key novelty is not generic signal fusion, but closed-loop estimation under delayed observations, where feedback is explicitly gated by predictive uncertainty so the system can suppress unstable or overconfident updates when the surrogate signal becomes unreliable. Feasibility is supported by existing simultaneous acquisition setups and by the fact that the method only requires regional feedback rather than full-brain real-time reconstruction. If successful, this approach could turn fMRI from a purely delayed feedback tool into a spatially anchored controller for near-real-time neurofeedback, enabling better training of deep or distributed circuits that EEG alone cannot localize well. The main risk is that the auxiliary modality may dominate the estimate, reducing true fMRI-specific spatial fidelity or yielding misleading control when uncertainty is miscalibrated. A minimal validation experiment would compare standard framewise fMRI neurofeedback, simple multimodal fusion, and the proposed delayed-correction controller on a region-targeting task, measuring effective feedback latency, regional specificity, and feedback stability.

idea: We propose a place-based evidence reconciliation model for high school environmental science in which students investigate a single local question, such as why one campus area is hotter, more polluted, or less biodiverse than another, using short field protocols with low-cost tools and then compare their measurements with authoritative public datasets such as weather, land-use, air-quality, or water records. The core novelty is that hands-on work is not treated as a standalone lab or generic citizen-science activity; instead, students must reconcile differences between their own noisy observations and larger-scale datasets through structured claim-evidence-reasoning, uncertainty notes, and revision cycles, producing a community-facing brief or map-based explanation. This design is feasible because it can be embedded into existing units, uses one focal phenomenon per cycle, and relies on repeatable routines for calibration, replication, or triangulation rather than specialized infrastructure. The expected impact is stronger scientific literacy through authentic question formulation, data interpretation, and understanding of uncertainty while making environmental science visibly relevant to students’ own surroundings. The main risk is teacher burden and uneven data quality, especially if public data access or student measurements are difficult to align. A minimal validation experiment would compare one class using this reconciliation cycle against a standard environmental science lab on students’ quality of evidence-based explanations and handling of conflicting data.

idea: This project proposes to treat microplastics as an unmodeled geomorphic control by testing whether particle morphology and aging state shift rainfall-runoff and erosion thresholds in agricultural soils. Specifically, it will compare fibers and fragments, each in fresh and environmentally aged forms, across contrasting cropland textures to determine how they alter pore connectivity, aggregate stability, surface sealing, and crust formation, thereby changing runoff onset, rill initiation, and fine-sediment export during storms. The novelty is not simply asking whether microplastics influence soil properties, but linking morphology-specific microplastic effects to threshold behavior that geomorphology routinely uses to explain detachment and channelization, yet rarely applies to plastic-contaminated soils. The work is feasible with standard rainfall simulators, runoff collection, aggregate-stability tests, dye-tracing or X-ray imaging of preferential flow, and sediment sizing, and it could provide parameters for incorporating microplastic-sensitive erodibility into agricultural erosion models and land-management guidance. A minimal validation experiment would amend replicated soil boxes of sandy loam and clay loam with realistic concentrations of aged fibers or fragments, then measure time to runoff, sediment yield, and the rainfall intensity required for first rill formation under identical simulated storms. The main risk is that effects may be small or highly contingent on soil texture and moisture history, but even null or conditional outcomes would clarify when microplastics matter for sediment dynamics.

idea: We propose that a clinically meaningful subset of Alzheimer’s disease is driven by an inflammatory gut-dysbiosis axis in which depletion of short-chain fatty acid- and indole-producing microbes, together with enrichment of endotoxin-associated taxa, weakens intestinal barrier integrity, increases circulating microbial inflammatory products, and biases peripheral myeloid cells and brain microglia toward NLRP3-dominant activation, thereby accelerating amyloid seeding, tau propagation, and neuroinflammatory injury. The novelty is not a generic microbiome-AD association, but a subtype framework that integrates a specific causal checkpoint with a multi-compartment biomarker strategy: stool metagenomics to quantify dysbiosis, plasma markers of permeability, endotoxemia, and microbial metabolite loss, and CSF or imaging readouts of neuroinflammation and amyloid/tau burden. This design is feasible because each component is measurable with existing assays and can support patient stratification for adjunctive therapy that combines microbiome or metabolite restoration with anti-inflammatory or anti-amyloid treatment. The expected impact is improved biological stratification and a rational path to identify patients most likely to benefit from gut-brain targeted intervention. The main risk is mechanistic over-attribution, since diet, medication exposure, and disease stage may confound the signature or reveal parallel pathways beyond NLRP3. A minimal validation experiment would test, in a well-phenotyped AD cohort, whether the proposed stool signature co-occurs with plasma permeability and endotoxin markers and correlates with CSF or imaging evidence of heightened neuroinflammation and greater amyloid/tau pathology.

idea: We propose a closed-loop real-time learning architecture that reduces both energy consumption and convergence time by separating adaptation into two timescales: a compact front-end adapter updates frequently on streaming data, while a larger backbone remains frozen except for rare correction steps triggered by sustained uncertainty or distribution shift. A lightweight controller monitors confidence, prediction volatility, and an explicit compute budget to decide whether to reuse the current state, update only the adapter, or invoke a sparse backbone refresh, thereby coupling optimization efficiency with conditional computation rather than treating training and inference separately. The novelty is the coordinated policy over when to update, what parameter subset to update, and how much computation to spend per input under latency constraints, which distinguishes the method from standard parameter-efficient tuning, pruning, or early-exit schemes alone. The design is feasible because it can be built from existing adapter modules, uncertainty estimators, and budget-aware schedulers without specialized hardware. If successful, it could enable more responsive edge and streaming AI systems that adapt quickly while avoiding unnecessary full-model updates. The main risk is that controller overhead or unstable triggers may erase the savings or degrade robustness under bursty nonstationary streams. A minimal validation experiment would compare this system against full fine-tuning and fixed-adapter online adaptation on a streaming benchmark, measuring updates-to-target accuracy, latency, and energy-relevant update frequency.

idea: We propose a Bayesian multimodal reconstruction framework for non-destructive fossil analysis that fuses low-dose micro-CT, high-resolution surface microscopy, and sparse Raman or infrared spectroscopic measurements into a single probabilistic model of internal anatomy and fossil-matrix boundaries. The core mechanism is a latent 3D representation whose geometry, material classes, and feature maps are inferred jointly from all modalities while explicitly modeling measurement noise, missing views, and cross-modality registration error, so the output is not just a reconstruction but posterior probability maps and calibrated uncertainty for cavities, vascular channels, growth structures, and interface locations. The novelty is a fossil-specific statistical inverse model that turns complementary but incomplete scans into conservative anatomical inference and a practical decision rule for when uncertainty remains too high to justify avoiding destructive sectioning. Feasibility is supported by using existing scanners and benchmark specimens rather than requiring new hardware, with priors regularizing inference without forcing expected morphology. The expected impact is to reduce unnecessary sampling while giving paleontologists more reliable internal structural information. The main risk is weak contrast or prior bias making some features unidentifiable. A minimal validation experiment would digitally degrade a small set of high-resolution scanned specimens into sparse multimodal observations and test whether posterior intervals and boundary probabilities remain calibrated against the original volumes.

idea: We propose a reproducibility-planning copilot for psychology that converts a researcher’s free-text hypothesis and draft protocol into an auditable design-and-analysis contract before data collection. The system would identify the target estimand, sampling plan, exclusion rules, stopping criteria, power target, primary and secondary analyses, robustness checks, and points of analytic flexibility, then recommend matched safeguards such as stronger preregistration fields, blinded decisions, or independent code review. Its main novelty is not another checklist, but an operational translation layer that turns vague protocol language into explicit commitments while preserving a machine-readable planned-versus-executed deviation log that can follow the study into manuscript submission. Feasibility is high because the inputs already exist in ordinary lab workflows and the outputs can be reviewed and edited by humans rather than enforced automatically. The expected impact is a reduction in hidden researcher degrees of freedom and clearer separation of confirmatory versus exploratory analyses, improving transparency without requiring every study to become a registered report. The main risk is over-standardizing legitimate exploratory work or producing poor recommendations from underspecified hypotheses, so the tool must label uncertainty and keep researchers in the loop. A minimal validation experiment would compare psychology protocols prepared with and without the copilot, measuring whether independent methodologists judge the copilot-assisted plans as more complete, less ambiguous, and easier to replicate.

idea: This project investigates when misinformation corrections actually suppress diffusion in social networks by testing the interaction of correction timing, messenger identity, and network position. The core mechanism is that corrections do not spread or persuade on content alone: they depend on whether the correcting actor is socially legitimate to the recipients and structurally able to cross community boundaries. I propose comparing early versus late corrections delivered by three actor types: highly central accounts within a community, ordinary local peers, and bridge-positioned users who connect otherwise separated groups. The central hypothesis is that early corrections from bridge actors who are seen as identity-congruent or at least locally credible will reduce downstream resharing and cascade depth more effectively than either generic high-centrality corrections or out-group corrections, especially in polarized or high-homophily networks. The novelty is to move beyond asking whether corrections work toward specifying how legitimacy and brokerage jointly condition correction success. The study is feasible with platform trace data that include repost networks and inferred communities, or with a controlled online network experiment that randomizes correction timing and sender type. A minimal validation experiment would expose participants in small artificial networks to the same false claim, vary whether correction appears early or late and from a peer, central node, or bridge node, and measure resharing and cross-community uptake. The main risk is separating true correction effects from prior beliefs and endogenous network selection.

idea: We propose an adaptive-boundary microfluidic platform that sustains laminar transport without requiring tightly optimized channel geometry by coating channel walls with a shear-activated lining made of soft microstructures or stimulus-responsive polymer brushes whose effective slip length and tangential damping change only when local transverse disturbances emerge. Under nominal flow the lining remains hydraulically quiet, preserving throughput and avoiding continuous energy input, but when curvature, fabrication defects, bends, or moderate Reynolds-number excursions generate incipient secondary motion, the wall locally shifts into a higher-damping state that attenuates cross-stream velocity fluctuations and re-centers the main stream before full instability develops. The novelty is to treat laminarization as a programmable boundary-condition problem rather than a fixed-geometry or global-feedback problem, making the stabilizing function modular and portable across many channel layouts. The concept is feasible because responsive coatings, compliant wall textures, and low-voltage electroresponsive surfaces are already manufacturable as thin post-fabrication layers on standard microchannels. If successful, this could relax geometric tolerances, reduce dependence on ultra-low-Re operation, and lower the complexity and power cost of active flow control. The main risk is that fouling, hysteresis, or poorly tuned response thresholds could either blunt the stabilizing effect or increase pressure drop. A minimal validation experiment is to compare coated and uncoated channels with deliberate width perturbations over a Reynolds-number sweep while measuring interface wandering and transverse velocity fluctuations.

idea: We propose a sequential, physics-guided probabilistic forecasting system for coronal mass ejections that aims to reduce the economic and operational inefficiencies caused by imprecise alerts. The model would issue an initial eruption-time forecast by fusing coronagraph image features, source-region magnetic characteristics, and outputs from heliospheric propagation models, then update that forecast as new observations arrive through a Bayesian or state-space mechanism. Rather than predicting only a single arrival time, it would produce calibrated distributions over Earth-arrival probability, arrival-time windows, and likely impact severity, allowing operators to act on quantified uncertainty instead of unstable point estimates. The main novelty is the combination of multimodal physics-informed fusion with event-lifecycle updating and decision-aware evaluation, which could improve precision without requiring new instruments or abandoning interpretable physical priors. Feasibility is high because the approach can be built on existing CME catalogs, solar observations, and operational propagation outputs, although a key risk is that heterogeneous labels and missing real-time inputs may limit calibration quality. A minimal validation experiment would retrospectively compare this system against deterministic and static probabilistic comparisons on historical CME events, measuring calibration, interval coverage, arrival-time error, and false-alarm tradeoffs under a stylized grid or satellite-operations cost matrix.

idea: We propose a distributed microplastic-capture system that replaces pore-size filtration with polymer-selective, magnetically recoverable flocculation in sidestream treatment nodes such as stormwater basins, retention ponds, and wastewater polishing units. The core mechanism uses biodegradable bridging ligands or mineral-supported biopolymers engineered to adsorb preferentially onto hydrophobic and mildly oxidized plastic surfaces, forming mesoscale aggregates that are then rapidly collected by reusable magnetic particles under an external field and removed by settling or skimming. The novelty is not magnet use alone, but the combination of environmentally benign transient bridging, surface-chemistry selectivity for mixed and weathered polymers, and closed-loop magnetic recovery designed for diffuse-source interception where fine membranes foul or become impractical. Feasibility is supported by the modular nature of the process, compatibility with existing basins and sidestreams, and the possibility of regenerating the magnetic collectors over multiple cycles rather than continuously replacing filters. If successful, this approach could lower energy use and fouling while expanding microplastic removal to decentralized water infrastructure. The main risk is poor selectivity in the presence of natural organic matter, clays, algae, surfactants, and biofilms, which could increase sludge production or reduce capture efficiency. A minimal validation experiment would compare capture and recovery of PE, PP, PS, and PET particles, including weathered samples, in synthetic freshwater with and without added organic matter, quantifying both microplastic removal and residual collector leakage.

idea: We propose a pre-release anti-predator training framework for captive-bred animals that combines social learning, adaptive cue exposure, and release-site matching to build predator responses that transfer beyond a single training scenario. Naive individuals would first observe experienced conspecifics, trained demonstrators, or species-appropriate surrogates responding to predator odors, calls, models, and movement patterns, then progress to individualized practice in semi-natural enclosures containing realistic refuge and escape options. Training intensity, cue combinations, and habitat context would be varied across sessions to reduce habituation and overfitting, while repeated behavioral assays would adjust dose and determine release readiness based on stable vigilance, timely refuge use, appropriate escape decisions, and controlled boldness under partially novel predator presentations. The novelty is not a single cue-exposure method, but an integrated operational pipeline that links social scaffolding, multimodal anti-habituation design, site-specific ecology, and closed-loop release gating into one deployable conservation protocol. The approach is feasible because it can be layered onto existing soft-release workflows and scaled by species using locally relevant predator cues and simple standardized assays. Its expected impact is lower post-release mortality caused by behavioral naivete, although a central risk is inducing chronic stress or excessive fear that reduces foraging or settlement. A minimal validation experiment would compare this integrated protocol against standard one-off predator exposure and measure pre-release generalization, retention, and short-term post-release behavioral proxies.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-gated rolling-horizon dispatch framework for emergency response that integrates real-time spatiotemporal demand prediction with fast constrained resource allocation. A short-horizon forecaster continuously estimates incident intensity, call mix, and calibrated uncertainty for each region and time window; these uncertainty signals are then translated into optimization controls such as ambiguity budgets, reserve requirements, and repositioning penalties inside a tractable dispatch-and-staging model. When predictions are confident, the controller proactively repositions units and allocates reserve capacity toward emerging hotspots; when confidence is low or shifts are detected, it falls back toward conservative coverage-preserving decisions that limit overreaction and maintain fairness and workload constraints. The novelty is not merely forecast-then-optimize, but using predictive uncertainty as an explicit operational control signal that determines how aggressive or robust the allocation should be at each decision epoch. This design is feasible because the optimization can be restricted to reserve and staging choices with warm starts for repeated solves. The expected impact is lower unmet demand and more stable response quality under volatile conditions. The main risk is that uncertainty calibration may fail during rare surges, causing either excessive conservatism or unsafe reallocations. A minimal validation experiment would compare static allocation, point-forecast rolling optimization, and the proposed uncertainty-gated controller on simulated nonstationary incident streams with delayed signals, measuring response time, coverage, stability, and constraint violations.

idea: We propose a microclimate-aware climate adaptation prioritization system for extreme heat that converts coarse regional adaptation planning into neighborhood-scale resource allocation. The core mechanism is to fuse sparse air temperature and humidity sensors with satellite land-surface indicators, topography, land cover, street morphology, imperviousness, and built-environment data to infer localized heat exposure at decision-relevant spatial units, then pass those estimates into an uncertainty-aware optimizer that allocates a fixed adaptation budget across interventions such as cooling centers, shade investments, or urban greening. The main novelty is not simply finer-resolution mapping, but the end-to-end linkage between microclimate inference, calibrated uncertainty, and intervention placement, including transfer to sensor-poor areas through similarity-based or physics-informed constraints so places without dense monitoring can still receive actionable guidance. The approach is feasible because most predictors are already available from public remote-sensing, GIS, and municipal sources, while low-cost sensors can provide limited calibration data. Expected impact is more efficient protection of populations in micro-hotspots that are invisible in coarse climate layers or population-only heuristics. The main risk is that predictions may overfit static urban form proxies and be weakly validated where sensors are sparse. A minimal validation experiment would compare budget-constrained intervention zones selected by this framework versus coarse-grid planning rules in two cities, testing whether the chosen zones cover more high-exposure residents and whether uncertainty correctly identifies where adding sensors would change decisions.

idea: We propose a closed-loop combinatorial chemistry platform that replaces brute-force high-throughput experimentation with nanoliter-to-droplet-scale adaptive synthesis guided by multi-objective active learning. The workflow begins with a diversity- and synthesizability-constrained seed panel spanning scaffold, reagent, and condition space, executes these reactions in ultra-miniaturized format, and scores crude outcomes using rapid inline MS or spectroscopy rather than full purification. A learning policy then selects the next reaction batch by jointly optimizing expected information gain, predicted product value, developability, reaction quality confidence, and material cost, while advancing only the most promising regions to confirmatory synthesis at larger scale. The novelty is not miniaturization or machine learning alone, but their integration into a medicinal-chemistry-ready decision system that treats solvent use, reagent consumption, and waste generation as first-class optimization targets. Feasibility is supported by existing liquid-handling, droplet microfluidic, and crude-analytics tools, with the main engineering effort being calibration of noisy crude signals and accommodating heterogeneous reaction classes. If successful, the approach could reduce experiment count, cost, and waste while preserving or improving discovery of chemically relevant hits. The main risk is that crude analytical noise or hardware bias could misdirect the acquisition loop. A minimal validation experiment would compare this workflow against random and conventional plate-based HTE for two representative reaction classes, measuring confirmable hits found per 1,000 reactions and reagent or solvent consumed per actionable hit.

idea: We propose a regime-aware crypto trading framework that treats strategy selection and risk control as separate but coupled problems under market nonstationarity. A lightweight latent-state model first identifies a small set of recurring market regimes, such as trend, mean-reversion, and stress, from multi-horizon features including returns, realized volatility, volume imbalance proxies, and cross-asset correlation shifts. For each regime, a specialist policy generates directional trades or portfolio weights using simple, reproducible learners rather than a single monolithic predictor. A meta-controller then scales exposure by predictive uncertainty and explicit penalties for transaction costs, slippage, and drawdown, so the system can reduce risk during unstable periods even when a regime is detected with low confidence. The main novelty is the modular integration of regime inference, specialist decision policies, and uncertainty-calibrated position sizing in a crypto-specific setting, which should improve interpretability and make ablations clearer than end-to-end reinforcement learning approaches. The method is feasible with standard exchange data and offline backtesting infrastructure, and its expected impact is more robust strategy behavior across volatility spikes and distribution shifts rather than only higher average return. The main risk is unstable regime assignment causing noisy switching and turnover. A minimal validation experiment is a rolling-window backtest against static momentum, mean-reversion, and non-regime-aware predictive comparisons, with ablations on switching and uncertainty throttling under realistic cost assumptions.

idea: We propose an interpretable two-stage autoregulation system for resistance training that replaces fixed percentage- or repetition-maximum prescriptions with daily individualized load and volume recommendations that explicitly account for physiological variation. Before each session, the system computes a low-burden readiness estimate from wearable and self-report signals such as heart-rate variability, sleep quality, muscle soreness, and prior-session training load, then combines this with a standardized warm-up check using submaximal bar velocity to set an initial target load range and repetition goal for major lifts. During the session, the prescription is updated after the first working set using observed velocity loss and perceived exertion, allowing the system to raise or reduce working weight, adjust planned volume, and trigger stop rules when acute fatigue diverges from expectation. The novelty lies not in any single signal, but in a prespecified, coach-auditable workflow that integrates pre-session readiness and within-session performance feedback while remaining deployable with common wearables and affordable velocity sensors. Expected impact is more stable training quality, fewer under- or over-prescribed sessions, and broader practical adoption of personalized strength programming. The main risk is that noisy or conflicting readiness signals could destabilize recommendations, requiring clear signal hierarchy and fallback rules. A minimal validation experiment would prospectively compare this method against fixed-percentage, RPE-only, and velocity-only prescriptions over several weeks in common barbell lifts, measuring prescription agreement with expert coaches, session consistency, adherence, and missing-data robustness.

idea: We propose a culturally and resource-adaptive guideline translation framework that converts rigid evidence-based recommendations into modular decision pathways with three explicit layers: a protected evidence core that should not be altered, an adaptable periphery covering delivery details, and a justification rule set that permits specific modifications when triggered by documented resource shortages, local cultural practices, or patient preferences. The key novelty is to treat anthropological context and preference information not as informal barriers noted after implementation fails, but as structured inputs to a transparent adaptation logic that preserves fidelity to the evidentiary core while making deviations auditable. In practice, clinics would use a compact adaptation matrix and justification log to classify which recommendation elements are fixed, which are negotiable, and what kinds of local evidence or deliberation authorize change, making the approach feasible even in low-resource settings with variable staffing or supply chains. The expected impact is improved uptake, acceptability, and transparency of evidence-based practice across culturally diverse settings. The main risk is that adaptation rules may either become too coarse to capture real-world nuance or too permissive and erode consistency with the underlying evidence. A minimal validation experiment would ask multiple clinicians and local stakeholders to apply the framework to the same guideline scenarios in contrasting settings and measure agreement on core-versus-adaptable elements, consistency of chosen adaptations, and perceived feasibility relative to fixed-guideline use.

idea: We propose a physics-informed multi-task molecular foundation model that accelerates both drug-design property prediction and materials-reaction screening by jointly learning from three data sources: large unlabeled molecular corpora, quantum-mechanical calculations, and curated reaction datasets. The core mechanism is a conformer- and symmetry-aware equivariant encoder trained to predict standard molecular properties together with coarse pathway surrogates such as barrier rankings, transition-state plausibility scores, and approximate reaction coordinates, rather than attempting full ab initio mechanism discovery. A calibrated uncertainty head then serves as a triage policy: predictions judged reliable are used directly, while ambiguous compounds or reaction candidates are escalated to higher-fidelity quantum calculations, allowing expensive simulation budgets to be concentrated where they matter most. The main novelty is the combination of joint property-plus-pathway learning, physically constrained outputs, and decision-theoretic uncertainty budgeting within a single transferable model that can be adapted across drug-like and materials-relevant chemistry. This design is feasible because it narrows pathway supervision to ranking-style targets that are more obtainable than full trajectories. Expected impact is a substantial reduction in costly trial-and-error computation during virtual screening and mechanistic prioritization. The main risk is that sparse, heterogeneous pathway labels may limit calibration and cross-domain transfer. A minimal validation experiment would test whether uncertainty-guided escalation reaches a fixed error target on property prediction and reaction-path ranking with fewer high-fidelity QM evaluations than separate single-task comparisons.

idea: We propose a consistency-first Bayesian arbitration framework for the Hubble tension that jointly analyzes Cepheid- and TRGB-calibrated supernova ladders, strong-lens time delays, BAO/CMB summaries, and standard sirens using two new ingredients: a small set of probe-independent consistency coordinates that localize where inference disagreements enter the distance-redshift chain, and a low-rank shared-latent systematic layer that can represent physically interpretable calibration or selection drifts common across multiple probes without giving any single dataset unlimited freedom. The framework then performs explicit model comparison among three explanation families within one hierarchy: hidden cross-probe systematics, pre-recombination sound-horizon shifts, and residual late-time expansion-history mismatches. The novelty is that it turns the Hubble tension from a sequence of probe-specific fits into a falsifiable diagnosis problem, asking which class of explanation is actually needed once complexity penalties and external constraints from BBN, BAO, and structure growth are imposed. Feasibility is high because the method can be built from public likelihood-level summaries and existing simulation pipelines. Its impact would be a clearer decision boundary for whether future effort should target new early-universe physics or calibration/inference systematics. The main risk is over-flexibility of the latent layer, so the minimal validation experiment is a blinded synthetic-injection study testing whether the model can correctly recover known systematic-driven, early-physics-driven, and late-time-driven scenarios without misclassifying them under realistic noise and probe coverage.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-aware shared-autonomy co-pilot for surgical robots that reduces surgeon fatigue by automating bounded, repetitive micro-actions while preserving full human authority over strategic decisions. The system fuses endoscopic video, robot kinematics, and available force or torque signals to infer procedure phase and near-term surgeon intent, then selects from a library of safety-constrained motion primitives for tasks such as camera centering, needle regrasp alignment, suture tension maintenance, and knot-tightening assistance. Its key novelty is the combination of multimodal intent inference with calibrated uncertainty gating: autonomy is invoked only inside a clearly defined envelope, and control is handed back instantly when confidence drops, anatomy becomes visually uncertain, or motion approaches protected regions. Feasibility is strengthened by limiting scope to reusable subtasks that can be trained in digital twins and retrospective robot logs rather than requiring end-to-end autonomous surgery. If successful, the approach could reduce repetitive manipulations, lower cognitive and physical workload, and improve consistency of low-level maneuvers across procedures. The main risk is that intent inference may fail under occlusion, bleeding, anatomy variation, or surgeon-specific style, causing disruptive handbacks or unsafe autonomy attempts. A minimal validation experiment would test one subtask such as suturing assistance in simulation or bench-top phantoms, measuring completion time, override rate, handback latency, and safety-constraint violations against manual teleoperation.
task_context:

idea: This project proposes a community-facing policy prioritization framework that helps marginalized neighborhoods translate uneven pollution exposure and health vulnerability into actionable local advocacy targets. The system would combine publicly available air pollution estimates, census-based vulnerability indicators, land-use and traffic data, and administrative records on permitting, zoning, truck routing, and monitoring enforcement to produce neighborhood-level rankings of which policy levers are most likely to reduce inequitable exposure burdens. Its core novelty is moving beyond standard environmental justice dashboards that only display hotspots by adding a transparent action-mapping layer, uncertainty-aware counterfactual scoring, and brief-generation features tailored to hearings, public comments, and enforcement petitions. Feasibility is strong because the approach is designed around data that exist in many jurisdictions and avoids requiring individual health records, instead using carefully labeled health-risk proxies and auditable assumptions. Expected impact is a more credible and usable evidence base for community groups seeking distributive policy change, while the main risk is that rankings may inherit bias from observational confounding, coarse proxies, or jurisdiction-specific policy mappings. A minimal validation experiment would apply the framework in two cities, compare ranking stability across alternative modeling assumptions, and assess whether advocates and policy experts judge the resulting briefs as more actionable than conventional disparity maps alone.

idea: We propose a wearable closed-loop gait coaching system for real-time rehabilitation that combines foot-mounted inertial measurement units with thin pressure insoles to estimate gait phase, stance-time symmetry, and toe-clearance proxies directly on an edge device, then delivers phase-specific haptic or audio cues only when deviations from a clinician-anchored personal target are both large enough and persistent enough to be actionable. The key novelty is not merely multimodal sensing, but a confidence-aware feedback policy that learns an individual comparison online while preventing cue fatigue through sparse triggering and user-adjustable sensitivity, making feedback practical during everyday walking rather than only in laboratory assessments. Feasibility is supported by low-bandwidth wearable sensors, lightweight gait-event inference, and simple actuator hardware that can run without continuous cloud connectivity. Expected impact is a shift from retrospective gait scoring toward continuous, adaptive correction for patients with rehabilitation needs, while also providing clinicians with interpretable metrics and progression controls. The main risk is that online personalization could drift toward reinforcing maladaptive gait or suppress needed feedback under unusual conditions such as turning, uneven terrain, or assistive-device use. A minimal validation experiment would compare end-to-end latency, gait-deviation detection agreement, and cue-timing accuracy against motion-lab references in a small walking study across multiple speeds, while collecting comfort and cognitive-load ratings to verify that sparse cueing remains usable.

idea: We propose a constrained reduced-order plate-tectonics sandbox that makes tectonic reasoning accessible for education and rapid hypothesis testing by replacing computation-heavy geodynamics solvers with an interpretable graph-and-rule model. In the system, plates are represented as graph entities, boundaries as typed interactions, and driving influences such as slab pull, ridge push, and mantle forcing as a small set of user-editable parameters; state-transition rules then generate qualitative outcomes including spreading, subduction, transform motion, and mountain building, while hard constraints prevent physically implausible combinations. The novelty is not merely an interactive visualization, but a middle layer between expert simulation codes and static classroom demos: users can directly manipulate causal mechanisms, inspect which rules produced each tectonic feature, and compare alternative scenarios in seconds without domain-specific software expertise. Feasibility is supported by the fact that the model targets qualitative textbook-consistent behavior rather than quantitative Earth forecasting, allowing implementation from canonical tectonic cases and selected calibration to existing simulation outputs. The expected impact is a novice-facing platform for causal learning, classroom experimentation, and early-stage scientific ideation. The main risk is oversimplification that could create misleading confidence, so the interface should explicitly label validity bounds and non-quantitative intent. A minimal validation experiment would test whether students can use the sandbox to distinguish and explain canonical ridge, subduction, transform, and collision scenarios more accurately than with a conventional animation-only tool.

idea: We propose a sensor-triggered, spectrally selective canopy screen for heat-stressed cropping systems that reduces thermal load without the yield penalty of conventional shading by reflecting a large fraction of near-infrared radiation while transmitting most photosynthetically active radiation. The system would use retractable films or nets mounted on existing support structures and deploy only during acute heat-risk windows identified from canopy temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and short-term weather forecasts, then retract when thermal stress subsides so crops recover full light exposure. The novelty is the combination of wavelength-selective filtering with temporal control, separating heat mitigation from continuous light reduction rather than treating all incoming sunlight as equally undesirable. Because retractable shade infrastructure already exists in many protected and high-value field systems, the concept is feasible as a retrofit pathway if durable low-energy materials can be identified. Expected impacts include cooler canopies, reduced heat injury, better photosynthetic retention during extreme events, and potentially lower irrigation demand, with a more favorable greenhouse balance than static shading if deployment time and embodied emissions remain low. The main risk is that altered spectra or mistimed deployment could still affect plant signaling, coloration, pests, or net carbon gain. A minimal validation experiment would compare dynamic selective screening, conventional shade netting, and no cover in one heat-sensitive crop while measuring spectral transmission, canopy temperature, gas exchange, yield, and a simple life-cycle emission estimate.

idea: We propose a modular tolerogenic nanoparticle platform for autoimmune disease that aims to replace broad immunosuppression with antigen-specific immune reprogramming. The particle would be engineered for preferential uptake by dendritic cells and would co-deliver two coordinated signals: interchangeable disease-relevant autoantigen peptides to identify the pathogenic immune response, and a defined tolerogenic cue that biases antigen presentation toward regulatory T-cell expansion and anergy or deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes rather than inflammatory activation. The main novelty is not generic antigen delivery, but the combination of APC-biased targeting, programmable paired antigen-plus-tolerogenic signaling, and a development strategy explicitly optimized to preserve unrelated antimicrobial immunity. Feasibility is supported by the modular backbone design, which can be reused across indications while swapping antigen payloads or small disease-specific antigen panels for different autoimmune settings. If successful, this approach could control disease while reducing infection risk, vaccine attenuation, and other liabilities of systemic immune suppression. The main risk is biological heterogeneity: relevant autoantigens may differ across patients or evolve through epitope spreading, and established inflammatory environments may weaken tolerance induction. A minimal validation experiment would test whether the nanoparticle selectively reprograms dendritic cells in vitro and suppresses responses to the target autoantigen while preserving recall responses to an unrelated microbial antigen.

idea: We propose Budget-Aware Structured Compute Routing, a deep learning framework that reduces computation by learning, for each input and each layer, which grouped compute units should be activated while keeping the active pattern aligned with efficient hardware execution. Instead of relying on unstructured sparsity or simple early exiting, the method applies differentiable gates over blockwise units such as token groups, channel groups, or attention-head groups, and trains these gates jointly with the backbone under an explicit budget loss that targets FLOPs, activation memory, or latency proxies. A key novelty is the combination of per-instance adaptive routing with accelerator-friendly structure and stabilization terms that encourage balanced utilization, preventing routing collapse in which only a few paths dominate. The approach is feasible because it can be added to existing transformer-style models without new hardware and can use standard grouped kernels at deployment. If successful, it could narrow the gap between theoretical efficiency gains and practical speedups, making large models cheaper to train and run while preserving accuracy on hard examples by allocating more capacity only when needed. The main risk is that routing complexity or regularization may reduce accuracy or produce limited real latency gains if the block design poorly matches runtime behavior. A minimal validation experiment would train a transformer on one benchmark under fixed compute budgets and compare accuracy, FLOPs, and measured latency against matched-budget pruning, token reduction, and early-exit comparisons.

idea: We propose a Bayesian excursion-reconstruction framework for workplace contaminant monitoring that addresses the core statistical failure of periodic air sampling: missing short, hazardous exposure spikes. The method fuses sparse reference-grade measurements with continuous low-cost proxy sensors and lightweight work-context signals such as task phase, location, or ventilation state in a latent-state hierarchical model that infers the probability, timing, and magnitude of unobserved short-term excursion episodes. Rather than predicting only average exposure, the model is designed around threshold exceedance risk, using change-point structure and extreme-value components to estimate when transient peaks likely occurred and how uncertain those estimates are under sensor noise, drift, and cross-sensitivity. The main novelty is shifting occupational exposure assessment from intermittent compliance snapshots to calibrated inference over rare, decision-relevant events, while remaining feasible because it only requires occasional reference sampling plus deployable continuous sensing already common in industrial settings. Expected impact is earlier identification of high-risk tasks and more targeted confirmatory sampling or intervention without requiring dense reference-grade monitoring everywhere. The main risk is weak identifiability when proxy sensors correlate poorly with the true contaminant under some conditions, which could lead to overconfident spike estimates unless calibration is carefully constrained. A minimal validation experiment would compare periodic sampling alone against the proposed fused model on retrospective or simulated high-frequency exposure series, evaluating calibration and missed-spike detection for short-term exposure limits.

idea: We propose an uncertainty-adaptive psychophysics protocol that replaces rigid staircase step sizes with online control of both stimulus placement and step magnitude, aiming to estimate perceptual thresholds in far fewer trials for participants with limited attention or mobility. After each response, a Bayesian psychometric-function update estimates the posterior distribution over threshold, slope, and lapse rate; the next stimulus is then selected to maximally reduce threshold uncertainty, while the step size automatically shrinks near the inferred boundary and expands when the observer is clearly above or below it. Testing stops early once posterior threshold precision reaches a preset criterion, yielding an interpretable threshold with a user-specified confidence target rather than a fixed trial budget. The main novelty is combining dynamic step-size adaptation, precision-based stopping, and lapse-aware estimation in one clinically practical workflow that remains compatible with standard psychometric reporting. Feasibility is high because the method can be implemented as software around existing sensory tasks without new hardware. Its expected impact is shorter, less fatiguing assessments with better accessibility. The main risk is biased estimation under nonstationary attention or atypical psychometric shapes, so a minimal validation experiment would compare trial count, bias, and confidence-interval width against conventional fixed-step and standard staircase methods in simulated observers with varying lapse rates and slopes.

idea: We propose a sociotechnical platform layer for large collective-intelligence projects that reduces cognitive bottlenecks by replacing a single global discussion feed with diversity-aware micro-panels and structured reconciliation. For each decomposable subproblem, the system algorithmically forms small heterogeneous groups using complementary expertise signals, then requires outputs in a lightweight schema including claims, evidence tags, confidence, and explicit dissent. Rather than promoting the most visible thread or highest-status contributor, the platform routes these intermediate outputs into cross-panel reconciliation episodes where different panels compare overlaps, unresolved conflicts, and omitted perspectives, and rotating integration roles distribute summarization labor instead of concentrating it in a few moderators. The novelty is the integration of expertise routing with dissent-preserving aggregation: existing platforms often help find contributors or collect arguments, but rarely redesign synthesis itself to retain minority expertise while keeping the process tractable. The design is feasible because it builds from deployable components already common in collaboration systems, including expertise profiles, task decomposition, templated contribution forms, and transparent allocation rules. Expected impact is improved representation of diverse knowledge in final syntheses and less premature convergence. A central risk is that structured reporting may increase participation costs or oversimplify nuanced contributions. A minimal validation experiment would compare this workflow against a global-thread platform on a complex collaborative problem, measuring concentration of integration labor, diversity of retained claims, and coverage of low-frequency expertise.

idea: We propose a hybrid solver for PDEs on irregular domains that combines an unfitted finite-element method on a simple background mesh with a geometry-conditioned local boundary corrector applied only near cut cells, sharp corners, and mixed-boundary junctions. The base solver handles the bulk physics using a consistent variational formulation, avoiding expensive body-fitted meshing, while the learned corrector predicts discretization-error corrections from local signed-distance samples, boundary type indicators, coarse FEM residuals, and simple curvature or corner descriptors. The key novelty is not to learn the full solution, but to learn the geometry-induced error created by non-body-fitted discretization, which should make the method more interpretable, more data-efficient, and easier to analyze than end-to-end neural PDE solvers. This design is feasible because it leaves stability-critical bulk computation classical and confines learning to the narrow region where irregular geometry causes the largest accuracy loss. If successful, the method could reduce meshing burden while improving boundary fidelity across Dirichlet, Neumann, and mixed conditions. The main risk is limited generalization near singular boundary features where smooth geometric descriptors may not capture the true local behavior. A minimal validation experiment would compare standard unfitted FEM and the proposed corrected solver on 2D Poisson problems over several unseen irregular domains, measuring global error and boundary-localized error near corners and cut cells.

idea: We propose a physics-informed, real-time tectonic nowcasting system that updates fault-segment-level probabilities of elevated seismic activity by fusing continuous GNSS displacement, local seismic waveforms, distributed acoustic sensing where available, and intermittent satellite deformation or thermal proxies within a multimodal probabilistic model. A causal anomaly-screening layer first estimates counterfactual comparisons for weather, hydrology, seasonal deformation, and human vibration so that non-tectonic disturbances are filtered before data enter the forecasting model, reducing spurious precursor claims. The core novelty is not deterministic earthquake prediction, but an operational framework that combines heterogeneous sensing, explicit confounder suppression, uncertainty calibration, and missing-modality robustness to produce trustworthy short-horizon risk updates under uneven global coverage. Feasibility is supported by the fact that most inputs already exist in regional monitoring networks, while asynchronous satellite streams can be treated as optional auxiliary evidence rather than mandatory signals. If successful, the approach could improve warning support, prioritization of inspections, and disaster-response readiness while also clarifying where predictive information is genuinely present. The main risk is that short-term precursory signal may be weak, unstable across regions, or overwhelmed by rare-event imbalance, limiting gains over standard seismicity models. A minimal validation experiment would prospectively compare rolling nowcasts against persistence, ETAS-style comparisons, and single-modality models, measuring calibration, lead-time-dependent precision-recall, and false-alarm burden.
